Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: A public body governs all of its projects with PRINCE2 Project Management. One project will build its product through a single linear sequence of design, build and test. How does the PRINCE2 Agile book regard this arrangement?
o: As a recognized use of PRINCE2 Project Management, which can govern any delivery method
As a breach of PRINCE2 Project Management, which requires agile delivery
As PRINCE2 Agile, because PRINCE2 Agile is designed for linear-sequential delivery
As acceptable once the board approves a waiver from two of the principles
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: PRINCE2 Project Management can host any delivery method, and the book recognizes that some organizations use it for governance without agile delivery. PRINCE2 Agile is the variant specifically for iterative-incremental delivery (book 1.3.4, 3.1).

n.1: PRINCE2 Project Management does not require agile delivery; it can govern linear-sequential work too (1.3.4).
n.2: PRINCE2 Agile is specifically for iterative and incremental delivery, not linear-sequential delivery (1.3.4).
n.3: No waiver is involved: all seven principles still apply, and the delivery method is a matter of project context (1.3.4, 5.2).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q:
Which two statements about PRINCE2 Agile Version 2 are correct?
1. Project performance is managed across seven aspects, including sustainability.
2. The former 'change' theme is now covered by the issues practice.
3. The five 'focus areas' remain a separate syllabus heading.
4. The Scrum master is one of the named PRINCE2 Agile roles.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: V2 judges performance across seven aspects, with sustainability added, and the old 'change' theme is now the issues practice (book 1.3.2, Table 3.1; issues practice, chapter 11).

n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: the focus areas heading has gone in V2, with its content moved into practices and people (e.g. the Agilometer into risk).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: 'Scrum master' is not one of the 11 named V2 roles; the V2 role set includes a team coach instead.
n.3: Both are wrong: focus areas are no longer a heading, and the Scrum master is not a named V2 role.

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: An older revision guide groups the Agilometer, requirements, rich communication, frequent releases and contracts under five 'focus areas'. How does Version 2 treat this material?
o: The heading has gone, and the Agilometer now sits within the progress practice
The focus areas are kept and examined as a fifth learning outcome
The focus areas have been renamed as the seven practices of PRINCE2 Agile
The heading has gone, and the Agilometer now sits within the risk practice
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Version 2 dropped the focus areas heading: the Agilometer moved into the risk practice (book 10.3.2), requirements into plans and quality, rich communication into mindset and people, frequent releases into business case and OCM, and contracts into the commercial management approach.

n.0: The Agilometer assesses the risk of agile working, so it sits in the risk practice, not progress (book 10.3.2).
n.1: The Foundation syllabus has four learning outcomes, and focus areas are not one of them.
n.2: The seven practices replace the old themes, not the focus areas, whose content is spread across several practices.

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile keep a project governed while still giving delivery teams room to decide how they do their work?
o: Tolerances restrict what is delivered but allow flexibility in time and cost
Tolerances restrict time and cost but allow flexibility in what is delivered
The board approves each iteration plan before the team starts work on it
Tolerances are removed so that teams can agree changes directly with users
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Manage by exception is at the heart of letting people self-manage while staying in control: in agile, tolerance is allowed on what is delivered and restricted on time and cost (book Table 5.1, Table 3.1).

n.0: This is the reverse: time and cost have zero tolerance by default, while scope below the Musts can flex (Table 3.1).
n.2: The board authorizes stages; iterations are planned by the teams themselves within the stage (5.2.1.4).
n.3: Tolerances are not removed; manage by exception still applies and is how the board stays in control (Table 5.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which statement BEST describes agile as PRINCE2 Agile presents it?
o: A set of prescribed processes that every team follows in the same way on each project
A delivery approach based on detailed upfront planning and formal sign-off of each phase
A set of software tools that track team tasks and report progress to managers
A way of thinking and working that favours adaptation, collaboration and learning from feedback
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: The book presents agile as a way of thinking and working that favours adaptation, collaboration, experimentation, learning from feedback and quick pivots, to cut waste and delay and deliver user-focused solutions (book 2.3).

n.0: Agile is not a fixed set of prescribed processes; the book stresses that it is less about rigid adherence to a framework (2.3).
n.1: Detailed upfront planning with sequential sign-off describes the waterfall approach (2.2).
n.2: Tools can support agile working, but agile is a way of thinking and working, not a tool set (2.3).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: An organization buys an agile planning tool and trains every team in a popular framework, expecting faster delivery and higher quality within months. Why does PRINCE2 Agile warn that this may not deliver the expected benefits?
o: The benefits appear once the framework has been in use for a full year
The value comes from a shift in mindset and culture that lets teams self-manage
Agile frameworks are designed for software teams rather than whole organizations
Tools and frameworks add costs that outweigh any gain in delivery speed
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Adopting a framework does not by itself bring faster delivery or higher quality; the value lies in changing mindsets and building a culture that empowers teams to self-manage and make decisions (book 2.3).

n.0: The book sets no waiting period; the issue is mindset and culture, not elapsed time (2.3).
n.2: Agile is used across many kinds of work; the warning is about mindset, not the type of team (2.3).
n.3: The book does not argue that tools cost too much; it says tools and frameworks without a change of mindset do not secure the benefits (2.3).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: A company renames its project phases 'sprints' and holds daily stand-ups, but managers still decide every task and team members may not change how they work. Why are agile benefits unlikely to follow?
o: Daily stand-ups are too frequent for teams that work in sprints
Managers should run the stand-ups so that tasks are assigned faster
People are not allowed to think and act in an agile way
The team needs a longer planning phase before the first sprint starts
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Calling processes agile means little if people are not allowed to think and act in an agile way; the benefits depend on teams being empowered to self-manage, not on new labels (book 2.3).

n.0: Frequent stand-ups are normal in agile teams; the problem is the lack of empowerment (2.3).
n.1: More direction from managers would deepen the problem; agile relies on teams self-managing (2.3).
n.3: A longer upfront planning phase is a waterfall habit and does not address the missing agile mindset (2.2, 2.3).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. PRINCE2 Agile explains that agile is less about rigid adherence to a [?] and more about collaboration, creativity and adaptability.
o: framework
mindset
user need
timebox
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: The book says agile is less about rigidly sticking to a framework and more about collaboration, creativity and adaptability (book 2.3).

n.1: The agile mindset is what the book wants teams to adopt, so it is not what agile is 'less about'.
n.2: Agile is user-focused; the book does not say it is less about meeting user needs.
n.3: Timeboxes are an agile technique, but the sentence in the book contrasts collaboration and adaptability with rigid use of a framework.

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, agile ways of working aim to deliver user-focused solutions while keeping which two things to a minimum?
o: Stakeholder involvement and feedback
Change and experimentation
Team autonomy and decision-making
Waste and delays
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Agile favours adaptation, collaboration, experimentation and feedback in order to minimise waste and delays and deliver user-focused solutions (book 2.3).

n.0: Agile seeks more stakeholder involvement and feedback, not less (2.3).
n.1: Agile embraces change and favours experimentation rather than minimising them (2.3).
n.2: Agile empowers teams to self-manage and decide, so autonomy is encouraged (2.3).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q:
Which two statements about agile are correct according to PRINCE2 Agile?
1. Agile favours experimentation and quick pivots in response to feedback.
2. Adopting a recognized framework is enough to secure agile benefits.
3. Agile aims to deliver user-focused solutions with less waste and delay.
4. Agile depends on following one prescribed framework rigidly.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: agile favours experimentation, feedback and quick pivots, and aims to cut waste and delay while delivering user-focused solutions (book 2.3).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: adopting a framework does not by itself secure the benefits; mindset and culture must change (2.3).
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: a framework alone does not secure benefits, and agile is less about rigid adherence to a framework (2.3).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: agile is less about rigid adherence to any framework (2.3).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: A team leader says: 'We are agile because we follow every rule in our chosen framework exactly.' Which response reflects PRINCE2 Agile's view?
o: That is correct, because agile is defined by complete adherence to a framework
Agile depends more on collaboration, creativity and adaptability than on following rules
That is correct, because Scrum is the framework that PRINCE2 Agile requires
Agile depends more on detailed upfront planning than on following framework rules
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: The book describes agile as less about rigid adherence to a framework and more about collaboration, creativity and adaptability; following rules without the mindset is 'doing' without 'being' (book 2.3).

n.0: The book says the opposite: agile is less about rigid adherence to a framework (2.3).
n.2: PRINCE2 Agile does not require Scrum; the project chooses which frameworks to use when tailoring (5.2.1.7).
n.3: Detailed upfront planning is typical of waterfall; agile relies on adaptability and feedback (2.2, 2.3).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of agile as PRINCE2 Agile describes it?
o: Learning from feedback and adapting the work in response
Collaborating closely to create user-focused solutions
Fixing the full solution in detail before any work begins
Being ready to pivot quickly when circumstances change
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Agile favours adaptation, experimentation, feedback and quick pivots. Fixing the whole solution in detail upfront is the linear-sequential (waterfall) way, whose main limitation is a lack of adaptability (book 2.2, 2.3).

n.0: Learning from feedback and adapting is a core feature of agile (2.3).
n.1: Collaboration and user-focused solutions are central to agile (2.3).
n.3: Quick pivots are named among the things agile favours (2.3).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: A trainer contrasts different ways of delivering a product. In PRINCE2 Agile terms, which description fits the waterfall approach?
o: An iterative approach in which each timebox delivers a usable increment of the product
A linear, sequential approach in which each phase is completed before the next begins
A flow-based approach in which work is pulled through stages as capacity allows
A hybrid approach in which design runs in parallel with build and test
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Waterfall is linear-sequential delivery: each phase finishes before the next starts (book Glossary, 2.2).

n.0: Delivering usable increments in repeated timeboxes is iterative-incremental (agile) delivery, not waterfall.
n.2: Pulling work through a system as capacity frees up describes Kanban, not waterfall (Glossary).
n.3: Running phases in parallel is not waterfall, which completes each phase before the next (2.2).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, what is the main limitation of a waterfall approach to delivery?
o: It needs more people than iterative delivery to finish the same work
It is unsuited to governance through management stages and tolerances
It offers little ability to adapt once the process is under way
It produces too little documentation for the business to review
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Waterfall is linear and sequential, and its main limitation is the lack of adaptability during the process (book 2.2).

n.0: The book does not judge waterfall on head count; its limitation is a lack of adaptability (2.2).
n.1: PRINCE2 Project Management can govern linear-sequential delivery with stages and tolerances (1.3.4).
n.3: Waterfall is usually documentation-heavy; the limitation the book names is adaptability (2.2).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: PRINCE2 Agile recognizes three levels of timebox in a project. Which list names them?
o: Iteration, release and stage
Sprint, epic and project
Iteration, increment and phase
Release, work package and stage
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: The Glossary defines three levels of timebox: iteration, release and stage. A release usually contains two to four iterations, and in agile a stage contains timeboxed releases and iterations (book Glossary, 8.3.2.5, 5.2.1.4).

n.1: An epic is a large user story, not a timebox, and 'sprint' is the Scrum word for an iteration (Glossary).
n.2: An increment is a product output, not a timebox, and 'phase' is not one of the named levels (Glossary).
n.3: A work package is a set of work agreed between project manager and product owner, not a timebox level (Glossary).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which definition of a timebox matches the way PRINCE2 Agile uses the term?
o: A fixed set of features that must be finished before the period can end
A flexible period that extends until the agreed scope is complete
A fixed budget that a team may spend in each stage of the project
A fixed period of time within which work is planned and delivered
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: A timebox is a fixed period of time; PRINCE2 Agile uses three levels (iteration, release, stage), and time is held fixed while lower-priority content can flex (book Glossary, Table 3.1).

n.0: Fixing the features and letting the period run on reverses the idea: the time is fixed and the content flexes (Table 3.1).
n.1: A timebox does not extend; time has zero tolerance at all levels of plan (Table 3.1).
n.2: A timebox is a period of time, not a budget (Glossary).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: A project manager is drafting a release map that clusters user stories from the story map into releases. In PRINCE2 Agile, how many iterations does each release usually span?
o: One
Two to four
Five to eight
Ten to twelve
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: The release map groups user stories into releases, each usually made up of two to four iterations; the release map serves as the project and stage plan (book 8.3.2.5, 8.4.4).

n.0: A release usually spans several iterations, typically two to four, rather than one (8.3.2.5).
n.2: Five to eight is more than the usual range of two to four iterations (8.3.2.5).
n.3: Ten to twelve iterations would be far beyond the usual release length of two to four (8.3.2.5).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: What distinguishes iterative-incremental delivery from linear-sequential delivery?
o: The whole product is designed in full before any part of it is built, tested or released to users
The product is delivered in one handover once every requirement is complete
The product is built in repeated cycles, with usable parts delivered and reviewed along the way
The scope is fixed and the timeboxes are extended until all of it is complete
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Iterative-incremental delivery builds the product in repeated timeboxed cycles, so parts are delivered early and feedback shapes what follows; linear-sequential delivery completes each phase before the next (book 1.3.4, 2.2).

n.0: Designing everything before building is the linear-sequential (waterfall) pattern (2.2).
n.1: A single final handover is typical of linear-sequential delivery, not iterative-incremental (2.2).
n.3: In agile delivery time is fixed and lower-priority scope flexes, not the reverse (Table 3.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q:
Which two statements about delivery approaches are correct?
1. In PRINCE2 Agile the iteration is the longest of the three timeboxes.
2. In a waterfall approach each phase is finished before the next one starts.
3. Iterative-incremental delivery lets users give feedback on early increments.
4. A release in PRINCE2 Agile usually lasts a single iteration.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Statements 2 and 3 are correct: waterfall completes each phase before the next, and iterative-incremental delivery produces early increments that users can give feedback on (book 2.2, 1.3.4).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: the iteration is the shortest timebox, since a release usually contains two to four iterations (Glossary, 8.3.2.5).
n.1: Statements 1 and 4 are both wrong: the iteration is the shortest timebox, and a release usually spans two to four iterations (Glossary, 8.3.2.5).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: a release usually spans two to four iterations (8.3.2.5).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Near the end of an iteration, a team realises it cannot finish every user story it planned. Following the PRINCE2 Agile default for time, what should normally happen?
o: The iteration ends on time and the unfinished lower-priority work is reprioritised
The iteration is extended until all of the planned user stories are finished
The project board is asked to approve extra time for this iteration
The iteration is cancelled and replanned from the start with a longer duration
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Time has zero tolerance at all levels of plan, including the iteration timebox, while Should and Could haves can flex. The timebox ends as planned and unfinished work goes back for prioritisation (book Table 3.1, Glossary).

n.1: Extending the iteration breaks the fixed timebox; time has zero tolerance by default (Table 3.1).
n.2: Iterations are timeboxes with zero time tolerance; the board does not grant extra time for an iteration (Table 3.1).
n.3: Cancelling and lengthening the timebox flexes time, which is fixed by default (Table 3.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile argue that complex work suits an agile approach?
o: Complexity disappears once the requirements have been written down in full
Complexity can be avoided by giving each phase to a separate specialist team
Complexity creates ambiguity, so there is rarely one perfect solution to plan for
Complexity makes costs unknown, so agile projects work without a budget
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Complexity brings ambiguity, so a single perfect solution rarely exists; it is better to stay adaptable and able to pivot quickly than to hunt for perfection (book 2.4).

n.0: Writing requirements down does not remove complexity; the book's answer is adaptability, not fuller upfront specification (2.4).
n.1: Handing phases between specialist teams is a sequential pattern and does not remove ambiguity (2.2, 2.4).
n.3: Agile projects still have budgets; cost has zero tolerance by default in PRINCE2 Agile (Table 3.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: On a traditional project, defects in a new billing system are found in the final testing phase, months after the code was written, and are expensive to fix. Which problem of traditional delivery does this illustrate?
o: Quality is assessed late, so early chances to fix it are missed
Progress is hard to measure without complicated metrics
Too much focus is placed on benefits rather than on time and cost
Teams self-manage too much, so quality checks are skipped
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: One problem of traditional projects is that quality is assessed late, so opportunities to put things right early are missed (book Table 2.2).

n.1: This is a real problem of traditional delivery, but the case is about late discovery of defects, not measuring progress (Table 2.2).
n.2: Traditional projects tend to focus too much on time and cost and too little on benefits, the reverse of this option (Table 2.2).
n.3: Self-management is an agile feature, not a problem of traditional delivery, and nothing in the case suggests it (2.3).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: A sponsor says she cannot tell how far her traditional project has really progressed without studying several pages of complex calculations. Which problem of traditional delivery is she describing?
o: Quality is assessed too late in the life cycle
Too much focus falls on time and cost rather than on value
The project board meets too often to review each stage
Progress is hard to measure without complicated metrics
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Traditional projects can make progress hard to measure without complicated metrics; agile shows progress through working output and simple visual tools such as burn charts (book Table 2.2, 12.4.3).

n.0: Late quality assessment is a real Table 2.2 problem, but the sponsor's complaint is about measuring progress.
n.1: This Table 2.2 problem concerns priorities, not how easily progress can be seen.
n.2: Board meeting frequency is not the problem described; the sponsor cannot read progress easily (Table 2.2).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: A project board judges its traditional projects mainly on finishing on time and within budget, and rarely asks whether the expected benefits will be achieved. Which problem does PRINCE2 Agile associate with this?
o: Too much focus on benefits, and too little control of time and cost
Too much focus on time and cost, and too little on benefits and value
Quality is assessed early, so teams spend too long on testing
Progress is reported too often, so teams lose time on reporting
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: PRINCE2 Agile lists an excessive focus on time and cost, with too little attention on benefits and value, among the problems of traditional projects (book Table 2.2).

n.0: This reverses the problem: traditional projects over-focus on time and cost, not benefits (Table 2.2).
n.2: The traditional problem is that quality is assessed late, not early (Table 2.2).
n.3: The progress problem in traditional delivery is that progress is hard to measure, not over-reported (Table 2.2).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: A product team faces shifting customer needs in a market that changes from month to month. Which response does PRINCE2 Agile favour?
o: Spend longer on analysis so that a perfect solution can be specified upfront
Fix the full scope early so that the changing market cannot disrupt the plan
Stay adaptable and ready to pivot quickly rather than search for a perfect solution
Pause the work until the market settles and the requirements become stable
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: In complex, ambiguous situations the book favours staying adaptable and able to pivot quickly over trying to find the perfect solution upfront (book 2.4).

n.0: Hunting for a perfect solution upfront is what the book advises against in complex situations (2.4).
n.1: Fixing all scope early removes the flexibility needed to respond to change; only Must haves are fixed by default (Table 3.1).
n.3: Waiting for stability delays value; the book's response to complexity is to stay adaptable (2.4).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q:
Which two statements about why organizations need agile are correct?
1. Agile removes uncertainty from complex projects.
2. Complexity creates ambiguity, so one perfect solution is rare.
3. Traditional projects tend to assess quality early in the life cycle.
4. Traditional projects can focus on time and cost at the expense of benefits.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Statements 2 and 4 are correct: complexity creates ambiguity so there is rarely one perfect solution, and traditional projects can over-focus on time and cost at the expense of benefits and value (book 2.4, Table 2.2).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: agile helps teams cope with uncertainty by adapting; it does not remove it (2.4).
n.1: Statements 1 and 3 are both wrong: agile does not remove uncertainty, and traditional projects assess quality late (2.4, Table 2.2).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: a problem of traditional projects is that quality is assessed late, not early (Table 2.2).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: How do frequent, inspected increments of the product help to address problems that PRINCE2 Agile identifies in traditional delivery?
o: Quality is checked early and often, and working output shows real progress
Detailed status reports replace the need to inspect the working output
Costs stop being tracked, so teams can focus on benefits instead
The full scope is fixed early, so progress can be measured against it
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Two Table 2.2 problems are late quality assessment and progress that is hard to measure. Frequent increments are checked as they are produced, and working output makes progress visible (book Table 2.2, 2.4).

n.1: Agile relies on inspecting working output, not on replacing it with detailed reports (Table 2.2).
n.2: Costs are still controlled; cost has zero tolerance by default (Table 3.1).
n.3: Only Must haves are fixed by default; Should and Could haves flex (Table 3.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which situation gives the STRONGEST reason for an organization to use agile ways of working?
o: Replacing equipment like for like against a fixed and proven specification
Running a monthly payroll process that follows the same steps each time
Submitting a regulatory return whose content and deadline are set in law
Building a new service for users whose needs are unclear and likely to change
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Agile is needed where complexity and ambiguity mean the right solution is not known upfront and must emerge through feedback and adaptation (book 2.4).

n.0: With a fixed, proven specification there is little ambiguity, so the case for agile is weakest here (2.4).
n.1: Repetitive, well-understood routine work has little of the complexity and ambiguity that drive the need for agile (2.4).
n.2: Content and deadline fixed in law leave little uncertainty to adapt to, so the need for agile is low (2.4).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Agile helps teams navigate change and adapt while prioritizing work that serves organizational objectives, leaving the organization better equipped for uncertainty. Which benefit of agile is this?
o: Organizational resilience and alignment
Responsiveness and innovation
More efficient teams and engaged people
Cost certainty and predictability
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Resilience and alignment: teams navigate change and adapt while prioritizing work that serves organizational objectives, so the organization copes better with uncertainty (book 2.4).

n.1: Responsiveness and innovation come from feedback loops and continual improvement, not from alignment to objectives (2.4).
n.2: This benefit is about collaboration and self-management within teams, not organizational alignment (2.4).
n.3: Cost certainty and predictability are not among the agile benefits the book describes (2.4).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: A department lets its cross-functional teams decide how to organize their own work. Staff report a stronger sense of ownership and purpose, and morale and productivity rise. Which benefit of agile is this?
o: Organizational resilience and alignment
Responsiveness and innovation
Stronger contract control with suppliers
More efficient teams and engaged people
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Collaboration and transparent communication in cross-functional teams, with teams empowered to self-manage, build trust, ownership, purpose, morale and productivity (book 2.4).

n.0: Resilience and alignment concern adapting to change while serving organizational objectives, not team morale (2.4).
n.1: Responsiveness and innovation come from feedback loops and continual improvement (2.4).
n.2: Contract control is not an agile benefit named in the book, and the case says nothing about suppliers (2.4).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: A team gathers user feedback after every iteration and keeps improving how it works, which cuts wasted effort and leads to a new way of solving a difficult problem. Which benefit of agile does this BEST illustrate?
o: Organizational resilience and alignment
Responsiveness and innovation
Efficient teams and engaged people
Standardization and compliance
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Feedback loops and continual improvement reduce waste and produce innovative solutions to complex problems: the responsiveness and innovation benefit (book 2.4).

n.0: Resilience and alignment concern prioritizing work that serves organizational objectives in changing conditions (2.4).
n.2: This benefit comes from collaboration and self-management, whereas the case centres on feedback and innovation (2.4).
n.3: Standardization and compliance are not agile benefits named in the book (2.4).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which list correctly names benefits of agile described in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Resilience and alignment; fixed scope and budget; responsiveness and innovation
Predictability and control; efficient, engaged teams; responsiveness and innovation
Resilience and alignment; efficient, engaged teams; responsiveness and innovation
Resilience and alignment; efficient, engaged teams; a reduced need for governance
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: The book describes organizational resilience and alignment, more efficient teams and engaged people, and responsiveness and innovation among the benefits of agile (book 2.4).

n.0: Fixed scope is not an agile benefit; scope below the Must haves flexes in PRINCE2 Agile (2.4, Table 3.1).
n.1: Predictability and control are not named agile benefits; resilience and alignment is (2.4).
n.3: Agile does not reduce the need for governance; PRINCE2 Agile keeps governance and control throughout (3.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which feature of agile working does PRINCE2 Agile link MOST directly to the benefit of responsiveness and innovation?
o: Feedback loops and continual improvement
Detailed upfront requirements and sign-off
A fixed scope agreed in the contract
Formal written reports at fixed intervals
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Feedback loops and continual improvement reduce waste and lead to innovative solutions to complex problems (book 2.4).

n.1: Detailed upfront requirements reduce the room to respond to feedback, the opposite of this benefit (2.2, 2.4).
n.2: Fixed contractual scope limits responsiveness; it is not linked to this benefit (2.4).
n.3: Formal reports do not create the feedback loops the book links to innovation (2.4).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, how does agile make teams more efficient?
o: Through specialist teams that hand work to each other in sequence
Through managers assigning each task and checking it every day
Through longer iterations that cut the time spent in meetings
Through collaboration and open communication in cross-functional teams
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Agile improves team efficiency through collaboration and transparent communication in cross-functional teams, with empowerment to self-manage (book 2.4).

n.0: Sequential hand-offs between specialists describe waterfall working, not agile teams (2.2).
n.1: Close task-by-task direction runs against the self-management the book links to efficiency (2.4).
n.2: The book links efficiency to collaboration and communication, not to longer iterations (2.4).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which statement about the benefits of agile is correct according to PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Self-managing teams tend to need closer supervision to stay productive
Self-managing teams tend to show greater ownership, morale and productivity
Agile builds resilience by fixing the full scope at the start of a project
Agile drives innovation by reducing contact with users between releases
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Empowering teams to self-manage builds trust, ownership, purpose, morale and productivity (book 2.4).

n.0: The book links self-management to higher productivity and ownership, not a need for closer supervision (2.4).
n.2: Resilience comes from adapting to change while staying aligned to objectives, not from fixing all scope (2.4).
n.3: Innovation comes from feedback loops, which need more user contact, not less (2.4).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which of the following is an example of the 'responsiveness and innovation' benefit of agile?
o: A team keeps its priorities aligned with strategy during a reorganization
A team reports higher morale after being trusted to plan its own work
A team uses rapid user feedback to find a new way to solve a complex problem
A team agrees a fixed price and fixed scope with its supplier at the outset
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Responsiveness and innovation come from feedback loops and continual improvement that reduce waste and produce innovative solutions to complex problems (book 2.4).

n.0: Staying aligned to organizational objectives through change is resilience and alignment (2.4).
n.1: Higher morale from self-management is the efficient teams and engaged people benefit (2.4).
n.3: A fixed price and scope is a contracting choice, not an example of an agile benefit (2.4).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile describe the relationship between business as usual (BAU) and projects?
o: A project identifies a need for change, and BAU is the means of introducing it
BAU identifies a need for change, and a project is the means of introducing it
BAU and projects are the same work managed under different budgets
A project permanently replaces BAU once its products have been delivered
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: BAU identifies the need for change and a project is the means by which that change is introduced; once the project ends, BAU adopts the change (book 1.1, 1.3.1).

n.0: This reverses the roles: BAU identifies the need and the project introduces the change (1.3.1).
n.2: Projects are temporary and unique, whereas BAU is repetitive and ongoing, so they are not the same work (1.3.1).
n.3: BAU continues after the project and adopts the change; the project does not replace it (1.3.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: A project to introduce a new online booking system reaches its planned end. What happens next to the change it has delivered?
o: The project team stays together to run the system as a service
The project is extended until every benefit has been measured
BAU adopts the change and goes on to realise its benefits
The change is held back until the next project has been approved
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: A project is temporary: it has a start and an end, after which BAU takes on the change and the benefits (book 1.3.1).

n.0: Running an ongoing service is BAU work; the temporary project team does not carry on as the operator (1.3.1).
n.1: Projects are temporary; many benefits are realised in BAU after the project has closed (1.3.1).
n.3: The delivered change passes to BAU at the end of the project; it does not wait for another project (1.3.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: An organization brings together people from several functional divisions, and from a partner organization, to work as one team on a new product. Which characteristic of a project does this BEST illustrate?
o: Cross-functional
Temporary
Introduces change
Repetitive and ongoing
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Projects are cross-functional: their teams span functional divisions and sometimes more than one organization (book 1.3.1).

n.1: Temporary refers to the project having a start and an end, which the case does not describe (1.3.1).
n.2: Introducing change into BAU is a project characteristic, but it is not what this case illustrates (1.3.1).
n.3: Repetitive, ongoing work is a feature of BAU, not a characteristic of a project (1.3.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which statement correctly contrasts a project with business as usual (BAU)?
o: A project is repetitive, while BAU work is unique and temporary
A project has no fixed end, while BAU work has a start and an end
A project avoids change, while BAU work introduces the change
A project is unique, while BAU work is repetitive and ongoing
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: A project is unique (a different team, customer, product, location or timeframe), whereas BAU is repetitive and ongoing (book 1.3.1).

n.0: This reverses the contrast: BAU is repetitive and ongoing, and projects are unique and temporary (1.3.1).
n.1: Projects are temporary with a start and an end; BAU is ongoing (1.3.1).
n.2: Projects introduce change; BAU identifies the need for it and adopts it afterwards (1.3.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which statement about agile in projects and in business as usual (BAU) is correct?
o: Agile suits projects, so BAU teams are expected to use waterfall methods
Agile is used in BAU as well as in projects; PRINCE2 Agile is for projects
PRINCE2 Agile is for BAU, and agile is kept out of project delivery
Agile is used in BAU once a project board has been set up to govern it
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: PRINCE2 Agile is designed for projects, but agile ways of working are also used in BAU, for example in ongoing product work (book 1.1, 1.3.1).

n.0: Agile is widely used in BAU, for example on ongoing product work (1.1).
n.2: PRINCE2 Agile is for projects, and agile delivery is at the centre of it (1.1, 3.1).
n.3: A project board governs a project, not BAU; agile in BAU does not depend on one (1.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: A team uses agile techniques to maintain and improve a company's customer app. The work has no planned end date and new requests arrive continually. How should this work be classified?
o: As a project, because the team uses agile techniques to do the work
As a project, because the stream of new requests keeps changing the product
As BAU, because it is ongoing product work with no defined end
As BAU, because agile techniques are not used within projects
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Work that is ongoing and repetitive, with no defined end, is BAU; agile is used in BAU as well as in projects, so using agile does not make it a project (book 1.1, 1.3.1).

n.0: Using agile does not make work a project; agile is also used in BAU (1.1).
n.1: Continual change requests to a live product are typical of ongoing BAU product work; a project is temporary (1.3.1).
n.3: Agile techniques are used in projects too; PRINCE2 Agile exists for exactly that (1.1, 3.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q:
Which two statements about projects and business as usual (BAU) are correct?
1. BAU introduces change, while projects identify the need for it.
2. PRINCE2 Agile is designed for running BAU operations.
3. A project has a defined start and a defined end.
4. Agile ways of working are used in BAU as well as in projects.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Statements 3 and 4 are correct: a project is temporary, with a start and an end, and agile is used in BAU as well as in projects (book 1.1, 1.3.1).

n.0: Both are wrong: BAU identifies the need for change and projects introduce it, and PRINCE2 Agile is designed for projects (1.1, 1.3.1).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: projects introduce change, and BAU identifies the need for it (1.3.1).
n.2: Statement 2 is wrong: PRINCE2 Agile is designed for projects, not for running BAU (1.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. A project is the means by which [?] is introduced into business as usual.
o: change
risk
routine
governance
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Projects are the means of introducing change into BAU; BAU identifies the need for change and adopts it after the project (book 1.3.1).

n.1: Projects manage risk, but the book describes them as the means of introducing change (1.3.1).
n.2: Routine, repetitive work is BAU itself, not something a project introduces (1.3.1).
n.3: Governance directs the project; the project's purpose is to introduce change (1.3.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which of the following is one of the four values of the Agile Manifesto?
o: Processes and tools over individuals and interactions
Comprehensive documentation over working software
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Following a plan over customer collaboration
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: The first Manifesto value prefers individuals and interactions to processes and tools (Agile Manifesto, 2001; book Table 2.1).

n.0: This reverses the value: individuals and interactions are valued more than processes and tools.
n.1: This reverses the value: working software is valued more than comprehensive documentation.
n.3: This mixes two values and reverses the preference; the Manifesto values responding to change over following a plan.

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: How does the Agile Manifesto regard the items on the right-hand side of its value statements, such as comprehensive documentation and following a plan?
o: They still have value, but the items on the left are valued more
They belong to traditional projects and are dropped once agile is adopted
They are valued equally with the items on the left in every agile team
They are valued more than the items on the left on large or regulated work
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: The Manifesto states that while there is value in the items on the right, the items on the left are valued more (Agile Manifesto, 2001; book Table 2.1).

n.1: The Manifesto keeps value in the right-hand items; agile teams still plan and document, just with less emphasis.
n.2: The Manifesto is a statement of preference: the left-hand items are valued more.
n.3: The Manifesto does not reverse its preference for larger or regulated work.

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Identify the missing words in the following Agile Manifesto value. Customer collaboration over [?].
o: comprehensive documentation
following a plan
processes and tools
contract negotiation
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: The third Manifesto value prefers customer collaboration to contract negotiation (Agile Manifesto, 2001; book Table 2.1).

n.0: Comprehensive documentation is the right-hand item of the working software value.
n.1: Following a plan is the right-hand item of the responding to change value.
n.2: Processes and tools is the right-hand item of the individuals and interactions value.

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: A team stops writing a lengthy specification and instead shows stakeholders a working version of the product every two weeks. Which Agile Manifesto value does this BEST reflect?
o: Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
Working software over comprehensive documentation
Responding to change over following a plan
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Replacing a long specification with a working version of the product reflects valuing working software over comprehensive documentation (Agile Manifesto, 2001; book Table 2.1).

n.0: The case is about replacing documentation with working output, not about how the customer relationship or contract is handled.
n.2: Nothing in the case concerns changing a plan; it replaces documentation with working output.
n.3: The case does not contrast people with processes or tools; it contrasts a specification with working output.

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Midway through a stage, user feedback shows that a planned feature is no longer needed, so the team replaces it with one that users now value more. Which Agile Manifesto value does this BEST reflect?
o: Working software over comprehensive documentation
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
Responding to change over following a plan
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Swapping a planned feature for one users now value more shows responding to change being valued over following a plan (Agile Manifesto, 2001; book Table 2.1).

n.0: The case is not about documentation versus working output; it is about changing the plan in response to feedback.
n.1: No contract or negotiation is involved; the team is adapting its plan to new information.
n.3: The case does not set people against processes or tools; it concerns adapting the plan.

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Team members are encouraged to walk over and talk to each other about a problem instead of raising a ticket in the workflow system. Which Agile Manifesto value does this BEST reflect?
o: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Working software over comprehensive documentation
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
Responding to change over following a plan
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Preferring a direct conversation to a ticket in a system reflects valuing individuals and interactions over processes and tools (Agile Manifesto, 2001; book Table 2.1).

n.1: The case is not about documentation versus working output.
n.2: The case concerns team members talking to each other, not the customer relationship or a contract.
n.3: The case is not about changing a plan; it is about how team members communicate.

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: When a customer asks for a change, the supplier works with the customer to agree new priorities instead of reopening the terms of their agreement. Which Agile Manifesto value does this BEST reflect?
o: Responding to change over following a plan
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Working software over comprehensive documentation
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Working with the customer on priorities rather than renegotiating the agreement reflects customer collaboration over contract negotiation (Agile Manifesto, 2001; book Table 2.1).

n.0: Responding to change is involved, but the key contrast in the case is collaboration versus reopening the contract.
n.1: The case does not set people against processes or tools; it concerns the customer agreement.
n.2: The case is not about documentation versus working output.

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: How many value statements does the Agile Manifesto contain, and how is each one structured?
o: Twelve, each describing a practice that an agile team follows
Four, each preferring one item over another that still has value
Four, each rejecting one item completely in favour of another
Five, each linked to one layer of the Agile Onion model
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: The Manifesto has four values, each preferring the item on the left over the item on the right while recognizing that the right-hand item still has value (Agile Manifesto, 2001; book Table 2.1).

n.0: The Manifesto has twelve principles, but four values; and the values are preferences, not practices.
n.2: The right-hand items are not rejected: they still have value, just less than the left.
n.3: There are four values, not five; the Agile Onion has five layers, which is a different model (2.6.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which agile approach improves flow by visualising work and limiting work in progress, using a pull system that exposes bottlenecks?
o: Scrum
Lean Startup
eXtreme Programming (XP)
Kanban
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Kanban improves flow and prompts improvement of the system by visualising work and controlling work in progress; as a pull system it limits items in circulation, which exposes bottlenecks (book Glossary).

n.0: Scrum organizes work into timeboxed sprints; limiting WIP in a pull system is the defining feature of Kanban (Glossary).
n.1: Lean Startup is about getting products to customers quickly and learning from them, not WIP limits (Glossary).
n.2: XP is known for engineering practices such as test-first programming, not WIP limits (Glossary).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which agile approach is a lightweight, iterative framework in which work is organized into short, timeboxed sprints to tackle complex problems?
o: Kanban
Scrum
Lean
Lean Startup
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Scrum is an iterative, timeboxed approach to product delivery; the Scrum Guide describes it as a lightweight framework for generating value through adaptive solutions to complex problems, using sprints (book Glossary).

n.0: Kanban focuses on flow and WIP limits; iterations are optional rather than built around sprints (Glossary).
n.2: Lean is a way of thinking about removing waste, not a sprint-based framework.
n.3: Lean Startup is about quickly getting products to customers and learning, not sprint timeboxes (Glossary).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which approach was originally developed for creating and managing start-up companies but is now applied by many kinds of business to get products to customers quickly?
o: Lean
eXtreme Programming (XP)
Lean Startup
Kanban
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: The Glossary describes Lean Startup as originally intended for creating and managing start-ups and now used by any business to deliver products to customers quickly (book Glossary).

n.0: Lean focuses on removing waste and improving flow; the start-up origin belongs to Lean Startup.
n.1: XP is a set of engineering practices such as test-first programming, not a start-up method (Glossary).
n.3: Kanban is a flow method using WIP limits, not a start-up method (Glossary).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: What is the central aim of Lean thinking, one of the agile-related approaches recognized in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Removing waste so that the flow of value to the customer is maximised
Limiting each sprint to one month or less to keep feedback frequent
Testing a minimum viable product with early users to validate ideas
Writing tests before writing code to improve technical quality
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Lean is about eliminating waste to maximise the flow of value to the customer (book Glossary; Lean Enterprise Institute).

n.1: Sprint length limits belong to Scrum, not Lean.
n.2: Testing an MVP to validate ideas is the hallmark of Lean Startup, which builds on Lean but is a separate approach.
n.3: Test-first programming comes from eXtreme Programming (XP) (Glossary).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Why does a Kanban team limit the number of work items in progress at any one time?
o: To fix the length of each iteration so that velocity can be measured
To make sure each item is estimated in story points before it starts
To keep the team small enough to meet in a daily stand-up
To expose bottlenecks and improve the flow of work through the system
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Kanban is a pull system that limits the items in circulation; this exposes bottlenecks and improves flow (book Glossary).

n.0: Kanban does not depend on fixed iterations; they are optional (Glossary, 14.2.2.1).
n.1: WIP limits control how much work is in progress, not how it is estimated (Glossary).
n.2: WIP limits apply to work items, not to team size (Glossary).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: A new company builds a minimum viable product, measures how customers use it, and then decides whether to pivot or persevere. Which approach is it following?
o: Kanban
Lean Startup
Scrum
eXtreme Programming (XP)
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Build, measure, learn, then pivot or persevere using a minimum viable product is the Lean Startup approach, aimed at getting products to customers quickly (book Glossary; Ries, The Lean Startup).

n.0: Kanban manages flow with WIP limits; it does not centre on MVPs and pivot decisions (Glossary).
n.2: Scrum organizes work in sprints with set events; the build-measure-learn loop is Lean Startup's.
n.3: XP centres on engineering practices such as test-first programming (Glossary).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile relate to agile frameworks such as Scrum and Kanban?
o: It replaces them with its own delivery techniques so that they are not used
It requires Scrum for project delivery and allows Kanban for BAU work
It adds direction and management around them, and the project chooses which to use
It treats them as alternatives to the PRINCE2 processes, chosen stage by stage
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: PRINCE2 Agile covers project direction and management as well as delivery, and under 'tailor to suit the project' the project decides which agile frameworks, artifacts and workshops to use (book 3.1, 5.2.1.7).

n.0: PRINCE2 Agile works with agile frameworks rather than replacing them (3.1).
n.1: PRINCE2 Agile does not mandate Scrum; the choice of framework is part of tailoring (5.2.1.7).
n.3: The PRINCE2 processes stay in place; agile frameworks are used for product delivery within them (3.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which statement about Kanban is correct?
o: Iterations are optional, because work is pulled when there is capacity
Work is pushed to the team in fixed batches at the start of each sprint
Work in progress is left unlimited so that the team stays fully busy
Each Kanban team appoints a Scrum master to manage its board
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Kanban is a pull system with limits on work in progress; iterations are optional (book Glossary, 14.2.2.1; Kanban Guide).

n.1: Kanban pulls work as capacity frees up; pushing batches per sprint is not how it works (Glossary).
n.2: Limiting work in progress is central to Kanban (Glossary).
n.3: Scrum master is a Scrum accountability, not part of Kanban.

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: PRINCE2 Agile describes a project in terms of three broad areas of work and aims to cover all of them while keeping governance and control throughout. Which three areas are these?
o: Project direction, project management and product delivery
Business justification, project management and service transition
Project direction, team leadership and benefits realization
Portfolio direction, project management and operational support
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: The book divides a project into project direction, project management and product delivery. PRINCE2 Agile covers all three, keeping governance and control in place throughout (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 3.1, Figure 3.1).

n.1: Service transition is not one of the three areas; the book names direction, management and product delivery (3.1).
n.2: Team leadership and benefits realization are not the named areas; the third area is product delivery, where agile is strongest (3.1).
n.3: The first area is project direction, not portfolio direction, and operational support belongs to BAU rather than the three project areas (3.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: PRINCE2 Agile compares the strengths of traditional project management with those of agile ways of working. Which statement reflects that comparison?
o: Project management is strong on product delivery, while agile is strong on governance and control
Project management and agile are equally strong across direction, management and delivery
Agile is strong on project direction, while project management is strong on responding to change
Project management is strong on governance and control, while agile is strong on product delivery
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Project management brings governance and control but says little about product delivery; agile is strong on product delivery and responding to change but light on direction and management. Blending them covers both (book 3.1).

n.0: This reverses the comparison: product delivery is agile's strength and governance is project management's (3.1).
n.1: They are not equally strong; each has gaps, which is why the book blends them (3.1).
n.2: Agile is light on direction and management, and responding to change is an agile strength, not a project management one (3.1).

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. In PRINCE2 Agile Version 2, business case, organization, plans, quality, risk, issues and progress are described as the seven [?].
o: themes
practices
processes
aspects
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: Version 2 follows PRINCE2 7 and calls these seven elements practices; the old word 'themes' is no longer used (Agile V2 syllabus 2.1.2; book chapters 6 to 12, one per practice).

n.0: 'Themes' is the term from the 6th edition and PRINCE2 Agile Version 1; V2 calls them practices.
n.2: The seven processes are starting up, directing, initiating, controlling a stage, managing product delivery, managing a stage boundary and closing, not these seven.
n.3: The seven aspects of performance are benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk, not this list.

Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.q: Which statement BEST describes what PRINCE2 Agile is?
o: An agile delivery framework that replaces the PRINCE2 processes with Scrum events and roles
A version of PRINCE2 that drops whichever principles conflict with agile ways of working
PRINCE2 Project Management tailored with an agile mindset, frameworks, artifacts and workshops
A team-level method for product delivery that leaves project governance to BAU
Agile: Basics & PRINCE2 Agile.w: PRINCE2 Agile keeps the PRINCE2 principles, practices and processes and tailors them with the agile mindset, agile frameworks, artifacts, techniques and workshops, so it covers direction, management and delivery (book 3.1).

n.0: The PRINCE2 processes stay; PRINCE2 Agile adds workshops to them and can work with Scrum or other frameworks (3.1).
n.1: No principle is dropped: all seven PRINCE2 principles apply, and only their application is tailored (5.2).
n.3: PRINCE2 Agile keeps governance and control throughout the project; it is not a team-level delivery method (3.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: A transport authority's agile project has three delivery teams. Which statement correctly distinguishes the project backlog from a product backlog?
o: The project backlog holds mostly epics and is owned by the CPO; a product backlog holds one team's stories
The project backlog holds one team's detailed stories; a product backlog holds the epics for the project
The project backlog is owned by the product owner; a product backlog is owned by the project executive
The project backlog replaces the business case; a product backlog replaces the work package description
Agile: Techniques.w: The project backlog is high level, mostly epics, replaces the project product description and is owned by the chief product owner. Each team's product backlog holds its detailed user stories, links the team DoD and is owned by that team's product owner (book 8.3.2.1, Table B.1).

n.1: This reverses the two: epics sit in the project backlog and detailed stories sit in each team's product backlog (book 8.3.2.1).
n.2: The CPO owns the project backlog and each product owner owns a product backlog; the project executive owns neither (book Table B.1).
n.3: The business case is tailored into the project canvas, and the work package description becomes a set of user stories; the backlogs replace the project product description and product descriptions (book 6.3.2, 8.3.2.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: A project manager at a building society shows the board a release map. Which statement best describes this artifact?
o: A chart of the story points still to do in an iteration, updated each day by the team
A visual plan clustering user stories into releases, used as the project and stage plan
A list of the criteria an item must meet before the team can start working on it
A summary of the business justification, including the costs, benefits and major risks
Agile: Techniques.w: A release map is a visual plan in which user stories, often taken from a story map, are clustered into releases of usually two to four iterations. In PRINCE2 Agile it serves as the project plan and the stage plan (book 8.3.2.5, 8.4.4).

n.0: Story points remaining in an iteration, updated daily, describes a burn-down chart, a progress technique rather than a plan (book 12.4.3).
n.2: Criteria an item must meet before work starts make up the Definition of Ready, a quality artifact (book 9.3.2.1).
n.3: The business justification with costs, benefits and risks is set out in the project canvas, not the release map (book 6.3.2.1).

Agile: Techniques.q:
Which two statements about dashboards in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report.
2. The project dashboard replaces the work package description.
3. The project dashboard replaces the highlight report and the end stage report.
4. The team dashboard is reviewed mainly in progress review workshops.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
Agile: Techniques.w: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: the team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report, and the project dashboard replaces both the highlight report and the end stage report (book Table 12.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the work package description becomes a set of user stories agreed between the project manager and product owner, not a dashboard (book 8.3.2).
n.1: Both are wrong: the work package description is not replaced by a dashboard, and the team dashboard is reviewed in team planning and retrospective workshops, while progress review workshops use the project dashboard (book Table 12.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is wrong: progress review workshops review the project dashboard, while the team dashboard is reviewed in team planning and retrospective workshops (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: A housing association's agile project will deliver an online repairs portal for tenants. Which of these is a benefit, as PRINCE2 Agile defines the term?
o: The online repairs portal released to tenants at the end of stage 2
The release map showing three releases across the first two stages
The project canvas approved by the project executive at the start
A 20% fall in repair calls to the contact centre within one year
Agile: Techniques.w: A benefit is a measurable improvement, resulting from an outcome, that the investing organization sees as an advantage and that contributes to its objectives. A measured fall in repair calls fits this (book Glossary).

n.0: The portal is an output, a specialist product the project delivers; an output is not a benefit (book Glossary).
n.1: The release map is a plan, a management artifact; it is not a measurable improvement for the organization (book 8.3.2.5).
n.2: The project canvas is the agile form of the business case that records expected benefits; the approved document is not itself a benefit (book 6.3.2.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: User stories are a popular way of expressing requirements in a PRINCE2 Agile project. Which three elements does the user story format capture?
o: Who needs it, when it is due and how much it will cost
What is needed, how it will be built and where it will be used
Who wants it, what they want and why they want it
Why it is needed, when it is due and who will approve it
Agile: Techniques.w: A user story describes who wants something, what they want and why, typically written as 'As a ... I want ... so that ...' (book 8.3.2.3).

n.0: Due dates and cost are planning information held elsewhere, such as the release map and budget; the story format captures the user, the need and the reason (book 8.3.2.3).
n.1: How a feature will be built is left to the delivery team; the story format deliberately states the user's need and its value, not the design (book 8.3.2.3).
n.3: Due dates and approvers are not part of the story format; it names the user (who), the need (what) and the value (why) (book 8.3.2.3).

Agile: Techniques.q: The chief product owner of a hospital trust's patient app has added several broad requirements to the project backlog as epics. What is an epic in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: A user story that has met the Definition of Done and been released
A timebox at project level made up of two to four iterations
A set of user stories agreed between the PM and a product owner
A large or vague user story that is broken down into detailed stories
Agile: Techniques.w: An epic is a large or vague user story that is broken down into more detailed user stories; the term comes from Mike Cohn (book 8.3.2.2, Glossary).

n.0: A story that has met the Definition of Done is a completed story; size and vagueness, not completion, make a story an epic (book 8.3.2.2, 9.3.2.2).
n.1: A timebox of two to four iterations describes a release, not an epic (book 8.3.2.5, Glossary).
n.2: A set of user stories agreed between the project manager and a product owner is a work package description (book 8.3.2).

Agile: Techniques.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.

In PRINCE2 Agile, a work package description is typically expressed as a set of [?] agreed between the project manager and the product owner.
o: user stories
release maps
team dashboards
risk responses
Agile: Techniques.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the project manager and product owner agree work as work package descriptions in the form of sets of user stories, within agreed tolerances (book 7.3, 8.3.2).

n.1: The release map is the project and stage plan; a work package covers a smaller set of work for one team (book 8.3.2.5).
n.2: Team dashboards replace checkpoint reports and show the team's progress; they do not describe the work to be done (book Table 12.1).
n.3: Risk responses are planned in the risk practice and may sit in a risk-adjusted backlog, but a work package is described as a set of user stories (book 10.4.1, 8.3.2).

Agile: Techniques.q: A council's waste team writes this story: 'As a resident, I want a text reminder the evening before collection, so that I do not miss my bin day.' What does the final clause, 'so that I do not miss my bin day', provide?
o: The who: the user role the story serves
The why: the value the user gains
The what: the feature being requested
The acceptance criterion to be tested
Agile: Techniques.w: The 'so that' clause states why the user wants the feature, which is the value they gain; 'As a resident' is the who and 'I want a text reminder' is the what (book 8.3.2.3).

n.0: The who is given by 'As a resident', the user role at the start of the story (book 8.3.2.3).
n.2: The what is the requested feature, 'a text reminder the evening before collection' (book 8.3.2.3).
n.3: Acceptance criteria are added to the story as separate, testable conditions; the 'so that' clause gives the reason for the request (book 9.3.2.1, Table 13.13).

Agile: Techniques.q: Which statement best explains how epics and user stories relate to each other in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: Epics sit in each team's product backlog, while user stories sit in the project backlog
Epics are written after the user stories are finished, to summarize what was delivered
Epics are high level and often vague, so they are broken down into detailed user stories
Epics replace user stories when the project uses a linear, waterfall delivery method
Agile: Techniques.w: Requirements often start large or vague; these epics are high-level stories that are broken down into more detailed user stories as work approaches (book 8.3.2.2). The project backlog holds mostly epics, and team product backlogs hold the detailed stories (book 8.3.2.1).

n.0: This reverses the levels: the project backlog holds mostly epics and each team's product backlog holds detailed user stories (book 8.3.2.1).
n.1: Epics come first, as broad requirements, and are decomposed into stories; they are not written afterwards as a summary (book 8.3.2.2).
n.3: Epics and user stories are agile requirement formats used for iterative delivery; they are not a substitute format for waterfall projects (book 8.3.2.2).

Agile: Techniques.q: During the user story refinement topic of the team planning workshop, what should the team make sure of for each story's acceptance criteria?
o: They are set by the project executive and approved at the stage boundary
They are recorded in the risk register so that they can be monitored
They are left open until the demo so that users can add to them later
They are clear and testable, so the team knows what counts as done
Agile: Techniques.w: User story refinement in the team planning workshop makes sure each story's acceptance criteria are clear and testable, so the team shares a view of what counts as done (book Table 13.13).

n.0: Acceptance criteria are refined by the delivery team with its product owner for the next iteration; the project executive does not set story-level criteria at stage boundaries (book Table 13.13, Table B.1).
n.1: The risk register records risks, not acceptance criteria; criteria belong with the story in the product backlog (book 10.3.2, 8.3.2.1).
n.2: Leaving criteria open would stop the story being ready; a ready story has measurable, prioritized acceptance criteria before work starts (book 9.3.2.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: In a PRINCE2 Agile delivery team, which role prepares and maintains the product backlog and its user stories?
o: Product owner
Chief product owner
Project support
Tester
Agile: Techniques.w: The product owner owns the team's product backlog, prepares and maintains it and its user stories, and keeps it aligned with the project backlog (book Table B.1).

n.1: The chief product owner owns the project backlog and sets priorities across teams; each team's product backlog belongs to its product owner (book Table B.1).
n.2: Project support gives administrative help and maintains dashboards; it does not own or maintain a product backlog (book Table B.1).
n.3: The tester checks products against acceptance criteria and the team DoD; it does not prepare the backlog (book Table B.1).

Agile: Techniques.q:
Which two statements about user stories in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. The user story format captures who wants something, what they want and why.
2. Acceptance criteria are added to a user story after it has been delivered.
3. A large or vague user story is known as an epic and is broken down further.
4. User stories are held in the project backlog, while product backlogs hold epics.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Techniques.w: Statement 1 is the who, what and why format (book 8.3.2.3), and statement 3 describes an epic, which is decomposed into detailed stories (book 8.3.2.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: a story is ready to start when it already has measurable, prioritized acceptance criteria, so they come before delivery (book 9.3.2.1).
n.2: Both are wrong: acceptance criteria are needed before work starts (book 9.3.2.1), and the project backlog holds mostly epics while product backlogs hold detailed stories (book 8.3.2.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 reverses the backlogs: epics sit mainly in the project backlog and detailed stories in team product backlogs (book 8.3.2.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: A delivery team at an insurance broker is about to estimate its user stories for the first time. What kind of estimates does PRINCE2 Agile recommend?
o: Relative estimates that compare the size of items with each other
Actual estimates of the hours each task will take to complete
Estimates prepared by the project manager and given to the team
Estimates taken from a similar project run by another supplier
Agile: Techniques.w: PRINCE2 Agile estimation starts from relative rather than actual estimates and draws on the knowledge of the whole team, so everyone can contribute without being swayed by others (book 8.4.3).

n.1: Predicting actual hours is the absolute approach that agile estimation moves away from; items are sized relative to one another (book 8.4.3).
n.2: Estimation harnesses the knowledge of the whole delivery team; it is not handed down by the project manager (book 8.4.3).
n.3: Forecasts should rest on the team's own measured experience; another organization's figures do not reflect this team (book 8.3, 8.4.3).

Agile: Techniques.q: A product owner asks the team to give each user story a number of story points. In PRINCE2 Agile, what does a story point value represent?
o: A fixed number of working hours agreed for one user story
The size of a story relative to other stories in the backlog
A priority rating showing whether a story is a Must or a Should
A mark awarded when a story passes all its acceptance tests
Agile: Techniques.w: Story points are the most common form of relative estimation: a story gets a points value that means something in relation to another story or requirement (book 8.4.3).

n.0: Story points are not hours; they express relative size, which is why they are a relative rather than an actual estimate (book 8.4.3).
n.2: Priority is set with MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't have this time), which is separate from estimating size (book 9.3.2, 8.4.3).
n.3: Passing acceptance tests relates to the Definition of Done; points are assigned before the work, as an estimate (book 9.3.2.2, 8.4.3).

Agile: Techniques.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

In [?] sizing, a team places user stories into broad relative size bands, labelled with clothing sizes such as small, medium and large.
o: velocity
MoSCoW
t-shirt
burn-up
Agile: Techniques.w: T-shirt sizing is one of the agile estimation techniques named in the syllabus: items are put into relative size bands labelled like clothing sizes (book 8.4.3).

n.0: Velocity is the average number of story points a team delivers per timebox; it is used for forecasting, not for sizing individual stories (book 12.4.3).
n.1: MoSCoW sets priority (Must, Should, Could, Won't have this time), not relative size (book 9.3.2).
n.3: A burn-up chart shows completed work against a deadline; it is a progress technique, not a way of sizing stories (book 12.4.3).

Agile: Techniques.q: When a delivery team estimates a story using numbered cards, why does PRINCE2 Agile have every member reveal their estimate at the same moment?
o: So the project manager can take the lowest estimate for the plan
So the most experienced member's estimate can be adopted quickly
So each estimate can be turned straight into hours for the budget
So everyone contributes without being influenced by the others
Agile: Techniques.w: Revealing estimates simultaneously harnesses the whole team's knowledge in a way that lets everyone contribute without being prejudiced by other team members (book 8.4.3).

n.0: Estimating is a whole-team activity aimed at a shared view; the project manager does not pick a figure from the cards (book 8.4.3).
n.1: Deferring to the most experienced person is the bias the simultaneous reveal is designed to avoid (book 8.4.3).
n.2: The estimates are relative sizes, not hours; converting them into hours would turn them back into actual estimates (book 8.4.3).

Agile: Techniques.q: A city museum's agile project has just started, and the team must size about 150 high-level stories for the project backlog quickly. Which estimation technique is intended for this situation?
o: Magic estimation
Card-based estimating of each story in turn
A cumulative flow diagram
Velocity from the last three iterations
Agile: Techniques.w: Magic estimation is a quick, collaborative technique used in early planning, for example at project product level, to size many items relative to each other without lengthy discussion (book 8.4.3).

n.1: Card-based estimating discusses and estimates one story at a time, which is too slow for sizing a very large early backlog (book 8.4.3).
n.2: A cumulative flow diagram shows work items in each workflow state over time to reveal bottlenecks; it does not estimate size (book 12.4.2).
n.3: At the very start there are no completed iterations, so there is no velocity yet; velocity also forecasts delivery rather than sizing stories (book 12.4.3).

Agile: Techniques.q: A delivery team completed 24, 18 and 21 story points in its last three iterations, and 105 points remain in its backlog. If conditions stay the same, about how many more iterations will it need?
o: Four iterations
Five iterations
Six iterations
Seven iterations
Agile: Techniques.w: Velocity is the average rate of story points delivered per timebox: (24 + 18 + 21) / 3 = 21 points. 105 / 21 = 5 more iterations, assuming conditions stay the same (book 12.4.3).

n.0: Four iterations would need about 26 points per iteration, above every iteration the team has delivered so far (book 12.4.3).
n.2: Six iterations implies a velocity of about 18 points, which is the team's lowest iteration rather than its average (book 12.4.3).
n.3: Seven iterations implies a velocity of 15 points, below anything the team has recorded (book 12.4.3).

Agile: Techniques.q: Two delivery teams work on the same project. Team A delivers about 30 points per iteration and team B about 18. The project manager wants to forecast when team B will finish its backlog. What should the forecast be based on?
o: Team A's velocity, as it is the higher and more ambitious rate
The average of both teams' rates, about 24 points per iteration
Team B's own velocity of about 18 points per iteration
The product owner's estimate of the hours left on each story
Agile: Techniques.w: Empirical forecasting uses the measured rate of the team doing the work: PRINCE2 Agile says to use your own team's velocity, not another person's or team's, so team B's 18 points is the basis (book 8.3, 12.4.3).

n.0: Team A is a different team; PRINCE2 Agile warns against forecasting with another team's velocity (book 8.3).
n.1: Blending two teams' rates still brings in another team's data; the forecast should use the team doing the work (book 8.3).
n.3: Converting stories to hours returns to actual estimates; agile forecasting divides remaining points by the team's velocity (book 8.4.3, 12.4.3).

Agile: Techniques.q: Before selecting stories for the next iteration, a delivery team agrees a shared view of how much effort or complexity each story involves. Under which workshop topic does this happen?
o: Product demo, in the progress review workshop
Release planning, in the release planning workshop
The learning, in the team retrospective workshop
Effort estimation, in the team planning workshop
Agile: Techniques.w: The team planning workshop includes an effort estimation topic, where the team builds a shared view of the effort or complexity of each story before iteration planning (book 13.6.4.1, Table 13.13).

n.0: The product demo shows completed features to users to gather acceptance and feedback; it does not estimate future stories (book Table 13.10).
