n.1: Release planning, at a stage boundary, breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map; detailed effort for the next iteration is the team planning workshop's job (book 13.7.4.1).
n.2: The learning collects lessons and improvement ideas from the last iteration; it does not size the next iteration's stories (book Table 13.14).

Agile: Techniques.q: A team coach at a logistics firm puts a burn-down chart on the team dashboard. What does a burn-down chart show?
o: Completed work rising towards a total scope line across stages
The number of work items in each workflow state over time
Outstanding work falling over time, often across an iteration
Total risk exposure falling as risk responses take effect
Agile: Techniques.w: A burn-down chart is a run chart of outstanding work over time, typically used at team level to show story points remaining over the days of an iteration (book 12.4.3).

n.0: Completed work rising against a scope line over stages describes a burn-up chart, usually used at project or product level (book 12.4.3).
n.1: Items in each workflow state over time is a cumulative flow diagram, used to reveal bottlenecks (book 12.4.2).
n.3: Falling total risk exposure is shown by a cumulative risk burn-down chart, a risk technique, not a progress burn-down (book 10.4.2).

Agile: Techniques.q: The chief product owner of a university's student-records project uses a burn-up chart at project level. What does a burn-up chart show?
o: The story points still to do in the current iteration, day by day
The number of risks closed in each iteration of the current stage
The hours each team member has logged against each user story
Completed work against a deadline, used to forecast completion
Agile: Techniques.w: A burn-up chart is a run chart of completed work against a deadline, often used at project or product level to show story points over stages or iterations and forecast when work will finish (book 12.4.3).

n.0: Remaining points day by day within an iteration is a burn-down chart, usually used at team level (book 12.4.3).
n.1: Risk exposure across iterations is tracked with a cumulative risk burn-down chart, not a burn-up chart (book 10.4.2).
n.2: Burn charts show work completed and work remaining, for example in story points over stages or iterations, not the hours each person has logged (book 12.4.3).

Agile: Techniques.q: At which level of a PRINCE2 Agile project are burn charts a suitable way of showing progress, and why?
o: At every level, because what is delivered is the main aspect that flexes
At team level, because the board tracks spend against budget instead
At project level, because teams report progress in checkpoint reports
At stage level, because time tolerance is the main measure of progress
Agile: Techniques.w: Flexibility in what is delivered is the aspect of performance of most interest to the whole project management team, so showing it in a burn chart suits every level of the project (book 12.3.1).

n.1: Cost has zero tolerance on all levels of plan in PRINCE2 Agile, so tracking spend against budget adds little; the board also benefits from burn charts (book 12.3.1, Table 3.1).
n.2: Checkpoint reports are replaced by team dashboards, and burn charts are used at team level as well as project level (book Table 12.1, 12.3.1).
n.3: Time also has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, so time tolerance is not the progress measure; scope delivered is (book 12.3.1, Table 3.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: Halfway through an iteration, a team's burn-down chart shows the actual line well above the ideal line. What does this indicate, and what should the team focus on?
o: It is ahead of plan, so it can pull extra stories into the iteration
It is behind plan, so it should focus on the highest-priority items
It is behind plan, so the iteration end date should be moved back
It is on plan, because the actual line is expected to stay above ideal
Agile: Techniques.w: An actual line above the ideal line means work is not being completed fast enough to finish everything, so the team should concentrate on the highest-priority backlog items (book 12.4.3).

n.0: A team that is ahead would have its actual line below the ideal line, with less work remaining than planned (book 12.4.3).
n.2: The reading is right but the action is wrong: time has zero tolerance in PRINCE2 Agile, so the timebox is kept and lower-priority scope flexes (book Table 3.1).
n.3: The ideal line shows the planned rate; sitting above it means more work remains than planned, which is behind, not on plan (book 12.4.3).

Agile: Techniques.q: On a project's burn-up chart, the completed-work line is rising steadily, but the total scope line has stepped upwards twice during the stage. What do the steps in the scope line show?
o: The delivery teams' velocity has fallen
Work has been completed faster than forecast
Work has been added to the scope being delivered
The cost tolerance for the stage has been exceeded
Agile: Techniques.w: A burn-up chart shows completed work against a separate line for total scope; when the scope line rises, work has been added, which moves the forecast finish (book 12.4.3).

n.0: Velocity shows in the slope of the completed-work line, which is rising steadily here, not in the scope line (book 12.4.3).
n.1: Faster completion would show as a steeper completed-work line; the scope line measures the total to be delivered (book 12.4.3).
n.3: A burn-up chart tracks work delivered, not money, and cost has zero tolerance in PRINCE2 Agile (book 12.4.3, Table 3.1).

Agile: Techniques.q:
Which two statements about burn charts in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. A burn-down chart typically shows story points remaining over the days of an iteration.
2. A burn-up chart is mainly a team-level chart of hours spent each day.
3. Burn charts are used in place of budget tracking because cost is the aspect that flexes.
4. An updated burn chart can reveal that a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
Agile: Techniques.w: Statement 1 describes the team-level burn-down chart (book 12.4.3). Statement 4 is correct because an exception can be triggered by an updated burn chart at iteration or release level (book Table 12.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: a burn-up chart shows completed work against a deadline, usually at project or product level, in story points rather than hours (book 12.4.3).
n.1: Both are wrong: a burn-up chart is not an hours chart (book 12.4.3), and cost has zero tolerance in PRINCE2 Agile, so it does not flex (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is correct, but statement 3 is wrong: what flexes is what is delivered, while cost is fixed with zero tolerance (book 12.3.1, Table 3.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: A project board at a regional airport wants to see the project's burn charts between progress reviews. Where would the board normally find them?
o: On the project dashboard, from which the board pulls information
In the team plan, which the product owner sends to the board
In the quality register, which records each completed story
In the daily log, which project support sends to the board
Agile: Techniques.w: The project dashboard replaces the highlight and end stage reports and shows items such as release status, burn charts, current risks and issues; the board pulls information from it (book 12.3.2.1, Table 12.1).

n.1: The team plan is the delivery team's task-level plan for the next iteration; it is not a reporting tool for the board (book 8.3.2).
n.2: The quality register records planned and completed quality activities and their results, not burn charts (book 9.3.2).
n.3: The daily log is the project manager's own working record, created in starting up; it is not where the board finds burn charts (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: A team coach wants a chart that shows how many tasks sit in each workflow state over time, so that bottlenecks become visible. Which technique fits this need?
o: A burn-up chart
A cumulative flow diagram
A cumulative risk burn-down chart
A release map
Agile: Techniques.w: A cumulative flow diagram shows the number of tasks in each workflow state over time and reveals bottlenecks; it is mostly used at team level (book 12.4.2).

n.0: A burn-up chart shows completed work against a deadline, not the spread of tasks across workflow states (book 12.4.3).
n.2: A cumulative risk burn-down chart tracks total risk exposure across iterations, not workflow states (book 10.4.2).
n.3: A release map is a plan of releases and their features; it does not chart work in progress over time (book 8.3.2.5).

Agile: Techniques.q: A garden-centre chain is planning an agile project for an online ordering service. How does PRINCE2 Agile describe a minimum viable product (MVP)?
o: A basic version built with minimal cost and time to gather early feedback
The finished product with every Must, Should and Could have delivered
The lowest-cost business option chosen when the project canvas is drafted
The set of products that must be handed over at project closure
Agile: Techniques.w: An MVP is a basic version of the product, built with minimal cost and time, so the team can gather early feedback and test core features; it is refined using that feedback (book 6.3.1).

n.1: An MVP is deliberately not a finished product; delivering every Must, Should and Could have describes a complete product (book 6.3.1).
n.2: Business options are compared in the project canvas to choose a way forward; an MVP is an early version of the product itself (book 6.3.2.1, 6.3.1).
n.3: Handover at closure concerns the final project product; the MVP comes early, to learn from real use (book 6.3.1, Table 13.18).

Agile: Techniques.q: A charity's project board asks why the team plans to release an MVP of its volunteer app early in the project. What is the main purpose of an MVP?
o: To meet every requirement in the project backlog in a single release
To test core features and assumptions with users at minimal cost
To give the board a fixed final cost before the project is initiated
To remove the need for a business case in an agile project
Agile: Techniques.w: The MVP helps assess product viability by testing core features with minimal investment and gathering early feedback from users (book 6.3.1).

n.0: An MVP holds the essential features, not every requirement; the rest follow in later releases as feedback is used (book 6.3.1).
n.2: Costs are set out in the project canvas and plans; the MVP is about learning from real use, not fixing a budget (book 6.3.2.1, 6.3.1).
n.3: All projects need business justification; the project canvas identifies the MVP where one is used rather than replacing the business case (book 6.3.1, Table 6.1).

Agile: Techniques.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

An MVP is not a finished product: its essential features are refined over time using user [?].
o: tolerances
sign-off
feedback
training
Agile: Techniques.w: An MVP is built to gather early feedback, and its essential features are then refined using what users say (book 6.3.1).

n.0: Tolerances are permitted deviations set for plans and targets; they do not refine a product's features (book Table 3.1).
n.1: Formal sign-off accepts a finished product; an MVP is refined through what users report, not approved as final (book 6.3.1).
n.3: User training supports adoption of change; the MVP's features are improved through the feedback users give (book 6.3.1, 4.2.4).

Agile: Techniques.q: A product owner says the MVP and the first full release are the same thing. Which statement about an MVP compared with a full first release is correct?
o: An MVP contains all the Must, Should and Could haves, so it is a full release
An MVP is built after the full product, as a cut-down version for user training
An MVP and a full first release are the same product under different names
An MVP holds just enough to learn from real use, so it is less than a full release
Agile: Techniques.w: An MVP is a basic version built with minimal cost and time to gather early feedback and test core features, so it holds less than a complete release (book 6.3.1).

n.0: Delivering every Must, Should and Could have is a full product; the MVP is deliberately minimal (book 6.3.1).
n.1: The MVP comes early, before the full product, so feedback can shape what is built next (book 6.3.1).
n.2: They differ in purpose and size: the MVP exists to test core features and learn, not to deliver the full set of features (book 6.3.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: A new energy company is building an app in a highly innovative market where much is unknown. According to PRINCE2 Agile, what is defining an MVP likely to involve in this context?
o: Exploring key assumptions so they can be validated as quickly as possible
Fixing the full feature list in detail before any build work begins
Delaying the first release until all the Could haves are complete
Matching the features of a product that a competitor has released
Agile: Techniques.w: How an MVP is defined depends on the level of uncertainty; in highly innovative contexts it often means exploring key assumptions and validating them fast (book 6.3.1).

n.1: Fixing every feature up front works against learning from feedback, which is the MVP's purpose in an uncertain market (book 6.3.1).
n.2: Could haves are the first scope to flex; holding the release for them delays the early feedback an MVP exists to gather (book 6.3.1, Table 3.1).
n.3: Copying a competitor does not test this organization's own key assumptions about its users (book 6.3.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: Why should the project canvas identify the MVP when a PRINCE2 Agile project plans to use one?
o: So the team can skip the usual quality checks on the first release
So an exception can be raised if the MVP is forecast to be late
So the senior supplier can approve each user story before it is built
So the MVP can be used in place of the project product description
Agile: Techniques.w: The project canvas must identify the MVP, if one is used, so that an exception can be raised if delivery of the MVP is forecast to be late (book Table 6.1).

n.0: An MVP is still delivered to the quality criteria and Definition of Done agreed for it; naming it does not remove quality checks (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: Stories are prepared and prioritized by product owners within the backlog; the canvas names the MVP for control, not for supplier approval of stories (book Table B.1, Table 6.1).
n.3: The project product description becomes the project backlog, not the MVP (book 8.3.2.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: A council is procuring an external agile supplier. Which management product could include a definition of the MVP and its tolerances, so that the contract supports agile delivery?
o: The quality register
The communication management approach
The commercial management approach
The risk register
Agile: Techniques.w: The commercial management approach should support agile product development, for example with fixed teams or costs per iteration, a definition of the MVP and possible tolerances, and an agreed Definition of Done (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3).

n.0: The quality register records planned and completed quality activities and their results, not contract terms (book 9.3.2).
n.1: The communication management approach sets the means and frequency of communication and feedback with stakeholders, not procurement or contract form (book 4.4).
n.3: The risk register records identified risks and their status; it does not define what the supplier must deliver (book 10.3.2).

Agile: Techniques.q: PRINCE2 Agile's fix and flex defaults include a row for benefits. What does that row say about minimum viability?
o: Benefits are flexed below minimum viability and fixed above it
Benefits have zero tolerance at every level of plan, like time
Benefits are fixed for Could haves and flexed for Must haves
Benefits are fixed for minimum viability and flexed above it
Agile: Techniques.w: Table 3.1 fixes benefits at minimum viability and allows them to flex above it, in the same way that sustainability is fixed at its minimum criteria (book Table 3.1).

n.0: This reverses the rule: minimum viability is the floor that is fixed, and benefits above it may flex (book Table 3.1).
n.1: Zero tolerance on all levels of plan is the default for time and cost, not benefits (book Table 3.1).
n.2: MoSCoW categories drive the scope row (fixed for Musts, flexed for Shoulds and Coulds), and even there the Musts are fixed, not flexed (book Table 3.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: A delivery team at a payroll bureau agrees a Definition of Ready (DoR). What does a DoR set out?
o: The criteria an item must meet to be considered complete
The criteria an item must meet before work on it begins
The order in which items will be released to the users
The tolerances the project board sets for the stage
Agile: Techniques.w: The Definition of Ready is a shared team agreement on the criteria a task, deliverable or user story must meet before work begins, so the item is fully prepared (book 9.3.2.1).

n.0: Criteria for an item to be considered complete form the Definition of Done, which applies at the end of the work (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: The order and timing of releases is shown in the release map, a plans artifact (book 8.3.2.5).
n.3: Stage tolerances are set by the project board under the progress practice; a DoR is the team's agreement about starting work (book Table 3.1, 9.3.2.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: A delivery team at a hotel group agrees a Definition of Done (DoD). What does a DoD set out?
o: The criteria a piece of work must meet to be considered complete
The criteria an item must meet before the team can start on it
The date by which each user story in the backlog must be released
The risks that must be closed before a release can go to users
Agile: Techniques.w: The Definition of Done is a shared agreement within the team on the criteria a task, deliverable or piece of work must meet to be considered complete, such as review, validation and approval (book 9.3.2.2).

n.1: Criteria to meet before work starts form the Definition of Ready (book 9.3.2.1).
n.2: Release timing is shown in the release map; the DoD defines completeness, not dates (book 8.3.2.5, 9.3.2.2).
n.3: Risks are recorded and managed through the risk register and risk practice; the DoD sets quality criteria for completed work (book 10.3.2, 9.3.2.2).

Agile: Techniques.q: At the end of an iteration, a developer describes a user story as 'almost done'. How does PRINCE2 Agile treat this story against the Definition of Done?
o: It counts as done if most of its acceptance criteria have passed
It counts as done if the product owner agrees that it is close
It counts as half done and earns half of its story points
It is not done, as an item is either done or not done
Agile: Techniques.w: Against the Definition of Done an item is either done or not done; there is no 'almost done' in agile (book 9.3.2.2).

n.0: Meeting most criteria is not meeting the DoD; any criterion still unmet means the item is not done (book 9.3.2.2).
n.1: The DoD is a shared, fixed set of criteria; a product owner's view that work is close does not change whether it is done (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: There is no partial credit for a story; the finished part can be split off, and the rest returns to the backlog (book 9.3.2.2).

Agile: Techniques.q: A delivery team at a ferry operator has agreed its own team Definition of Done. In which artifact should it be included or linked?
o: The project canvas
The risk register
The product backlog
The project dashboard
Agile: Techniques.w: A product backlog is a regular backlog that also includes, or links to, the team Definition of Done (book 8.3.2.1).

n.0: The project canvas is the one-page business justification; it does not hold team quality criteria (book 6.3.2.1).
n.1: The risk register records risks and their status, not completion criteria (book 10.3.2).
n.3: The project dashboard shows progress for the board; the team DoD sits with the team's product backlog (book 12.3.2.1, 8.3.2.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: When an iteration ends, one user story is only partly complete. Following PRINCE2 Agile guidance on the Definition of Done, what should happen to it?
o: Split it: the finished part is done, and the rest returns to the backlog
Extend the iteration by a few days so that the whole story can finish
Mark it as done and record the missing work as a risk in the register
Count it as done because most of its acceptance criteria were met
Agile: Techniques.w: A partly finished story is split: the completed part goes to done and the remainder returns to the backlog for reprioritization (book 9.3.2.2).

n.1: Time has zero tolerance at every level of plan, so the timebox is kept rather than extended (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Unfinished work cannot be marked done; there is no 'almost done', and missing scope is not a risk entry (book 9.3.2.2).
n.3: Meeting most criteria is not meeting the DoD; the story is either done or not done (book 9.3.2.2).

Agile: Techniques.q: In a PRINCE2 Agile project, the project-level Definition of Ready and Definition of Done are agreed as topics of which workshop?
o: The team retrospective workshop
The project initiation workshop
The project closure workshop
The progress review workshop
Agile: Techniques.w: The project initiation workshop includes topics for the project Definition of Ready (product-wide criteria to start work) and the project Definition of Done (criteria for work to be acceptable to users and the CPO) (book 13.4.4.1, Table 13.7).

n.0: The team retrospective reflects on the last iteration (the good, the bad, the learning, team building); it does not set project-level criteria (book Table 13.14).
n.2: The project closure workshop confirms the final product and captures lessons at the end; the project DoR and DoD are needed from initiation (book Table 13.19).
n.3: The progress review workshop reviews dashboard metrics, risks and issues and holds a product demo during delivery (book Table 13.10).

Agile: Techniques.q:
Which two statements about the Definition of Ready and the Definition of Done are correct?

1. A user story can be ready when it states who, what and why and has measurable, prioritized acceptance criteria.
2. The DoR is checked once work is finished, to decide whether it can be released.
3. Work that is finished but still contains defects meets the DoD.
4. The DoD is a shared agreement within the team on what complete means.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
Agile: Techniques.w: Statement 1 is the book's example of a ready user story (book 9.3.2.1), and statement 4 describes the DoD as a shared team agreement on completion criteria (book 9.3.2.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the DoR applies before work begins; deciding whether finished work is complete is the DoD's job (book 9.3.2.1, 9.3.2.2).
n.1: Both are wrong: the DoR applies before work starts (book 9.3.2.1), and work with defects is not done (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: Statement 4 is correct, but statement 3 is wrong: completed work that still has defects does not meet the DoD (book 9.3.2.2).

Agile: Techniques.q: Within a PRINCE2 Agile delivery team, which role is described as reviewing products against their acceptance criteria and the team Definition of Done?
o: Project assurance
Developer
Tester
Agile coach
Agile: Techniques.w: The tester ensures quality and reliability by designing and running tests and quality reviews, and reviews products against acceptance criteria and the team DoD (book Table B.1).

n.0: Project assurance independently monitors adherence to PRINCE2 Agile principles and practices for the board; it is not the team role that checks each product against the DoD (book Table B.1).
n.1: The developer designs, builds and maintains increments of the product; checking them against acceptance criteria and the DoD is the tester's role (book Table B.1).
n.3: The agile coach works across the organization to remove systemic blockers to agile adoption, not inside a team testing products (book Table B.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: A delivery team at a recycling company wants to reflect regularly on how it works together. In PRINCE2 Agile, when does the team hold its retrospective?
o: At the start of each iteration, before planning begins
Each day, as the last item of the daily stand-up
Once, at the end of the final stage of the project
At the end of each iteration, looking back on it
Agile: Techniques.w: Retrospectives are recurring events held at the end of an iteration, not during it; the team retrospective workshop reflects on the iteration just finished (book 5.6.3.3, 13.6.4.2).

n.0: The start of an iteration is for the team planning workshop, which prepares the coming iteration (book 13.6.4.1).
n.1: The daily stand-up keeps the day's work visible (book Table 12.1); the retrospective is a separate event, held at the end of each iteration (book 5.6.3.3).
n.2: Lessons are captured throughout, with a retrospective after every iteration; waiting for the final stage loses the regular feedback loop (book 5.6.3.3, 13.6.4.2).

Agile: Techniques.q: A team coach is preparing a team planning workshop in the 'managing product delivery' process. What is the purpose of this workshop?
o: To prepare the next iteration and agree a realistic team plan
To review the project dashboard with the project board
To agree the project canvas before the project is initiated
To confirm the final product is ready for handover to users
Agile: Techniques.w: The team planning workshop prepares the next iteration through backlog refinement, user story refinement, effort estimation and iteration planning, ending with a realistic team plan (book 13.6.4.1, Table 13.13).

n.1: Reviewing project dashboard metrics belongs to the progress review workshop in controlling a stage (book Table 13.10).
n.2: The project canvas is built in the project canvas workshop when the project is being started up (book 6.3.2.1).
n.3: Confirming the final product is ready for handover happens in the project closure workshop (book Table 13.19).

Agile: Techniques.q: PRINCE2 Agile attaches named workshops to each of its processes. How does it describe a workshop?
o: An informal daily meeting where each member reports progress
A training course run by the agile coach for the project board
A facilitated session with a set purpose, agenda and outputs
A formal meeting at which the board authorizes the next stage
Agile: Techniques.w: A workshop is a facilitated, collaborative session with a defined purpose, participants, agenda topics and outputs; PRINCE2 Agile V2 names workshops for every process (book 5.6.3.1).

n.0: A short daily progress meeting is the daily stand-up, which the project manager may attend only with the team's agreement; it is not a workshop with a set agenda and outputs (book Table 12.1, 5.6.3.1).
n.1: Training and coaching raise agile maturity, but a workshop is a working session with its own agenda and outputs, not a course (book 2.7.3, 5.6.3.1).
n.3: Authorizing a stage is a board decision in directing a project; it does not describe what a workshop is (book 5.6.3.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: A project manager would like to join the delivery team's daily stand-ups to stay close to progress. What does PRINCE2 Agile say about this?
o: The project manager chairs the stand-ups and assigns daily tasks
The project manager may attend with the delivery team's agreement
The project manager attends to present progress to the team daily
The project manager attends weekly to collect checkpoint reports
Agile: Techniques.w: The project manager may attend daily stand-ups with the delivery team's agreement, which respects the team's self-management (book Table 12.1).

n.0: Delivery teams self-manage their daily work; the project manager does not run the stand-up or hand out tasks (book Table 12.1, 2.6.2).
n.2: The stand-up is the team's own event for making its work visible; the project manager presenting progress to the team weakens transparency and self-management (book 2.6.2, Table 12.1).
n.3: Checkpoint reports are replaced by the team dashboard, which the project manager pulls from; stand-ups are daily, not a weekly collection point (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: During a progress review workshop at an engineering firm, the team shows newly completed features so that users can give acceptance and feedback. Under which topic does this happen?
o: Project highlights
Current risks and issues
Welcome
Product demo
Agile: Techniques.w: In the progress review workshop, the product demo topic shows completed features and gathers user acceptance and feedback (book 13.5.4.1, Table 13.10).

n.0: Project highlights reviews the project dashboard metrics, not a demonstration of the product (book Table 13.10).
n.1: Current risks and issues looks at open risks and issues, not at completed features (book Table 13.10).
n.2: The welcome introduces the facilitators, presenters and stakeholders at the start (book Table 13.10).

Agile: Techniques.q: Which of these should NOT be used to track progress during an iteration?
o: The retrospective
A burn-down chart
The team dashboard
The daily stand-up
Agile: Techniques.w: Retrospectives happen at the end of an iteration, not during it, so they are not a way of tracking progress within the iteration (book 4.2.4, 5.6.3.3).

n.1: A burn-down chart shows outstanding work over the days of an iteration, so it tracks progress within it (book 12.4.3).
n.2: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report, and the project manager pulls progress from it during delivery (book Table 12.1).
n.3: The daily stand-up makes the team's daily progress visible, and the project manager may attend with the team's agreement (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: In a team retrospective workshop, the team lists suggestions for improving the way it tests stories in the next iteration. Under which topic do these suggestions belong?
o: The good
The learning
The bad
Team building
Agile: Techniques.w: The learning topic captures lessons, improvement suggestions and actionable insights for the next iteration (book 13.6.4.2, Table 13.14).

n.0: The good celebrates what went well; it does not hold improvement actions (book Table 13.14).
n.2: The bad identifies issues, risks and challenges and their causes; turning them into improvements belongs to the learning (book Table 13.14).
n.3: Team building, such as a game or shared food, strengthens bonds rather than recording improvements (book Table 13.14).

Agile: Techniques.q:
Which two statements about agile events in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. Detailed task-level planning for the next iteration takes place in the team planning workshop.
2. The retrospective reviews the product with users, while the demo reviews the team's way of working.
3. The release planning workshop is held at stage boundaries and updates the release map.
4. The daily stand-up removes the need for iteration planning.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
Agile: Techniques.w: Task-level planning is done for the next iteration in managing product delivery, through the team planning workshop (book 8.3, 13.6.4.1). The release planning workshop belongs to managing a stage boundary and updates the release map (book 13.7.4.1).

n.0: Statement 2 reverses the two: the demo shows the product to users, and the retrospective looks at the team's way of working (book Table 13.10, Table 13.14).
n.1: Both are wrong: the demo and retrospective are swapped in statement 2, and the stand-up does not replace iteration planning, which is a topic of the team planning workshop (book Table 13.13).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is wrong: iteration planning is still needed and takes place in the team planning workshop (book Table 13.13).

Agile: Techniques.q: A delivery team at a regional water company keeps its requirements in a backlog. How does PRINCE2 Agile define a backlog?
o: A prioritized list of the requirements for a product, which may be epics or user stories
A record of the risks and issues the team has raised during the current iteration
A visual plan that groups user stories into releases of two to four iterations
A one-page summary of the project's vision, value, costs, benefits and major risks
Agile: Techniques.w: In the PRINCE2 Agile glossary a backlog is a prioritized list of requirements for a product, and the items can be epic user stories, user stories or other requirement formats (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, Glossary).

n.1: Risks and issues are recorded in the risk register and issue register; a backlog holds requirements, not risks and issues (book 10.3.2, Glossary).
n.2: Grouping user stories into releases of two to four iterations describes the release map, which is the project and stage plan (book 8.3.2.5).
n.3: A one-page summary of vision, value, costs, benefits and risks is the project canvas, the agile form of the business case (book 6.3.2.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, several management products are tailored into agile artifacts. Which management product does the project backlog replace?
o: The product description for each team's products
The project product description
The project brief
The stage plan for the current stage
Agile: Techniques.w: The project backlog is the PRINCE2 Agile tailoring of the project product description: a high-level backlog, mostly of epics, that shows or links to the project DoR and DoD and names who accepts the project product (book 8.3.2.1).

n.0: Product descriptions at team level are replaced by each team's product backlog, not by the project backlog (book 8.3.2.1).
n.2: The project brief remains a business case product in PRINCE2 Agile, outlining flexible scope and quality areas; it is not replaced by the project backlog (book Table 6.1).
n.3: The stage plan, like the project plan, takes the form of a release map, not the project backlog (book 8.3.2.5).

Agile: Techniques.q: A product owner would traditionally send checkpoint reports to the project manager. In PRINCE2 Agile, which artifact takes the place of the checkpoint report?
o: The project dashboard
The release map
The team dashboard
The product backlog
Agile: Techniques.w: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report. It is updated and reviewed in team planning and retrospective workshops, and the project manager pulls progress information from it (book Table 12.1).

n.0: The project dashboard replaces the highlight report and end stage report, used by the board, not the checkpoint report (book Table 12.1).
n.1: The release map is the agile form of the project and stage plans; it is a plan, not a progress report from the team (book 8.3.2.5).
n.3: The product backlog replaces product descriptions and holds the team's user stories; it does not report progress to the project manager (book 8.3.2.1).

Agile: Techniques.q: PRINCE2 Agile uses timeboxes at more than one level of a project. Which three levels of timebox does it define?
o: Sprint, iteration and release
Iteration, increment and project
Release, stage and project
Iteration, release and stage
Agile: Techniques.w: A timebox is a fixed period of time, and PRINCE2 Agile names three levels of it: the iteration, the release and the stage (book Glossary).

n.0: Sprint is Scrum's name for an iteration, so it is not a separate level; the stage level is missing from this list (book Glossary).
n.1: An increment is a piece of product delivered, not a period of time, and the project is not one of the three timebox levels (book Glossary).
n.2: The project is not one of the named timebox levels, and the iteration, the shortest timebox, is missing (book Glossary).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Lindqvist Logistics adopts an agile framework, renames its meetings with agile terms and trains every team in the new vocabulary. Team leaders still approve every task before work starts. Which explanation fits PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: The organization is being agile, but it has not yet adopted enough agile frameworks, processes and terms
The organization has not yet scaled agile, so the framework should first be extended to more teams
The organization is doing agile, but people are not yet free to apply an agile mindset through self-management
The organization lacks a project canvas, so the value of the change has not been summarized on one page
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Frameworks, processes and terminology are doing agile. Being agile also needs people to be allowed to apply the mindset within appropriate self-management, which task-by-task approval prevents (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3.1).

n.0: The teams have adopted a framework, processes and terminology, which is doing agile; what is missing is the freedom to self-manage, which is being agile (book 2.3.1).
n.1: Scaling extends agile across many teams and products (book 3.2); it does not address leaders approving every task within a team.
n.3: The project canvas is the one-page business justification for a project (book 6.3.2.1); it does not explain the missing freedom to self-manage.

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, what is the likely result when an organization does agile without being agile?
o: Short-term efficiency gains that lack a lasting, sustainable impact
A cultural shift that builds long-term resilience across the organization
Lower efficiency at first, followed by a lasting change in culture
Strong adaptability, as the framework's events require critical thinking
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: In the 'long-term impact versus short-term mechanics' contrast, doing agile alone can bring short-term efficiency gains but not a sustainable impact; being agile creates the cultural shift (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3.1).

n.1: A cultural shift and long-term resilience come from being agile, not from doing agile alone (book 2.3.1).
n.2: This reverses the contrast: doing agile alone tends to give short-term efficiency, not a lasting cultural change (book 2.3.1).
n.3: Doing agile alone may mean following a framework rigidly without knowing why, which limits adaptability (book 2.3.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q:
Which two statements about being agile and doing agile are correct?

1. Being agile includes being allowed to apply an agile mindset within suitable levels of self-management.
2. Doing agile covers the use of agile frameworks, techniques and terminology.
3. Adopting an agile framework is enough to bring faster delivery and higher quality.
4. Being agile concerns short-term mechanics, while doing agile creates long-term cultural change.
o: 1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 2
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Statement 1 is the definition of being agile and statement 2 the definition of doing agile (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3.1). Statement 3 is the misconception the book warns against (book 2.3), and statement 4 reverses the long-term versus short-term contrast.

n.0: Statement 1 is correct, but statement 3 is the classic misconception: a framework does not by itself bring faster delivery or higher quality; the value lies in shifting mindsets and culture (book 2.3).
n.1: Statement 2 is correct, but statement 4 reverses the contrast: being agile brings long-term cultural change and doing agile alone short-term mechanics (book 2.3.1).
n.2: Both are wrong: statement 3 is the framework misconception (book 2.3) and statement 4 reverses the long-term versus short-term contrast (book 2.3.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile warn that adopting an agile framework does not by itself guarantee faster delivery or higher quality?
o: Frameworks give structure, so speed and quality depend mainly on choosing the right framework for the work
The value comes from shifting mindsets and building a culture that empowers teams to self-manage and decide
Faster delivery depends on adding developers to each team rather than on how the work is organized
Quality is protected by project board approvals at each stage rather than by the delivery teams
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: PRINCE2 Agile calls it a misconception that a framework alone brings speed or quality. The value lies in changing mindsets and creating a culture where teams are empowered to self-manage and make decisions (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3).

n.0: This is the misconception the book corrects: the benefit lies in mindset and culture, not in the choice of framework (book 2.3).
n.2: PRINCE2 Agile does not link agility to team size; it links the value of agile to mindset and an empowering culture (book 2.3).
n.3: Board approvals are part of governance; the reason given in the book is that agility depends on mindset and culture, not on the framework (book 2.3).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile describe the agile mindset?
o: Formal processes that guide teams on when to deliver value and how to manage work
Techniques and activities, such as prioritization and workshops, used in frameworks
A way of thinking about work that fosters adaptability and continual learning
Guidelines drawn from the Agile Manifesto that explain why agile behaviour matters
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The agile mindset is a way of thinking and approaching work that fosters adaptability and encourages continual learning, improvement and flexibility (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1).

n.0: This describes the processes layer of the Agile Onion, which gives structure but does not guarantee agility (book 2.6.1).
n.1: This describes the practices layer of the Agile Onion, the most visible part of adoption (book 2.6.1).
n.3: This describes the principles layer of the Agile Onion (book 2.6.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Where does the agile mindset sit in the Agile Onion?
o: At the core, as the innermost layer that drives the others
At the surface, as the layer people notice first in adoption
As the values layer defined by the Agile Manifesto
Between processes and practices, linking structure to technique
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The mindset is the innermost layer of the Agile Onion: the way of thinking that drives values, principles, practices and processes (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1).

n.1: The most visible layer is practices; the mindset is the deepest layer (book 2.6.1).
n.2: Values are a separate layer, defined by the Agile Manifesto; the mindset is the innermost layer beneath them (book 2.6.1).
n.3: Processes and practices are outer layers; the mindset is at the centre (book 2.6.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which concept does PRINCE2 Agile say is often seen as the core of the agile mindset itself?
o: Servant leadership: the leader serves the team and puts members' needs first
Rich communication: sharing emotions, body language and visuals as well as words
Training and coaching: theory supported by practical coaching on the job
Growth mindset: the belief that anyone can learn, adapt to change and grow
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The growth mindset, the belief that any person can learn, adapt to change and grow, is often regarded as the core of the agile mindset (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1, 2.7.3).

n.0: Servant leadership is a leadership style linked to agile maturity, not the belief described as the core of the mindset (book 2.7.3).
n.1: Rich communication helps avoid misunderstandings in short iterations; it is not described as the core of the mindset (book 2.7.3).
n.2: Training and coaching help people apply change; the book names the growth mindset as the core (book 2.7.3).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile place the agile mindset at the core of agility?
o: It is the part of agile that stakeholders can see most easily while adoption is under way
It is the way of thinking that shapes how people use values, principles, practices and processes
It replaces processes, so teams no longer need structure for planning and delivery
It is the set of four values that the Agile Manifesto defines for agile teams
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The mindset is the innermost layer: the way of thinking from which the other layers follow. Without it, processes and practices give the appearance of agility without its substance (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1).

n.0: The most visible part of adoption is the practices layer, not the mindset (book 2.6.1).
n.2: Processes still give structure; the mindset does not replace them but gives them meaning (book 2.6.1).
n.3: The four Manifesto values form the values layer, which is separate from the mindset (book 2.6.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Teams at Kestrel Freight follow every event of a new agile framework, yet they resist changing plans when user feedback arrives. Which explanation fits PRINCE2 Agile guidance on the agile mindset?
o: The teams lack the formal processes that tell them when to deliver value to their users
The teams need more framework events, since adaptability grows with each review
The teams have adopted visible practices without a mindset of adaptability and learning
The teams have no approved agile transformation plan from the project board
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Practices are the most visible layer and teams that stop there can look agile without the mindset that fosters adaptability and continual learning (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1).

n.0: The teams already follow the framework's events and processes; the gap is the mindset, as processes alone do not guarantee agility (book 2.6.1).
n.1: Adding events adds practices; adaptability comes from the mindset, the innermost layer (book 2.6.1).
n.3: An agile transformation plan guides enterprise adoption (book 2.7.1); it does not explain why teams resist adapting to feedback.

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which statement reflects the agile mindset described in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Agile is less about strict adherence to a framework and more about collaboration and adaptability
Agile is mainly about choosing one framework and applying its rules consistently in every team
Agile is about finding the one perfect solution through detailed analysis before work starts
Agile is mainly about reducing documentation so that teams can spend more time building
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: PRINCE2 Agile describes agile as less about rigid adherence to a framework and more about collaboration, creativity and adaptability (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3).

n.1: The book stresses that agile is less about rigid adherence to a framework (book 2.3).
n.2: Complexity creates ambiguity, so there is rarely one perfect solution; staying adaptable is preferred (book 2.4).
n.3: Reduced paperwork is not what the book identifies as the heart of agile; it emphasizes collaboration, creativity and adaptability (book 2.3).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q:
Which two statements about the agile mindset are correct?

1. It fosters adaptability and encourages continual learning.
2. It is the most visible layer of the Agile Onion.
3. A growth mindset is often seen as its core.
4. It is made up of the four values of the Agile Manifesto.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The mindset fosters adaptability and continual learning, improvement and flexibility (statement 1), and the growth mindset is often seen as its core (statement 3) (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1, 2.7.3).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: practices are the most visible layer; the mindset is the innermost (book 2.6.1).
n.2: Both are wrong: practices are the most visible layer, and the Manifesto values form their own layer, separate from the mindset (book 2.6.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is wrong: the four Manifesto values are the values layer, not the mindset (book 2.6.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: In a complex environment, why does PRINCE2 Agile favour an agile mindset over searching for a perfect solution?
o: Complex work needs a fixed, detailed plan agreed before delivery so that change can be avoided
Complexity removes the need for governance, so teams can make every decision themselves
Perfect solutions can be found by doing more detailed upfront analysis in each stage
Complexity brings ambiguity, so staying adaptable and able to pivot is worth more than perfection
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Because complexity creates ambiguity, there is rarely one perfect answer; it is better to stay adaptable and able to pivot quickly than to chase perfection (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.4).

n.0: A fixed plan that avoids change is the opposite of the agile response to complexity (book 2.4).
n.1: PRINCE2 Agile keeps governance and control; self-management works within agreed tolerances (book 3.1).
n.2: The book says there is rarely one perfect solution in complex work, so more upfront analysis does not find one (book 2.4).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which list names the five layers of the Agile Onion used in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Processes, practices, principles, roles and mindset
Practices, principles, values, behaviours and culture
Processes, practices, products, values and mindset
Processes, practices, principles, values and mindset
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The Agile Onion has five layers: processes, practices, principles, values and mindset (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1).

n.0: Roles are not an Agile Onion layer; the fourth layer is values, defined by the Agile Manifesto (book 2.6.1).
n.1: Behaviours and culture are not layers; the onion includes processes and has mindset at its core (book 2.6.1).
n.2: Products are a PRINCE2 focus, not an onion layer; the third layer is principles (book 2.6.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which layer of the Agile Onion does PRINCE2 Agile describe as the most visible aspect of agile adoption?
o: Values, such as those set out in the Agile Manifesto
Practices, such as prioritization techniques and workshops
Principles, such as welcoming late changes to requirements
Mindset, such as believing that anyone can learn and grow
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Practices, the specific techniques (for example prioritization) and activities (for example events and workshops), are the most visible aspects of agile adoption (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1).

n.0: Values are the foundation that encompasses everything else, not the most visible layer (book 2.6.1).
n.2: Principles explain the why behind agile behaviour; they are less visible than practices (book 2.6.1).
n.3: The mindset is the innermost layer, the least visible, not the most visible (book 2.6.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which Agile Onion layer is defined by the Agile Manifesto and described as the foundation that encompasses all else?
o: Values
Practices
Processes
Mindset
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Values are defined by the Agile Manifesto and form the foundation of agile, shifting focus from rigid processes to people, collaboration and user value (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1).

n.1: Practices are techniques and activities, the most visible layer, not the foundation (book 2.6.1).
n.2: Processes give structure to agile implementations but do not guarantee agility (book 2.6.1).
n.3: The mindset is the innermost way of thinking; the layer defined by the Manifesto as the foundation is values (book 2.6.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

In the Agile Onion, the [?] is derived from the Agile Manifesto and helps teams understand the 'why' behind agile behaviour.
o: practices layer
processes layer
principles layer
mindset layer
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Principles are core guidelines derived from the Agile Manifesto, such as welcoming changing requirements; teams that internalize them understand why agile works (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1).

n.0: Practices are techniques and activities such as prioritization and workshops; they are the 'what', not the 'why' (book 2.6.1).
n.1: Processes give structure, such as when to deliver value, but they do not explain the why (book 2.6.1).
n.3: The mindset is the innermost way of thinking; the layer derived from the Manifesto's guidelines that explains the why is principles (book 2.6.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: A team at Brightwell Insurance holds daily stand-ups and retrospectives and uses MoSCoW prioritization, yet its managers say it looks agile but does not respond well to change. Which Agile Onion layer has the team adopted without going deeper?
o: Practices
Principles
Values
Mindset
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Events such as stand-ups and techniques such as prioritization are practices, the most visible layer. Teams that stop there can look agile but lack the depth needed for long-term success (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1).

n.1: Principles explain the why; a team that had internalized them would understand why responding to change matters (book 2.6.1).
n.2: Values shift the focus to people, collaboration and user value; they are part of what the team is missing (book 2.6.1).
n.3: The mindset of adaptability is exactly what is missing; it is the deepest layer (book 2.6.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: What does PRINCE2 Agile say about the processes layer of the Agile Onion?
o: Processes are the core of agility, so changing them is the surest way to create lasting change
Processes are defined by the Agile Manifesto values and form the foundation of all other layers
Processes are the specific techniques and events that teams use, such as prioritization
Processes give structure, such as when to deliver value, but do not guarantee agility by themselves
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The formal processes of agile frameworks give structure, guiding when to deliver value and how to manage work, but must be supported by principles and values to allow change and innovation (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1).

n.0: The core of the onion is the mindset; processes alone do not guarantee agility (book 2.6.1).
n.1: The layer defined by the Manifesto that encompasses all else is values (book 2.6.1).
n.2: Techniques and events such as prioritization and workshops are practices (book 2.6.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile caution teams against stopping at the practices layer of the Agile Onion?
o: Practices are the least visible layer, so stakeholders cannot see how the team is progressing
Practices come from Scrum and are not permitted in a PRINCE2 Agile project without approval
They may look agile but lack the deeper principles, values and mindset needed for long-term success
Practices must be approved by the project board before each stage, which slows adoption
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Practices only scratch the surface. Teams that adopt them without the deeper layers can appear agile without the mindset needed for lasting success (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1).

n.0: Practices are the most visible layer, not the least (book 2.6.1).
n.1: Practices such as prioritization and workshops are used throughout PRINCE2 Agile; the concern is depth, not permission (book 2.6.1).
n.3: The book's concern is that teams stopping at practices lack depth, not board approval (book 2.6.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: How do the values in the Agile Onion change a team's focus?
o: From user value towards detailed documentation and fixed plans
From rigid processes towards people, collaboration and user value
From team self-management towards central control of decisions
From short iterations towards a single long delivery phase
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Values, defined by the Agile Manifesto, shift attention from rigid processes to people, collaboration and user value (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1).

n.0: This reverses the shift; values move focus away from rigid processes towards people and user value (book 2.6.1).
n.2: The agile mindset favours empowerment and self-management, not central control (book 2.6.1, 2.6.2).
n.3: A single long delivery phase describes waterfall, which the values do not promote (book 2.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which key characteristic of the agile mindset is about fostering autonomy and self-management within teams?
o: Respect
Adaptability
Empowerment
Transparency and rich communication
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Empowerment fosters autonomy and self-management within teams (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.2).

n.0: Respect is rooted in empathy and open-mindedness, not autonomy (book 2.6.2).
n.1: Adaptability concerns inspection and adaptation in response to change (book 2.6.2).
n.3: Transparency concerns open, rich information flow, not freedom to decide (book 2.6.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which key characteristic of the agile mindset is rooted in empathy and open-mindedness?
o: Collaboration
Empowerment
Adaptability
Respect
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Respect is rooted in empathy and open-mindedness, so that all voices are valued and diverse perspectives are welcomed (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.2).

n.0: Collaboration is about working closely together with shared ownership and co-creation (book 2.6.2).
n.1: Empowerment fosters autonomy and self-management (book 2.6.2).
n.2: Adaptability is about inspection and adaptation in response to change (book 2.6.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which key characteristic of the agile mindset refers to inspecting and adapting in response to change?
o: Transparency and rich communication
Adaptability
Empowerment
Collaboration
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Adaptability reflects the agile values of inspection and adaptation in response to change (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.2).

n.0: Transparency is about open information flow and visible work status, not adapting to change (book 2.6.2).
n.2: Empowerment is about autonomy and self-management (book 2.6.2).
n.3: Collaboration is about shared ownership and co-creating solutions (book 2.6.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which key characteristic of the agile mindset involves working closely with team members, stakeholders and users, with shared ownership and co-creation of solutions?
o: Collaboration
Respect
Empowerment
Transparency and rich communication
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Collaboration means working closely with the team, stakeholders and users in a culture of shared ownership, mutual support and co-created solutions (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.2).

n.1: Respect is rooted in empathy and open-mindedness, valuing all voices (book 2.6.2).
n.2: Empowerment fosters autonomy and self-management (book 2.6.2).
n.3: Transparency concerns open, rich information flow rather than co-creation (book 2.6.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: At Fernlea Housing, the delivery team keeps its work status visible on a shared board, raises obstacles openly at regular meetings and explains ideas with sketches as well as written notes. Which key characteristic of the agile mindset is the team showing?
o: Empowerment of a self-managing team
Respect for every team member's view
Adaptability through inspection
Transparency and rich communication
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Transparency and rich communication mean information flows openly and is richer than text alone; regular meetings, open documentation and visible work status build trust and alignment (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.2).

n.0: Empowerment is about autonomy and self-management; the behaviours described are about open, rich information flow (book 2.6.2).
n.1: Respect is about empathy and open-mindedness towards others' views (book 2.6.2).
n.2: Adaptability is about inspecting and adapting to change, not about how openly information is shared (book 2.6.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: In a workshop at Corvan Engineering, the team coach makes sure quieter members and new joiners are heard, and that differing views are explored rather than dismissed. Which key characteristic of the agile mindset does this BEST show?
o: Empowerment
Respect
Adaptability
Transparency and rich communication
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Respect is rooted in empathy and open-mindedness: every voice is valued and diverse perspectives are embraced (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.2).

n.0: Empowerment is about autonomy and self-management in decisions, not about valuing every voice (book 2.6.2).
n.2: Adaptability is about responding to change through inspection and adaptation (book 2.6.2).
n.3: Transparency is about open information flow and visible work; hearing and valuing differing views is respect (book 2.6.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: A release review at Ashdown Libraries shows that users struggle with a new search feature, so the team reworks its plan for the next iteration. Which key characteristic of the agile mindset does this show?
o: Adaptability
Empowerment
Respect
Self-organization
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Inspecting what happened and adapting the plan in response is adaptability (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.2).

n.1: Empowerment is about the team's autonomy to decide; the behaviour here is inspecting results and adapting the plan (book 2.6.2).
n.2: Respect is about empathy and open-mindedness towards people (book 2.6.2).
n.3: Self-organization was a Version 1 behaviour; V2 lists key mindset characteristics and uses self-management (under empowerment) (book 2.6.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q:
Which two statements about the key characteristics of the agile mindset are correct?

1. Empowerment fosters autonomy and self-management within teams.
2. Respect refers to inspection and adaptation in response to change.
3. Collaboration builds shared ownership and co-creation of solutions.
4. Adaptability is rooted in empathy and open-mindedness.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Empowerment fosters autonomy and self-management (1) and collaboration builds shared ownership and co-created solutions (3) (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.2). Statements 2 and 4 swap the meanings of respect and adaptability.

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: inspection and adaptation describe adaptability, not respect (book 2.6.2).
n.1: Both are wrong: statements 2 and 4 swap respect (empathy, open-mindedness) and adaptability (inspection and adaptation) (book 2.6.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: empathy and open-mindedness are the roots of respect, not adaptability (book 2.6.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: What is an agile transformation plan in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: A plan guiding the adoption of more agility, with strategic goals and short-term objectives
A plan that clusters user stories into releases, each usually made up of two to four iterations
A plan for one delivery team's work in its next iteration, drawn from that team's product backlog
A plan for handing the project's products over to operations at the end of the final stage
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The agile transformation plan guides an initiative to adopt (more) agility. It sets high-level goals that align target states to the organization's strategy, plus short-term objectives for practical implementation (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.1).

n.1: Clustering user stories into releases of two to four iterations describes the release map (book 8.3.2.5).
n.2: A plan for one team's iteration is a team plan built from its product backlog, not a transformation plan (book 8.3.2).
n.3: Handover planning is part of transition to operations and the project closure workshop (book 13.8.4).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: What does an agile transformation plan typically span?
o: A single iteration of one delivery team within a management stage
One management stage, after which the stage plan replaces it
Several projects or initiatives working towards enterprise-wide agility
The initiation stage of a single project, ending when the PID is approved
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: An agile transformation plan typically covers several projects or initiatives, as it aims at enterprise-wide adoption of agility (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.1).

n.0: An iteration is a short timebox for one team; a transformation plan covers organization-wide adoption (book 2.7.1).
n.1: A transformation plan is not tied to one stage; it typically spans several projects or initiatives (book 2.7.1).
n.3: The plan is broader than one project's initiation; for a single pilot it may not even be needed (book 2.7.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.

In the project initiation workshop, the agile transformation plan can, if needed, replace the [?].
o: communication management approach
change management approach
quality management approach
benefits management approach
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Among the management approaches co-created in the project initiation workshop, the change management approach can be replaced by the agile transformation plan if needed (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.7).

n.0: The communication management approach is still agreed in initiation; the transformation plan can replace the change management approach (Table 13.7).
n.2: The quality management approach covers quality methods and responsibilities; it is not the approach the transformation plan can replace (Table 13.7).
n.3: The benefits management approach covers how benefits are measured and reviewed; the plan can replace the change management approach (Table 13.7).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Morrow Foods is running one pilot project to try agile ways of working before any wider roll-out. According to PRINCE2 Agile, what may be done instead of creating an agile transformation plan at this point?
o: Add the transformation goals to the project canvas
Record the planned changes in the risk register
List the transformation steps in the team skill matrix
Update the project's change management approach
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: For a single pilot project an agile transformation plan may not be needed yet; the change management approach can be updated instead (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.1).

n.0: The project canvas summarizes the project's business justification, not how the organization changes its ways of working (book 6.3.2.1).
n.1: The risk register records risks; it does not set out how the organization moves to a new target state (book 10.3.2).
n.2: A team skill matrix maps skills and gaps in a team; it is not a substitute for planning the change (book 7.4.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which two kinds of content does an agile transformation plan combine?
o: Release dates for each product increment, plus a burn-up chart of finished work
Risks to agile adoption, plus the probability and impact of each one
Skills of each team member, plus the training needed to close any gaps
High-level goals aligned to strategy, plus short-term objectives for implementation
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The plan aligns new target states with the organization's mission and vision through high-level goals and adds short-term objectives for practical implementation (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.1).

n.0: Release dates and burn charts belong to the release map and progress reporting (book 8.3.2.5, 12.4.3).
n.1: Assessing agile adoption risks is done with the Agilometer and in the agile enablement workshop (Table 13.5).
n.2: Mapping skills and gaps is the team skill matrix; training and coaching plans support maturity (book 7.4.1, 2.7.3).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: A pilot project at Hollins Water produces an agile transformation plan for the wider organization. How should the plan be described in terms of the business case?
o: As a benefit, because it is a measurable improvement in agility
As an output, because it is a deliverable the project produces
As an outcome, because it is the change in ways of working
As a tolerance, because it limits how far teams may change
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: An agile transformation plan created by a project is a deliverable, so it is an output (part of scope), not a benefit (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Glossary; official V2 sample rationale).

n.0: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome; a plan the project produces is an output, never a benefit (book Glossary).
n.2: An outcome is the result of the change once outputs are used; the plan itself is a deliverable, an output (book Glossary).
n.3: Tolerances are permitted deviations set on performance targets such as time and cost under manage by exception; a plan the project produces is an output (book 5.2.1.5, Glossary).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile link an agile transformation to organizational change management (OCM)?
o: It replaces OCM, because agile teams adapt as they go and do not need a defined target state
It changes the delivery teams' tools and techniques but leaves the organization's culture as it is
It moves the organization from its current state, via interim states, to an agile target state
It is finished in starting up a project, before any initiation or delivery work begins
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: OCM moves an organization from its current state to a target state. The change management approach can define the target state for introducing the agile mindset and values and how the business moves through interim states (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).

n.0: PRINCE2 Agile uses OCM and the change management approach to define the target state; adaptability does not remove the need for it (book 4.2.1).
n.1: Culture is central: changes stick when the culture evolves, so a transformation is not limited to tools (book 4.2.1, 4.2.3).
n.3: A transformation spans several projects or initiatives; it is not completed within one process (book 2.7.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: When the change management approach is used to guide an agile transformation, what does PRINCE2 Agile say it should consider so that the change lasts?
o: The evolving culture and how to stop changes being rolled back afterwards
Financial rewards for the teams that adopt the new agile framework the fastest
Strict compliance checks on any team that departs from the new agile processes
A single announcement explaining the change to all of the affected staff
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: In deciding the detail of the change management approach, PRINCE2 Agile asks for consideration of the evolving culture and of how to ensure changes are not reversed once the transformation ends (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).

n.1: Rewards are not what the book names; it asks for the evolving culture to be considered (book 4.2.1).
n.2: Compliance checks do not make change stick; the book points to culture and preventing roll-back (book 4.2.1).
n.3: One-off communication is not enough; people need training, coaching and a culture that sustains the change (book 2.7.3, 4.2.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which leadership style, credited to Robert Greenleaf, does PRINCE2 Agile describe under agile maturity?
o: Transformational leadership
Servant leadership
Directive leadership
Situational leadership
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Servant leadership, credited to Robert Greenleaf, holds that the best way to lead a team is to serve it, putting team members' needs above the leader's own (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.3).

n.0: Transformational leadership is not the Greenleaf style the book names; it describes servant leadership (book 2.7.3).
n.2: A directive style conflicts with self-management; Greenleaf's style is servant leadership (book 2.7.3).
n.3: Situational leadership is a different model; the book credits servant leadership to Greenleaf (book 2.7.3).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, what is meant by a growth mindset?
o: A leader serving the team and putting members' needs first
Sharing emotions, body language and visuals as well as words
Combining theoretical training with practical coaching on the job
The belief that any person can learn, adapt to change and grow
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The growth mindset is the fundamental belief that anyone can learn, adapt to change and grow; it is often seen as the core of the agile mindset (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.6.1, 2.7.3).

n.0: This is servant leadership, credited to Robert Greenleaf (book 2.7.3).
n.1: This is rich communication, which reduces misunderstandings in short iterations (book 2.7.3).
n.2: This is training and coaching, which helps people apply the changes (book 2.7.3).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: What does PRINCE2 Agile mean by rich communication?
o: Sharing emotions, body language and visuals as well as words
The belief that any person can learn, adapt to change and grow
A leader serving the team and putting members' needs first
Combining theoretical training with practical coaching on the job
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Rich communication conveys not just words but emotions, body language, visuals and graphics, to reduce misunderstandings in short agile iterations (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.3).

n.1: This is the growth mindset, often seen as the core of the agile mindset (book 2.7.3).
n.2: This is servant leadership, credited to Robert Greenleaf (book 2.7.3).
n.3: This is training and coaching, which helps people apply the changes (book 2.7.3).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile recommend combining theoretical training with practical coaching on the job?
o: Coaching on the job removes the need for formal training courses during an agile change
Training must be completed before a person may join a delivery team in PRINCE2 Agile
People must understand how to apply the change, not just be told, which reduces frustration
Coaching lets the project manager direct each team member's daily tasks more closely
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: People must understand how to apply proposed changes through theoretical training and practical coaching on the job. This combats frustration, a leading cause of demotivation and resistance to change (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.3).

n.0: The book asks for both theoretical training and practical coaching, not coaching in place of training (book 2.7.3).
n.1: PRINCE2 Agile does not set training as an entry condition for teams; it uses training and coaching to build understanding (book 2.7.3).
n.3: Directing daily tasks conflicts with self-management; coaching helps people apply the change (book 2.7.3, 2.6.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: What does PRINCE2 Agile suggest including to support training and coaching during an agile change?
o: A one-off training event at the start, after which teams learn independently
A training and coaching plan mapped to the needs of each stage of the change
A delegation matrix showing who may approve each request for training
A communication plan that informs people of the new ways of working by email
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: PRINCE2 Agile suggests a training and coaching plan, ideally mapped to the different needs at each stage of the agile change initiative (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.3).

n.0: Leaving people to fend for themselves after informing them undermines the change; the book suggests a plan across the stages (book 2.7.3).
n.2: A delegation matrix makes decision authority transparent; it is not the plan the book suggests for training (book 7.4.3).
n.3: Being informed is not enough; people need training and practical coaching (book 2.7.3).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q:
Which two statements about agile maturity in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. Agile maturity assessments are first carried out in starting up a project or initiating a project.
2. Agile maturity is assessed once, at project closure, for the lessons report.
3. The agile enablement workshop uses regular Agilometer assessments so that agile maturity and agile risks are reviewed regularly.
4. Agile maturity is a delivery measure calculated from each team's velocity.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Agile maturity assessments are first made in starting up or initiating a project (statement 1, PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.4.1), and the agile enablement workshop reassesses agile maturity and agile risks regularly through the Agilometer (statement 3, Table 13.5).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: maturity is first assessed in starting up or initiating and reassessed regularly, not once at closure (book 12.4.1, Table 13.5).
n.1: Both are wrong: maturity is assessed early and regularly, not once at closure, and it is a key metric for agility, not a velocity calculation (book 12.4.1, 2.7.6).
n.2: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is wrong: agile maturity is one of the key metrics for agility, not derived from velocity (book 2.7.6).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Early in an agile transformation at Pennant Bank, staff are emailed a guide to the new ways of working and then left to apply it themselves. According to PRINCE2 Agile, what is the most likely result?
o: Frustration, leading to demotivation and resistance to the change
Rapid adoption, as written guidance gives everyone the same understanding
Higher psychological safety, as people can learn at their own pace
Stronger agile sustainability, as no reliance on coaches is created
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: PRINCE2 Agile warns that informing people and leaving them to cope undermines change; without training and on-the-job coaching, frustration grows, a leading cause of demotivation and resistance (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.3).

n.1: Being informed is not the same as understanding how to apply the change; the book warns this causes frustration (book 2.7.3).
n.2: Leaving people unsupported does not build psychological safety; it breeds frustration (book 2.7.3, 2.7.4).
n.3: Without training and coaching the change is resisted, which works against agility lasting (book 2.7.3).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which statement about servant leadership is correct in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: The leader assigns each task and checks it daily so that the team stays within tolerance
The leader is the product owner, who serves users by owning the project backlog
The leader serves the team, making sure members are supported and have what they need
The leader steps back and leaves all team support to the agile coach
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Servant leadership holds that the best way to lead a team is to serve it: the leader puts members' needs first and makes sure everyone is supported and has what they need (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.3).

n.0: Close daily direction is a command-and-control style; servant leadership supports a self-managing team (book 2.7.3).
n.1: Servant leadership is a style, not a role; and the project backlog is owned by the chief product owner (book 2.7.3, 7.3).
n.3: A servant leader actively supports the team; the agile coach works across the organization on systemic blockers (book 2.7.3, Table 7.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: What does psychological safety mean in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: People are assured that they will keep their project roles until the project closes
Project data is protected under the digital and data management approach
The team's physical workplace has passed a health and safety assessment
People feel able to speak up, take risks and question ideas without fear of blame
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Psychological safety means people feel safe to express themselves, take risks and challenge ideas without fearing judgment or negative consequences (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.4).

n.0: Job or role security is not what the book means; psychological safety is about speaking up and taking risks without fear (book 2.7.4).
n.1: Data protection is covered by the digital and data management approach, not psychological safety (book 2.7.4).
n.2: Physical safety is a separate matter; psychological safety concerns how safe people feel to express themselves (book 2.7.4).
