Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which three success factors of agile transformations does the PRINCE2 Agile Foundation syllabus name?
o: Agile maturity, team velocity and agile sustainability
Psychological safety, the Agilometer and agile scaling
Agile maturity, psychological safety and agile sustainability
Agile sustainability, servant leadership and the project canvas
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The syllabus lists agile maturity (2.7.3), psychological safety (2.7.4) and agile sustainability (2.7.5) as success factors of agile transformations (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.3 to 2.7.5).

n.0: Velocity is a team delivery measure, not a transformation success factor; the second factor is psychological safety (book 2.7.3 to 2.7.5).
n.1: The Agilometer is a risk tool and scaling is a separate concept; the factors are maturity, safety and sustainability (book 2.7.3 to 2.7.5, 10.3.2).
n.3: Servant leadership is a concept under agile maturity and the project canvas is a business case artifact (book 2.7.3, 6.3.2.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile describe psychological safety as essential in an agile organization?
o: It lets the project board remove tolerances, since teams will report every problem
Rapid feedback, collaboration and continual learning rely on people being willing to speak up
It means fewer defects reach the product, so testing can be reduced in each iteration
It is a contract term in the commercial management approach for agile suppliers
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Where rapid feedback, collaboration and continual learning are key, people need to feel safe to express themselves, take risks and challenge ideas; this makes psychological safety essential for a productive, innovative agile environment (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.4).

n.0: Tolerances remain part of governance under manage by exception in PRINCE2 Agile; psychological safety does not replace them (book 5.2.1.5).
n.2: Testing and quality checks stay part of every iteration; the book links safety to feedback and learning (book 2.7.4, 9.3.2).
n.3: The commercial management approach covers procurement and contracts, not psychological safety (book Table 7.3).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which type of psychological safety is present when a team member feels accepted and valued as part of the team?
o: Inclusion safety
Contributor safety
Learner safety
Challenger safety
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Inclusion safety is feeling accepted and valued as part of the team and able to be yourself (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.4).

n.1: Contributor safety is about being encouraged to share ideas and skills, with contributions respected (book 2.7.4).
n.2: In Timothy Clark's model, learner safety is about feeling safe to learn and ask questions, not about belonging.
n.3: In Timothy Clark's model, challenger safety is about feeling safe to question the status quo, not about belonging.

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which type of psychological safety is present when people are encouraged to share their ideas and skills and their contributions are respected?
o: Inclusion safety
Challenger safety
Contributor safety
Learner safety
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Contributor safety is being encouraged to share ideas and skills, knowing contributions will be respected (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.4).

n.0: Inclusion safety is about feeling accepted and valued as part of the team (book 2.7.4).
n.1: In Timothy Clark's model, challenger safety is about feeling safe to question the way things are done.
n.3: In Timothy Clark's model, learner safety is about feeling safe to learn, ask questions and make mistakes.

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: In which PRINCE2 Agile workshop is a psychological safety assessment one of the agenda topics?
o: Team planning workshop
Release planning workshop
Project canvas workshop
Project kickoff workshop
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The project kickoff workshop includes a psychological safety assessment alongside team introductions, team values and norms, the skill matrix and dashboards (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 13.4.4.2, Table 13.8).

n.0: The team planning workshop covers backlog refinement, user story refinement, estimation and iteration planning (Table 13.13).
n.1: The release planning workshop covers OKR definition and release planning at a stage boundary (13.7.4.1, Table 13.16).
n.2: The project canvas workshop builds the one-page business justification in starting up (13.2.4.1, Table 13.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: A team coach at Orla Health notices that developers have stopped raising concerns in retrospectives since a manager publicly criticized a mistake. Which success factor of agile transformation is MOST at risk?
o: Psychological safety
Agile scaling
Agile sustainability
Rich communication
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: People holding back concerns for fear of criticism shows a loss of psychological safety: feeling safe to speak up, take risks and challenge ideas without fear of negative consequences (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.4).

n.1: Scaling concerns many teams and products; the problem here is people no longer feeling safe to speak up (book 3.2, 2.7.4).
n.2: Agile sustainability is a different success factor; silence after public criticism points directly to psychological safety (book 2.7.4, 2.7.5).
n.3: Rich communication is a concept under agile maturity about richer information, not the safety to speak up (book 2.7.3).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: In the project closure workshop, which agenda topic can draw on trends from psychological safety assessments?
o: Final handover planning
Lessons report
Final product demo
Progress review
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The lessons report topic of the project closure workshop defines actionable lessons and can include insights and trends from the Agilometer and psychological safety assessments (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.19).

n.0: Final handover planning covers support responsibilities, operational requirements and benefits actions (Table 13.19).
n.2: The final product demo confirms user acceptance and readiness for handover (Table 13.19).
n.3: The progress review topic updates the PID, logs, project dashboard and Agilometer (Table 13.19).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which statement about agile sustainability in PRINCE2 Agile is correct?
o: It is a success factor of agile transformation and a key metric for agility
It is the performance target covering the project's impact on the wider environment
It is the Agilometer slider that measures how easily the teams communicate
It is the rate at which a team completes user stories in each iteration
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Agile sustainability is one of the three success factors of agile transformations and one of the key metrics for agility, with agile maturity and psychological safety (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.5, 2.7.6).

n.1: Impact on the wider environment is the sustainability performance target, a different concept (book 1.3.2, Table 3.1).
n.2: 'Ease of communication' is an Agilometer slider in the risk practice, not agile sustainability (book 10.3.2).
n.3: The rate of completing work is velocity, a planning measure, not agile sustainability (book 8.3).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: How is agile sustainability assessed in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: Through the sustainability management approach, reviewed at each stage boundary
Through burn-up charts showing the work completed across releases and stages
Through the cumulative flow diagram, which shows bottlenecks in the workflow
Through agile maturity assessments, first made in starting up or initiating a project
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Agile maturity assessments, first carried out in starting up or initiating a project, are based on the key metrics for agility: psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.4.1, 2.7.6).

n.0: The sustainability management approach deals with the sustainability performance target; agile sustainability is assessed through agile maturity assessments (book 12.4.1).
n.1: Burn charts show delivery progress; they do not assess agile sustainability (book 12.4.3).
n.2: A cumulative flow diagram tracks work in each workflow state; it is not an agility metric assessment (book 12.4.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: A board member at Thornbury Council says that 'agile sustainability' refers to the carbon impact of the project's products. Why is this incorrect?
o: Carbon impact is covered by agile maturity, which includes environmental criteria for each team
Agile sustainability refers to keeping the project within the cost tolerance set by the board
That is the sustainability performance target; agile sustainability is a transformation success factor
Agile sustainability is the benefits target, which is fixed at the minimum viable level
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The project's impact on the wider environment is the sustainability performance target (fixed at minimum criteria, flexed above). Agile sustainability is a success factor of agile transformations and a key metric for agility (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.2, Table 3.1, 2.7.5).

n.0: Agile maturity is a separate success factor about agile capability; carbon impact belongs to the sustainability performance target (book 2.7.3, 1.3.2).
n.1: Cost tolerance is about the cost performance target; agile sustainability is a transformation success factor (book 2.7.5, Table 3.1).
n.3: Benefits fixed at minimum viability is the fix and flex default for benefits, a different concept (book Table 3.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: One of the principles behind the Agile Manifesto concerns sustainable development. What does it say sponsors, developers and users should be able to do?
o: Increase their pace in every iteration
Maintain a constant pace indefinitely
Work extra hours before each release
Match the pace of the fastest team
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The Agile Manifesto principles state that agile processes promote sustainable development, with sponsors, developers and users able to keep a constant pace indefinitely (agilemanifesto.org/principles). This supports agility that lasts rather than short bursts.

n.0: The principle asks for a pace that can be kept up, not one that keeps rising (agilemanifesto.org/principles).
n.2: Bursts of overtime before releases are the opposite of a sustainable, constant pace (agilemanifesto.org/principles).
n.3: Each team works at a pace it can sustain; matching another team's pace is not the principle (agilemanifesto.org/principles).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: What does scaling up agile mean in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Raising one team's velocity so that it can deliver more user stories in each iteration
Adopting agile values and principles beyond small teams for multi-team, multi-product work
Giving each team its own separate governance so that teams can act independently
Focusing every team on short-term goals so that releases can be delivered sooner
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Scaling up agile means adopting agile values and principles beyond small teams to support larger multi-team and multi-product environments (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 3.2).

n.0: Scaling is about many teams and products, not one team's output (book 3.2).
n.2: Scaling keeps sufficient governance and control; governance is not re-created for each team (book 3.2).
n.3: Short-term goals are not the focus; scaling aligns teams to shared goals (book 3.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: In a PRINCE2 Agile project with several delivery teams, which role sets priorities across the teams?
o: Chief product owner
Product owner of each team
Team coach of each team
Agile coach for the organization
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: The chief product owner represents the user community, owns the project backlog and sets priorities across teams, such as consistent branding for every team's output (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2, 7.3).

n.1: A product owner owns one team's product backlog and does not prioritize across teams (book Table 7.2).
n.2: A team coach works with one or two teams on self-management and workshops, not cross-team priorities (book Table 7.2).
n.3: The agile coach works across the organization on systemic blockers to adoption, not on product priorities (book Table 7.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: A project at Calder Rail has four delivery teams. Which arrangement fits PRINCE2 Agile guidance on scaling?
o: A project manager for each team, each reporting to a separate project board
One product owner across all the teams, with a chief product owner inside each team
One team coach for all four teams, taking over the work of the product owners
One project manager, a chief product owner across the teams and a product owner per team
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: With multiple teams there is one project manager, possibly several product owners (one per team) and one chief product owner prioritizing across the teams (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 7.3.1, Figure 7.2).

n.0: Scaling keeps one project manager and one set of governance; it does not create a project and board per team (book 3.2, 7.3.1).
n.1: This reverses the roles: the chief product owner works across teams and each team has its own product owner (book 7.3.1).
n.2: A team coach works with one or two teams and does not replace product owners (book Table 7.2).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q:
Which two statements about scaling agile in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. It aligns multiple teams towards shared goals and streamlined processes.
2. Each team re-creates its own governance and control.
3. It keeps sufficient governance and control while gaining agile flexibility.
4. Team composition changes completely when more teams are added.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Scaling aligns many teams to shared goals and streamlined processes (statement 1) while keeping sufficient governance and control (statement 3) (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 3.2). Team composition stays as in a single-team project (book 7.3.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: governance is maintained across teams, not re-created for each team (book 3.2).
n.1: Both are wrong: governance is not re-created per team, and team composition stays the same as in a single-team project (book 3.2, 7.3.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is wrong: team composition is the same as in a single-team project (book 7.3.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, what does 'being agile' mean?
o: Applying agile frameworks, following agile processes and techniques, and adopting agile terminology in the team
Thinking in an agile way and being allowed to apply that mindset to work within suitable levels of self-management
Holding recognized agile certifications and using the vocabulary of a chosen framework in daily team work
Following the events and artifacts of one agile framework closely so that every team works in the same way
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Being agile combines an agile way of thinking with permission to apply it to your work within appropriate self-management. Thinking alone is not enough if people are not allowed to act on it (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3.1).

n.0: This is the definition of 'doing agile': the practical application of frameworks, processes, techniques and terminology (book 2.3.1).
n.2: Certifications and framework vocabulary sit on the 'doing' side (terminology); being agile is a way of thinking plus the freedom to apply it (book 2.3.1).
n.3: Following a framework closely is doing agile, and following it rigidly without knowing why is the 'routine' side of the contrast (book 2.3.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: Which description matches 'doing agile' in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: A way of thinking that people are free to apply within agreed levels of self-management
A cultural shift in the organization that builds long-term resilience and adaptability
The belief that any person can learn, adapt to change and grow over time
The practical application of agile frameworks, processes, techniques and terminology
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Doing agile is the hands-on use of agile frameworks, processes and techniques and the adoption of agile terminology (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3.1).

n.0: Thinking in an agile way with freedom to apply it is 'being agile', not doing agile (book 2.3.1).
n.1: Cultural shift and long-term resilience are what being agile brings; doing agile alone gives short-term gains (book 2.3.1).
n.2: This is the growth mindset, often seen as the core of the agile mindset, not doing agile (book 2.6.1, 2.7.3).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q: PRINCE2 Agile contrasts being agile and doing agile under the heading 'adaptability versus routine'. Which statement reflects this contrast?
o: Being agile lets teams adapt and think critically, while doing agile alone may mean following a framework rigidly without knowing why
Doing agile lets teams adapt and think critically, while being agile alone may leave them following routines with no structure
Being agile delivers short-term efficiency gains, while doing agile creates a lasting cultural shift in the organization
Doing agile relies on stable routines suited to business as usual, while being agile is reserved for project work
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Under 'adaptability versus routine', being agile allows teams to adapt to change and think critically, whereas doing agile on its own can leave them applying a framework rigidly without understanding the reasons (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3.1).

n.1: This reverses the contrast: it is being agile that supports adaptation and critical thinking (book 2.3.1).
n.2: This reverses the 'long-term impact versus short-term mechanics' contrast: doing agile alone gives short-term gains (book 2.3.1).
n.3: The contrast is about mindset versus mechanics, not about splitting agile between business as usual and projects; agile is used in both (book 2.3.1, 1.1).

Agile: Mindset & Transformation.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.

If an organization labels its processes 'agile' but its people are not allowed to think and act in an agile way, there is a gap between [?] agile.
o: scaling and sustaining
planning and delivering
being and doing
valuing and practising
Agile: Mindset & Transformation.w: Calling processes agile means little if people are not permitted to think and act in an agile way; PRINCE2 Agile describes this as the gap between being and doing agile (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3).

n.0: Scaling and sustaining are separate topics (book 3.2, 2.7.5); the gap between labels and freedom to act is between being and doing agile (book 2.3).
n.1: Planning and delivering are activities in any project; the gap described is between mindset with freedom (being) and mechanics (doing) (book 2.3).
n.3: Values and practices are layers of the Agile Onion; the book names this gap as being versus doing agile (book 2.3, 2.6.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A water company has upgraded pumping stations before. The next upgrade, however, uses a new supplier, a different site and a newly formed team. Which characteristic of a project does this illustrate?
o: Temporary
Unique
Cross-functional
Change
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Unique: every project differs from others in some way, for example in its team, customer, supplier, location or timeframe, even when similar work has been done before. BAU, by contrast, is repetitive and ongoing (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.1).

n.0: Temporary is about the project having a start and an end; the stem stresses how this upgrade differs from earlier ones, not its duration (book 1.3.1).
n.2: Cross-functional is about the team spanning functional divisions or organizations; the stem does not describe the mix of functions in the team (book 1.3.1).
n.3: Change is about BAU identifying a need and the project introducing it; the stem focuses on what makes this upgrade different (book 1.3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q:
Which two statements about projects and business as usual (BAU) are correct?
1. BAU identifies a need for change and a project is the means of introducing it.
2. A project continues until the product it delivers is retired from use.
3. Project teams normally sit within one functional department of BAU.
4. When a project ends, BAU adopts the change, which leads to the expected benefits.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Statement 1 is the 'change' characteristic and statement 4 the 'temporary' characteristic: a project has a start and an end, after which BAU adopts the change and the expected benefits follow (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: a project is temporary and ends once the change is handed to BAU; running the product until retirement is BAU (book 1.3.1).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: projects end when the change is adopted, and project teams are cross-functional, working across BAU's functional divisions (book 1.3.1).
n.2: Statement 3 is wrong: project teams are cross-functional, working across functional divisions and sometimes across organizations (book 1.3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A retailer's store managers report that customers want to collect online orders in store. The retailer then sets up a project to introduce a click-and-collect service. Which project characteristic is shown by the link between the store managers' report and the project?
o: Change, because BAU spotted the need and the project introduces it
Unique, because the retailer has not offered this service before
Temporary, because the service will be handed to stores after launch
Cross-functional, because store and online teams will work together
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Change: BAU identifies a need for change and projects are the means by which that change is introduced. Here the store managers (BAU) spotted the need and the project brings in the new service (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.1).

n.1: Unique is about how a project differs from other projects (team, supplier, location, timeframe); it does not describe BAU raising a need that a project then meets (book 1.3.1).
n.2: Temporary is about the project ending and BAU adopting the change; the stem asks about the link between BAU identifying the need and the project, which is change (book 1.3.1).
n.3: Cross-functional is about the make-up of the project team; the stem does not describe the team, and the link it asks about is BAU identifying a need for change (book 1.3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: An IT operations team improves its service desk every week as part of its normal work, using a backlog and short iterations. Which feature would show that a new piece of work should instead be run as a project?
o: It will be carried out by people from within the IT operations team
It will use agile techniques such as product backlogs and iterations
It has a defined end, after which operations takes over the new capability
It will repeat on a regular cycle whenever demand from service users rises
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: A project is temporary: it has a start and an end, after which BAU adopts the change. Agile techniques are also used in BAU, so they do not by themselves make work a project (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.1, 1.1).

n.0: Work done within one functional team is typical of BAU; project teams are cross-functional, so this does not point to a project (book 1.3.1).
n.1: Agile ways of working are used in business as usual as well as in projects, so backlogs and iterations do not distinguish a project (book 1.1).
n.3: Repetitive, ongoing work that recurs with demand is a feature of BAU, not of a project, which is unique and temporary (book 1.3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: PRINCE2 Agile Version 2 aligns its performance targets with PRINCE2 Project Management (PRINCE2 7). How many performance targets are there, and which one did PRINCE2 7 add to the earlier set?
o: Six targets, with benefits added to the earlier set
Seven targets, with sustainability added to the earlier set
Six targets, with sustainability added to the earlier set
Seven targets, with risk added to the earlier set
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: There are seven performance targets: benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk. Sustainability is the PRINCE2 7 addition, which is why older material shows only six aspects (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.2).

n.0: Benefits was already one of the six aspects in older material; the current set has seven, and the addition is sustainability (book 1.3.2).
n.2: Sustainability is the addition, but the result is seven targets, not six; six aspects is the older, pre-PRINCE2 7 set (book 1.3.2).
n.3: Risk was already an aspect in the older six; the target added by PRINCE2 7 is sustainability (book 1.3.2).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which statement best describes a performance target in PRINCE2 Project Management, as used in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: A permitted deviation the project manager may use before escalating to the board
A measurable improvement the business expects from the change the project enables
A criterion that a user story must meet before a delivery team starts work on it
The expected level of success against which management of the project is judged
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: A performance target sets the expected success level against which the management of the project will be judged; targets exist for benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.2).

n.0: A permitted deviation before escalation is a tolerance, set under the 'manage by exception' principle; tolerances are set against the targets but are not the targets themselves (book 5.2.1.5).
n.1: A measurable improvement expected from the change is a benefit, which is one of the seven targets rather than the definition of a target (book 1.3.2).
n.2: Criteria an item must meet before work begins form the Definition of Ready, a quality artifact, not a performance target (book 9.3.2.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A local authority wants its new depot project to limit carbon emissions and reduce waste sent to landfill. Which performance target is this, and how does PRINCE2 Agile treat it by default?
o: Sustainability: fixed for minimum criteria and flexed above them
Quality: fixed for the minimum criteria and flexed above them
Benefits: fixed for minimum viability and flexed above it
Scope: fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Sustainability is the performance target covering how the project will impact the wider environment, and PRINCE2 Agile fixes it for the minimum criteria and flexes anything above them (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.2, Table 3.1).

n.1: Quality concerns the characteristics that make products fit for purpose and in line with expectations, not the project's impact on the wider environment, so the target is wrongly identified (book 1.3.2).
n.2: Benefits are the measurable improvements the business expects from the change; limiting emissions and waste concerns impact on the wider environment, which is sustainability (book 1.3.2).
n.3: Scope is what the project will and will not deliver; the stem describes the project's environmental impact, which is the sustainability target (book 1.3.2).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A project board asks for a clear statement of which features the new online booking system will include and which it will not include. Which performance target does this statement relate to?
o: Quality
Benefits
Scope
Time
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Scope is the performance target describing what the project will deliver and what it will not deliver (out of scope) (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.2).

n.0: Quality is about the characteristics that make products fit for purpose, not which features are in or out of the project (book 1.3.2).
n.1: Benefits are the measurable improvements expected from the change, not a list of included and excluded features (book 1.3.2).
n.3: Time concerns when the project and its products will be delivered, not which features are in or out (book 1.3.2).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
In PRINCE2 Project Management, [?] are the measurable improvements that the business expects as a result of the change enabled by the project.
o: outputs
tolerances
benefits
requirements
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Benefits are the measurable improvements the business expects as a result of the change the project enables; benefits is one of the seven performance targets (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.2; Glossary).

n.0: Outputs are the deliverables (specialist products) the project produces; an output is never itself a benefit (Glossary).
n.1: Tolerances are permitted deviations set against performance targets under 'manage by exception', not improvements the business expects (book 5.2.1.5).
n.3: Requirements describe what users need from the products, for example as user stories in a backlog; they are not the measurable improvements that result from the change (book 8.3.2).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A digital team asks what makes the project's products fit for purpose and in line with the expectations of the people who will use them. Which performance target does this concern?
o: Quality
Scope
Benefits
Sustainability
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Quality is the performance target covering the characteristics of the project's products that make them fit for purpose and in line with expectations (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.2).

n.1: Scope describes what will and will not be delivered, not the characteristics that make products fit for purpose (book 1.3.2).
n.2: Benefits are measurable improvements from the change, not the characteristics of the products themselves (book 1.3.2).
n.3: Sustainability concerns the project's impact on the wider environment, not whether products are fit for purpose (book 1.3.2).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which list contains four of the performance targets set out in PRINCE2 Project Management and used in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Scope, risk, team velocity and benefits
Time, cost, business value and quality
Time, cost, quality and team happiness
Scope, risk, sustainability and benefits
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The seven performance targets are benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk, so scope, risk, sustainability and benefits are all targets (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.2).

n.0: Velocity is an agile measure of story points delivered per timebox, used for forecasting; it is not one of the seven performance targets (book 12.4.3).
n.1: Value is central to agile business justification, but the performance target is benefits, not value (book 1.3.2).
n.2: Team happiness matters in agile teams, but it is not one of the seven performance targets (book 1.3.2).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Under the 'manage by exception' principle, a project board sets tolerances so it can delegate authority. Against which aspects of project performance can these tolerances be set?
o: The six aspects: time, cost, quality, scope, benefits and risk
The seven aspects: benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk
The three aspects of time, cost and quality, as the classic project triangle
The four aspects of time, cost, scope and benefits, with quality left to teams
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Manage by exception sets tolerances for the seven performance aspects: benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 5.2.1.5, 1.3.2).

n.0: This is the older six-aspect set without sustainability; PRINCE2 7 and PRINCE2 Agile V2 use seven aspects (book 1.3.2, 5.2.1.5).
n.2: The time, cost and quality triangle is not the PRINCE2 set; tolerances cover all seven aspects, including scope, benefits, sustainability and risk (book 5.2.1.5).
n.3: Quality is one of the seven aspects with tolerances set through governance, and sustainability and risk are also included (book 5.2.1.5).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A city council hires an external software company to build its new parking permit app, while council staff act as the users. Which project context does PRINCE2 say must be taken into account because of this arrangement?
o: Commercial
Organizational
Scale
Delivery method
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The commercial context recognizes that the suppliers of a project's products may be external to the sponsoring organization, as with the software company here (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.4).

n.1: The organizational context is about whether the project is standalone or part of a programme or portfolio, not about external suppliers (book 1.3.4).
n.2: Scale is about how simple or complex the project is and how formal its governance must be, not about who supplies the products (book 1.3.4).
n.3: The delivery method context is about how the work is delivered, for example linear-sequential or iterative-incremental, not about external suppliers (book 1.3.4).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A project team is deciding whether to build its product through a series of sequential phases or through repeated cycles that each add new features. Which project context covers this choice?
o: Scale
Commercial
Delivery method
Organizational
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The delivery method context concerns the way project work is delivered, such as linear-sequential or iterative-incremental (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.4).

n.0: Scale concerns how simple or large and complex the project is, which affects the formality of control, not how the work is sequenced (book 1.3.4).
n.1: The commercial context concerns suppliers that may be external to the sponsoring organization, not the way the work is delivered (book 1.3.4).
n.3: The organizational context concerns whether the project is standalone or part of a programme or portfolio (book 1.3.4).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A project to replace a bank's mortgage application system is one of six projects within the bank's wider digital transformation programme. Which project context does this describe?
o: Commercial
Organizational
Scale
Delivery method
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The organizational context recognizes that projects do not operate in a vacuum: they may be part of a programme or portfolio, or be standalone (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.4).

n.0: The commercial context concerns suppliers external to the sponsoring organization; the stem describes the project's place within a programme (book 1.3.4).
n.2: Scale concerns how simple or complex the project is; being one of six projects in a programme is about its organizational setting (book 1.3.4).
n.3: The delivery method context concerns linear-sequential or iterative-incremental delivery, which the stem does not mention (book 1.3.4).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which project context has the most direct influence on how formal a project's governance, documentation, project structure and tolerances need to be?
o: Commercial
Organizational
Delivery method
Scale
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Scale: projects range from relatively simple to large and complex, and the scale influences how the project is managed and controlled, including the formality of governance, documentation, structure and tolerances (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.4).

n.0: The commercial context concerns suppliers that may be external to the sponsoring organization; the book links formality of control to scale (book 1.3.4).
n.1: The organizational context concerns whether the project is standalone or part of a programme or portfolio; the book links formality of control to scale (book 1.3.4).
n.2: The delivery method context concerns linear-sequential or iterative-incremental work; the book links formality of control to scale (book 1.3.4).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile differ from PRINCE2 Project Management in relation to the delivery method context?
o: PRINCE2 Agile can host any delivery method, while PRINCE2 Project Management is designed for linear delivery
Both are designed for linear-sequential delivery, with agile techniques added during the delivery stages
PRINCE2 Agile is designed for hybrid delivery, mixing linear and iterative work within each delivery stage
PRINCE2 Agile is designed for iterative-incremental delivery; PRINCE2 Project Management can host any method
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: PRINCE2 Project Management is configured so a project can use any chosen delivery method, whereas PRINCE2 Agile is specifically designed for projects using iterative and incremental (agile) delivery (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.4).

n.0: This reverses the position: it is PRINCE2 Project Management that can host any delivery method, while PRINCE2 Agile is designed for iterative-incremental delivery (book 1.3.4).
n.1: PRINCE2 Agile is specifically designed for iterative and incremental delivery, not for linear-sequential delivery with agile add-ons (book 1.3.4).
n.2: PRINCE2 Agile is described as designed for iterative and incremental (agile) delivery, not as a hybrid method (book 1.3.4).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
When a project buys in some of its products from a company outside the organization paying for the project, its [?] context must be taken into account.
o: organizational
commercial
scale
delivery method
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The commercial context applies when the project's products come from suppliers outside the sponsoring organization (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.4).

n.0: The organizational context concerns whether the project is standalone or part of a programme or portfolio (book 1.3.4).
n.2: The scale context concerns how simple or complex the project is and therefore how formally it is controlled (book 1.3.4).
n.3: The delivery method context concerns whether work is linear-sequential or iterative-incremental (book 1.3.4).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which statement about the organizational context of a project is correct?
o: It describes whether the project stands alone or forms part of a programme or portfolio
It describes whether the project's suppliers sit inside or outside the sponsoring organization
It describes how formal governance and documentation need to be for the project's size
It describes whether products are built in sequence or through repeated iterations
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The organizational context recognizes that a project may be part of a programme or portfolio, or may be a standalone project introducing a single change into the operational environment (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.4).

n.1: Whether suppliers are external to the sponsoring organization is the commercial context, not the organizational context (book 1.3.4).
n.2: How formal governance and documentation need to be is driven by the scale context (book 1.3.4).
n.3: Whether products are built sequentially or iteratively is the delivery method context (book 1.3.4).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A housing charity will build a tenant mobile app in two-week iterations, releasing new features to users every month. Which project context most clearly makes PRINCE2 Agile, rather than PRINCE2 Project Management on its own, a suitable choice?
o: Commercial
Scale
Delivery method
Organizational
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The delivery method context: PRINCE2 Project Management can host any delivery method, but PRINCE2 Agile is specifically designed for iterative and incremental delivery such as two-week iterations with frequent releases (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.4).

n.0: The commercial context concerns suppliers external to the sponsoring organization; the stem says nothing about suppliers (book 1.3.4).
n.1: Scale shapes the formality of governance and documentation; the feature that points to PRINCE2 Agile here is the iterative-incremental delivery (book 1.3.4).
n.3: The organizational context concerns programme, portfolio or standalone status, which the stem does not mention (book 1.3.4).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: PRINCE2 Agile Version 2 builds on PRINCE2 Project Management. Which list gives the five integrated elements of PRINCE2 Project Management?
o: Principles, themes, processes, roles and tailoring
Principles, practices, processes, products and tolerances
Principles, people, practices, processes and performance targets
Principles, people, practices, processes and the project context
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The five integrated elements are principles, people, practices, processes and the project context (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.3; syllabus 1.2.3).

n.0: Themes and tailoring belong to the older four-element model; the current elements are principles, people, practices, processes and the project context (book 1.3.3).
n.1: Management products and tolerances are parts of the method, not integrated elements; the list lacks people and the project context (book 1.3.3).
n.2: Performance targets are what management of the project is judged against, not an integrated element; the fifth element is the project context (book 1.3.2, 1.3.3).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which integrated element of PRINCE2 Project Management covers factors such as commercial arrangements, delivery method, organizational setting and scale, which shape how the method is applied?
o: People
Project context
Practices
Tailoring to the environment
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The project context is the integrated element covering the setting the project operates in (commercial, delivery method, organizational, scale), which shapes how principles, practices and processes are applied (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.3, 1.3.4).

n.0: People covers the needs, capabilities and motivations of those involved in and affected by the project, not commercial or scale factors (PRINCE2 7 manual 1.2).
n.2: Practices are the aspects of project management applied throughout the lifecycle, such as risk and progress, not the setting of the project (book 1.3.3).
n.3: 'Tailoring to the project environment' was part of the older four-element model; the current element is the project context (book 1.3.3).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which integrated element consists of seven guiding obligations and good practices that decide whether a project is genuinely being managed using PRINCE2?
o: Practices
Processes
Principles
Performance targets
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The principles are the seven guiding obligations and good practices; if they are not all applied, the project is not a PRINCE2 project (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.3, 5.2).

n.0: There are seven practices too, but they are aspects of project management applied throughout the lifecycle, not the obligations that decide whether a project is PRINCE2 (book 1.3.3).
n.1: The seven processes describe the lifecycle from pre-project to closure; they are not the guiding obligations (book 1.3.3).
n.3: Performance targets are the success levels against which management of the project is judged; they are not an integrated element (book 1.3.2).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which integrated element describes the project lifecycle from pre-project activity through to closure, with recommended activities and the responsibilities for them?
o: Processes
Practices
Principles
People
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The processes describe the whole project lifecycle, from before the project starts to its closure, with recommended activities and responsibilities (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.3; PRINCE2 7 manual 1.2).

n.1: Practices are aspects of project management, such as risk and progress, applied continually throughout the lifecycle rather than a lifecycle sequence (book 1.3.3).
n.2: Principles are the guiding obligations that apply to every project; they do not set out lifecycle activities (book 1.3.3).
n.3: People covers the needs, capabilities and motivations of those involved; it does not describe the lifecycle activities (book 1.3.3).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which integrated element covers aspects of project management, such as risk, quality and progress, that must be applied consistently and continually throughout the project lifecycle?
o: Practices
Processes
Principles
People
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The practices are the seven aspects of project management (business case, organization, plans, quality, risk, issues and progress) that are applied continually throughout the lifecycle (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.3; chapters 6 to 12).

n.1: Processes set out activities in sequence through the lifecycle, from pre-project to closure; risk, quality and progress are practices (book 1.3.3).
n.2: Principles are the guiding obligations, such as manage by exception; risk, quality and progress are practices (book 1.3.3).
n.3: People concerns those involved in and affected by the project; risk, quality and progress are practices (book 1.3.3).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which is NOT one of the five integrated elements of PRINCE2 Project Management on which PRINCE2 Agile Version 2 is built?
o: People
Project context
Themes
Practices
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Themes belong to older editions of PRINCE2; in PRINCE2 7 and PRINCE2 Agile V2 they are practices. The five elements are principles, people, practices, processes and the project context (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.3).

n.0: People is one of the five integrated elements (book 1.3.3).
n.1: The project context is one of the five integrated elements (book 1.3.3).
n.3: Practices are one of the five integrated elements; they replaced the older themes (book 1.3.3).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which statement about the people element of PRINCE2 Project Management is correct?
o: It covers the project board members and leaves out the users affected by the change
It covers both the people working on the project and the people affected by it
It was one of the four integrated elements in earlier editions of PRINCE2
It replaces the organization practice in projects that use agile delivery
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The people element covers the needs, capabilities and motivations of everyone involved, including those working on the project and those affected by it (PRINCE2 7 manual 1.2; PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.3, chapter 4).

n.0: People is not limited to the board: it includes those working on the project and those affected by the change (PRINCE2 7 manual 1.2).
n.2: The older four elements were principles, themes, processes and tailoring to the project environment; people became a named element in PRINCE2 7 (PRINCE2 7 manual 1.2).
n.3: The organization practice remains one of the seven practices in PRINCE2 Agile; the people element does not replace it (book chapter 7).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A project manager says: 'Our method has four elements: principles, themes, processes and tailoring to the project environment.' Why is this out of date for PRINCE2 Agile Version 2?
o: Version 2 has six elements, adding agile workshops and artifacts to the original four
Version 2 keeps the four elements but renames the themes as agile focus areas
Version 2 drops processes as an element, because agile delivery teams self-manage
Version 2 builds on five elements, adding people and using practices and project context
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: PRINCE2 Agile V2 builds on PRINCE2 Project Management's five integrated elements: principles, people, practices, processes and the project context. Themes became practices and people is a new named element (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.3).

n.0: There are five elements, not six; workshops and artifacts are agile tailoring, not integrated elements (book 1.3.3).
n.1: Focus areas were a Version 1 heading that no longer appears; the themes became practices within five elements (book 1.3.3).
n.2: Processes remain one of the five integrated elements; self-managing teams work within them (book 1.3.3).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: PRINCE2 Agile uses the seven PRINCE2 principles. Which list contains three of those seven principles?
o: Learn from experience, manage by iterations, focus on products
Learn from experience, manage by exception, focus on products
Ensure continued business justification, manage by sprints, focus on value
Tailor to suit the project, manage by exception, collaborate with customers
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Learn from experience, manage by exception and focus on products are all PRINCE2 principles. The full set is: ensure continued business justification, learn from experience, define roles, responsibilities and relationships, manage by stages, manage by exception, focus on products, and tailor to suit the project (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 5.2).

n.0: 'Manage by iterations' is not a principle; the principle is manage by stages, and stages contain timeboxed iterations (book 5.2).
n.2: 'Manage by sprints' and 'focus on value' are not PRINCE2 principles; the principles are manage by stages and focus on products (book 5.2).
n.3: 'Collaborate with customers' echoes the Agile Manifesto, not a PRINCE2 principle (book 5.2).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which PRINCE2 principle requires that a project has a valid reason for being undertaken, and that this reason remains valid throughout the project lifecycle?
o: Ensure continued business justification
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Manage by stages
Learn from experience
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Ensure continued business justification: a project must have a valid business justification that stays relevant throughout its lifecycle, otherwise it may proceed with minimal benefit or poor strategic fit (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 5.2.1.1).

n.1: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships concerns having the right people in clear roles with stakeholders engaged, not the project's justification (book 5.2.1.3).
n.2: Manage by stages concerns planning, monitoring and controlling the project stage by stage, not whether it remains justified (book 5.2.1.4).
n.3: Learn from experience concerns seeking, recording and acting on lessons, not keeping a valid reason for the project (book 5.2).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which principle means a project is planned, monitored and controlled stage by stage, with the project board authorizing one stage at a time?
o: Manage by exception
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Ensure continued business justification
Manage by stages
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Manage by stages: the project is planned, monitored and controlled stage by stage, and the board authorizes one stage at a time, delegating day-to-day control within tolerances to the project manager (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 5.2.1.4).

n.0: Manage by exception sets tolerances for the seven performance aspects so authority can be delegated; authorizing one stage at a time is manage by stages (book 5.2.1.5).
n.1: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships concerns clear roles and engaged stakeholders, not stage-by-stage control (book 5.2.1.3).
n.2: Ensure continued business justification concerns keeping a valid justification, not authorizing the project one stage at a time (book 5.2.1.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which principle establishes governance by delegating responsibilities and setting tolerances for the seven performance aspects, such as cost, time and scope?
o: Manage by stages
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Manage by exception
Tailor to suit the project
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Manage by exception establishes governance by delegating responsibilities and setting tolerances for benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 5.2.1.5).

n.0: Manage by stages is about authorizing and controlling the project one stage at a time; setting tolerances for the seven aspects is manage by exception (book 5.2.1.4).
n.1: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships concerns clear roles and engaged stakeholders, not tolerances on performance aspects (book 5.2.1.3).
n.3: Tailor to suit the project concerns adapting the method to size, complexity, risk and context, not setting tolerances (book 5.2.1.7).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which principle emphasizes delivering well-defined outputs rather than focusing on activities, which helps avoid unnecessary work and prevent scope creep?
o: Ensure continued business justification
Manage by stages
Learn from experience
Focus on products
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Focus on products: delivering well-defined outputs rather than concentrating on activities avoids unnecessary work, prevents scope creep, sets clear expectations and supports controlled closure (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 5.2.1.6).

n.0: Ensure continued business justification is about the project remaining worthwhile, not about defining outputs to prevent scope creep (book 5.2.1.1).
n.1: Manage by stages is about stage-by-stage planning and control, not defining the products to be delivered (book 5.2.1.4).
n.2: Learn from experience is about using lessons throughout the project, not defining outputs (book 5.2).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which principle states that PRINCE2 should be adapted to suit the project's size, complexity, risk and organizational context?
o: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Tailor to suit the project
Manage by exception
Learn from experience
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Tailor to suit the project: PRINCE2 is flexible and should be adapted to the project's size, complexity, risk and organizational context (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 5.2.1.7).

n.0: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships concerns clear roles and stakeholder engagement, not adapting the method to the project (book 5.2.1.3).
n.2: Manage by exception concerns tolerances and delegation, not adapting the method to the project's size and context (book 5.2.1.5).
n.3: Learn from experience concerns lessons; tailoring decisions may draw on lessons, but adapting the method is the tailoring principle (book 5.2.1.7).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q:
Which two statements about the PRINCE2 principles are correct?
1. All seven principles must be applied for a project to be a PRINCE2 project.
2. A small, simple project may leave out the 'manage by stages' principle.
3. The principles are not tailored; tailoring adapts how the method is applied.
4. 'Learn from experience' applies at project closure rather than throughout.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Statement 1 is correct: all seven principles must be applied for a project to be PRINCE2. Statement 3 is correct: the principles themselves are not tailored; tailoring adapts the way the method is applied (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 5.2; PRINCE2 7 manual ch 2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: even a simple project applies manage by stages, with at least an initiation stage and one further stage (PRINCE2 7 manual 2.4).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: no principle may be left out, and lessons are sought and applied throughout the project, not only at closure (PRINCE2 7 manual ch 2, 2.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: lessons are sought, recorded and acted on from the start and throughout the project as well as at closure (PRINCE2 7 manual 2.2).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: At the start of a new project, the project manager reviews lessons from similar past projects and talks to people who have delivered comparable work elsewhere. Which principle is being applied?
o: Learn from experience
Ensure continued business justification
Manage by stages
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Learn from experience: lessons from previous projects are sought at the start and applied throughout, especially when the work is new to the organization (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 5.2; PRINCE2 7 manual 2.2; 'assess previous lessons' in starting up, book Table 13.1).

n.1: Ensure continued business justification is about the project remaining worthwhile, not about reviewing lessons from earlier projects (book 5.2.1.1).
n.2: Manage by stages is about stage-by-stage authorization and control, not about gathering lessons (book 5.2.1.4).
n.3: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships is about clear roles and stakeholder engagement; consulting others here is to gather lessons (book 5.2.1.3).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: PRINCE2 Agile explains that many agile concepts support the 'learn from experience' principle. Which group of agile concepts does it link most closely to this principle?
o: Swarming, trading and MoSCoW prioritization of the product backlog
Delegation matrices, team skill matrices and agreed role descriptions
Short feedback loops, continual customer involvement and retrospectives
Zero time and cost tolerance combined with flexible delivered scope
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: PRINCE2 Agile names shortening the feedback loop to the customer, continual customer involvement, and inspect and adapt with retrospectives as agile ways of applying 'learn from experience' (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 5.1).

n.0: Swarming and trading are issues practice techniques and MoSCoW is a prioritization technique; they are not the concepts the book links to learning from experience (book 11.4, 9.3.2).
n.1: Delegation and skill matrices and role descriptions support the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle through the organization practice (book 7.4).
n.3: Restricting time and cost while flexing what is delivered is how 'manage by exception' is applied in agile (book Table 5.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, how is the 'manage by exception' principle applied when working in an agile way?
o: Tolerance is allowed on time and cost, while what is delivered is held fixed
Tolerances are replaced by each team's Definition of Done for the iteration
Tolerance is set on team velocity, so teams escalate when story points fall
Tolerance is allowed on what is delivered and restricted on time and cost
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Working in an agile way emphasizes allowing tolerance on what is delivered and restricting tolerance on time and cost (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 5.1; Table 3.1).

n.0: This reverses the agile position: time and cost have zero tolerance by default, while what is delivered is flexed (book Table 3.1, Table 5.1).
n.1: The Definition of Done is a quality artifact setting when an item is complete; it does not replace tolerances set by the board (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: Velocity is used to forecast empirically; tolerances are set against the seven performance aspects, not against velocity (book 12.4.3, 5.2.1.5).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile describe the 'manage by exception' principle as being at the heart of empowering people to self-manage?
o: Clear tolerances let teams make their own decisions while the board stays in control
Exceptions are raised by teams directly to the board, bypassing the project manager
Teams agree their own tolerances each iteration without reference to the board
The board reviews every user story, so teams know exactly what to build next
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Manage by exception lets people self-manage within agreed tolerances while the project keeps the right level of governance; decisions inside the limits stay with the team, and only forecast breaches are escalated (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 5.1, 5.2.1.5).

n.1: Escalation follows the governance structure: deviations beyond tolerance go through the project manager to the board, not around the project manager (book 5.2.1.5, Table 12.1).
n.2: Tolerances are set by the level above (the board sets project and stage tolerances); teams work within them rather than setting their own (book 5.2.1.5).
n.3: A board reviewing every user story would be the opposite of management by exception, which delegates day-to-day decisions (book 5.2.1.5).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which statement describes how the 'focus on products' principle supports working in an agile way?
o: Products are fully specified at the start so that delivery teams can build them without change
Product descriptions and quality criteria can be prioritized and decomposed so what is delivered can flex
Products are replaced by activities and tasks, which are easier to timebox in each iteration
Products are approved by the board one at a time, at each stage boundary, before the next starts
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: In agile, product descriptions, quality specifications and quality tolerances can be prioritized and decomposed so that what is delivered can flex, making it easier to stay in control and focus on value (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 5.1).

n.0: Agile does not fix every product detail up front; change is embraced and requirements are prioritized so that what is delivered can flex (book Table 5.1, Table 11.1).
n.2: Focus on products means delivering well-defined outputs rather than concentrating on activities, so products are not replaced by tasks (book 5.2.1.6).
n.3: The board authorizes stages, not individual products; products are delivered by teams within each stage (book 5.2.1.4).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
In PRINCE2 Agile, timeboxed releases and iterations sit within management stages, and the project board authorizes one stage at a time. This reflects the '[?]' principle.
o: manage by exception
manage by stages
focus on products
tailor to suit the project
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Manage by stages: the board authorizes one stage at a time, and in PRINCE2 Agile each stage contains timeboxed releases and iterations (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 5.2.1.4; Glossary, timebox).

n.0: Manage by exception concerns tolerances and delegation; authorizing one stage at a time with iterations inside stages reflects manage by stages (book 5.2.1.5).
n.2: Focus on products concerns delivering well-defined outputs, not the stage-by-stage structure of authorization (book 5.2.1.6).
n.3: Tailor to suit the project concerns adapting the method to the project; the stage-by-stage authorization described is manage by stages (book 5.2.1.7).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile apply the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle?
o: Agile roles are added where needed and PRINCE2 roles are tailored carefully to the agile context
PRINCE2 roles are replaced by Scrum roles, so a project board is not needed in agile projects
Roles are left undefined so that self-managing teams can decide among themselves who does what
The project manager takes over the chief product owner's duty of making sure user needs are met
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: In agile, additional agile roles may be needed and PRINCE2 Project Management roles should be tailored carefully to the agile context; PRINCE2 Agile V2 has 11 roles, including the chief product owner, product owner, team coach and agile coach (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 5.1, Table 7.2).

n.1: PRINCE2 Agile keeps governance roles such as the project executive and project board; it adds agile roles rather than replacing the PRINCE2 roles (book Table 5.1, 7.3.1).
n.2: The principle requires defined and agreed roles; self-management happens within clear roles and boundaries, not in place of them (book 5.2.1.3).
n.3: It is the chief product owner, not the project manager, who makes sure user requirements are met (book 5.2.1.3, Table B.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which agile practices does PRINCE2 Agile relate most closely to the 'ensure continued business justification' principle?
o: Holding a retrospective at the end of every iteration to improve
Agreeing a delegation matrix with each delivery team at kickoff
Breaking product descriptions down into prioritized user stories
Focusing on value, using an MVP and keeping a project canvas current
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: In agile, continued business justification is supported by a focus on value, a minimum viable product to test viability early, the project canvas as the business case, and frequent releases that bring benefits earlier (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 5.2.1.1, 6.3.1, 6.3.2).

n.0: Retrospectives support the 'learn from experience' principle (book Table 5.1).
n.1: A delegation matrix supports the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle through the organization practice (book 7.4.3).
n.2: Prioritizing and decomposing product descriptions supports the 'focus on products' principle (book Table 5.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q:
Which two statements about the PRINCE2 principles in an agile context are correct?
1. PRINCE2 Agile replaces some of the principles with the Agile Manifesto values.
2. Retrospectives are one way of applying the 'learn from experience' principle.
3. Tailoring includes choosing which agile frameworks, artifacts and workshops to use.
4. Differences in agile maturity between teams should be escalated as an exception.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Statement 2 is correct: retrospectives, with inspect and adapt, apply learn from experience. Statement 3 is correct: tailoring in agile means deciding which agile frameworks, artifacts and workshops to use, recorded in the PID (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 5.1, 5.2.1.7).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: all seven principles still apply in PRINCE2 Agile; agile techniques help to apply them rather than replacing them (book 5.2).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: the principles are kept, and varying agile maturity is handled transparently as lessons rather than escalated (book 5.2, Table 5.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: varying agile maturity is handled transparently with the team as lessons; an exception arises when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded (book Table 5.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: PRINCE2 Agile describes a project in terms of three areas that all need to be addressed. Which three areas are these?
o: Project direction, project management and product delivery
Project governance, team coaching and product support
Project initiation, stage control and project closure
Business layer, delivery teams and business operations
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: PRINCE2 Agile identifies three areas: project direction, project management and product delivery, and addresses all three while keeping governance and control throughout (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 3.1, Figure 3.1).

n.1: Team coaching and product support are not the three areas of Figure 3.1; the areas are project direction, project management and product delivery (book 3.1).
n.2: Initiation, stage control and closure are parts of the process lifecycle, not the three areas PRINCE2 Agile uses to show how project management and agile blend (book 3.1).
n.3: The three areas are project direction, project management and product delivery; the business layer and operations sit outside the project (book 3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, where does the main strength of a project management method such as PRINCE2 lie?
o: In product delivery and responding quickly to change
In the governance and control of the project
In building and testing products in short iterations
In coaching delivery teams to manage their own work
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The strength of project management lies in governance and control, while it gives relatively little focus to product delivery (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 3.1).

n.0: Product delivery and responding to change are the strengths the book gives to agile, not to project management (book 3.1).
n.2: Building and testing in short iterations is agile product delivery, where project management gives little focus (book 3.1).
n.3: Coaching teams to self-manage comes from agile ways of working, not the stated strength of project management, which is governance and control (book 3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, which areas does agile on its own provide relatively little guidance on?
o: Product delivery and responding to change
Product delivery and project management
Responding to change and project direction
Project direction and project management
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Agile has a very strong focus on product delivery and responding to change but relatively little on project direction and project management, which is why PRINCE2 Agile blends it with PRINCE2 (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 3.1, Figure 3.1).

n.0: Product delivery and responding to change are agile's strengths, not its gaps (book 3.1).
n.1: Product delivery is agile's strength; the gaps are direction and management (book 3.1).
n.2: Responding to change is one of agile's strengths, so this pairing is wrong (book 3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which statement best describes PRINCE2 Agile?
o: An agile framework that replaces the PRINCE2 processes with iterations and sprints
A version of Scrum that adds monthly progress reports for senior managers
PRINCE2 Project Management tailored with agile mindset, frameworks and techniques
A delivery method that removes management stages so teams can release continuously
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: PRINCE2 Agile is PRINCE2 Project Management (principles, practices and processes) tailored with the agile mindset, agile frameworks, artifacts, techniques and workshops, covering direction, management and delivery (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 3.1).

n.0: PRINCE2 Agile keeps the seven PRINCE2 processes and tailors them; it does not replace them with iterations (book 3.1, chapter 13).
n.1: PRINCE2 Agile is not a version of Scrum; Scrum is one agile framework that can be used for delivery within it (book 3.1).
n.3: PRINCE2 Agile keeps management stages, with the board authorizing one stage at a time; releases and iterations sit inside stages (book 5.2.1.4).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile combine PRINCE2 Project Management with agile ways of working?
o: Each is strong where the other is light, so together they cover direction, management and delivery
Agile teams need PRINCE2 reports in order to calculate their velocity for each new iteration
PRINCE2 needs agile in order to replace its stage boundaries with continuous release cycles
Combining them lets the project board take over product prioritization from the teams
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Project management is strong on governance and control but light on product delivery, while agile is strong on delivery and responding to change but light on direction and management. PRINCE2 Agile brings them together so all three areas are covered with governance throughout (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 3.1).

n.1: Velocity comes from the team's own record of delivered work, not from PRINCE2 reports, and this is not the reason for the blend (book 8.3, 12.4.3).
n.2: Stage boundaries remain in PRINCE2 Agile: in managing a stage boundary the project manager gives the board the information it needs to review the stage and approve the next stage plan (updated release map); stages are not replaced by continuous release cycles (book 13.7.1).
n.3: Prioritizing work stays with the product owner and chief product owner; the board directs through stages and tolerances (book Table 7.2, 5.2.1.5).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: An organization wants the governance and control of PRINCE2 but prefers not to use agile delivery methods, as it feels agile does not suit its needs. How does PRINCE2 Agile view this choice?
o: It treats the project as PRINCE2 Agile, since governance is the core of the method
It advises the organization to drop PRINCE2 governance until agile is adopted
It requires agile delivery before the board can authorize project initiation
It recognizes that some organizations use PRINCE2 for governance without agile
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: The book recognizes that some businesses choose not to use agile in project delivery and adopt PRINCE2 Project Management for overall governance and control because they feel agile does not suit them (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 3.1).

n.0: PRINCE2 Agile is designed for iterative and incremental delivery; a project using PRINCE2 governance without agile delivery is using PRINCE2 Project Management (book 1.3.4, 3.1).
n.1: The book does not advise dropping governance; it keeps governance and control throughout, and accepts that some organizations use PRINCE2 without agile (book 3.1).
n.2: Authorizing initiation does not depend on agile delivery; the book recognizes PRINCE2 can be used for governance without agile (book 3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q:
Which two statements about PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. Project management methods are strong on governance and control.
2. Agile frameworks are strong on project direction.
3. PRINCE2 Agile keeps governance and control throughout all three areas.
4. PRINCE2 Agile is designed mainly for linear-sequential delivery.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Statement 1 is correct: project management's strength is governance and control. Statement 3 is correct: PRINCE2 Agile addresses direction, management and delivery while keeping governance and control throughout (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 3.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: agile focuses relatively little on project direction and project management (book 3.1).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: agile is light on direction, and PRINCE2 Agile is designed for iterative and incremental delivery (book 3.1, 1.3.4).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: PRINCE2 Agile is designed for iterative and incremental (agile) delivery (book 1.3.4).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: In a PRINCE2 Agile project, which pairing of area and typical activity is correct?
o: Product delivery: the project board prioritizes the user stories for each iteration
Project direction: the project board authorizes stages and sets tolerances
Project management: delivery teams agree project tolerances with the board
Project direction: the project manager plans the tasks for each iteration
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Project direction is the board's area: it authorizes one stage at a time and sets tolerances, delegating day-to-day control to the project manager (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 3.1, 5.2.1.4, 5.2.1.5).

n.0: Prioritizing user stories within an iteration is done at team level by the product owner and team, not by the board (book Table 7.2, 13.6.4.1).
n.2: Tolerances are set by the level above: the board sets stage tolerances for the project manager, who in turn agrees work package tolerances with the teams. Delivery teams do not agree project tolerances with the board (book 5.2.1.5).
n.3: Task-level planning for the next iteration is done by the delivery team in managing product delivery, not by the project manager as a direction activity (book 8.3, Table 13.12).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: PRINCE2 Agile sets a default position for each aspect of project performance. What is the default tolerance for time?
o: Fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves
Fixed for minimum viability and flexed above it
Flexed at team level and fixed at project level
Zero tolerance for extra time on all levels of plan
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: By default PRINCE2 Agile sets zero tolerance for extra time on all levels of plan, so deadlines are kept and what is delivered flexes instead (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1).

n.0: Fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves is the default for scope, not time (book Table 3.1).
n.1: Fixed for minimum viability and flexed above it is the default for benefits, not time (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, including team and project levels (book Table 3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile treat scope by default?
o: Zero tolerance for extra scope on all levels of plan
Flexed for every requirement, including the Must haves
Fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves
Fixed for minimum criteria and flexed above them
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Scope is fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should haves and Could haves, which lets time and cost stay fixed (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1).

n.0: Zero tolerance on all levels of plan is the default for time and cost, not scope (book Table 3.1).
n.1: Must haves are fixed; only Should and Could haves are flexed (book Table 3.1).
n.3: Fixed for minimum criteria and flexed above them is the default for sustainability, not scope (book Table 3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A project board agrees that a new claims system must cut average processing time by at least 10% to be worth doing, and that any further improvement would be welcome. Which aspect is being fixed at its minimum and flexed above it?
o: Scope
Benefits
Quality
Sustainability
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: A minimum level of measurable improvement with room for more describes the benefits target, which PRINCE2 Agile fixes for minimum viability and flexes above it (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.2, Table 3.1).

n.0: Scope is about which features are delivered, fixed for Must haves; the stem describes a measurable improvement, which is a benefit (book 1.3.2).
n.2: Quality concerns the characteristics that make products fit for purpose; a measurable business improvement is a benefit (book 1.3.2).
n.3: Sustainability concerns the project's impact on the wider environment, not a cut in processing time (book 1.3.2).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which pairing of a performance aspect with its PRINCE2 Agile default is correct?
o: Sustainability: fixed for minimum criteria, flexed above them
Time: fixed for Must haves, flexed for Should and Could haves
Benefits: zero tolerance on all levels of plan
Scope: fixed for minimum viability, flexed above it
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Sustainability is fixed for the minimum criteria and flexed for anything above them (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1).

n.1: Time has zero tolerance for extra time on all levels of plan; the Must, Should and Could split is the scope default (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Benefits are fixed for minimum viability and flexed above it; zero tolerance on all levels applies to time and cost (book Table 3.1).
n.3: Scope is fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves; minimum viability is the benefits default (book Table 3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q:
Which two statements about the PRINCE2 Agile fix and flex defaults are correct?
1. There is zero tolerance for extra cost on all levels of plan.
2. Time may be extended to protect Should have features.
3. Must have requirements are fixed.
4. Benefits may be flexed below minimum viability.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Statement 1 is correct: cost has zero tolerance on all levels of plan. Statement 3 is correct: scope is fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: time has zero tolerance, so Should haves are flexed to protect the date, not the other way round (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Both statements are wrong: time is not extended to protect Should haves, and benefits are fixed for minimum viability, flexing only above it (book Table 3.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: benefits are fixed for minimum viability and are flexed above it, not below it (book Table 3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A delivery team forecasts that it cannot finish every planned feature before a fixed release date. Following the PRINCE2 Agile fix and flex defaults, what should normally happen?
o: Extend the release date so that every planned feature can be delivered
Add budget for extra developers so that all the features fit the date
Remove a Must have feature so that the Should haves can be kept
Drop or defer lower-priority Should and Could haves to keep the date
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Time and cost have zero tolerance, while scope is flexed for Should and Could haves, so lower-priority features are dropped or deferred to protect the date (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1, Table 5.1).
