n.0: Time has zero tolerance for extra time on all levels of plan, so extending the date breaks the default (book Table 3.1).
n.1: Cost has zero tolerance for extra cost on all levels of plan, so adding budget breaks the default (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Must haves are fixed; it is Should and Could haves that flex (book Table 3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Why are burn charts a natural way to display progress at every level of a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: Flexibility in what is delivered is of most interest, and burn charts show it
They track spend against budget, which is the main tolerance used in agile
They show how much of the time tolerance has been used in each stage
They replace the need for retrospectives at the end of each iteration
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: In PRINCE2 Agile, flexibility in what is delivered is the aspect of performance of most interest to the project management team, so showing it in a burn chart is natural at any level (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.3.1).

n.1: Cost has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, so there is little point tracking spend against a cost tolerance (book 12.3.1, Table 3.1).
n.2: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, so there is no time tolerance to track being used up (book 12.3.1, Table 3.1).
n.3: Retrospectives are held at the end of iterations to learn lessons; burn charts show progress and do not replace them (book 4.2.4, 12.4.3).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A project manager plans to report each week how much of the time and cost tolerance has been used. Why is this of little value in a PRINCE2 Agile project using the default tolerances?
o: Time and cost are tracked by the delivery team, so the board does not need them
Time and cost tolerances are reviewed at stage end, so weekly reports duplicate them
Time and cost have zero tolerance, so the useful measure is what is being delivered
Time and cost are flexed by default, so their tolerances change every iteration
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: With zero tolerance for extra time and cost on all levels of plan, there is no tolerance to use up; progress is better shown by what is being delivered, for example in burn charts (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.3.1, Table 3.1).

n.0: The board does govern time and cost, which are fixed; the reason the report adds little is that their tolerance is zero (book Table 3.1, 12.3.1).
n.1: The issue is not duplication: with zero tolerance there is nothing to measure against, so flexing what is delivered is tracked instead (book 12.3.1).
n.3: Time and cost are fixed, not flexed, by default in PRINCE2 Agile (book Table 3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A housing association runs a repairs helpdesk that answers tenant calls every day of the year. It also sets up a team to replace its tenant records system by next spring. Which characteristic of the second piece of work shows that it is a project rather than business as usual?
o: It uses staff with specialist technical and engineering skills
It must be delivered within a budget agreed by senior managers
It has a defined start and end, after which BAU adopts the change
It serves the association's tenants and responds to their needs
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Temporary is one of the five characteristics that distinguish a project from business as usual: a project has a start and an end, after which BAU takes on the change and the benefits follow. The helpdesk runs indefinitely, so it is BAU (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.1).

n.0: Specialist skills are used in both pieces of work, so they do not set the project apart from the helpdesk; skills are not one of the project characteristics (book 1.3.1).
n.1: BAU operations such as the helpdesk also run to budgets, so a budget does not distinguish a project from BAU (book 1.3.1).
n.3: Both the helpdesk and the new system serve tenants, so serving customers is not what makes the second piece of work a project (book 1.3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: A hospital trust forms a team to introduce electronic prescribing. The team includes pharmacists, ward nurses, IT staff and engineers from an external software company. Which characteristic of a project does this team composition illustrate?
o: The project is cross-functional
The project is unique
The project is temporary
The project introduces change
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Cross-functional: project teams work across the functional divisions of BAU and sometimes span different organizations, as here with several departments and an external supplier (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.1).

n.1: Unique is about a project differing from others, for example in team, customer, supplier, location or timeframe; the stem describes who is in the team, not how the project differs (book 1.3.1).
n.2: Temporary is about the project having a start and an end; nothing in the stem concerns its duration (book 1.3.1).
n.3: Change is about BAU identifying a need and the project introducing it; the stem is about the mix of people, not the change itself (book 1.3.1).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which statement describes project management, as defined in PRINCE2 Project Management and used in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: The running of business as usual operations within agreed service levels
The agreed limits within which a manager may act before escalating
The expected success level against which a project's management is judged
Applying methods, tools, techniques and competencies to meet project objectives
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: Project management is the application of methods, tools, techniques and competencies to a project so that it meets its objectives (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 1.3.2).

n.0: Running day-to-day operations is business as usual, which projects change; it is not project management (book 1.3.1).
n.1: Agreed limits of authority before escalation describe tolerances under the 'manage by exception' principle, not project management (book 5.2.1.5).
n.2: The expected success level against which management of the project is judged is the definition of a performance target, not of project management (book 1.3.2).

Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.q: Which of the following best describes a project, as PRINCE2 Project Management defines the term?
o: A permanent team that runs and continually improves an organization's services
A temporary organization set up to deliver products under an agreed business case
A timeboxed period in which a delivery team builds and demonstrates user stories
A group of related initiatives managed together to achieve strategic outcomes
Agile: PRINCE2 Essentials.w: PRINCE2 defines a project as a temporary organization created to deliver one or more products according to an agreed business case (PRINCE2 Project Management 1.3; PRINCE2 Agile builds on this definition, book 1.3).

n.0: A permanent team running and improving services is business as usual; a project is temporary, with a start and an end (book 1.3.1).
n.2: A short timeboxed period in which a team builds and demonstrates stories is an iteration, one of the three timebox levels, not a project (PRINCE2 Agile Glossary).
n.3: A group of related initiatives managed together for strategic outcomes describes a programme or portfolio, which a project may form part of (book 1.3.4).

Agile: People & Change.q: How does applying the 'focus on products' principle to people help a change to succeed, according to PRINCE2 Project Management?
o: Products are fully specified before users are consulted, so later rework is avoided
Co-creating with the business, users and suppliers improves adoption and eases handover
Suppliers own the product descriptions, so users face fewer decisions during delivery
Each product gets one named owner, so the wider community is spared review effort
Agile: People & Change.w: Co-creating products and their descriptions with business, user and supplier communities unites perspectives, improves adoption, reduces handover risks and makes sure operational needs are considered (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.5.1).

n.0: Specifying products in full before involving users runs against co-creation, which involves users in designing products so they are adopted (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.3).
n.2: Product descriptions are agreed collaboratively; handing them to the supplier would weaken user involvement and adoption (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Keeping the wider community out of reviews loses the shared perspectives that co-creation is meant to bring (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.5.1).

Agile: People & Change.q: How does the 'manage by exception' principle apply to the people in a project, according to PRINCE2 Project Management?
o: Decisions sit with the project board so that delivery teams can concentrate on building
Delegation levels are agreed at initiation and stay the same for the whole project
Team members refer each decision to the product owner, who holds authority over the team
Decisions are made at the most local level where the knowledge to make and own them sits
Agile: People & Change.w: Applied to people, managing by exception means deciding at the most local level where the knowledge to make and own the decision resides, escalating when a decision could affect other areas (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.5.1).

n.0: Holding decisions at board level is the opposite of local decision-making; the board directs by exception and delegates day-to-day matters (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.5.1).
n.1: The extent of delegation depends on confidence and trust in key relationships and changes as skills grow, so it is not fixed at initiation (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.5.1).
n.2: Referring every decision upward moves it away from where the knowledge sits; decisions are escalated when they could affect other areas (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.5.1).

Agile: People & Change.q: Why does PRINCE2 Project Management say that learning about team behaviours, culture and relationships is best achieved through social learning?
o: Much of this knowledge is hidden in the project ecosystem and is hard to write down
Lessons about people must be kept out of the lessons log for confidentiality reasons
The lessons log records product defects, so people lessons go in the issue register
Social learning replaces the need to assess previous lessons during starting up
Agile: People & Change.w: Applying 'learn from experience' to people, much valuable knowledge is hidden in the project ecosystem; behaviours, culture and relationships are hard to document, so they are best learned socially in a collaborative, knowledge-sharing environment (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.5.1).

n.1: There is no rule keeping people lessons out of the lessons log; the method's point is that such knowledge is hard to capture in writing (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.5.1).
n.2: The lessons log records lessons, not product defects, and the issue register holds formal issues, not lessons (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, management products map).
n.3: Assessing previous lessons remains an activity in starting up a project; social learning adds to it rather than replacing it (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.1).

Agile: People & Change.q:
Which two statements about how PRINCE2 Project Management addresses people are correct?
1. People is one of the five integrated elements of the method.
2. People guidance starts to apply once the project board has approved the PID.
3. Projects should involve key people critical to success even if they hold no formal role.
4. The people element replaces the need for defined roles and responsibilities.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
Agile: People & Change.w: People is one of the five integrated elements (statement 1), and projects must involve key people who are impacted or critical to success even when they hold no formal role (statement 3) (PRINCE2 7 manual 1.2 and 3.1, PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: people factors are addressed throughout the lifecycle, from pre-project onwards, not from PID approval (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.5.1).
n.1: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: people guidance applies throughout, and the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle still applies (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: defined roles, responsibilities and relationships remain a principle; the people element works alongside them (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.5.1).

Agile: People & Change.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile define organizational change management (OCM)?
o: The procedure for controlling changes to approved baselines within the issues practice
A plan that guides the adoption of agility across several projects and initiatives
The means by which an organization moves from its current state to a target state
The arrangements that define how finished products are accepted into operational use
Agile: People & Change.w: OCM is the means by which an organization transitions from its current state to a target state (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).

n.0: Controlling changes to baselines is change control, handled by the issues practice; OCM is about the organization's transition (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1, 11.3).
n.1: A plan for adopting agility across several initiatives is the agile transformation plan, a product that can support OCM rather than its definition (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.1).
n.3: Acceptance into operational use concerns transition to operations and closure, not the definition of OCM (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).

Agile: People & Change.q: PRINCE2 Agile notes that one PRINCE2 Project Management product can be tailored for use outside a project to define the target organizational state for introducing the agile mindset and values. Which management product is this?
o: Change management approach
Communication management approach
Quality management approach
Benefits management approach
Agile: People & Change.w: The change management approach can be tailored for use outside a project to define the target organizational state for the agile mindset and values, and how the business moves there from the current state (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1, Table 4.1).

n.1: The communication management approach defines the means and frequency of communication and feedback, not the target organizational state (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4, Table 4.1).
n.2: The quality management approach covers quality standards, agile ways of working and testing for the project's products, not the organization's target state (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, quality practice).
n.3: The benefits management approach defines benefits management actions and reviews, not the target organizational state (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 6.1).

Agile: People & Change.q: Besides the target state, what can a change management approach describe, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
o: The procedure for raising requests for change against the project backlog
The schedule of benefits reviews to be held after the final release
The criteria the CPO uses to prioritize the epics in the project backlog
Any interim states the business passes through on the way to the target
Agile: People & Change.w: The change management approach can define the target organizational state and how the business will shift from the current state through any interim states (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1, Table 4.1).

n.0: Raising and handling requests for change is set out in the issue management approach, not the change management approach (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, issues practice).
n.1: The schedule of benefits reviews belongs in the benefits management approach (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 6.1).
n.2: How the CPO prioritizes epics is part of managing the project backlog in the plans practice, not the change management approach (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, plans practice).

Agile: People & Change.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.

During the project initiation workshop, the team may decide that the [?] should replace the change management approach when the organization's move to agile working needs it.
o: project canvas
agile transformation plan
communication management approach
release map
Agile: People & Change.w: When the management approaches are co-created in the project initiation workshop, the agile transformation plan can replace the change management approach if needed (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.7).

n.0: The project canvas summarizes the project and its business case; it is refined in initiation but does not replace the change management approach (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.7).
n.2: The communication management approach is a separate approach agreed alongside the change management approach, not a replacement for it (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.6).
n.3: The release map replaces the project and stage plans, not the change management approach (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, plans practice).

Agile: People & Change.q: A water company is deciding how much detail to put in the change management approach for its move to agile working. Which consideration does PRINCE2 Agile highlight as key to making the changes last?
o: The size of the budget set aside for external training courses
The number of delivery teams that will work in parallel
The reporting frequency agreed for the project dashboards
The evolving culture and ways to stop changes being rolled back
Agile: People & Change.w: Among the points that shape the approach's level of detail, the evolving culture and ways to make sure changes are not rolled back after the transformation are what make the change last (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).

n.0: Learning and upskilling needs are a consideration, but the size of a training budget is not what the book highlights for making change last (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).
n.1: The number of delivery teams affects the organization practice and scaling, not how the change management approach secures lasting change (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 7.3.1).
n.2: Dashboard frequency is a progress control; it does not stop new ways of working being rolled back (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).

Agile: People & Change.q: A bank is piloting agile working on one project and asks whether it needs an agile transformation plan yet. What does PRINCE2 Agile suggest?
o: Write an agile transformation plan before the pilot's initiation stage begins
Record the transition steps in the project canvas instead of a separate product
Update the change management approach, as a plan may not be needed for one pilot
Ask the agile coach to replace the communication management approach with a plan
Agile: People & Change.w: An agile transformation plan typically spans several projects for organization-wide adoption; for a single pilot it may not be needed yet, and the change management approach can be updated instead (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.1).

n.0: The book suggests a transformation plan may not be needed for a single pilot, so writing one first is not its suggestion (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.1).
n.1: The project canvas summarizes the project and its business case; the transition is described in the change management approach (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).
n.3: Where a transformation plan is used, it can replace the change management approach, not the communication management approach (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.7).

Agile: People & Change.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes organizational change management (OCM) from change control in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: OCM is handled by the issues practice; change control by the change management approach
OCM moves the organization to a target state; change control manages changes to baselines
OCM covers user groups outside the project; change control covers supplier contracts
OCM is used in traditional projects; change control is used in agile projects
Agile: People & Change.w: OCM is about the organization's transition from current to target state, supported by the change management approach; change control handles changes to approved baselines through the issues practice (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1, 11.3).

n.0: This reverses the two: change control sits in the issues practice, while the change management approach supports OCM (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).
n.2: OCM covers everyone affected by the change, and change control covers changes to baselines, not supplier contracts (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1, 4.2.2).
n.3: Both apply in agile projects; PRINCE2 Agile uses OCM for people's transition and the issues practice for controlling baseline changes (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).

Agile: People & Change.q:
Which two statements about organizational change management (OCM) in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. OCM is the means of moving an organization from its current state to a target state.
2. OCM is a technique used to control changes to the project backlog.
3. The change management approach can describe how the business moves through interim states.
4. The change management approach is replaced by the release map in agile projects.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: People & Change.w: OCM is the move from current to target state (statement 1), and the change management approach can describe the shift through any interim states (statement 3) (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1, Table 4.1).

n.1: Statement 2 is wrong: controlling changes to the project backlog is change control in the issues practice, not OCM (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 11.3).
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: OCM is not backlog change control, and the release map replaces project and stage plans, not the change management approach (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: if anything replaces the change management approach it is the agile transformation plan, not the release map (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.7).

Agile: People & Change.q: How does PRINCE2 Project Management, on which PRINCE2 Agile builds, define culture?
o: The formal structure of authority and reporting lines in an organization
The set of shared attitudes, values, goals and practices of a group
The agreed ways of working recorded in the project's management approaches
The policies and standards an organization requires its projects to follow
Agile: People & Change.w: Culture is the set of shared attitudes, values, goals and practices; PRINCE2 Agile builds on this when it asks how the evolving culture will be handled in organizational change (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3, PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).

n.0: Authority and reporting lines describe organizational structure, which is only one thing a change may alter; it is not the definition of culture (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3).
n.2: Agreed ways of working are written down in the management approaches; culture is how people actually think and behave, and the two can drift apart (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3).
n.3: Policies and standards are formal requirements set by the organization; culture is the shared attitudes, values, goals and practices behind behaviour (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3).

Agile: People & Change.q: An organization trained its staff in agile techniques, but most teams soon returned to their old ways of working. According to PRINCE2 Agile, what was MOST LIKELY missing?
o: A larger budget for agile tools, software licences and coaching
More frequent progress reports from the teams to senior managers
Stricter compliance audits on the use of the new agile techniques
Work on evolving the culture so the changes were not rolled back
Agile: People & Change.w: When planning the change, PRINCE2 Agile highlights the evolving culture and ways to make sure changes are not rolled back after the transformation; training without a cultural shift does not make change stick (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).

n.0: Money for tools and licences does not by itself make new behaviours last; the book points to the evolving culture (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).
n.1: Communication and reporting matter, but they are not what the book identifies as most important for preventing change being rolled back (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1).
n.2: Compliance checks address symptoms; persistent non-compliance signals that ways of working no longer fit the culture (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3).

Agile: People & Change.q: In PRINCE2 Project Management, what is persistent non-compliance with the project's agreed processes a leading indicator of?
o: The agreed ways of working no longer fit the emerging culture
The project has exceeded its stage tolerances and needs an exception plan
The project assurance role has not yet been appointed by the executive
The team members need formal disciplinary action from the project manager
Agile: People & Change.w: Persistent non-compliance with project processes is a leading indicator that the agreed ways of working no longer match the emerging culture, so feedback should be gathered and acted on (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3).

n.1: A forecast breach of stage tolerance is an exception raised through an exception report; non-compliance with processes signals a culture mismatch (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, progress practice).
n.2: Project assurance gives independent assurance to the board; its absence is not what non-compliance indicates (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 7.3.1).
n.3: The method treats the pattern as a signal to review the fit of the ways of working, not as a disciplinary matter (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3).

Agile: People & Change.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile treat culture as important in organizational change management (OCM), rather than focusing on new processes and tools alone?
o: Culture sets the tolerances within which the project board can approve change
Culture is recorded in the project canvas and stays fixed for the whole project
New ways of working last when the culture evolves to support them
Culture determines which agile framework the delivery teams must use
Agile: People & Change.w: Processes and tools can be introduced quickly, but new ways of working only stick when the culture evolves with them, which is why the change management approach considers the evolving culture and how to stop changes being rolled back (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1, 4.2.3).

n.0: Tolerances are set by the business layer and project board; they are not set by culture (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, progress practice).
n.1: The project canvas summarizes the project and its business case; culture evolves over time rather than being fixed in a document (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3).
n.3: The choice of agile approach is a tailoring decision made for the project, not something culture prescribes (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, tailoring).

Agile: People & Change.q: A retail chain rewards teams with bonus points for modelling agile values. What does PRINCE2 Agile say about relying on such incentives to make change last?
o: They need balancing with intangible motivators such as purpose and recognition
They are the most reliable way to stop teams returning to old ways of working
They should replace retrospectives as the main way to reinforce agile values
They should be set by the project executive and recorded in the project canvas
Agile: People & Change.w: Value-based incentives such as points can help, but they cannot guarantee that changes stay; they should be balanced with intangible motivators, such as purpose and recognition, and with personal values (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.5).

n.1: The book warns that financial or points incentives cannot by themselves guarantee lasting change; evolving the culture is what makes change stick (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1, 4.5).
n.2: Retrospectives remain the place to learn and improve; team values can even be used in peer assessment during retrospectives (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4, 4.5).
n.3: Team incentives are not a project canvas item; the canvas summarizes the project and its business case (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, business case practice).

Agile: People & Change.q: Teams have adopted stand-ups and iterations but follow them by rote. Which statement about 'doing agile' and 'being agile' explains the effect on culture?
o: Doing agile changes the culture; being agile changes the processes and tools
Being agile brings a lasting cultural shift; doing agile alone may give short-term gains
Being agile applies to delivery teams; doing agile applies to the project board
Doing agile builds long-term resilience; being agile brings short-term efficiency
Agile: People & Change.w: Being agile is thinking in an agile way and being allowed to apply that mindset; it creates cultural shift and long-term resilience, whereas doing agile on its own may give short-term efficiency without lasting impact (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3.1).

n.0: This reverses the two: doing agile is applying frameworks, processes and terms, and being agile is the mindset that shifts culture (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3.1).
n.2: Being and doing agile are not split by level of the project management team; both apply to everyone involved (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3.1).
n.3: This reverses the contrast: long-term resilience comes from being agile, short-term efficiency from doing agile alone (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3.1).

Agile: People & Change.q: Leaders order every team to work in two-week iterations without explaining why. In PRINCE2 Agile terms, which risk to the change does this create?
o: The teams will exceed their time tolerance in the first iteration
The project canvas will need to be rewritten by the delivery teams
Teams may follow the new routine without the mindset, so it may not last
The agile coach will have to take over the role of project executive
Agile: People & Change.w: Imposing a framework without the 'why' risks doing agile without being agile: teams follow the routine rigidly, and without a cultural shift the change gives short-term mechanics rather than lasting impact (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3.1, 4.2.1).

n.0: Time has zero tolerance at every level of plan in PRINCE2 Agile, and nothing in the situation forecasts a breach (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1).
n.1: The project canvas is led by the project executive and refined in initiation; the announcement does not affect it (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.1).
n.3: The agile coach removes organization-level blockers and supports leaders; it does not take over the project executive role (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, roles).

Agile: People & Change.q: In PRINCE2 Project Management, what should the project management team do to keep the agreed ways of working aligned with the emerging culture?
o: Fix the ways of working in the PID and treat any deviation as an exception
Ask project assurance to audit compliance at the end of every stage
Replace the team members who do not follow the agreed processes
Gather and act on feedback about how people are actually working
Agile: People & Change.w: Feedback should be gathered and acted on so that the defined ways of working stay aligned with how people actually work, as culture keeps evolving (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3).

n.0: Exceptions concern forecast breaches of tolerance; freezing the ways of working ignores the evolving culture the method asks teams to respond to (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3).
n.1: Audits can show non-compliance, but the method's response is to understand and adapt through feedback, not to rely on stage-end checks (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3).
n.2: Non-compliance is treated as a sign that ways of working no longer fit the culture, not as a reason to replace people (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.3).

Agile: People & Change.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile define a stakeholder in organizational change management?
o: Any person who holds a formal role within the project management team structure
Any member of the business layer who funds or sponsors the change initiative
Any user who will operate the new products once they are released into service
Anyone who can affect, be affected by, or feel affected by the change initiative
Agile: People & Change.w: A stakeholder is any individual, group or organization that can affect, be affected by, or perceive itself to be affected by the change initiative (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).

n.0: Holders of formal project roles are stakeholders, but so are many people with no project role who are affected by the change (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).
n.1: Funders and sponsors are stakeholders, but the definition reaches anyone who can affect or is affected by the change (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).
n.2: Future users are stakeholders, but the definition also covers those who influence the change or perceive themselves to be affected (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).

Agile: People & Change.q: In organizational change management, PRINCE2 Agile asks the project to identify key influencers as well as stakeholders. Which description fits key influencers?
o: Senior managers who approve the funding for the change initiative
Specialists with the deepest technical knowledge of the new products
People whose network lets them shape how the majority view the change
Suppliers whose delivery teams build and maintain the new products
Agile: People & Change.w: Key influencers are those who can shape the perception of the majority in the organizational ecosystem and, through their network, have the greatest influence on adoption of the change and realization of benefits (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).

n.0: Seniority and budget approval do not make someone a key influencer; influence over adoption comes through their network (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).
n.1: Technical expertise does not by itself give someone the network influence over how the majority view the change (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).
n.3: Suppliers build the products, but they do not usually shape how the people adopting the change perceive it (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).

Agile: People & Change.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

Key influencers matter in organizational change management because their [?] allows them to sway how widely the change is adopted and whether its benefits are realized.
o: formal authority
network
budget control
technical expertise
Agile: People & Change.w: It is through their network that key influencers shape the perception of the majority and most influence adoption of the change outcomes and realization of benefits (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).

n.0: Formal authority comes from a role; key influencers are defined by their influence through their network, and may hold no formal role (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).
n.2: Control of a budget belongs to roles such as the project executive; it is not what defines a key influencer (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).
n.3: Technical experts may know the product best, but expertise is not what lets someone shape the majority's view (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).

Agile: People & Change.q: A housing association is rolling out a new repairs app to its tenant liaison officers. Which person is MOST LIKELY to be a key influencer for adoption of the app among the officers?
o: A long-serving liaison officer whom colleagues turn to for advice
The supplier's lead developer who designed the app's architecture
The finance director who signed off the project's budget
A newly appointed tester who checks the app against acceptance criteria
Agile: People & Change.w: A trusted, well-connected officer can shape how the majority of colleagues perceive the app, which is what makes someone a key influencer (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).

n.1: The supplier's developer has technical knowledge but little network influence among the liaison officers who must adopt the app (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).
n.2: The finance director is a stakeholder with authority over money, but seniority is not what shapes the officers' view of the app (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).
n.3: A tester assures quality against acceptance criteria; a new appointee has little network influence over the officers (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).

Agile: People & Change.q: A health board's project manager plans to identify key influencers in each clinic early in the project. Why is this useful, according to PRINCE2 Agile and PRINCE2 Project Management?
o: They approve each release before it goes into operational use
They replace the chief product owner in prioritizing the project backlog
They can help co-create products and messages that drive adoption
They hold the authority to set the project's time and cost tolerances
Agile: People & Change.w: Users and key influencers can be involved in co-creating products and ways of working, and messaging works better when shaped with key influencers, both of which help the change to be adopted (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.3, PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2, 4.4).

n.0: Release and acceptance decisions follow the agreed acceptance arrangements in the project backlog and Definition of Done, not approval by key influencers (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, quality practice).
n.1: The CPO owns the project backlog and sets priorities across teams; key influencers do not replace that role (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, roles).
n.3: Project tolerances are set by the business layer and the project board, not by key influencers (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, progress practice).

Agile: People & Change.q: Which statement about stakeholders in an agile change initiative is correct, according to PRINCE2 Agile and PRINCE2 Project Management?
o: Key people critical to success may hold no formal role in the project
Stakeholders are limited to those named in the project management team structure
The list of stakeholders is fixed at initiation and is not revisited later
People who merely believe they are affected fall outside the stakeholder definition
Agile: People & Change.w: Projects must involve key people who are impacted by the change or critical to its success, even when they hold no formal role (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.1, PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).

n.1: The definition reaches anyone who can affect or is affected by the change, well beyond the project management team (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).
n.2: Stakeholder relationships change over time, and stages often mark a change in influencers, so engagement is revisited (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.2, 3.5.1).
n.3: The definition explicitly includes those who perceive themselves to be affected by the change (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).

Agile: People & Change.q: In PRINCE2 Project Management, how should stakeholder relationships be treated as a project moves through its stages?
o: They are set in the starting up workshop and remain stable until closure
They are owned by project support, who keep the stakeholder records up to date
They are handed to the business layer once the PID has been approved
They change over time, so engagement continues and is reviewed throughout
Agile: People & Change.w: Stakeholder relationships change over time, and stage boundaries often mark a change in influencers and key relationships, so engagement is kept under review (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.2, 3.5.1).

n.0: The starting up workshop aligns on roles and lessons; relationships keep changing after it, and new influencers often appear at stage boundaries (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.2, 3.5.1).
n.1: Project support can help with administration and stakeholder analysis, but managing relationships in the project ecosystem is not handed to it (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, roles).
n.2: The business layer commissions the project; stakeholder engagement stays with the project management team throughout (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.2.2).

Agile: People & Change.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an OCM stakeholder from a key influencer?
o: A stakeholder holds a formal project role; a key influencer advises the project board
Anyone affected is a stakeholder; a key influencer shapes how the majority view the change
A stakeholder works inside the organization; a key influencer is an external expert
A stakeholder funds the change initiative; a key influencer delivers the new products
Agile: People & Change.w: A stakeholder is anyone who can affect, be affected by, or perceive themselves affected by the change; a key influencer is a stakeholder who, through their network, shapes the perception of the majority and so drives adoption (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).

n.0: Stakeholders need not hold a project role, and key influencers are defined by network influence, not by advising the board (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).
n.2: Stakeholders can be inside or outside the organization, and key influencers are defined by the influence their network gives them, not by being external experts (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).
n.3: Funding is not what makes someone a stakeholder, and delivering products is the work of delivery teams, not the mark of a key influencer (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.2).

Agile: People & Change.q: How do frequent releases support organizational change management, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
o: They allow the change to be adopted incrementally and smoothly
They let the teams postpone testing until the final release
They remove the need for a benefits management approach
They let the project board leave out stage boundaries
Agile: People & Change.w: Frequent releases support OCM by allowing incremental and smooth adoption of the change (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).

n.1: Agile projects test frequently, and frequent testing is itself listed as an OCM enabler because it increases user engagement (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).
n.2: Frequent releases bring benefits earlier, which the benefits management approach still plans and reviews (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, business case practice).
n.3: Management stages and their boundaries remain part of PRINCE2 Agile governance whatever the release frequency (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, processes).

Agile: People & Change.q: How does having users represented in the delivery team support organizational change management, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
o: It replaces the need for progress reviews and demos with users
It lets the project board delegate benefits reviews to the users
It means the system can be released without user acceptance
It facilitates adoption of the change across the organization
Agile: People & Change.w: Having users represented in the delivery team facilitates organizational adoption of the change (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).

n.0: Progress reviews with demos are a separate OCM enabler that engages users and speeds adoption; user representation does not replace them (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).
n.1: Benefits reviews are planned in the benefits management approach; user representation is about adoption, not delegating benefits reviews (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).
n.2: Products are still accepted against agreed criteria and the Definition of Done; having users in the team does not remove acceptance (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, quality practice).

Agile: People & Change.q: Which benefit to organizational change management does PRINCE2 Agile link to progress reviews that include demos?
o: They give the project board a formal point to approve the next stage
They replace retrospectives as the place to agree process improvements
They engage users and help to speed up adoption of the change
They set the time and cost tolerances for the next iteration
Agile: People & Change.w: Progress reviews, including demos, enable user engagement and improve the speed of adoption (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).

n.0: Approval of the next stage is a project board decision in directing a project after managing a stage boundary, not the purpose of a progress review (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, processes).
n.1: Retrospectives are the separate enabler for learning lessons and improving adoption; demos do not replace them (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).
n.3: Time and cost have zero tolerance at every level of plan in PRINCE2 Agile, and tolerances are not set in progress reviews (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1).

Agile: People & Change.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, what do retrospectives contribute to organizational change management?
o: A way to track progress against the iteration goal while the iteration runs
A chance to learn lessons and act on them to improve adoption of the change
A formal review of the benefits realized since the previous release
A decision point for the CPO to reprioritize the whole project backlog
Agile: People & Change.w: Retrospectives give opportunities to learn lessons and act on them to improve adoption of the change (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).

n.0: Retrospectives happen at the end of an iteration, so they are not used to track progress while it is running (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).
n.2: Benefits reviews are planned in the benefits management approach; a retrospective looks at how the team works and what it has learned (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).
n.3: The CPO prioritizes the project backlog as part of managing it; that is not what retrospectives contribute to OCM (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, roles).

Agile: People & Change.q: How does frequent testing support organizational change management, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
o: It lets the business delay user training until after project closure
It increases the engagement of users with the change
It replaces the need for a Definition of Done for each team
It moves acceptance decisions from the users to the testers
Agile: People & Change.w: Frequent testing increases user engagement with the change, which supports its adoption (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).

n.0: Frequent testing engages users during delivery; it gives no reason to delay training until after closure (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).
n.2: The Definition of Done remains the agreed standard that work must meet; frequent testing checks against it rather than replacing it (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, quality practice).
n.3: Testers check work against acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done, but acceptance stays with the users and the agreed acceptor (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, roles).

Agile: People & Change.q: Which is NOT one of the agile ways of working that PRINCE2 Agile links to supporting organizational change management?
o: Regular feedback during iterations and after releases
User representation in the delivery team
One release of the complete product at the end of the project
Retrospectives whose lessons improve how the change is adopted
Agile: People & Change.w: PRINCE2 Agile links OCM to frequent releases, user representation, frequent testing, progress reviews with demos, retrospectives and regular feedback; a single release at the end works against incremental adoption (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).

n.0: Regular feedback, during iterations and after releases, is one of the listed ways agile working supports OCM (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).
n.1: User representation in the delivery team is listed because it facilitates organizational adoption (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).
n.3: Retrospectives are listed because they give opportunities to learn lessons and improve adoption (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).

Agile: People & Change.q: PRINCE2 Agile lists regular feedback as one way agile working supports organizational change management. At which points does it say this feedback can be incorporated?
o: At stage boundaries and in the project closure workshop
In the project initiation workshop and at project closure
In end stage reports and in the end project report
During iterations and after a release
Agile: People & Change.w: Regular feedback can be incorporated both during iterations and after a release, so the change is shaped while it is being delivered (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).

n.0: Stage boundaries and closure are governance points; the OCM enabler is feedback built into iterations and after releases (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).
n.1: Initiation and closure are too far apart to give the regular feedback the book describes (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).
n.2: End stage and end project reports are progress reports to the board, not the user feedback loops the book links to OCM (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).

Agile: People & Change.q: A charity's delivery team holds demos with volunteers at each progress review and releases new features every month. Which pair of organizational change management effects does PRINCE2 Agile link to these two practices?
o: Demos engage users and speed adoption; frequent releases allow smooth, incremental adoption
Demos replace user acceptance; frequent releases remove the need for training volunteers
Demos let the board approve each stage; frequent releases fix the full scope early
Demos record lessons in the lessons log; frequent releases reduce the testing needed
Agile: People & Change.w: Progress reviews with demos enable user engagement and faster adoption, and frequent releases allow incremental and smooth adoption of change (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).

n.1: Demos engage users but do not replace acceptance, and frequent releases do not remove the need to prepare people for the change (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).
n.2: Stage approval is a project board decision, and agile projects flex scope below the Must haves rather than fixing it all early (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1).
n.3: Lessons are linked to retrospectives, and frequent releases go with frequent testing rather than less of it (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4).

Agile: People & Change.q: What does PRINCE2 Agile say about allocating people to the roles in a project team?
o: Agile teams are self-managing, so the defined roles are not used in agile projects
The project board should hold all delivery roles itself to keep control of the work
One person per role is ideal but often impractical, so roles may be combined or shared
Each person should hold at least two roles so that knowledge is spread across the team
Agile: People & Change.w: Ideally each role is held by one person, but this is often impractical, so roles can be combined or shared (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.2).

n.0: PRINCE2 Agile defines 11 roles and keeps them in agile projects; self-management works within the boundaries those roles set (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.2, 7.3.1).
n.1: The board directs and delegates; delivery roles sit with product owners, team coaches, developers and testers (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 7.3.1).
n.3: Combining roles is an allowance when one person per role is impractical, not a target for every team member (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.2).

Agile: People & Change.q: A rail infrastructure project uses delivery teams from two companies and several external advisers. According to PRINCE2 Agile, what helps people work effectively across these organizational and cultural boundaries?
o: Placing every external adviser under the direct authority of the product owner
Setting clear boundaries within which people are free to flex
Asking each company to keep following its own decision-making rules
Holding all decisions at project board level until trust has been built
Agile: People & Change.w: When working across organizations and cultures, PRINCE2 Agile recommends clear boundaries within which people can flex, for example a delegation matrix showing what advisers decide or advise on (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.1).

n.0: The product owner has direct authority over delivery team members; the guidance for advisers is to clarify what they decide or advise on, not to place them under the PO (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.1, 7.3.1).
n.2: Separate decision-making rules in each company leave people unclear about who decides what; the book asks for shared, clear boundaries (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.1).
n.3: Holding decisions at board level runs against local decision-making and the freedom to flex within agreed boundaries (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.1).

Agile: People & Change.q: A project uses external legal and data protection advisers alongside its delivery teams. Which tool does PRINCE2 Agile suggest for making clear which decisions these advisers take and which they advise on?
o: Delegation matrix
Team skill matrix
Project canvas
Burn-up chart
Agile: People & Change.w: A delegation matrix makes responsibilities and decision-making authority transparent, for example what external advisers decide or advise on (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.1, 7.4.3).

n.1: A team skill matrix shows current and planned skills, strengths and gaps, not decision-making authority (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 7.4.1).
n.2: The project canvas is a one-page summary of the project and its business case (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, business case practice).
n.3: A burn-up chart shows work completed over time, not who makes decisions (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, progress practice).

Agile: People & Change.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, which action is MOST LIKELY to build social cohesion in a hybrid team whose members are spread across several cities?
o: Requiring all team members to work from the same office every day
Running all online meetings to a strict, formal agenda
Replacing face-to-face workshops with written status updates
Arranging synchronized co-location days for key people and teams
Agile: People & Change.w: For remote and hybrid teams, PRINCE2 Agile suggests synchronized co-location days for key people and teams, plus time for less structured conversation online, to build social cohesion (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.3).

n.0: Mandating full-time co-location is not the book's answer; it suggests planned, synchronized co-location days for key people (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.3).
n.1: Strict formal agendas leave no room for the less structured conversation that helps remote people build cohesion (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.3).
n.2: Written updates reduce contact between people; social cohesion grows when people meet purposefully and regularly (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.3).

Agile: People & Change.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile suggest allowing time for less structured conversation when teams meet online?
o: It reduces the number of formal reports the team must produce
It removes the need for team planning and retrospective workshops
It lets the project manager monitor each person's productivity
It helps build social cohesion and trust within the team
Agile: People & Change.w: Allowing time for less structured conversation online is one of the ways PRINCE2 Agile suggests remote and hybrid teams build social cohesion (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.3, PRINCE2 7 manual 3.3.3).

n.0: Informal conversation does not change the reporting the team agreed; dashboards and reports are set by the progress practice (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, progress practice).
n.1: Team planning and retrospectives are still held; informal time adds to them rather than replacing them (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, managing product delivery).
n.2: The purpose is cohesion and trust between people, not monitoring individuals (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.3).

Agile: People & Change.q: According to PRINCE2 Project Management, why do temporary project teams often need a different leadership style from established teams?
o: Authority is harder to exercise, and members may be more senior than the PM
Temporary teams sit outside the organization's policies and standards
Temporary teams need little trust, as they disband after project closure
The project board leads temporary teams directly, bypassing the PM
Agile: People & Change.w: A temporary leader finds authority harder to exercise, and it is not unusual for team members to be more senior than the project manager, so leadership relies on collaboration and influence (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.3, summarized in PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3).

n.1: Projects work within the organizational ecosystem and its policies and standards, so temporary teams are not outside them (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.1).
n.2: Building trust across silos and social cohesion matters especially in temporary teams (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.3.3).
n.3: The project manager manages the project day to day within tolerances set by the board; the board directs rather than leading teams directly (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 7.3.1).

Agile: People & Change.q: What does PRINCE2 Project Management mean by cultural intelligence when leading teams across organizations?
o: Knowing the history and structure of each organization involved
The ability to relate to and work with people across different cultures
Adopting the culture of the largest supplier for the whole project
Measuring each organization's culture with the Agilometer before initiation
Agile: People & Change.w: Cultural intelligence is the ability to relate and work across cultures within the organizational ecosystem, which leaders need when teams span organizational boundaries (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.3.1).

n.0: Knowing an organization's history and structure is useful background, but cultural intelligence is the ability to relate and work across cultures (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.3.1).
n.2: Imposing one organization's culture ignores the others; cultural intelligence is about working across cultures (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.3.1).
n.3: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working, not each organization's culture (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 10.3.2).

Agile: People & Change.q:
Which two statements about leading teams across organizations are correct, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
1. Clear boundaries should be set within which people can flex.
2. Mandating full-time co-location is the best way to build social cohesion.
3. Roles may be combined or shared when one person per role is impractical.
4. External advisers should take all decisions in their own specialist area.
o: 1 and 4
2 and 3
1 and 3
2 and 4
Agile: People & Change.w: PRINCE2 Agile recommends clear boundaries within which people can flex (statement 1) and accepts that roles may be combined or shared (statement 3) (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.1, 4.3.2).

n.0: Statement 4 is wrong: a delegation matrix clarifies which decisions advisers take and which they only advise on (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.1).
n.1: Statement 2 is wrong: the book suggests synchronized co-location days for key people, not mandated full-time co-location (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.3).
n.3: Both statements are wrong: co-location is planned for key people rather than mandated, and advisers' decision rights are set out in a delegation matrix (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.3.1, 4.3.3).

Agile: People & Change.q: What is the purpose of the communication management approach in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: To describe the agile behaviours and ways of working expected of the teams
To describe how changes to the project backlog will be controlled
To set out the reports that the project manager sends to the project board
To define how and how often information and feedback flow across the ecosystem
Agile: People & Change.w: The communication management approach defines the means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, everyone across the project ecosystem (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4, Table 4.1).

n.0: Agile behaviours and ways of working are described in the quality management approach, not the communication management approach (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 4.1, quality practice).
n.1: Controlling changes to the project backlog is set out in the issue management approach (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, issues practice).
n.2: Reports to the board are part of communication, but the approach covers communication and feedback with the whole ecosystem, not one reporting line (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).

Agile: People & Change.q: A project manager says the communication management approach must give a controlled, bidirectional flow of information. What does PRINCE2 Agile mean by describing communication in this way?
o: Listening and gathering feedback matter as much as sending information out
The project manager and the CPO share responsibility for sending messages
Each message is sent twice, once in writing and once in a meeting
Users and suppliers receive the same messages at the same time
Agile: People & Change.w: Bidirectional communication is as much about listening as about broadcasting: it gathers feedback and concerns as well as sending information (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).

n.1: Bidirectional refers to information flowing both out to and back from stakeholders, not to two senders sharing the work (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).
n.2: Repeating a message in two formats is still one-way broadcasting; bidirectional means receiving feedback too (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).
n.3: Sending identical messages to all groups is generic messaging, which the book says is rarely effective (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).

Agile: People & Change.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile say that generic messaging is rarely effective in organizational change?
o: Generic messages breach the confidentiality terms in the commercial management approach
Different groups have different concerns, so messages should be tailored to each
Generic messages need approval from project assurance before they are released
Agile teams rely on dashboards, so written messages are seldom read by anyone
Agile: People & Change.w: Generic messaging is rarely effective; the communication management approach allows messages to be tailored to each group, working with key influencers from user, supplier and business groups (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).

n.0: The commercial management approach covers procurement and contracts; the problem with generic messages is that they do not fit each group's concerns (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).
n.2: Project assurance monitors adherence and governance for the board; it is not an approval step for messages (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, roles).
n.3: Dashboards support transparency, but the book's reason is that untailored messages miss what each group cares about (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).

Agile: People & Change.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, why is periodic reporting on its own not enough for project communication?
o: Reports are usually too detailed for the project board to read in time
Reports come from project support and so carry too little authority
People may shape reports to what seems acceptable, so they can be biased
Reports are replaced by Agilometer assessments in agile projects
Agile: People & Change.w: Periodic reporting alone is not sufficient because reports can be biased: people adjust what they report to what seems acceptable, so other feedback routes are needed (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).

n.0: The book's concern is bias in what is reported, not the level of detail (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).
n.1: Who compiles a report is not the issue the book raises; its concern is that people adjust what they report to what seems acceptable, so reports can be biased (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).
n.3: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working; it does not replace progress reporting (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 10.3.2).

Agile: People & Change.q: A project manager notices that most news about the project spreads through informal chats and messaging groups rather than formal channels. What does PRINCE2 Agile recommend in response?
o: Restrict project information to formal reports so that messages stay consistent
Ask project assurance to monitor informal conversations between the teams
Accept it, and give people shareable formats and several feedback paths
Hold a weekly briefing to replace informal exchanges between team members
Agile: People & Change.w: Most communication happens outside formal channels; the book advises accepting this, providing information in formats people can share, and offering multiple feedback paths (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).

n.0: Trying to restrict information to formal reports fights how people actually communicate; the book says to accept informal channels (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).
n.1: Project assurance provides independent assurance to the board; monitoring informal conversations is not its role (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, roles).
n.3: A briefing can help, but replacing informal exchanges is not the aim; the book says to work with them (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).

Agile: People & Change.q: How should communication for a remote team differ from that for a co-located team, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
o: It can rely on information being shared organically between colleagues
It is handed over to project support to reduce the load on the team
It is limited to the written reports defined in the project initiation documentation
It needs a more deliberate, structured approach, including how information flows
Agile: People & Change.w: Remote teams need a more deliberate and structured approach: clarity on how information flows, suitable formats, key relationships identified, and agreed structured and unstructured time together (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).

n.0: Organic sharing is what co-located teams benefit from; remote teams need deliberate methods instead (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4, PRINCE2 7 manual 3.3.3).
n.1: Project support helps with administration, but communication for remote teams needs agreed structure involving the team itself (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).
n.2: Relying on written reports alone is not enough, and the book asks for both structured and unstructured time together (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).

Agile: People & Change.q: How does a well-designed communication management approach help with risk, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Listening to stakeholders can surface concerns before they become risks
It replaces the risk register as the record of stakeholder threats
It sets the risk appetite that the board agrees with the business
It removes the need for Agilometer assessments during initiation
Agile: People & Change.w: Because the approach is as much about listening as broadcasting, it helps surface concerns before they turn into risks (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).

n.1: Identified risks are still recorded in the risk register; the communication approach does not replace it (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book, risk practice).
n.2: Risk appetite is the amount of risk the business is willing to take; it is set by the business and applied by the project board, not set through the communication management approach (PRINCE2 7 manual ch 9).
n.3: The Agilometer is still assessed in the project initiation workshop; communication does not remove that need (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.7).

Agile: People & Change.q:
Which two statements about communication in a PRINCE2 Agile project are correct?
1. The communication management approach describes the agile behaviours the teams will follow.
2. Working with key influencers from user, supplier and business groups helps to tailor messages.
3. Communication should be as much about listening as about broadcasting.
4. Periodic reports give a full and unbiased picture of how people feel about the change.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
Agile: People & Change.w: Working with key influencers from user, supplier and business groups helps tailor messages (statement 2), and communication is as much about listening as broadcasting (statement 3) (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: agile behaviours belong in the quality management approach, not the communication management approach (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 4.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: periodic reporting alone is not enough and can be biased (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4).
n.3: Both statements are wrong: agile behaviours sit in the quality management approach, and periodic reports can be biased (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.4, Table 4.1).

Agile: People & Change.q: PRINCE2 Project Management, on which PRINCE2 Agile builds, is made up of five integrated elements. Which element covers the needs, capabilities and motivations of those involved in a project and the relationships between them?
o: People
Principles
Project context
Practices
Agile: People & Change.w: People is the integrated element concerned with the needs, capabilities and motivations of everyone involved and the relationships between them; it sits at the centre of the method (PRINCE2 7 manual 1.2, summarized in PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.1).

n.1: The principles are the guiding obligations and good practices that decide whether a project is genuinely PRINCE2; they do not describe people's needs and relationships (PRINCE2 7 manual 1.2).
n.2: The project context is the setting the method is applied in, such as the organizational and commercial context, delivery method and scale (PRINCE2 7 manual 1.2).
n.3: The practices are the seven aspects of project management, such as business case and risk, applied throughout the lifecycle (PRINCE2 7 manual 1.2).

Agile: People & Change.q: Which group does the people element of PRINCE2 Project Management cover?
o: The project board and the project manager, who hold the formal decision-making roles
Both the people working on the project and the people affected by what it delivers
The delivery teams, because they create the products the project hands over
The users who will operate the new system once it is released into service
Agile: People & Change.w: The people element covers those working on the project and those affected by it, such as staff in the business who must integrate the new products into their area (PRINCE2 7 manual 1.2 and 3.1, PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.1).

n.0: Board members and the project manager are part of the people element, but it also reaches every other team member and everyone affected by the project (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.1).
n.2: Delivery teams are inside the project team, but the element also covers the governance roles and the people affected by the change (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.1).
n.3: Future users are among the people affected, but the element also covers everyone working on the project (PRINCE2 7 manual 1.2).

Agile: People & Change.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.

PRINCE2 Project Management contrasts the existing organizational ecosystem of business, users and suppliers with the [?], which is the temporary set of people, relationships, structures and ways of working set up for the project.
o: business layer
project management team structure
project ecosystem
delivery team
Agile: People & Change.w: The project ecosystem is temporary and created for the project, where the business, user and supplier interests meet; the organizational ecosystem is what already exists (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.1).

n.0: The business layer is the permanent commissioning level outside the project; it is part of the existing organizational ecosystem (PRINCE2 7 manual ch 6).
n.1: The project management team structure is a management product showing roles and reporting lines, not the wider set of relationships and ways of working (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 7.3.2).
n.3: A delivery team is one group inside the project; the temporary whole that includes relationships and ways of working is the project ecosystem (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.1).

Agile: People & Change.q: PRINCE2 Project Management places people at the centre of the method and groups its people guidance into four parts. Which list shows those four parts?
o: Motivating teams, resolving conflict, coaching individuals and building trust
Analysing stakeholders, planning communication, training users and coaching teams
Leading teams, managing suppliers, shaping the culture and setting governance rules
Leading change, leading teams, communication, and people at the centre of the method
Agile: People & Change.w: The people guidance is shown as leading successful change, leading successful teams and communication, with people at the centre of the method (PRINCE2 7 QRG figure 3.3, summarized in PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.1).

n.0: Motivation, conflict and trust are topics within leading teams, not the four named parts of the people guidance (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.3).
n.1: Stakeholder analysis and communication planning belong inside the communication part; training and coaching are not named parts of the model (PRINCE2 7 manual 3.4).
n.2: Supplier management and governance rules are covered by the organization practice and commercial management approach, not by the four parts of the people guidance (PRINCE2 7 QRG figure 3.3).

Agile: Practices & Business Case.q:
Which two statements about the purposes of the PRINCE2 Agile practices are correct?
1. The issues practice collects and assesses issues and controls changes to the project's baseline.
2. The progress practice identifies, assesses and controls uncertainty to improve the chance of success.
3. The plans practice defines what is to be delivered and the means of delivering it, including who, how, where, when and how much.
4. The organization practice documents the users' requirements of the project products.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Practices & Business Case.w: Statement 1 is the issues purpose and statement 3 is the plans purpose, which defines the 'what' and the 'who, how, where, when and how much' in support of the business case's 'why' (see PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.1, 11.1).

n.0: Statement 2 describes the risk practice, not progress, which compares actual achievement with plan and controls deviations (book 10.1, 12.1).
n.2: Statement 2 describes risk rather than progress, and statement 4 describes quality rather than organization (book 9.1, 10.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: documenting users' requirements of the products is the quality purpose; organization sets up accountability and responsibilities (book 7.1, 9.1).

Agile: Practices & Business Case.q: PRINCE2 Agile links each practice to a question it helps the project to answer. Which question is linked to the business case practice?
o: What is acceptable to the users, and how can this be measured?
What now, when a product deviates from what was agreed?
What if something unexpected happens, and how should responses be planned?
Why does the project exist, and what should it stay aligned to?
Agile: Practices & Business Case.w: The business case practice answers why the project exists and what it must stay aligned to, which is why it underpins every decision on continued investment (see PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 5.2, 6.1).

n.0: What is acceptable to users and how to measure it is the question for the quality practice (book Table 5.2).
n.1: What to do when a product deviates from what was agreed is the question for the issues practice (book Table 5.2).
n.2: What happens if something unexpected occurs and how to respond is the question for the risk practice (book Table 5.2).

Agile: Practices & Business Case.q: A tester finds that a finished feature does not meet the acceptance criteria that were agreed for it. Which practice provides the means to capture and assess this and to control any resulting change to the project's baseline?
o: Issues
Quality
Risk
Progress
Agile: Practices & Business Case.w: A product that deviates from what was agreed is an issue. The issues practice collects and assesses issues and controls changes to the baseline, answering 'what now, when a product deviates from what was agreed?' (see PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 11.1, Table 5.2).

n.1: Quality documents users' requirements and how they will be met; once a product has deviated from what was agreed, capturing it and controlling baseline change is the issues purpose (book 9.1, 11.1).
n.2: Risk deals with uncertain events that may happen; this deviation has already happened, so it is an issue (book 10.1, 11.1).
n.3: Progress compares actual achievement with plan and handles deviations that cause an exception, not the assessment of an individual off-specification (book 11.1, 12.1).

Agile: Practices & Business Case.q: Which of the following is NOT part of the purpose of the progress practice?
o: Monitoring and comparing actual achievements against those planned
Providing a forecast for the project objectives and continued viability
Controlling changes to the project's baseline
Controlling any deviations that would cause an exception
Agile: Practices & Business Case.w: Controlling changes to the project's baseline belongs to the issues practice. The other three options together make up the progress purpose (see PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 11.1, 12.1).

n.0: Comparing actual achievements with those planned is part of the progress purpose (book 12.1).
n.1: Forecasting the project objectives and continued viability is part of the progress purpose (book 12.1).
n.3: Controlling deviations that would cause an exception is part of the progress purpose (book 12.1).

Agile: Practices & Business Case.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, what is the main challenge when merging project management with agile, and how is it handled?
o: Agile has no governance of its own, so PRINCE2 terms replace agile terms throughout the project
Agile terms are better understood by teams, so they replace all PRINCE2 management product names
There is no common ground in terminology, so a combination of both sets of terms is used
The two use different lifecycles, so the PRINCE2 processes are dropped in favour of agile events
Agile: Practices & Business Case.w: Project management and agile share no common terminology, so PRINCE2 Agile deliberately uses a mix of project management and agile terms, for example stage plan alongside release map (see PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 5.8).

n.0: PRINCE2 Agile does not replace agile language with PRINCE2 terms; it combines the two sets of terms (book 5.8).
n.1: PRINCE2 management products are kept, tailored or paired with agile artifacts; agile terms do not simply replace them (book 5.8, Table 5.2).
n.3: PRINCE2 Agile keeps the seven PRINCE2 processes and supports them with agile workshops; the stated merging challenge is terminology (book 5.8).

Agile: Practices & Business Case.q: Which agile term is used in PRINCE2 Agile alongside, or in place of, the PRINCE2 project plan and stage plan?
o: Team plan
Story map
Product backlog
Release map
Agile: Practices & Business Case.w: The release map shows the releases and iterations over time and serves as the project plan and the stage plan, so the two terms are used together (see PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.5, Table 8.1).

n.0: The team plan is still a team plan in PRINCE2 Agile: a detailed task-level plan for the next iteration, not the project or stage plan (book Table 8.1).
n.1: A story map breaks products into user stories; it feeds the release map but is not itself the project or stage plan (book 8.3.2.4).
n.2: The product backlog is the team-level list of user stories that tailors the product descriptions, not the plans (book 8.3.2.1).

Agile: Practices & Business Case.q: Which pairing of a PRINCE2 management product with the agile artifact used for it in PRINCE2 Agile is correct?
o: Checkpoint report and team dashboard
Highlight report and team dashboard
Product description and project backlog
Work package description and release map
Agile: Practices & Business Case.w: The team dashboard is used in place of the checkpoint report; the PM pulls team progress from it (see PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1).

n.1: The highlight report pairs with the project dashboard, not the team dashboard (book Table 12.1).
n.2: The project backlog tailors the project product description; product descriptions pair with the team product backlog (book 8.3.2.1).
n.3: A work package description in agile is a set of user stories; the release map pairs with the project and stage plans (book Table 8.1).

Agile: Practices & Business Case.q: A project manager agrees 'a set of user stories' with a product owner before the team starts an iteration. Which PRINCE2 management product does this set of user stories represent?
o: Product description
Work package description
Team plan
Project product description
Agile: Practices & Business Case.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the work package description is expressed as a set of user stories agreed between the project manager and the product owner (see PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 8.1, 7.3.1).

n.0: Product descriptions are tailored into the team product backlog, which the product owner owns; the agreed set of stories is the work package (book 8.3.2.1, Table 8.1).
n.2: The team plan is the delivery team's detailed task plan for the iteration, produced when it accepts the work package (book Table 8.1).
n.3: The project product description describes the overall project product and is tailored into the project backlog, which the CPO owns; it is not the agreed work for one team (book 8.3.2.1).

Agile: Practices & Business Case.q:
