n.3: A team skill matrix maps team capabilities and gaps, not role responsibilities.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: Which of the following would be included in the commercial management approach for a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: The structure chart showing the reporting lines in the project
The skill level each team member has in the key techniques
The level of delegation agreed for each team decision area
The delivery model and the resources for contract management
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: Typical content of the commercial management approach includes the delivery model, the resources for market engagement, procurement and contract management, responsibilities, tools and techniques, and standards (book Table 7.3).

n.0: A structure chart is content of the project management team structure.
n.1: Team members' skill levels belong in the team skill matrix.
n.2: Agreed delegation levels per decision area are recorded in the delegation matrix.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: A project manager is documenting how the people on a PRINCE2 Agile project will work together, including team working practices, how performance reviews will run and how members gain access to project systems. Which product should hold this?
o: Role descriptions
Commercial management approach
Team skill matrix
Project management team structure
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: The project management team structure includes a section on working practices and arrangements, which is where performance reviews and access to project systems are described, alongside the structure chart and summary of authority (book Table 7.3).

n.0: Role descriptions set out each role's specific responsibilities; working practices and arrangements sit in the team structure.
n.1: The commercial management approach covers procurement and contracts, not internal working practices.
n.2: The team skill matrix maps capabilities and gaps; it does not hold working practices or system access.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: Which statement about the commercial management approach in a PRINCE2 Agile project is correct?
o: It sets out how each supplier's delivery team will run its iterations
It replaces the role descriptions when external suppliers are involved
It can define fixed teams and cost per iteration and an agreed DoD
It mainly records the skill levels of the supplier's team members
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: The commercial management approach makes procurement and contracts support agile delivery, for example through fixed delivery teams and costs per iteration, a defined MVP and tolerances, and an agreed Definition of Done (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3).

n.0: The approach covers selecting and contracting suppliers, not the supplier's own internal ways of working.
n.1: Role descriptions remain a separate product; the commercial approach does not replace them.
n.3: Skill levels are mapped in the team skill matrix, not in the commercial management approach.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q:
Which two statements about the project management team structure in a PRINCE2 Agile project are correct?
1. It describes who is involved in the project and how they relate to each other.
2. It holds the delivery model and the standards for procurement.
3. It can set out arrangements for co-located or remote working.
4. It assigns a level of delegation to each team decision.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: the team structure covers who is involved, their relationships and how they work together, including co-location or remote working arrangements (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the delivery model and procurement standards belong in the commercial management approach.
n.2: Both are wrong: procurement content belongs to the commercial management approach and delegation levels to the delegation matrix.
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: levels of delegation per decision area are shown in the delegation matrix.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
The commercial management approach, the project management team structure and the role descriptions are management products used by the [?] practice.
o: organization
plans
business case
progress
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: These three management products belong to the organization practice in PRINCE2 Agile (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3).

n.1: The plans practice uses the release map, team plans and backlogs, not these organization products.
n.2: The business case practice uses the project canvas and benefits and sustainability approaches; the commercial approach sits under organization in PRINCE2 Agile.
n.3: The progress practice uses dashboards, logs and reports, not these products.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: What is the main purpose of a team skill matrix in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: To agree who makes each type of decision within the delivery team
To give an overview of team capabilities, strengths and skill gaps
To show how much work remains to be done in the current iteration
To record the supplier contracts that provide the team's members
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: A team skill matrix gives an overview of the team's capabilities, strengths, gaps and development areas, helping to put the right people on tasks and identify training needs (book 7.4.1).

n.0: Agreeing who decides is the job of delegation poker and the delegation matrix.
n.2: Remaining work in an iteration is shown by a burn-down chart.
n.3: Supplier contracts are governed by the commercial management approach.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: A new delivery team is forming on a PRINCE2 Agile project. In which workshop is the team skill matrix typically completed collaboratively?
o: The project kickoff workshop
The project initiation workshop
The release planning workshop
The team retrospective workshop
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: The team skill matrix is a topic of the project kickoff workshop, where the team maps its skills and spots gaps or overlaps together (book 7.4.1, Table 13.8).

n.1: The project initiation workshop covers topics such as the Agilometer, management approaches and project DoR/DoD, not the team skill matrix.
n.2: The release planning workshop focuses on releases, the release map and OKRs.
n.3: A team retrospective reviews how the last iteration went; the skill matrix is first built in the kickoff workshop.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: Once a delivery team has built its skill matrix, where does PRINCE2 Agile suggest it is shown so that it stays visible to the team?
o: In the project canvas
In the role descriptions
In the project brief
On the team dashboard
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: For delivery teams, the skill matrix is displayed on the team dashboard (book 7.4.1).

n.0: The project canvas is the business case artifact; it does not hold team skills.
n.1: Role descriptions set out responsibilities per role, not the team's current skills and gaps.
n.2: The project brief is a starting up product; it is not where a team's skill matrix is kept visible.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: A team skill matrix shows that one developer is the sole person able to maintain the payment module. How does PRINCE2 Agile expect the team to use this finding?
o: Raise it as a baseline change and pass it to the project board
Move that developer into the team coach role to share knowledge
Plan training or pairing so that more members gain the skill
Add the module to the commercial management approach as a risk
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: The skill matrix exists to reveal gaps and development areas and to identify training needs, so the team plans training to spread the skill (book 7.4.1; training plans 4.5).

n.0: A skill gap is not a change to the project backlog baseline, so it is not raised as a baseline change.
n.1: Changing someone's role does not close the gap; the matrix is used to plan training and development.
n.3: The commercial management approach covers procurement and contracts, not internal skill gaps.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q:
Which two statements about the team skill matrix in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. It is owned by the project executive and approved at each stage boundary.
2. It can show current skills and the expertise planned for the future.
3. It helps assign the right people to tasks and identify training needs.
4. It replaces the role descriptions for members of a delivery team.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
1 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: Statements 2 and 3 are correct: the skill matrix shows current and planned skills and helps assign people and identify training needs (book 7.4.1, 4.5).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: the team builds the matrix collaboratively; it is not an executive-approved product.
n.2: Both are wrong: the matrix is the team's own tool, and role descriptions remain a separate product.
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: role descriptions remain a separate organization product.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: How does a team skill matrix help with resource planning in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: It gives a structured view of the competencies available and required
It forecasts the cost of each iteration from the team's past velocity
It sets the tolerances within which the team may plan its own work
It lists the dependencies between products built by different teams
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: The skill matrix gives a structured view of the competencies available and those required, which enhances resource planning and helps use complementary skills (book 7.4.1).

n.1: Forecasting from velocity is a planning and progress technique, not the purpose of the skill matrix.
n.2: Tolerances are set through the governance levels, not by a skill matrix.
n.3: Dependencies between products are shown in planning artifacts such as a product flow diagram.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: Why is the team skill matrix built collaboratively by the team in PRINCE2 Agile rather than drawn up by the project manager?
o: Because the project board approves every team member's skill rating
Because the matrix forms part of each supplier's commercial contract
Because the agile coach uses it to set a velocity target for each team
Because members can map their own skills and spot gaps and overlaps
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: The team completes the skill matrix together in the project kickoff workshop to map skills and find gaps or overlaps, which also empowers team members (book 7.4.1, Table 13.8, 4.5).

n.0: Skill ratings are not approved by the board; the matrix is a team tool.
n.1: Contracts are covered by the commercial management approach, not the skill matrix.
n.2: The agile coach works on organization-level adoption; the skill matrix does not set velocity targets.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: Which of the following is NOT a use of the team skill matrix in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Identifying the training needs of team members
Spotting skill gaps and overlaps in the team
Recording which person decides each decision area
Helping to assign the right people to the tasks
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: Recording who decides in each decision area is the purpose of the delegation matrix (book 7.4.3). The other three are uses of the team skill matrix (book 7.4.1).

n.0: Identifying training needs is a stated use of the team skill matrix.
n.1: Mapping skills to spot gaps and overlaps is what the team does with the matrix in the kickoff workshop.
n.3: Helping to assign the right people to tasks is a stated use of the team skill matrix.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: A team coach suggests using delegation poker at the start of a PRINCE2 Agile project. What is delegation poker?
o: A technique for estimating the relative size of user stories
A way for the team to rank risks by probability and impact
A collaborative technique for defining decision-making in teams
A game used in retrospectives to rate the team's morale
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: Delegation poker is a collaborative technique for defining how decisions are made within teams (book 7.4.2).

n.0: Sizing user stories is done with estimation techniques such as story points or magic estimation, not delegation poker.
n.1: Ranking risks by probability and impact is a risk assessment technique, not delegation poker.
n.3: Delegation poker concerns decision-making authority, not measuring morale in retrospectives.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: What is the purpose of a delegation matrix in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: To show the skills and development needs of each team member
To set out the contract terms that are agreed with each supplier
To map the dependencies between the delivery teams' products
To make clear who decides, and who is involved, per decision area
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: A delegation matrix makes responsibilities and decision-making authority transparent, showing who decides and who is involved for each decision area (book 7.4.3).

n.0: Skills and development needs are shown in the team skill matrix.
n.1: Contract terms are covered by the commercial management approach.
n.2: Product dependencies are shown in planning artifacts such as a product flow diagram.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: A new PRINCE2 Agile delivery team will agree its team delegation matrix as one of the topics of a workshop. Which workshop is this?
o: The project kickoff workshop
The agile enablement workshop
The project closure workshop
The release planning workshop
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: The team delegation matrix is a topic of the project kickoff workshop, aimed at simplifying decision-making and empowering self-management (book Table 13.8).

n.1: The agile enablement workshop is held with the board and agile coaches in directing a project; team delegation is a kickoff topic.
n.2: The project closure workshop is held at the end of the project, too late to agree how a team will make decisions.
n.3: The release planning workshop focuses on releases, the release map and OKRs.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: Which benefit does a delegation matrix bring to a PRINCE2 Agile delivery team?
o: It fixes the scope of each iteration before any work begins
It reduces confusion and duplicated effort over who decides
It records the velocity that each team member contributes
It lists the user stories that the team has agreed to deliver
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: By making decision authority transparent, a delegation matrix improves alignment, reduces confusion, streamlines communication and avoids duplicated effort (book 7.4.3).

n.0: Iteration scope is agreed in team planning; the delegation matrix is about decision authority.
n.2: Velocity is a team-level planning measure; the delegation matrix does not record it.
n.3: Agreed user stories sit in the product backlog and work package, not in the delegation matrix.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: How are delegation poker and the delegation matrix related in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Both clarify decision-making: poker is a way to define it, the matrix makes it visible
Poker sizes the user stories, and the matrix then assigns them to the developers
Poker scores the project risks, and the matrix records the agreed risk responses
Poker sets the team's tolerances, and the matrix is signed off by the executive
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: Both techniques in the organization practice deal with decision-making: delegation poker is a collaborative way to define how decisions are made in teams, and the delegation matrix makes responsibilities and decision authority transparent (book 7.4.2, 7.4.3).

n.1: Sizing user stories is an estimation activity; neither technique allocates stories to developers.
n.2: Risk scoring and responses belong to the risk practice and the risk register.
n.3: Tolerances for agile decision-making are approved by the project executive, not set by delegation poker.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: In the project kickoff workshop, what is the aim of the team delegation matrix topic?
o: To agree which supplier contracts each delivery team will use
To simplify decision-making and empower team self-management
To assess the team's psychological safety before work begins
To map the team's skills and spot any gaps and overlaps in them
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: The team delegation matrix topic in the kickoff workshop aims to simplify decision-making and empower self-management (book Table 13.8).

n.0: Supplier contracts are covered by the commercial management approach, not a kickoff workshop topic.
n.2: Psychological safety is a separate kickoff topic with its own assessment.
n.3: Mapping skills, gaps and overlaps is the aim of the team skill matrix topic.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: A PRINCE2 Agile project brings in external specialist advisers to work alongside its own staff. Which technique helps make clear which matters the advisers decide and which they advise on?
o: A team skill matrix
A cumulative flow diagram
A delegation matrix
The Agilometer
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: When working across organizations, PRINCE2 Agile suggests setting clear boundaries within which people can flex, for example a delegation matrix showing what external advisers decide or advise on (book 4.3.1, 7.4.3).

n.0: A skill matrix shows capabilities and gaps, not decision authority.
n.1: A cumulative flow diagram shows work moving through workflow states, not who decides.
n.3: The Agilometer assesses the risk of working in an agile way, not decision authority.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: A delivery team has used delegation poker to agree the levels at which its members make decisions. Which statement about the outcome is correct?
o: The agreed levels replace the tolerances set by the project board
The agreed levels are approved by the senior supplier each iteration
The agreed levels apply to the project board's decisions as well
The team still works within tolerances and escalates beyond them
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: Self-management in PRINCE2 Agile operates inside agreed boundaries: teams know the limits of self-management and when decisions must be escalated, and product owners deliver within tolerances agreed with the PM (book 4.5, Table 7.2).

n.0: Delegation within a team does not override the tolerances set through the governance levels.
n.1: Delegation levels are a team agreement; the senior supplier does not approve them each iteration.
n.2: Delegation poker defines decision-making within teams; it does not change the board's decisions.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: A new sponsor asks what the organization practice contributes to a PRINCE2 Agile project. Which statement describes the purpose of the organization practice?
o: To define and establish the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities
To control changes to the project's baseline once the project backlog has been agreed
To compare actual achievements with those planned and forecast the project's objectives
To document the users' requirements of the project products and how they will be met
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: The organization practice answers the 'who' question: it defines and establishes the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 7.1; practice purposes 6.1 to 12.1, paraphrased).

n.1: Controlling changes to the baseline is the purpose of the issues practice, not organization.
n.2: Comparing actual against planned achievement and forecasting objectives is the purpose of the progress practice.
n.3: Documenting users' requirements and the means of meeting them is the purpose of the quality practice.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: A product owner on a PRINCE2 Agile project asks where they sit in the project management team structure. Which role has the direct line of authority over the product owner?
o: The chief product owner, who sets priorities across the teams
The project manager, who runs the project day to day for the board
The team coach, who supports the product owner and the team
The agile coach, who advises the board on agile ways of working
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: In the PRINCE2 Agile structure (book Figure 7.1, Table 7.2) the project manager is the role with the direct line of authority over the product owner. The PO is a version of the team manager role and agrees work with the PM.

n.0: The CPO works closely with product owners and sets priorities across teams, but the structure does not give the CPO the line of authority over the PO.
n.2: The team coach supports and advises the PO and the delivery team; it holds no line authority over the PO.
n.3: The agile coach supports the board, project assurance and the PM at organization level; it is not in the PO's line of authority.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: In a PRINCE2 Agile project, a delivery team is made up of a product owner, a team coach, developers and testers. Which role has the direct line of authority over the developers and testers?
o: The project manager, through the work packages
The team coach, through the team's workshops
The product owner of that delivery team
The senior supplier, through supplier resources
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: The product owner, a version of the team manager role, is the role with the direct line of authority over delivery team members (book Figure 7.1, Table 7.2). The PM works through the PO rather than directly with team members.

n.0: The project manager's direct authority is over the product owner; the PM does not manage developers and testers directly.
n.1: The team coach helps the team self-manage and facilitates its workshops but has no line authority over team members.
n.3: The senior supplier represents the supplier side at governance level; the structure places the delivery team members under the product owner.

Agile: Organization & Roles.q: A project manager and a product owner need to agree the next piece of work for a delivery team in a PRINCE2 Agile project. How is this work normally agreed between them?
o: As a team plan that the product owner signs off before each iteration
As tasks that the project manager adds to the team's product backlog
As a checkpoint report that the project manager issues each iteration
As a work package description expressed as a set of user stories
Agile: Organization & Roles.w: The PM and the PO agree work as work package descriptions, which in PRINCE2 Agile take the form of a set of user stories, within the agreed tolerances and management approaches (book 7.3.1, Table 7.2).

n.0: A team plan is the team's own iteration-level plan; it is not the vehicle by which the PM and PO agree work.
n.1: The product owner owns and maintains the product backlog; the PM consults the PO on it rather than adding tasks directly.
n.2: Checkpoint reporting flows from the team to the PM (as the team dashboard in agile); it does not allocate work.

Agile: Plans.q:
Which two statements about calibration and velocity in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. Calibration means starting real work and measuring how much gets done.
2. Velocity is the rate of progress, typically the average story points delivered per timebox.
3. A new team should borrow a more experienced team's velocity until it has one of its own.
4. Velocity is set when the project is initiated and then held constant for the whole project.
o: 1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 2
Agile: Plans.w: Statement 1 matches the book's description of calibration, and statement 2 matches velocity as the average rate of story points delivered per timebox (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3, 12.4.3).

n.0: Statement 3 is wrong: a team should use its own velocity, not another person's or team's (book 8.3).
n.1: Statement 4 is wrong: velocity comes from measuring work actually done and is used to forecast while conditions stay the same, so it is not fixed at initiation (book 8.3, 12.4.3).
n.2: Both statements are wrong: velocity is not borrowed from another team, and it is not set at initiation and held constant (book 8.3).

Agile: Plans.q: A delivery team has completed 16, 20 and 24 story points in its first three iterations, and 120 story points remain in the release. Using the team's velocity, how many more iterations should the project manager forecast?
o: 4 more iterations
5 more iterations
6 more iterations
7 more iterations
Agile: Plans.w: Velocity is the average rate: (16 + 20 + 24) / 3 = 20 points per iteration, so 120 / 20 = 6 more iterations, assuming conditions stay the same (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3, 12.4.3).

n.0: Four iterations would need 30 points per iteration, faster than the team has achieved in any iteration so far.
n.1: Five iterations uses the best single iteration (24 points) instead of the average rate of 20 points.
n.3: Seven iterations implies about 17 points per iteration, below the team's measured average of 20.

Agile: Plans.q: A board member asks a newly formed delivery team to forecast its release date by using the velocity achieved by a sister team that built a similar product last year. Which response best reflects the PRINCE2 Agile plans practice?
o: Start the work, measure this team's own rate of delivery and forecast from it
Accept the sister team's velocity, as similar products need similar effort
Ask the most experienced developer to estimate the duration for the team
Fix the release date now and add a time tolerance to absorb any variation
Agile: Plans.w: Empirical planning starts the work and measures how much this team gets done; a team cannot use another team's or person's velocity (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3).

n.1: Borrowing another team's rate is not empirical for this team: velocity must come from the team's own measured progress (book 8.3).
n.2: One person's estimate is neither past velocity nor a collaborative team estimate, so it does not meet the plans practice guidance (book 8.3, 8.4.3).
n.3: Time normally has zero tolerance in PRINCE2 Agile; scope is flexed instead of adding time tolerance (book Table 3.1).

Agile: Plans.q: During a stage, the delivery team's measured progress shows that some features will arrive later than first forecast. How does the project manager keep the release map grounded in this evidence?
o: The chief product owner replaces the release map with a detailed task schedule when the stage is authorized
The project manager updates it with actuals, forecasts and adjustments when evaluating work package status
The project executive revises the team plan for each remaining iteration when giving ongoing direction
The delivery team recalculates the project canvas costs in the next team retrospective workshop
Agile: Plans.w: In controlling a stage, the project manager pulls progress from the team dashboard and updates the release map with actuals, forecasts and adjustments as part of evaluating work package status (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.9, 8.3).

n.0: The release map stays high level; task-level detail lives in team plans for the next iteration, and the CPO does not replace the plan (book 8.3.2.5).
n.2: Team plans are produced by the delivery team when accepting a work package, not revised by the executive (book Table 13.12).
n.3: The team retrospective reflects on the last iteration (the good, the bad, the learning, team building); it does not recalculate project canvas costs (book Table 13.14).

Agile: Plans.q: PRINCE2 Agile keeps the product-based planning technique but tailors it with agile artifacts. Which artifact is recommended to replace the product breakdown structure?
o: A product flow diagram
A release map
A user story map
A project canvas
Agile: Plans.w: In agile product-based planning, the product breakdown structure is recommended to be replaced by a user story map, which breaks the products down into user stories (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.1.1, 8.3.2.4).

n.0: A product flow diagram shows the sequence in which products are developed and their dependencies; it is not the recommended replacement for the PBS (book 8.4.2).
n.1: The release map is built from the story map and serves as the project and stage plan; it does not replace the breakdown step (book 8.3.2.5, 8.4.4).
n.3: The project canvas is the agile form of the business case, not a product breakdown (book 6.3.2.1).

Agile: Plans.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

When building a story map, the team starts from user descriptions such as [?], brainstorms the activities users carry out, orders them chronologically and breaks them into user stories.
o: epics
OKRs
work packages
personas
Agile: Plans.w: Story mapping starts from descriptions of the users, such as personas, then brainstorms user activities, orders them in time and breaks them into stories (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.4).

n.0: Epics are large user stories that are broken down; they are requirements, not descriptions of the users the map starts from (book 8.3.2.2).
n.1: OKRs are a goal-setting framework used in progress and release planning, not descriptions of users (book 12.3.2.3).
n.2: Work packages are sets of user stories agreed between the PM and PO; they come after the stories exist, not before (book Table 8.1).

Agile: Plans.q: Story mapping is used to define and break down the work needed to build a product that meets user needs. Under which PRINCE2 Agile practice is the story map described as an artifact?
o: Plans
Quality
Business case
Progress
Agile: Plans.w: The story map is a plans practice artifact: it supports product-based planning by breaking products into user stories (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.4).

n.1: The quality practice covers acceptance criteria, the Definition of Ready and Definition of Done, not the story map (book 9.3.2).
n.2: The business case practice uses the project canvas, not the story map (book 6.3.2.1).
n.3: The progress practice uses dashboards, burn charts and reports, not the story map (book 12.3.2).

Agile: Plans.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile say a separate product breakdown document is not needed when a story map is used?
o: The project canvas already lists every product and its components
Building the story map already breaks the products into user stories
Products are defined later by each team when it writes its team plan
The product flow diagram already shows the full product hierarchy
Agile: Plans.w: During story mapping the products are broken down into smaller user stories, so a separate product breakdown structure is not needed (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.1.1).

n.0: The project canvas summarizes the business justification (vision, value, options, costs, users, scope, benefits, risks); it is not a product breakdown (book 6.3.2.1).
n.2: Team plans hold task-level detail for the next iteration; they do not define the project's products (book Table 8.1).
n.3: A product flow diagram shows development sequence and dependencies, not the product hierarchy (book 8.4.2).

Agile: Plans.q: When a project manager and the teams turn a story map into a release map, what else is defined at the same time?
o: The team Definition of Done for each team's product backlog
The dependencies between products, which shape the releases
The project tolerances for time and cost for each stage
The velocity that fixes the deadline of each release
Agile: Plans.w: Turning the story map into a release map also defines the interdependencies between products, and the releases are planned accordingly (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.1.1).

n.0: The team Definition of Done is a quality criterion held in or linked from the product backlog; it is not defined by building the release map (book 8.3.2.1, 9.3.2.2).
n.2: Project tolerances are set as project controls in initiating a project, not while converting the story map (book Table 13.6).
n.3: Velocity is measured from work actually done once the team has started; it is not defined from the story map (book 8.3).

Agile: Plans.q: How are the user stories on a story map grouped to create the releases on a release map?
o: Into releases that make sense from both a priority and a development or technical point of view
Into releases of equal size, so that every release holds the same number of user stories
Into releases by persona, so that each release serves one user group from start to finish
Into releases by delivery team, so that each team owns one complete release of the product
Agile: Plans.w: The release map uses the story map: stories are clustered into releases that make sense from a priority and a development or technical point of view, then separated and given deadlines (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.5).

n.1: Releases are clustered by priority and technical sense, not by an equal story count (book 8.3.2.5).
n.2: Personas are where story mapping starts, but releases are not formed one persona at a time (book 8.3.2.4, 8.3.2.5).
n.3: Releases are formed by priority and technical sense; several teams can contribute to one release (book 8.3.2.5, 7.3.1).

Agile: Plans.q:
Which two statements about product-based planning in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. Planning still starts from the products that the project must deliver.
2. The budget covers the cost of producing and delivering the products plus the cost of project management activities.
3. The story map is the delivery team's task-level plan for the next iteration.
4. The story map is produced as an input to the product breakdown structure, which stays the main breakdown.
o: 1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 2
Agile: Plans.w: Product-based planning keeps its product focus in PRINCE2 Agile (statement 1), and the budget step covers product costs (people, equipment, materials, facilities) plus project management costs (statement 2) (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.1, 8.3.1.5).

n.0: Statement 3 is wrong: the task-level plan for the next iteration is the team plan, not the story map (book Table 8.1).
n.1: Statement 4 is wrong: the story map is recommended to replace the product breakdown structure, not feed it (book 8.3.1.1).
n.2: Both are wrong: the story map is neither the team plan nor an input to a PBS it is meant to replace (book Table 8.1, 8.3.1.1).

Agile: Plans.q: Which statement best describes the difference between the story map and the release map in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: The story map is the project plan; the release map is the team's task-level plan for the next iteration
The story map is part of the business case; the release map is part of the quality management approach
The story map breaks the products into user stories; the release map groups them into releases over time
The story map sets the order of priority; the release map shows the products as a component hierarchy
Agile: Plans.w: The story map is the breakdown (products into user stories), and the release map is the plan built from it, clustering stories into releases with deadlines (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.4, 8.3.2.5).

n.0: The release map, not the story map, represents the project plan, and task-level detail sits in team plans (book 8.4.4, Table 8.1).
n.1: Both maps are plans practice artifacts; the business case uses the project canvas (book 8.3.2, 6.3.2.1).
n.3: A component hierarchy is what a product breakdown structure shows; the release map shows releases over time (book 8.4.1, 8.4.4).

Agile: Plans.q: PRINCE2 Agile tailors several PRINCE2 management products into agile artifacts. Which artifact replaces the contents of the project product description?
o: Product backlog
Release map
Project canvas
Project backlog
Agile: Plans.w: The project backlog is tailored to replace the contents of the project product description; it usually holds high-level epics and shows or links to the project DoR and DoD (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.1).

n.0: The product backlog is used at team level and takes the place of product descriptions, not the project product description (book 8.3.2.1).
n.1: The release map represents the project plan and stage plan (book 8.4.4).
n.2: The project canvas is the agile form of the business case (book 6.3.2.1).

Agile: Plans.q: A project has three delivery teams, each working from its own product backlog. Which role owns the project backlog and sets priorities across all three teams?
o: The chief product owner
The product owner
The project manager
The project executive
Agile: Plans.w: The chief product owner represents the user community, owns the project backlog, keeps it aligned with the team product backlogs and sets priorities across teams (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2).

n.1: Each product owner owns one team's product backlog and does not prioritize across teams (book Table 7.2).
n.2: The project manager runs the project day to day and agrees work packages with product owners, but does not own the project backlog (book Table 7.2).
n.3: The project executive is accountable for the project and approves tolerances, but the project backlog is owned by the CPO (book Table 7.2).

Agile: Plans.q: A delivery team's product owner is preparing the backlog that the team will work from. Which statement describes a product backlog in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: A project-level list of high-level epics that names who will accept the project product
A team-level backlog of detailed user stories that includes or links to the team Definition of Done
A one-page visual summary of the project vision, benefits, costs, users, scope and major risks
A visual plan showing how many releases there will be, when they occur and what each contains
Agile: Plans.w: A product backlog has everything a regular backlog has, plus it includes or links to the team Definition of Done; it holds the detailed stories and is used at team level by the person responsible for the team's outputs (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.1).

n.0: High-level epics and naming who accepts the project product describe the project backlog (book 8.3.2.1).
n.2: A one-page summary of vision, benefits, costs and risks is the project canvas (book 6.3.2.1).
n.3: Showing how many releases, when, and their features describes the release map (book 8.4.4).

Agile: Plans.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

A backlog is a [?] list of the requirements for a product, which may be written as epic user stories, user stories or other requirement formats.
o: hierarchical
chronological
prioritized
costed
Agile: Plans.w: The Glossary defines a backlog as a prioritized list of requirements for a product, which may be (epic) user stories or other formats (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Glossary, 8.3.2.1).

n.0: A hierarchical breakdown of products into components is the product breakdown structure; a backlog is a list in priority order (book 8.4.1, Glossary).
n.1: Ordering user activities in time is part of building a story map; a backlog is ordered by priority (book 8.3.2.4).
n.3: Costs belong to the budget and the project canvas; the backlog is defined by being prioritized (book 8.3.1.5, Glossary).

Agile: Plans.q:
Which two statements about the project backlog in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. It usually holds high-level requirements in the form of epic user stories.
2. It includes or links to the team Definition of Done for each delivery team.
3. It shows or links to the project Definition of Ready and Definition of Done.
4. It is owned by the product owner of the largest delivery team.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Plans.w: The project backlog usually contains high-level epics (statement 1) and shows or links to the project DoR and DoD from the quality management approach (statement 3) (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.1).

n.1: Statement 2 is wrong: the team Definition of Done is included in or linked from each team's product backlog (book 8.3.2.1).
n.2: Both are wrong: the team DoD belongs with the product backlog, and the project backlog is owned by the chief product owner (book 8.3.2.1, Table 7.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the chief product owner owns the project backlog, not a product owner (book Table 7.2).

Agile: Plans.q: In which process is the project backlog first created in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Initiating a project, when the project Definition of Ready and Done are agreed in the project initiation workshop
Managing product delivery, when each team refines its backlog in the team planning workshop
Directing a project, when the board authorizes initiation and approves the project brief
Starting up a project, when the project manager works with the CPO, senior supplier and executive on what is to be delivered
Agile: Plans.w: In starting up a project, while the executive leads the project canvas, the project manager works with the CPO, senior supplier and executive to define what is to be delivered and creates the project backlog with its epics (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.1).

n.0: The project DoR and DoD are agreed in the project initiation workshop, and the project backlog is reviewed and updated if needed in initiation, but it already exists from starting up (book Tables 13.6, 13.7).
n.1: Teams refine their own product backlogs in the team planning workshop; the project backlog has existed since starting up (book Table 13.13).
n.2: Authorizing initiation approves the project brief and the release map for initiation; it does not create the project backlog (book Table 13.4).

Agile: Plans.q: A product owner maintains her team's product backlog. What should she keep it aligned with?
o: The other teams' product backlogs, prioritized by her across teams
The senior supplier's resource plan, which orders the stories
The project backlog, business justification and tolerances
The team plan, which fixes stories for all remaining releases
Agile: Plans.w: The product owner owns the product backlog and keeps it aligned with the project backlog, continued business justification and tolerances, working closely with the CPO (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2).

n.0: Prioritizing across teams is the chief product owner's job, not a product owner's (book Table 7.2).
n.1: The senior supplier represents those who design and build the products; the order of a team's stories is set by priority in its product backlog (book Table 7.2, Glossary).
n.3: The team plan covers the next iteration at task level, not all remaining releases (book Table 8.1).

Agile: Plans.q: During a stage, the users ask for a new Must-have epic that is not in the approved project backlog. How should this request be handled in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: As a detail change, which the product owner adds directly to the team's product backlog
As a baseline change to the project backlog, handled formally through the issues practice
As a new risk, which the team coach records on the team dashboard for the next iteration
As a quality matter, which the tester adds to the team Definition of Done for the stage
Agile: Plans.w: A change that alters the approved project backlog, such as a new Must-have, is a baseline change and is handled formally; changes within the project backlog are detail changes handled at team level (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 11.3, 8.3.2.1).

n.0: Detail changes sit within the existing project backlog; a new Must-have epic changes the project backlog itself, so it is not a detail change (book 11.3).
n.2: A request for new scope is an issue (a request for change), not a risk, and the team dashboard reports team progress (book 11.3.1, Table 12.1).
n.3: The team DoD sets completion criteria for the team's work; it is not where new scope is approved (book 9.3.2.2).

Agile: Plans.q: Which PRINCE2 Agile artifact represents the project plan, showing how many releases there will be, when they will happen and which features each will contain?
o: Story map
Release map
Project backlog
Project dashboard
Agile: Plans.w: The release map shows how many releases are planned, when, and which features they contain; it represents the project plan, and a stage plan is the same with a shorter horizon (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.4.4, Table 8.1).

n.0: The story map breaks products into user stories; it feeds the release map but is not the plan (book 8.3.2.4).
n.2: The project backlog replaces the project product description, not the project plan (book 8.3.2.1).
n.3: The project dashboard replaces the highlight report and end stage report; it reports progress rather than planning releases (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Plans.q: A release map clusters user stories into releases, and each release is visually separated and given a deadline. How many iterations does a release usually contain?
o: One iteration
Five to eight iterations
Two to four iterations
Nine to twelve iterations
Agile: Plans.w: Releases on a release map usually contain two to four iterations (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.5).

n.0: A single iteration is the smallest timebox; a release is a larger timebox that usually spans two to four iterations (book Glossary, 8.3.2.5).
n.1: Five to eight iterations is longer than the usual release length of two to four (book 8.3.2.5).
n.3: Nine to twelve iterations is far longer than the usual release length of two to four (book 8.3.2.5).

Agile: Plans.q: A project board member asks where the stage plan is in a PRINCE2 Agile project. How does a stage plan relate to the release map?
o: The stage plan replaces the release map once the project has been authorized
The stage plan is the team plan for the next iteration, made by the delivery team
The stage plan is held in the project backlog as a list of epics for that stage
The stage plan is also a release map, covering a shorter horizon than the project plan
Agile: Plans.w: Both the project plan and the stage plan are represented through a release map; the stage plan is the same thing with a shorter horizon (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.4.4, Table 8.1).

n.0: The release map is kept and updated throughout; the updated release map is approved when a stage is authorized (book Table 13.4).
n.1: Team plans are task-level plans for the next iteration produced by the delivery team; the stage plan is a release map (book Table 8.1).
n.2: The project backlog holds the project's requirements, mostly epics; it is not the stage plan (book 8.3.2.1).

Agile: Plans.q: The release map serves as the plan for a PRINCE2 Agile project. Which other plan elements should it include or refer to?
o: The budget, tolerances and assumptions for the plan
The team skill matrix, delegation matrix and team values
The Definition of Ready, Definition of Done and test results
The daily log, lessons log and issue register entries
Agile: Plans.w: As the agile form of a plan, the release map includes or refers to the budget, tolerances and assumptions (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 8.1).

n.1: Skill and delegation matrices and team values are organization and people topics set up in the project kickoff workshop, not plan elements (book Table 13.8).
n.2: Definitions of Ready and Done belong to the quality practice and the backlogs; test results are quality records (book 9.3.2).
n.3: Logs and registers are progress and issues records, not elements of the plan (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Plans.q: At a stage boundary, the release map for the next stage is being updated. Which of the following should NOT be done at this point?
o: Plan the next stage at a high level in the release planning workshop
Break key activities into user stories and update the release map
Define or update the team OKRs for the coming stage
Break each iteration of the next stage into detailed tasks
Agile: Plans.w: At a stage boundary the release map is planned at a high level; the next iterations can be outlined but not at task level, because plans are made just in time. Task-level plans are produced by the team for each iteration in managing product delivery (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.5, Table 13.16).

n.0: This should be done: the release planning workshop plans the next stage and reviews the release map at a high level (book Table 13.16).
n.1: This should be done: the release planning topic breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map (book Table 13.16).
n.2: This should be done: OKR definition is a topic of the release planning workshop (book Table 13.16).

Agile: Plans.q: At a stage boundary, the project manager runs a workshop whose topics include OKR definition and breaking key activities into user stories to plan the next stage. Which workshop is this?
o: Team planning workshop
Release planning workshop
Progress review workshop
Agile enablement workshop
Agile: Plans.w: The release planning workshop, held for initiation and for later stages, covers an introduction, OKR definition, release planning (breaking activities into stories and updating the release map) and wrap-up (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 13.7.4.1, Table 13.16).

n.0: The team planning workshop is held in managing product delivery to prepare the next iteration and the team plan (book Table 13.13).
n.2: The progress review workshop in controlling a stage reviews project dashboard metrics, risks and a product demo (book Table 13.10).
n.3: The agile enablement workshop in directing a project reviews Agilometer assessments and agile adoption risks (book Table 13.5).

Agile: Plans.q: Why is the release map kept at a high level at a stage boundary, rather than being planned at task level for every iteration in the stage?
o: Plans are made just in time, because planning too early has its own risks
Task-level detail for each iteration is held in the project backlog instead
The project board approves each task directly in the progress review workshop
Iterations are planned once the release they belong to has been completed
Agile: Plans.w: Plans are made just in time to avoid planning too early and its inherent risks; the team plans the next iteration at task level in managing product delivery (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.5).

n.1: The project backlog holds high-level requirements, mostly epics, not task-level detail (book 8.3.2.1).
n.2: The progress review workshop reviews dashboard metrics, risks and demos; the board does not approve tasks (book Table 13.10).
n.3: Each iteration is planned by the team at its start, in the team planning workshop, not after the release ends (book Table 13.13).

Agile: Plans.q: Which statement correctly describes how the release map is used across the PRINCE2 Agile processes?
o: It is first created in closing a project, when the end project report compares planned and actual releases
It is produced by each delivery team in accept a work package as the plan for the next iteration
The board approves a release map for initiation, and the PM documents the project release map in initiation
It is owned by the chief product owner and replaces the project product description for the board
Agile: Plans.w: Starting up produces a high-level release map for initiation, which the board approves when authorizing initiation; in initiating a project the project manager documents the release map while preparing the project plan (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Tables 13.1, 13.4, 13.6).

n.0: The release map exists from starting up onwards; closing a project does not create it (book Tables 13.1, 13.6).
n.1: Accepting a work package produces a team plan, not the release map (book Table 13.12).
n.3: The CPO owns the project backlog, which is what replaces the project product description (book 8.3.2.1, Table 7.2).

Agile: Plans.q: The project manager and a product owner agree the work that a delivery team will deliver next. In PRINCE2 Agile, what form does the work package description usually take?
o: A set of user stories
An updated release map
A team dashboard entry
A refined project canvas
Agile: Plans.w: In PRINCE2 Agile a work package description is usually expressed as a set of user stories, agreed between the project manager and the product owner (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 8.1, 7.3.1).

n.1: The release map is the project and stage plan, not a work package (book 8.4.4).
n.2: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report and shows team progress (book Table 12.1).
n.3: The project canvas is the agile form of the business case (book 6.3.2.1).

Agile: Plans.q: When a delivery team accepts a work package, a detailed plan of what it will do in the next iteration is created. Who produces this team plan?
o: The project manager
The delivery team
The chief product owner
Project support
Agile: Plans.w: The team plan is produced by the delivery team when it accepts a work package; it is a detailed task-level plan for the next iteration (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 8.1, Table 13.12).

n.0: The project manager reviews the team plan when authorizing the work package but does not produce it (book Table 13.9).
n.2: The chief product owner owns the project backlog and sets priorities across teams; team plans are made by the teams (book Table 7.2).
n.3: Project support gives administrative and planning help but does not produce the team's plan (book Table 7.2).

Agile: Plans.q: In a PRINCE2 Agile project with two delivery teams, between which two roles is each team's work package description agreed?
o: The project executive and the project manager
The chief product owner and the product owner
The project manager and the product owner
The team coach and the developers
Agile: Plans.w: The project manager and the product owner agree work as work package descriptions expressed as sets of user stories, within the tolerances and management approaches (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 7.3.1).

n.0: The executive and project manager agree stage-level matters such as tolerances, not team work packages (book Table 7.2).
n.1: The CPO works closely with product owners on priorities, but work packages are agreed with the project manager (book 7.3.1).
n.3: The team coach helps the team self-manage; work packages are agreed between the PM and PO (book Table 7.2, 7.3.1).

Agile: Plans.q: What level of detail does a team plan contain in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: A high-level plan of all releases in the current stage
A summary of epics for the whole of the project
A forecast of benefits for each of the planned releases
A detailed, task-level plan covering the next iteration
Agile: Plans.w: A team plan is a detailed task-level plan for the next iteration, produced when the team accepts a work package (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 8.1).

n.0: Releases across a stage are shown on the release map used as the stage plan (book 8.4.4).
n.1: A summary of epics for the whole project is the project backlog (book 8.3.2.1).
n.2: Benefits are forecast in the business case artifacts and the benefits management approach, not the team plan (book 6.3.2).

Agile: Plans.q:
Which two statements about team plans and work packages in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. The team plan is produced when the delivery team accepts a work package.
2. The chief product owner agrees each work package description with the delivery team.
3. On receiving a completed work package, the project manager confirms the set of user stories was delivered.
4. The team plan replaces the release map once a stage has been authorized.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
Agile: Plans.w: Statement 1: the team produces its team plan when accepting the work package. Statement 3: when receiving a completed work package, the project manager confirms the set of user stories or timebox features was delivered (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Tables 13.12, 13.9).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: work package descriptions are agreed between the project manager and the product owner (book 7.3.1).
n.1: Both are wrong: the PM and PO agree work packages, and the release map remains the stage plan alongside team plans (book 7.3.1, 8.4.4).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the release map stays as the stage plan; team plans add task detail for the next iteration (book 8.4.4, Table 8.1).

Agile: Plans.q: In managing product delivery, a delivery team refines its backlog, clarifies acceptance criteria, estimates effort and then selects stories by priority to agree what it can realistically deliver next. Which workshop is this?
o: Team planning workshop
Release planning workshop
Project kickoff workshop
Team retrospective workshop
Agile: Plans.w: The team planning workshop prepares the next iteration: product backlog refinement, user story refinement, effort estimation and iteration planning to build a realistic team plan (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 13.6.4.1, Table 13.13).

n.1: The release planning workshop is held at stage boundaries to define OKRs and update the release map (book Table 13.16).
n.2: The project kickoff workshop in initiation covers team intro, values, skill and delegation matrices and dashboards (book Table 13.8).
n.3: The team retrospective reflects on the last iteration (the good, the bad, the learning, team building) rather than planning the next (book Table 13.14).

Agile: Plans.q: What does the project manager do in the 'authorize a work package' activity?
o: Writes the team plan and assigns each of its tasks to a named developer
Asks the chief product owner to approve the team's tasks for the iteration
Updates the team dashboard and reports the team's progress to the board
Co-creates the description with the PO and team, then reviews the team plan
Agile: Plans.w: When authorizing a work package, the project manager co-creates and reviews the work package description with the product owner and team, confirms acceptance, reviews the team plan and authorizes the work (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.9).

n.0: The delivery team produces its own team plan and self-manages how the work is done (book Table 13.12).
n.1: The CPO prioritizes across teams but does not approve team tasks; the PM reviews the team plan (book Table 7.2, Table 13.9).
n.2: The delivery team updates its team dashboard when evaluating a work package; the PM pulls information from it (book Tables 13.12, 12.1).

Agile: Plans.q: Why does the project manager in PRINCE2 Agile agree work package descriptions with the product owner rather than directly with the developers?
o: The product owner prioritizes stories across every delivery team on the project
The PM has direct authority over the product owner, a version of the team manager
The developers are appointed by the project board and report to the executive
The product owner is accountable for the project's continued business justification
Agile: Plans.w: The project manager is the only role with direct authority over the product owner, who is a version of the team manager role; the product owner then has direct authority over the delivery team members (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 7.3.1).

n.0: Prioritizing across teams is the chief product owner's responsibility, not a product owner's (book Table 7.2).
n.2: Developers sit in the delivery team under the product owner; they do not report to the executive (book 7.3.1).
n.3: The project executive is accountable for the project and its business justification, not the product owner (book Table 7.2).

Agile: Plans.q: Which statement describes how estimates are normally produced in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Actual estimates in hours from the most experienced team member
Estimates set by the project manager and approved by the board
Estimates taken from similar past projects to fix the end date
Relative estimates from the whole team, so nobody is swayed by others
Agile: Plans.w: Agile estimation uses relative rather than actual estimates and harnesses the whole team so that everyone contributes without being swayed by others (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.4.3).

n.0: Estimates are relative (for example story points), not actual hours, and come from the whole team rather than one person (book 8.4.3, 8.3).
n.1: The delivery team estimates its own work collaboratively, for example in the effort estimation topic of the team planning workshop (book Table 13.13).
n.2: Forecasts come from the team's own measured velocity, not from other projects' figures (book 8.3).

Agile: Plans.q: Teams commonly size user stories in story points. What does a story point value represent?
o: A fixed number of hours agreed for each user story
A measure of the business value a story will deliver
A size that means something relative to another story
A score of how far a story meets the Definition of Done
Agile: Plans.w: Story points are the most common form of agile estimate: a points value that means something relative to another story (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.4.3).

n.0: Story points are relative estimates, not actual hours (book 8.4.3).
n.1: Business value is set out in the project canvas and used in prioritization; story points estimate size or effort (book 6.3.2.1, 8.4.3).
n.3: The Definition of Done is a set of criteria that work either meets or does not; story points do not score it (book 9.3.2.2).

Agile: Plans.q: Which estimating technique gives a quick, collaborative way to size the relative size or complexity of many items in early planning, such as at project product level, without lengthy discussion?
o: Delegation poker
Magic estimation
Product flow diagram
MoSCoW prioritization
Agile: Plans.w: Magic estimation is a quick, collaborative technique used in early planning, for example at project product level, to estimate the relative size or complexity of many pieces of work without lengthy discussion (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.4.3).

n.0: Delegation poker is an organization practice technique for agreeing decision-making levels, not for sizing work (book 7.4.2).
n.2: A product flow diagram shows the sequence and dependencies of products; it does not estimate size (book 8.4.2).
n.3: MoSCoW sets priority (Must, Should, Could, Won't), for example in product backlog refinement, not relative size or complexity (book Table 13.13).

Agile: Plans.q: What does a product flow diagram show in PRINCE2 Agile planning?
o: The sequence in which products are developed and the dependencies between them
The products to be delivered, broken down hierarchically into their components
The work completed and the work remaining, updated regularly over time
The number of tasks sitting in each workflow state over the course of time
Agile: Plans.w: A product flow diagram describes the sequence in which the products will be developed and the dependencies between them (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.4.2).

n.1: Breaking products down hierarchically into components describes the product breakdown structure (book 8.4.1).
n.2: Showing work done and work remaining over time describes a burn chart in the progress practice (book 12.4.3).
n.3: Counting tasks in each workflow state over time describes a cumulative flow diagram (book 12.4.2).

Agile: Plans.q: In card-based story point estimating, every team member picks a value privately on a pre-numbered card and all the cards are revealed at the same moment. Why is this done?
o: So that the product owner can adopt the highest card as the final value
So that each person gives an independent view without being swayed by others
So that the estimate can be turned straight into hours for the team plan
So that the project manager can log each member's estimate on the dashboard
Agile: Plans.w: Agile estimation draws on the whole team so everyone contributes without being swayed by others; revealing simultaneously keeps each estimate independent before differences are discussed (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.4.3).

n.0: The team discusses differences and agrees a shared value; the product owner does not simply take the highest card (book 8.4.3).
n.2: Story points stay relative estimates; they are not converted to hours (book 8.4.3).
n.3: The aim is unbiased team estimates; individual estimates are not dashboard content (book 8.4.3, Table 12.1).

Agile: Plans.q: In which process does the detailed estimation of user stories normally take place in PRINCE2 Agile, and in which part of it?
o: Directing a project, when the board reviews the release map in the agile enablement workshop
Closing a project, when actual effort is compared with the original estimates for each release
Starting up a project, when the project canvas workshop agrees the cost definition for the project
Managing product delivery, in the effort estimation topic of the team planning workshop
Agile: Plans.w: Estimation of work is part of the plans practice and takes place during managing product delivery; the team planning workshop includes an effort estimation topic to reach a shared view of each story's effort (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.13).

n.0: The agile enablement workshop reviews Agilometer assessments and agile adoption risks, not story estimates (book Table 13.5).
n.1: Closing a project reviews performance and confirms acceptance; estimating stories happens before they are built (book Table 13.13).
n.2: Cost definition in the project canvas workshop sets out the project's costs at a high level, not detailed story estimates (book Table 13.2).

Agile: Plans.q: A project includes physical products as well as software. How do the product breakdown structure (PBS) and product flow diagram (PFD) relate in planning?
o: The PFD is drawn first, and the PBS then orders the products by priority for each release
The PBS shows the order of delivery, and the PFD lists the requirements of each component
Building the PBS helps identify dependencies, which the PFD then shows as a sequence
Both are replaced by the project backlog, which holds the products and their sequence
Agile: Plans.w: A PBS divides each product hierarchically into components and collects their requirements; developing it helps identify dependencies, which the PFD describes as the sequence of development (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.4.1, 8.4.2).

n.0: The PBS comes first and is a hierarchy, not a priority order; the PFD follows from it (book 8.4.1, 8.4.2).
n.1: This swaps the two: the PBS holds the components and their requirements, while the PFD shows the order and dependencies (book 8.4.1, 8.4.2).
n.3: The project backlog replaces the project product description; the PBS and PFD remain plans practice techniques (book 8.3.2.1, 8.4).

Agile: Plans.q: In initiation, the whole team needs to size 50 epics quickly before building the release map. Later, each team will estimate individual stories in more detail. Which pairing of techniques best fits?
o: Magic estimation for the epics now, then card-based story points in each team planning workshop
Card-based estimating for the epics now, then magic estimation of tasks in each team retrospective
Delegation poker for the epics now, then story points set by the product owner for the team
A product flow diagram for the epics now, then hours estimated by the project manager per task
Agile: Plans.w: Magic estimation suits early planning, sizing many items quickly without lengthy discussion; detailed estimation of stories then happens in managing product delivery, in the team planning workshop's effort estimation topic (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.4.3, Table 13.13).

n.1: Team retrospectives reflect on the last iteration; they are not where work is estimated (book Table 13.14).
n.2: Delegation poker agrees decision-making levels, not sizes, and estimates come from the whole team rather than the product owner (book 7.4.2, 8.4.3).
n.3: A PFD shows sequence and dependencies, not size, and agile estimates are relative, made by the team rather than hours set by the PM (book 8.4.2, 8.4.3).

Agile: Plans.q: A new delivery team starts work, measures how much it completes in each iteration and uses that rate to forecast when the release will be finished. Which term does PRINCE2 Agile use for basing planning decisions on this kind of experience?
o: Rationalism
Empiricism
Timeboxing
Decomposition
Agile: Plans.w: Empiricism means making decisions from experience, meaning what is happening or has already happened: start the work, see how much gets done and forecast from that (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3).

n.0: Rationalism is the opposite of empiricism: it relies on reasoning and logic to predict and plan before evidence exists (book 8.3).
n.2: Timeboxing fixes the length of a period of work (iteration, release or stage); it does not describe forecasting from observed progress (Glossary).
n.3: Decomposition is breaking work into smaller parts, as a story map does; it is not the term for planning from experience (book 8.3.1).

Agile: Plans.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

Starting the work and then seeing how much a team actually gets done is sometimes called [?], by comparison with setting a pair of weighing scales to zero before using them.
o: calibration
refactoring
baselining
swarming
Agile: Plans.w: The plans practice describes starting work to see the real rate of progress as calibration, likened to zeroing scales, or as calculating velocity (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3).

n.1: Refactoring is improving the internal structure of a product without changing its behaviour; it is not a way of measuring the team's rate.
n.2: Baselining fixes an approved version of a product or plan for control purposes; the book's term for measuring the team's real rate is calibration (book 8.3).
n.3: Swarming is the whole team focusing on one item, often a blocker; it is not about measuring how much gets done.

Agile: Plans.q: Which statement describes the approach that the PRINCE2 Agile plans practice treats as the opposite of empiricism?
o: Iterative delivery, releasing the product in small increments
Self-management, where the team organizes its own work
Just-in-time planning of tasks for the next iteration
Rationalism, predicting and planning by reasoning and logic
Agile: Plans.w: The book contrasts empiricism, deciding from what is happening or has happened, with rationalism, which uses reasoning or logic to predict and plan (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3).

n.0: Iterative and incremental delivery is how agile teams deliver; it works alongside empirical planning rather than being its opposite (book 8.3).
n.1: Self-management describes how delivery teams organize their work; it is an agile characteristic, not the opposite of empiricism (book 2.6.2).
n.2: Planning task detail just in time for the next iteration is part of empirical agile planning, not its opposite (book 8.3.2.5).

Agile: Plans.q: A project manager tells the board that the release forecast is based on the delivery team's own measured velocity. Why does PRINCE2 Agile prefer this to other sources of estimate?
o: It removes the need to set time and cost tolerances for the current stage
It allows the team to estimate in hours rather than in relative story points
It reflects how fast this team is really delivering, so forecasts rest on evidence
It means the release map can be fixed at initiation and left unchanged afterwards
Agile: Plans.w: Velocity is the team's real rate of progress, found by starting work and measuring it, so a forecast built on it is empirical; another person's or team's rate does not reflect this team (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3, 12.4.3).

n.0: Tolerances are still set for every level of plan; time and cost normally have zero tolerance, which velocity does not change (book Table 3.1).
n.1: Velocity is normally measured in story points, which are relative estimates rather than hours (book 8.4.3).
n.3: Because forecasts come from measured progress, the release map is updated with actuals and forecasts during each stage (book Table 13.9).

Agile: Quality.q: An organization already has its own established procedures for designing, developing and testing products. How does PRINCE2 Agile suggest these are handled?
o: They are raised as a request for change for the change authority to approve
They are recorded in the quality register as planned quality activities
They are replaced by the testing practices in each team's product backlog
They may be used, with this recorded as a tailoring decision in the PID
Agile: Quality.w: PRINCE2 Agile allows an organization's own product design, development and testing procedures to be used instead, recording this as a tailoring decision in the PID (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.3.1).

n.0: Choosing to use the organization's procedures is a tailoring decision agreed in initiation, not a change to an approved baseline (book 9.3.1).
n.1: The quality register records individual planned and completed quality activities, not a decision about which procedures the project follows (book Table 9.1).
n.2: There is no requirement to replace existing procedures; the book allows them to be used and the decision to be recorded in the PID (book 9.3.1).

Agile: Quality.q:
Which two statements about the quality practice in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. Product descriptions, quality specifications and quality tolerances can be prioritized and decomposed so that what is delivered can flex.
2. Testing is grouped at the end of each release so that the iterations can focus on building features.
3. Products are aligned with the quality management approach through quality planning, quality control and product acceptance.
4. An organization's own testing procedures are set aside in favour of those in the quality register.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Quality.w: Statement 1 is how agile keeps the focus on products while letting what is delivered flex (book Table 5.1); statement 3 is the quality cycle (book 9.3.1). Statement 2 is wrong because testing is done first or as you go inside iterations (9.4.3); statement 4 is wrong because own procedures may be used and recorded in the PID, and the quality register records activities, not procedures (9.3.1, Table 9.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is false: agile tests first or as you go within iterations rather than grouping testing at the end of a release (book 9.4.3).
n.2: Both statements are false: testing is not deferred to the end of a release (9.4.3), and an organization's own procedures may be kept, with the quality register recording activities rather than procedures (9.3.1, Table 9.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is false: an organization's own procedures may be used as a tailoring decision recorded in the PID (book 9.3.1).

Agile: Quality.q: In the quality practice in agile, how is acceptance of products by the users normally obtained?
o: Once, when the complete project product is handed over at the end of the project
Frequently, as completed increments are shown and accepted against agreed criteria
By project assurance signing off each product on behalf of the users
By the project manager confirming that the product register is complete
Agile: Quality.w: Agile seeks frequent acceptance: completed features are demonstrated, for example in the product demo of a progress review, to gather user acceptance and feedback against acceptance criteria and the DoD (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.3.1, Table 13.10).

n.0: Waiting until the end for a single acceptance is the traditional pattern; agile obtains acceptance increment by increment (book 9.3.1, Table 13.10).
n.2: Project assurance monitors adherence to principles and governance; it does not accept products in place of the users (book Table 7.2).
n.3: The product register records product status and acceptance dates; updating it records acceptance, it does not obtain it from users (book Table 9.1).

Agile: Quality.q: In managing product delivery, what does the team do about quality while executing a work package?
o: Tells the project manager of completed quality activities and gets products approved
Raises an exception report for each product that fails a quality check in the iteration
Sends a checkpoint report to the project board listing each quality check performed
Updates the project canvas with the results of every quality check carried out
Agile: Quality.w: Executing a work package includes notifying the project manager of completed quality activities and products and obtaining approvals for completed products (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.12).

n.1: A failed check is normal work for the team; exception reports are for forecast breaches of tolerance, raised by the project manager (book Table 12.1).
n.2: In PRINCE2 Agile the team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report, and team-level reporting goes to the project manager, not the board (book Table 12.1).
n.3: The project canvas holds the business justification; quality results go in the quality register (book 6.3.2, Table 9.1).

Agile: Quality.q: Which management product describes the quality techniques and standards to be applied, and the roles and responsibilities for achieving the required quality, in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: The product backlog
The commercial management approach
The quality register
The quality management approach
Agile: Quality.w: The quality management approach describes the quality techniques and standards to be applied and the roles and responsibilities for meeting the quality specifications and acceptance criteria (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 9.1).

n.0: The product backlog holds a team's user stories and links to the team DoD; the approach to quality is set out elsewhere (book 8.3.2.1).
n.1: The commercial management approach covers procurement and contract forms that support agile delivery, not the quality techniques and standards for the project (book Table 7.3).
n.2: The quality register records individual quality activities and their results; it does not set out techniques and standards (book Table 9.1).

Agile: Quality.q: Where should the agile ways of working and agile behaviours expected on a PRINCE2 Agile project be documented so that they can be properly assured?
o: In the communication management approach
In the quality management approach
In the quality register
In the lessons log
Agile: Quality.w: Agile ways of working and agile behaviours should be incorporated and documented in the quality management approach, where they can be assured like any other quality standard (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 9.1).

n.0: The communication management approach covers how information is exchanged with stakeholders; it does not set out the agile behaviours to be assured (book 4.4, Table 9.1).
n.2: The quality register records planned and completed quality activities and their results, not expected ways of working (book Table 9.1).
n.3: The lessons log captures lessons learned during the project; it does not define the behaviours expected from the start (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Quality.q: A supplier will use its own automated testing methods for the components it builds. Where should these testing methods be documented?
o: In the commercial management approach
In the quality management approach
In the team dashboard
In the product register
Agile: Quality.w: Agile testing methods, including those used by external suppliers, are recorded in the quality management approach so that everyone knows how quality will be achieved and checked (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 9.1, 9.4.3).

n.0: The commercial management approach covers supplier selection and contracts, not the supplier's testing methods (book Table 7.3).
n.2: The team dashboard shows a team's progress for the iteration; it is not where testing methods are documented (book Table 12.1).
n.3: The product register lists each product and its status; it does not describe how testing is done (book Table 9.1).

Agile: Quality.q: In which process are the management approaches, including the quality management approach, agreed?
o: Controlling a stage
Starting up a project
Initiating a project
Managing a stage boundary
Agile: Quality.w: Agreeing the management approaches (change, communication, sustainability, benefits, commercial, quality, risk, issue, digital and data) is an activity of initiating a project (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.6).

n.0: Controlling a stage assigns and monitors work within an agreed approach; it does not agree the approaches in the first place (book Table 13.9).
n.1: Starting up checks whether the project is viable and worthwhile and produces the project brief; the detailed approaches come in initiation (book 13.2).
n.3: Stage boundaries may review and update approaches, but they are first agreed in initiating a project (book 13.7, Table 13.6).

Agile: Quality.q: The project backlog shows or links to the project Definition of Ready and Definition of Done. Which management product do these come from?
o: The commercial management approach
The team plan
