The quality management approach
The project canvas
Agile: Quality.w: The project backlog should show or link to the project DoR and DoD taken from the quality management approach, and name who accepts the project product (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.1).

n.0: The commercial management approach can support agile contracts, but it is not the source of the project DoR and DoD (book Table 7.3, 8.3.2.1).
n.1: A team plan covers one iteration's tasks; the project-level DoR and DoD come from the quality management approach (book 8.3.2, 8.3.2.1).
n.3: The project canvas sets out the business justification and scenarios; quality criteria come from the quality management approach (book 6.3.2, 8.3.2.1).

Agile: Quality.q: How should the management approaches, including the quality management approach, be developed in the project initiation workshop?
o: Replaced by the team dashboards that each team creates at kickoff
Copied from the previous project and approved by the board unchanged
Co-created, to give structured agility with governance and control
Drafted by project assurance and issued to the teams for compliance
Agile: Quality.w: The management approaches topic of the project initiation workshop co-creates the approaches to give structured agility, keeping flexibility while maintaining governance and control (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.7).

n.0: Team dashboards are created in the project kickoff workshop for transparency; they do not replace the management approaches (book Table 13.8).
n.1: The approaches are tailored to this project in the workshop; reusing old ones unchanged ignores the tailor principle (book Table 13.7).
n.3: Project assurance monitors and advises; the workshop co-creates the approaches with the people who will use them (book Table 7.2, Table 13.7).

Agile: Quality.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile ask for agile behaviours to be included in the quality management approach?
o: So that team members can be appraised one by one on their conduct
So that the board can compare each team's velocity against the plan
So that the communication management approach no longer needs to be produced
So agile ways of working are documented and assured like other standards
Agile: Quality.w: Agile ways of working must be incorporated and documented in the quality management approach, and agile behaviours form part of it so that they are properly assured (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 9.1).

n.0: The aim is to assure the agreed ways of working for the project, not to appraise individuals (book Table 9.1).
n.1: Velocity is a progress measure from the team's own history, not the reason behaviours sit in the quality approach (book 8.3, 12.4).
n.2: The communication management approach is still produced; it covers stakeholder communication, not the behaviours to be assured (book Table 13.6, 4.4).

Agile: Quality.q: Which role approves the management approaches, such as the quality management approach, in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: Project assurance
The chief product owner
The project executive
The project manager
Agile: Quality.w: The project executive is accountable for the project and approves the project brief, the management approaches and the team structure (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2).

n.0: Project assurance monitors adherence and advises the board and project manager; it does not approve the approaches (book Table 7.2).
n.1: The CPO represents the users and owns the project backlog; approving the management approaches is the executive's responsibility (book Table 7.2).
n.3: The project manager prepares the approaches with product owners and stakeholders, but approval sits with the executive (book Table 7.2, Table 13.6).

Agile: Quality.q: In the quality practice, what is the Definition of Ready?
o: A shared agreement on the criteria an item must meet to be considered complete
A checklist the project board uses before authorizing the next stage
A shared agreement on the criteria an item must meet before work on it begins
A list of the finished products and their approval and acceptance dates
Agile: Quality.w: The DoR is a shared team agreement on the criteria a task, deliverable or user story must meet before work begins, so the item is fully prepared (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.3.2.1).

n.0: Criteria for an item to count as complete form the Definition of Done, not the Definition of Ready (book 9.3.2.2).
n.1: Authorizing a stage is a board decision in directing a project; the DoR is a team-level agreement about work items (book 9.3.2.1).
n.3: Products with their status and acceptance dates are recorded in the product register (book Table 9.1).

Agile: Quality.q: At the end of an iteration a user story has been built, but a known defect is still open. How should the story be treated under the Definition of Done?
o: As done, because the defect can be fixed early in the next iteration
As done, with the defect recorded in the issue register for later
As not done, because work that still has defects does not meet the DoD
As almost done, shown as 90% complete on the team dashboard
Agile: Quality.w: An item is either done or not done; work that still contains defects is not done (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.3.2.2).

n.0: Planning a later fix does not change its status now; work with defects is not done (book 9.3.2.2).
n.1: Recording the defect does not make the work complete; work with defects is not done (book 9.3.2.2).
n.3: There is no 'almost done' state: an item is either done or not done (book 9.3.2.2).

Agile: Quality.q: In which workshop are the project Definition of Ready and the project Definition of Done agreed?
o: The project initiation workshop
The project canvas workshop in starting up
The project kickoff workshop
The team planning workshop
Agile: Quality.w: Project DoR and project DoD are agenda topics of the project initiation workshop in initiating a project (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 13.4.4.1, Table 13.7).

n.1: The project canvas workshop shapes the canvas, scope and user groups; DoR and DoD come later, in initiation (book Table 13.2, Table 13.7).
n.2: The kickoff workshop builds teamwork (values and norms, skill and delegation matrices, dashboards); it has no project DoR or DoD topic (book Table 13.8).
n.3: Team planning refines stories and their acceptance criteria for the next iteration; the project-level DoR and DoD are set in initiation (book Table 13.13, Table 13.7).

Agile: Quality.q: Where is the team Definition of Done included or linked in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: In the project backlog
In the project canvas
In the release map
In the product backlog
Agile: Quality.w: A product backlog should include or link to the team Definition of Done; it is used at team level by the product owner (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.1).

n.0: The project backlog shows or links to the project-level DoR and DoD, not each team's DoD (book 8.3.2.1).
n.1: The project canvas records the business justification, not team quality criteria (book 6.3.2).
n.2: The release map shows releases, their timing and features; it does not hold the team DoD (book 8.3.2).

Agile: Quality.q: At the end of an iteration, only part of a user story meets the Definition of Done. What does PRINCE2 Agile suggest?
o: Report the whole story as done and finish the rest in the next iteration
Split it: the finished part is done and the rest returns to the backlog
Extend the iteration by a few days so the whole story can be finished
Raise an exception report because the story was not completed in time
Agile: Quality.w: A partly completed story is split: the part meeting the DoD is done, and the remainder goes back to the backlog to be reprioritized (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.3.2.2).

n.0: Work that does not meet the DoD is not done; reporting it as done hides the true position (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: Iterations are timeboxes with fixed time; the unfinished part is returned to the backlog instead (book 9.3.2.2, Table 3.1).
n.3: One unfinished story is handled by splitting it; exceptions are for forecast breaches of tolerance (book 9.3.2.2, Table 12.1).

Agile: Quality.q:
Which two statements about the Definition of Ready are correct?

1. It helps prevent delays by making sure the team has what it needs before starting work.
2. A user story can be ready when it states who, what and why and has measurable, prioritized acceptance criteria.
3. It sets out the checks a product must pass before it is handed to the users.
4. It is agreed by the project board at each stage boundary for the next stage.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
Agile: Quality.w: The DoR makes sure items are fully prepared so work can start without delays, and a story is ready when it has who, what and why plus measurable, prioritized acceptance criteria (book 9.3.2.1). Checks before handover to users belong to the DoD (9.3.2.2), and the DoR is a team agreement, with the project DoR set in the project initiation workshop (Table 13.7).

n.1: Statement 4 is false: the DoR is a shared team agreement and the project DoR is set in the project initiation workshop, not by the board at each boundary (book 9.3.2.1, Table 13.7).
n.2: Statement 3 is false: the checks a product must pass before handover to users are the Definition of Done (book 9.3.2.2).
n.3: Both are false: handover checks belong to the DoD (9.3.2.2), and the DoR is not a board decision at stage boundaries (9.3.2.1, Table 13.7).

Agile: Quality.q: What is the goal of agreeing a project Definition of Done in the project initiation workshop?
o: A shared understanding of the quality needed before work is handed to the users or CPO
A shared view of the effort and complexity involved in each user story
A shared map of the skills, gaps and overlaps within each delivery team
A shared understanding of the quality needed before work is handed to development
Agile: Quality.w: The project DoD topic lists product-overarching criteria for work to be acceptable to users, so that everyone shares an understanding of the quality needed before work is handed to the users or CPO (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.7).

n.1: Sharing a view of effort per story is the effort estimation topic of the team planning workshop (book Table 13.13).
n.2: Mapping skills, gaps and overlaps is the team skill matrix topic of the project kickoff workshop (book Table 13.8).
n.3: That is the goal of the project Definition of Ready topic, which covers what must be in place before development starts (book Table 13.7).

Agile: Quality.q: Which PRINCE2 Agile role reviews products against the acceptance criteria and the team Definition of Done?
o: Project assurance
The developer
The team coach
The tester
Agile: Quality.w: The tester designs, runs and possibly automates tests and quality reviews, checking products against acceptance or quality criteria and the team DoD (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2).

n.0: Project assurance monitors adherence to principles, practices and governance; it does not review each product against the team DoD (book Table 7.2).
n.1: The developer designs, builds and maintains increments of the product; reviewing them against the criteria and DoD is the tester's role (book Table 7.2).
n.2: The team coach helps one or two teams self-manage and facilitates their workshops; reviewing products against the criteria and team DoD is the tester's role (book Table 7.2).

Agile: Quality.q: Which register summarizes all the quality management activities that are planned or have taken place on a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: The risk register
The product register
The quality register
The issue register
Agile: Quality.w: The quality register summarizes every planned and completed quality management activity, with method, dates, responsibilities and results (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 9.1).

n.0: The risk register records identified risks with their status and history, not quality activities (book Table 10.1).
n.1: The product register lists the products required by a plan and their status, not the quality activities carried out on them (book Table 9.1).
n.3: The issue register records issues being handled formally, such as requests for change and off-specifications (book 11.3.4).

Agile: Quality.q: A stakeholder asks whether a particular product has been approved and accepted yet. Which record should the project manager check?
o: The quality register
The product register
The project log
The issue register
Agile: Quality.w: The product register lists all the products required by a plan with their status and dates such as approval and acceptance, so status questions are answered there (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 9.1).

n.0: The quality register shows quality activities and their pass or fail results; product status and acceptance dates sit in the product register (book Table 9.1).
n.2: The project log holds the daily log and lessons log; product status is kept in the product register (book Table 12.1, Table 9.1).
n.3: The issue register tracks issues such as requests for change; it does not record whether products have been accepted (book 11.3.4).

Agile: Quality.q: Which information is recorded in the quality register?
o: The priority and severity of each request for change
The quality method and the pass or fail result of each check
The probability, impact and owner of each identified threat
The status of each product and the date it was accepted
Agile: Quality.w: Quality register entries include quality and product identifiers, the quality method, planned and actual dates, responsibilities, the result (pass or fail) and quality records (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 9.1).

n.0: Requests for change are recorded and prioritized in the issue register (book 11.3.4).
n.2: Probability, impact and ownership of risks are recorded in the risk register (book Table 10.1).
n.3: Product status and approval or acceptance dates are held in the product register (book Table 9.1).

Agile: Quality.q: What does the product register record in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: All the products required by a plan and their current status
All the user stories selected for the coming iteration
All planned and completed quality activities and their results
All the lessons learned about product quality so far
Agile: Quality.w: The product register lists all products required by a plan with their status, identifiers, approval and acceptance dates and references (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 9.1).

n.1: Stories selected for an iteration form the team plan agreed in the team planning workshop (book Table 13.13).
n.2: Planned and completed quality activities with results are the content of the quality register (book Table 9.1).
n.3: Lessons are recorded in the lessons log, part of the project log (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Quality.q:
Which two statements about the quality register and the product register are correct?

1. The product register records the quality method used to check each product.
2. The quality register records the result of each quality activity, such as pass or fail.
3. The quality register records the probability and impact of threats to quality.
4. The product register records each product's status and its approval and acceptance dates.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Quality.w: The quality register records each quality activity with its method and result, and the product register records each product's status with approval and acceptance dates (book Table 9.1). The quality method sits in the quality register, not the product register, and probability and impact of threats belong in the risk register (Table 10.1).

n.0: Statement 1 is false: the quality method is recorded in the quality register, not the product register (book Table 9.1).
n.1: Both are false: the quality method belongs in the quality register (Table 9.1) and probability and impact of threats belong in the risk register (Table 10.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is false: probability and impact of threats are recorded in the risk register, not the quality register (book Table 10.1).

Agile: Quality.q: In managing product delivery, during which activity does the team review registers and logs and update the team dashboard?
o: Evaluate a work package
Accept a work package
Authorize a work package
Notify work package completion
Agile: Quality.w: Evaluating a work package includes reviewing registers and logs and updating the team dashboard (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.12).

n.1: Accepting a work package covers reviewing the user stories, producing a team plan and agreeing to deliver (book Table 13.12).
n.2: Authorizing a work package is a project manager activity in controlling a stage, not a team activity in managing product delivery (book Table 13.9).
n.3: Notifying completion tells the project manager the work package is finished; reviewing registers and updating the dashboard come in evaluation (book Table 13.12).

Agile: Quality.q: A product has passed its quality review, but the chief product owner has not yet accepted it. How is this shown in the registers?
o: The quality register shows the product as accepted, since its review has passed
The product register shows the review result; the quality register shows acceptance
The issue register records an off-specification until the product is accepted
The quality register shows the pass; the product register shows it awaiting acceptance
Agile: Quality.w: The quality register records quality activities and results, so the pass is logged there; the product register records product status and acceptance dates, so it still shows the product awaiting acceptance (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 9.1).

n.0: Acceptance is a product status recorded in the product register; a passed review does not by itself record acceptance (book Table 9.1).
n.1: This reverses the two registers: results belong in the quality register and status in the product register (book Table 9.1).
n.2: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification; a product that passed review is not one (book 11.3.1).

Agile: Quality.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile treat the PRINCE2 quality register and product register?
o: It replaces both with the team dashboard for each delivery team
It merges both into the project backlog as part of each epic
It replaces both with the Definition of Done agreed by each team
It keeps both as quality practice artifacts with their usual purposes
Agile: Quality.w: Table 9.1 keeps the quality register and the product register as quality practice artifacts alongside the product backlog, the quality management approach and DoR/DoD (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 9.1).

n.0: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report in the progress practice; it does not replace the registers (book Table 12.1).
n.1: The project backlog replaces the project product description and holds epics; the registers remain separate artifacts (book 8.3.2.1, Table 9.1).
n.2: The DoD defines when an item is complete; it sits alongside the registers rather than replacing them (book 9.3.2.2, Table 9.1).

Agile: Quality.q: In MoSCoW prioritization, what does the W stand for?
o: Worth having later
Won't have this time
Would like to have
Wanted if time allows
Agile: Quality.w: MoSCoW stands for Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have (this time): items agreed not to be delivered in the current timeframe (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.3.2; DSDM origin).

n.0: 'Worth having later' is not a category name; the W is Won't have this time (book 9.3.2).
n.2: 'Would like to have' is not a MoSCoW category; the W is Won't have this time (book 9.3.2).
n.3: Requirements wanted if time allows fit the Could have category; the W is Won't have this time (book 9.3.2).

Agile: Quality.q: By default, how is scope treated in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: Fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves
Fixed for Must and Should haves and flexed for Could haves
Fixed for every priority, with time flexed to deliver them
Flexed for Must, Should and Could haves to protect the deadline
Agile: Quality.w: Table 3.1 sets scope as fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should haves and Could haves, while time and cost have zero tolerance (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1).

n.1: Should haves are flexed as well as Could haves; only the Must haves are fixed (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan; it is scope below the Must haves that flexes (book Table 3.1).
n.3: Must haves are fixed; flexing them would remove the minimum the product needs (book Table 3.1).

Agile: Quality.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

When an iteration is running late, the team protects the deadline by dropping lower-priority work, starting with the [?] haves.
o: Must
Won't
Could
Should
Agile: Quality.w: Could haves are desirable but less important and are the first to be dropped when time is short; scope flexes so that time and cost do not (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1; DSDM MoSCoW guidance).

n.0: Must haves are fixed in scope; they are the minimum that has to be delivered (book Table 3.1).
n.1: Won't have items are already agreed not to be delivered this time, so there is nothing to drop (book 9.3.2).
n.3: Should haves are important and are flexed after the Could haves have gone (book Table 3.1; DSDM).

Agile: Quality.q: In which workshop topic is MoSCoW used to review and prioritize requirements before an iteration?
o: Effort estimation in the team planning workshop
Team values and norms in the project kickoff workshop
Product backlog refinement in the team planning workshop
Project highlights in the progress review workshop
Agile: Quality.w: The product backlog refinement topic of the team planning workshop reviews and prioritizes requirements using MoSCoW (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.13).

n.0: Effort estimation builds a shared view of the complexity and effort of each story; prioritizing with MoSCoW is backlog refinement (book Table 13.13).
n.1: Team values and norms shape the agile culture and expectations of the team, not the order of requirements (book Table 13.8).
n.3: Project highlights reviews the metrics on the project dashboard; it does not prioritize the backlog (book Table 13.10).

Agile: Quality.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile pair MoSCoW prioritization with zero tolerance on time and cost?
o: So the deadline can move when Must haves take longer than estimated
So every feature in the backlog is delivered by the agreed end date
So extra budget can be released for Should haves at each stage end
So lower-priority features can flex to protect the agreed time and cost
Agile: Quality.w: Agile allows tolerance on what is delivered while restricting time and cost; MoSCoW shows which features can flex (Should and Could haves) when time or cost is under pressure (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1, Table 5.1).

n.0: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan; the response to pressure is to flex lower-priority scope (book Table 3.1).
n.1: MoSCoW assumes not everything will be delivered; Should and Could haves may be dropped (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Cost also has zero tolerance; Should haves flex rather than attracting extra money (book Table 3.1).

Agile: Quality.q: Which description best fits a Should have requirement?
o: Desirable but less important, and the first to be dropped from the timebox if time runs short
Agreed not to be delivered in this timeframe, and recorded so it does not creep back
Part of the minimum usable subset, without which the solution would not be worth deploying
Important but not vital: painful to omit, yet the solution stays viable, perhaps with a workaround
Agile: Quality.w: A Should have is important but not vital; leaving it out hurts, but the solution remains viable, possibly with a workaround (DSDM MoSCoW guidance, used in PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.3.2).

n.0: This describes a Could have, the main contingency (DSDM; book Table 3.1).
n.1: This describes a Won't have this time item (DSDM; book 9.3.2).
n.2: This describes a Must have, the fixed minimum that has to be delivered (DSDM; book Table 3.1).

Agile: Quality.q: How is MoSCoW used in the project canvas workshop?
o: To prioritize the scope, set out as epic user stories, under scope definition
To rank each team member's skills when building the team skill matrix
To prioritize the key user groups, ranked first to third, under user group definition
To prioritize the Agilometer sliders that need the most improvement
Agile: Quality.w: In the project canvas workshop, the scope definition topic defines the scope in epic user stories and prioritizes them with MoSCoW, then checks timeline and scope tolerances (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.2).

n.1: The team skill matrix maps skills, gaps and overlaps in the project kickoff workshop (book Table 13.8).
n.2: User group definition ranks one to three key user groups first to third; it does not use MoSCoW (book Table 13.2).
n.3: The Agilometer is assessed in the project initiation workshop and is a risk tool; it is not ranked with MoSCoW (book 10.3.2, Table 13.7).

Agile: Quality.q: Midway through a stage, the team forecasts that not all the Must have features can be delivered within the stage's time and cost. What does this indicate?
o: An exception, because the fixed Must have scope is forecast to be missed
A case for extending the stage end date while keeping all scope
A detail change that the product owner can approve within the iteration
A routine trade-off the team handles by moving some Must haves to Could
Agile: Quality.w: Must haves are fixed, so a forecast that they cannot all be delivered within fixed time and cost means tolerance will be exceeded: an exception for the project manager to escalate with an exception report (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1, Table 12.1).

n.1: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan; the project manager escalates the forecast breach instead (book Table 3.1, Table 12.1).
n.2: A forecast that fixed scope will be missed is a breach of tolerance, not a detail change inside the project backlog (book Table 12.1, 11.3.2).
n.3: Must haves are fixed; the team cannot downgrade them to stay within the timebox (book Table 3.1).

Agile: Quality.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, what is refactoring?
o: Changing a product's internal structure without changing its external behaviour
Rebuilding a product from scratch when its defects exceed tolerance
Changing a product's external behaviour so that it meets new acceptance criteria
Moving unfinished user stories from one iteration into the next one
Agile: Quality.w: Refactoring, a concept from Martin Fowler, changes the internal structure of a product without altering its external behaviour (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.1).

n.1: Refactoring improves structure step by step while behaviour stays the same; it is not a rebuild (book 9.4.1).
n.2: Changing what a product does is new or changed work, not refactoring, which leaves behaviour unchanged (book 9.4.1).
n.3: Returning unfinished work to the backlog is part of applying the DoD, not refactoring (book 9.3.2.2).

Agile: Quality.q: Which description best fits technical debt?
o: The cost overrun recorded when a stage goes beyond its agreed cost tolerance
The fees owed to a supplier for products accepted but not yet invoiced
The work still owed, due to poor design or development, before a job is truly complete
The backlog of Could have stories still left undelivered when the project closes
Agile: Quality.w: Technical debt, Ward Cunningham's metaphor, describes the eventual consequences of poor design, architecture or development: work that must still be done before a job is truly complete (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.2).

n.0: A cost overrun beyond tolerance is an exception in the progress practice, not technical debt (book Table 12.1).
n.1: Supplier payments are commercial matters under the commercial management approach, not technical debt (book Table 7.3).
n.3: Undelivered Could haves are flexed scope; technical debt is about the quality of work already built (book Table 3.1, 9.4.2).

Agile: Quality.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

If technical debt is not paid back, it builds up [?], making later changes harder and more costly.
o: tolerance
contingency
interest
velocity
Agile: Quality.w: Like financial debt, unpaid technical debt accumulates interest, making future change harder, raising disorder and lowering quality (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.2).

n.0: Tolerances may be set for technical debt, but tolerance is a permitted limit, not what unpaid debt accumulates (book 9.4.2).
n.1: Contingency is room kept in reserve, such as Could haves; it is not what unpaid technical debt accumulates (book 9.4.2).
n.3: Velocity is the rate at which a team delivers story points; debt tends to slow work rather than build velocity (book 12.4.3, 9.4.2).

Agile: Quality.q: Which statement about refactoring is correct in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: It is the technique a team uses to clear a blocker it is stuck on
It is carried out once, at the end of the project, before handover
The concept can be applied to any product, not just software
It changes what a product does so it meets the users' new needs
Agile: Quality.w: Although it comes from software, the refactoring concept applies to any product, software or not (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.1).

n.0: Clearing a blocker together is swarming; refactoring is not a blocker technique (book 11.4.2, 9.4.1).
n.1: Refactoring is ongoing good practice during development, not a single end-of-project step (book 9.4.1).
n.3: Refactoring keeps external behaviour the same; meeting new needs means changing requirements (book 9.4.1).

Agile: Quality.q: How can technical debt be controlled in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: It is logged in the quality register and closed once the product passes review
Tolerances can be set, and a forecast that it will be too significant is an exception
It is tracked by the agile coach across all the teams in the organization
It is accepted as normal and passed to the operations team after handover
Agile: Quality.w: Tolerances may be applied to technical debt; if it is forecast to become too significant, this causes an exception (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.2).

n.0: The quality register records quality activities and results; it is not the control for technical debt (book Table 9.1, 9.4.2).
n.2: The agile coach removes systemic blockers to agile adoption; technical debt is controlled through tolerances (book Table 7.2, 9.4.2).
n.3: Unpaid debt accrues interest and lowers quality; PRINCE2 Agile controls it with tolerances during the project (book 9.4.2).

Agile: Quality.q: Technical debt has grown so large that the remaining Must have features can no longer be delivered within the stage tolerances. Which report should the project manager use?
o: An exception report to the project board
A lessons report to the project board
A highlight report through the project dashboard
An issue report to the change authority
Agile: Quality.w: Technical debt forecast to become too significant causes an exception, and a forecast breach of stage tolerance is escalated to the board in an exception report (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.2, Table 12.1).

n.1: A lessons report shares lessons to improve ways of working; it does not escalate a forecast breach (book Table 12.1).
n.2: The project dashboard gives regular status; a forecast breach of tolerance needs an exception report (book Table 12.1).
n.3: An issue report covers one issue's impact and options; a forecast breach of stage tolerance goes to the board as an exception (book 11.3.4, Table 12.1).

Agile: Quality.q: Why does unpaid technical debt matter to a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: It requires a fresh Agilometer assessment at every stage boundary
It reduces the minimum viable benefits figure recorded in the project canvas
It increases the number of Won't have items recorded in the backlog
It raises disorder and lowers quality, so later changes become harder and costlier
Agile: Quality.w: Unpaid technical debt accumulates interest: it increases disorder, lowers quality and makes later change harder (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.2).

n.0: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working; it is not triggered by technical debt (book 10.3.2, 9.4.2).
n.1: Technical debt affects the quality and changeability of products; it does not alter the benefits figures in the canvas (book 9.4.2, 6.3.2).
n.2: Won't have items are an agreed scope decision, not a consequence of technical debt (book 9.3.2, 9.4.2).

Agile: Quality.q: A developer reorganizes the code behind an online booking form so that it is easier to maintain. Users notice no difference in how the form works. Which technique is this?
o: Swarming
Test-driven development
Refactoring
A/B testing
Agile: Quality.w: Improving a product's internal structure while its external behaviour stays the same is refactoring (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.1).

n.0: Swarming is the whole team focusing on one blocker or urgent task; one developer tidying code is not swarming (book 11.4.2).
n.1: TDD writes tests before code at unit level; the change described is a restructuring of existing code (Glossary, book 9.4.3).
n.3: A/B testing compares two versions with users and analyses their responses; here nothing is shown to users (book 9.4.3).

Agile: Quality.q: What does A/B testing involve in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Writing a unit test for each piece of code before the code itself is written
Comparing two versions of a feature with users and analysing how they respond
Splitting the testing of each story between a developer and a tester
Checking a product against its acceptance criteria before and after refactoring
Agile: Quality.w: A/B testing compares two versions of a product, design or feature with users and analyses their responses to guide decisions (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.3).

n.0: Writing tests first at unit level is test-driven development (Glossary).
n.2: Sharing testing between roles is a team arrangement, not A/B testing (book Table 7.2, 9.4.3).
n.3: Refactoring keeps behaviour unchanged, and checking against acceptance criteria is a quality check on one version; A/B testing compares two versions with users (book 9.4.1, 9.4.3).

Agile: Quality.q: In validation and verification, what does validation confirm?
o: That the product has been signed off by project assurance
That the right product is being built to meet the users' needs
That the product has passed every automated unit test
That the product is being built correctly to its specification
Agile: Quality.w: Validation is building the right thing; verification is building the thing right (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.3).

n.0: Project assurance monitors governance and adherence to principles; it does not validate products for users (book Table 7.2).
n.2: Passing unit tests shows the code works as written; it does not show the right product is being built (book 9.4.3).
n.3: Building the product correctly to its specification is verification, building the thing right (book 9.4.3).

Agile: Quality.q: What should be decided early about testing in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: Which stage end the testing of all products will be deferred to
How much testing can be done first, or at least as you go
Which supplier will carry out all the testing after delivery
How many defects each release may contain before acceptance
Agile: Quality.w: Early on, the project should decide how much testing and checking can be test or check first, or at least test or check as you go (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.3).

n.0: Deferring testing to stage ends repeats the traditional late-assessment problem; agile tests first or as you go (book 9.4.3).
n.2: Testing is built into the iterations, with testers in the teams; it is not handed to a supplier after delivery (book Table 7.2, 9.4.3).
n.3: Work with defects is not done under the DoD; the early decision is about testing first or as you go (book 9.3.2.2, 9.4.3).

Agile: Quality.q: Which statement best describes test-driven development (TDD)?
o: A test-first approach from XP that relies on automation, usually at unit level
An approach in which users test each release after it goes live
A collaborative approach that writes tests in language that users understand
An approach that compares two versions of a feature with groups of users
Agile: Quality.w: TDD comes from XP test-first programming, requires automation and usually operates at unit-testing level (PRINCE2 Agile V2 Glossary).

n.1: TDD writes tests before code during development, not user checks after release (Glossary).
n.2: Writing tests collaboratively in users' language is behaviour-driven development, which builds on TDD (Glossary).
n.3: Comparing two versions with users is A/B testing (book 9.4.3).

Agile: Quality.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile urge care when applying software testing practices to other kinds of product?
o: Products such as a campaign may not be rebuilt and retested quickly or by automation
Non-software products are tested by project assurance instead of testers
Testing practices are owned by suppliers and cannot be shared with users
Products that are not software do not need acceptance criteria or a Definition of Done
Agile: Quality.w: Software can be built and tested with automation in days, hours or minutes, but a product such as a marketing campaign may not be built that quickly or automatically, so the transfer needs care (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.3).

n.1: Testers design and run tests for any product; project assurance monitors governance (book Table 7.2).
n.2: Supplier testing methods are documented in the quality management approach; ownership is not the concern (book Table 9.1, 9.4.3).
n.3: Every product needs acceptance criteria and a DoD; the caution is about speed and automation of testing (book 9.3.2.2, 9.4.3).

Agile: Quality.q:
Which two statements about testing in an agile context are correct?

1. Verification checks that the right product is being built for the users.
2. Test-driven development is mainly used for end-to-end user acceptance.
3. Behaviour-driven development builds on test-driven development using language users understand.
4. A/B testing compares two versions of a feature by analysing users' responses.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Quality.w: BDD is based on TDD but is more collaborative and uses language users understand (Glossary), and A/B testing compares two versions with users and analyses their responses (book 9.4.3). Statement 1 describes validation, not verification (9.4.3); statement 2 is wrong because TDD usually works at unit-test level (Glossary).

n.0: Both are false: checking that the right product is built is validation (9.4.3), and TDD usually works at unit level, not end-to-end acceptance (Glossary).
n.1: Statement 1 is false: building the right product is validation; verification is building the thing right (book 9.4.3).
n.2: Statement 2 is false: TDD is a test-first technique that usually works at unit-testing level (Glossary).

Agile: Quality.q: A marketing team shows two versions of a sign-up page to different groups of customers and keeps the one that converts better. Which technique is this?
o: A/B testing
Verification
Refactoring
Behaviour-driven development
Agile: Quality.w: Comparing two versions of a product or feature with users and analysing their responses to decide between them is A/B testing (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.3).

n.1: Verification checks that a product is built correctly to its specification, not which version users prefer (book 9.4.3).
n.2: Refactoring changes internal structure without changing behaviour; here two different versions are compared (book 9.4.1).
n.3: BDD writes tests collaboratively in users' language before building; it does not compare live versions (Glossary).

Agile: Quality.q: A team confirms that a new payroll report calculates every figure exactly as set out in its specification. What is this an example of?
o: Validation
Refactoring
A/B testing
Verification
Agile: Quality.w: Checking that a product has been built correctly against its specification is verification, building the thing right (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.3).

n.0: Validation checks that the right product is being built for the users' needs, not conformance to the specification (book 9.4.3).
n.1: Refactoring restructures a product without changing its behaviour; it is not a check of results (book 9.4.1).
n.2: A/B testing compares two versions with users; here one report is checked against its specification (book 9.4.3).

Agile: Quality.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, what provides the starting point that drives the quality practice?
o: The lessons recorded in the project log
The requirements held in the project backlog
The tolerances shown on the project dashboard
The risk responses recorded in the risk register
Agile: Quality.w: In an agile context the quality practice is driven by the requirements in the project backlog, which replaces the project product description (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.3.1, 8.3.2.1).

n.0: The project log (daily and lessons log) supports the progress practice; it does not define what the products must be like (book Table 12.1).
n.2: The project dashboard reports progress to the board (it replaces the highlight report); it does not set the quality requirements (book Table 12.1).
n.3: Risk responses belong to the risk practice; quality starts from what the users require, held in the project backlog (book 10.3, 9.3.1).

Agile: Quality.q: Which cycle does the quality practice follow in PRINCE2 Agile to align the project products with the quality management approach?
o: Identify, assess, plan, implement and communicate
Develop, check, maintain and confirm
Capture, assess, recommend, decide and implement changes
Quality planning, quality control and product acceptance
Agile: Quality.w: The quality practice aligns the project products with the quality management approach through a cycle of quality planning, quality control and product acceptance (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.3.1).

n.0: These are the five steps of the risk management technique in the risk practice, not the quality cycle (book 10.3.1).
n.1: These steps describe how the business case is handled over the life of the project, not how quality is managed (book ch 6).
n.2: These are the steps of the issue management technique in the issues practice, used to control changes to the baseline (book 11.3; PRINCE2 7 issue technique).

Agile: Quality.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

The question the quality practice answers in an agile project is what is [?] to the users and how this can be measured.
o: affordable
acceptable
achievable
desirable
Agile: Quality.w: The quality practice asks what is acceptable to the users and how that can be measured, which is why acceptance criteria and the DoD matter so much (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 5.2).

n.0: Whether the project is affordable is a viability question for the business case practice, not the quality question (book 6.1).
n.2: Achievability is also a business case test of whether the project should continue; quality asks what the users will accept (book 6.1, Table 5.2).
n.3: Desirability is one of the three tests (desirable, viable, achievable) applied by the business case practice (book 6.1).

Agile: Quality.q: When does quality control mainly take place in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: At each stage boundary, before the board approves the next release map update
In closing a project, when acceptance of the project product is confirmed
In initiating a project, before any delivery work begins on the first stage
Throughout each iteration, as products are built, so problems are caught early
Agile: Quality.w: Agile builds quality checking into each iteration: testers incorporate quality assurance into iterations and testing is done first or as you go, avoiding the traditional problem of assessing quality late (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.3.1, 9.4.3, Table 7.2).

n.0: Stage boundaries review the stage and plan the next one; leaving quality checks until then repeats the traditional late-assessment problem (book 9.4.3, Table 2.2).
n.1: Closing a project confirms acceptance of the project product; quality control happens long before that, inside the iterations (book 9.3.1).
n.2: Initiation agrees the quality management approach and project DoR/DoD; it plans quality rather than controlling products not yet built (book Table 13.7).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: Which option correctly states the purpose of the risk practice AND how PRINCE2 Agile applies it?
o: To collect and assess issues and control changes to the baseline, by trading backlog items of similar effort
To monitor actual achievement against the plan and control deviations, by updating burn charts at every level
To document the users' requirements and the means to meet them, by checking stories against the Definition of Done
To identify, assess and control uncertainties affecting the objectives, by weaving the five risk steps into the iterations
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The risk practice exists to identify, assess and control uncertainties that would affect the project's objectives, improving its chance of success. PRINCE2 Agile adapts the five-step technique and builds it into planning sessions, retrospectives and iteration cycles (book Table 10.1, 10.3.1).

n.0: Collecting and assessing issues and controlling baseline changes is the purpose of the issues practice, and trading is an issues technique (book 11.1, 11.4.1).
n.1: Monitoring achievement against plan and controlling deviations that cause an exception is the purpose of the progress practice (book 12.1, 12.3.1).
n.2: Documenting user requirements and how they will be met is the purpose of the quality practice (book Table 9.1, 9.3.2.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q:
Which two statements about the risk technique in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. Risks can be raised at any point in the project, as well as in planning sessions and retrospectives.
2. The 'assess' step is where risks are first gathered and documented.
3. The 'plan' step is addressed by planning the necessary risk responses.
4. The 'communicate' step takes place once, when the stage is closed.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Statement 1 is true: planning sessions and retrospectives are the fixed points for identifying risks, but risks can surface at any time and in any workshop. Statement 3 is true: the plan step plans the necessary risk responses (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is false: risks are gathered and documented in the identify step; assess is where they are estimated and evaluated (book 10.3.1).
n.2: Both statements are false: gathering risks belongs to identify, and communicate is part of the continuous feedback loops in every iteration and stage, not a one-off at stage close (book 10.3.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is false: communicating risks happens through the established communication procedures and feedback loops throughout each iteration (book 10.3.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
In PRINCE2 Agile, the identify step of the risk technique is suggested to be a fixed part of every [?] and of every team and project retrospective.
o: product demo
highlight report
planning session
board meeting
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Identifying risks is suggested as a fixed part of every planning session and of team and project retrospectives, where risks are gathered and documented (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).

n.0: A product demo in the progress review shows completed features and gathers feedback; it is not named as the fixed point for identifying risks (book Table 13.10, 10.3.1).
n.1: In PRINCE2 Agile the highlight report takes the form of the project dashboard, which reports status; it is not a session where risks are gathered (book Table 12.1).
n.3: Board meetings are not where the team routinely identifies risks; the book places this in planning sessions and retrospectives (book 10.3.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: In a team planning workshop at a hospital trust, the team added a response to a supplier-delay risk to its backlog. During the next iteration, the developers carry out that response as part of their normal work. Which step of the risk technique is this, and where does PRINCE2 Agile place it?
o: Implement, which is part of the continuous iteration cycles
Plan, which is completed in the agile enablement workshop by the board
Assess, which is carried out when the team plan is produced
Communicate, which is handled by updating the project dashboard
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Carrying out planned risk responses is the implement step, which PRINCE2 Agile makes part of the continuous iteration cycles (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).

n.1: Planning the response happened when the team added it to the backlog; the agile enablement workshop deals with risks to agile adoption, not team-level responses (book 10.3.1, Table 13.5).
n.2: Assessing means estimating and evaluating the risk; carrying out a response that is already planned is implementation (book 10.3.1).
n.3: Carrying out the response is implement, not communicate; communicating uses the established procedures and feedback loops, and nothing is being reported here (book 10.3.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A project manager at a building society proposes using the Agilometer at the start of an agile project. What is the Agilometer used for in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: To forecast the likely completion date of a release from the team's velocity
To identify and monitor the risks of working in an agile way on the project
To decide whether a requested change alters the project backlog and needs the board
To measure how many user stories in each iteration meet the Definition of Done
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The Agilometer is a risk practice tool to identify and monitor the risks of agile working. It defines six areas where agile adoption could cause problems if left unmanaged, each graded from low to high (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 10.3.1, 10.3.2).

n.0: Forecasting completion from velocity is done with burn charts, especially burn-up charts, in the progress practice (book 12.4.3).
n.2: Whether a change affects the project backlog is an issues practice decision (baseline or detail change); the Agilometer does not deal with change requests (book 11.3.2).
n.3: Checking stories against the Definition of Done is part of the quality practice, not the purpose of the Agilometer (book 9.3.2.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A trainer who learned PRINCE2 Agile from the 2015 guide describes the Agilometer as part of a 'focus area'. In PRINCE2 Agile Version 2, which practice includes the Agilometer among its artifacts?
o: Progress
Quality
Organization
Risk
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Version 2 dropped the focus areas heading. The Agilometer is now listed with the risk management approach and risk register as an artifact of the risk practice (book 10.3.2, Table 10.1).

n.0: The progress practice uses dashboards, burn charts and OKRs; the project dashboard may show Agilometer trends, but the Agilometer itself belongs to the risk practice (book Table 12.1, Table 10.1).
n.1: The quality practice covers requirements, the Definition of Done and testing; it does not hold the Agilometer (book Table 9.1, Table 10.1).
n.2: The organization practice covers roles, team structure and the commercial management approach, not the Agilometer (book Table 7.3, Table 10.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: At a county council, the stakeholders treat every requirement as essential and are uneasy about the part they must play in prioritizing the work. Which Agilometer slider is MOST LIKELY to be given a low setting?
o: Flexibility on what is delivered
Level of collaboration
Ease of communication
Ability to work iteratively and deliver incrementally
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The flexibility on what is delivered slider is high when stakeholders are comfortable flexing scope and with their role in prioritizing the work. Treating everything as essential points to a low setting (book 10.3.2.2).

n.1: Level of collaboration concerns how well people work together; the problem described is stakeholders' unwillingness to flex and prioritize scope (book 10.3.2.2).
n.2: Ease of communication concerns how easily all parties communicate; nothing in the situation points to communication difficulties (book 10.3.2.2).
n.3: This slider concerns delivering benefit through regular partial deliveries; the issue here is attitudes to prioritizing and flexing what is delivered (book 10.3.2.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: The Agilometer defines several project areas in which agile adoption could cause problems if left unmanaged. How is each of these areas graded?
o: As red, amber or green according to its effect on stage tolerances
As a percentage of user stories completed in the current iteration
On a scale from low to high according to its suitability for agile
By probability and impact, in the same way as each entry in the risk register
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The Agilometer helps the project manager and team by defining six areas where agile adoption could cause problems, each graded on a scale from low to high according to agile suitability (book 10.3.1).

n.0: The Agilometer is not a tolerance status report; each area is graded from low to high for agile suitability (book 10.3.1).
n.1: Completed stories are tracked with burn charts in the progress practice, not with Agilometer grades (book 12.4.3, 10.3.1).
n.3: Individual risks are assessed by probability and impact; the Agilometer grades its areas on a low-to-high scale of agile suitability (book 10.3.1, Table 10.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: At a water utility, procurement rules and the standard supplier contract make it hard for teams to work in an agile way, and the wider working environment does not support agile working. Which Agilometer slider reflects this situation?
o: Level of collaboration
Ease of communication
Advantageous environmental conditions
Ability to work iteratively and deliver incrementally
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The advantageous environmental conditions slider asks whether the overall working environment supports agile working, including contract details that do not inhibit agile working and delivery (book 10.3.2.2).

n.0: Level of collaboration is about how well the people involved work together, not about contracts and the supportiveness of the working environment (book 10.3.2.2).
n.1: Ease of communication is about how easily all parties communicate; contract terms and procurement rules fall under environmental conditions (book 10.3.2.2).
n.3: This slider is about delivering benefit through regular partial deliveries; the situation describes an unsupportive environment and contracts (book 10.3.2.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: During the project initiation workshop for a new citizen-services app, the project manager introduces the Agilometer. How is it used in this workshop?
o: Everyone assesses the sliders, individually or in groups, and the views are combined into one project Agilometer
The project executive completes it before the workshop on behalf of everyone and presents it to the board
The agile coach sets each slider after the workshop and records the readings as entries in the risk register
The project manager sets each slider to match the targets in the project canvas and shares it with the team
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: In the project initiation workshop the Agilometer and its purpose are introduced, all participants assess it (anonymously or in groups) and the individual assessments are combined into one project Agilometer (book Table 13.7).

n.1: The initiation workshop involves all participants in the assessment; it is not a single executive's view presented for approval (book Table 13.7).
n.2: The assessment is made by all participants during the workshop and combined; the sliders are not set by one person afterwards (book Table 13.7, 10.3.2).
n.3: The sliders reflect participants' views of the environment, not targets copied from the project canvas (book Table 13.7, 10.3.2.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: PRINCE2 Agile expects the Agilometer to be reassessed regularly during the initiation stage and later stages. Which workshop provides this regular reassessment, and which process does it support?
o: The project kickoff workshop, in initiating a project
The team retrospective workshop, in managing product delivery
The release planning workshop, in managing a stage boundary
The agile enablement workshop, in directing a project
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The agile enablement workshop supports directing a project: the board, agile coaches and business representatives regularly review the Agilometer so that agile maturity and agile risks are reassessed in initiation and later stages (book Table 13.5).

n.0: The kickoff workshop builds the team, its values and its dashboards; it is held once and does not provide regular Agilometer reassessment (book Table 13.8).
n.1: The team retrospective reviews the last iteration (the good, the bad, the learning, team building); it is not where the board reassesses the Agilometer (book Table 13.14).
n.2: The release planning workshop updates the release map and OKRs for the next stage; regular Agilometer reassessment belongs to agile enablement (book Table 13.16, Table 13.5).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: The combined Agilometer for a hospital records project shows a low reading for flexibility on what is delivered. Which action does PRINCE2 Agile suggest to help improve this slider?
o: Co-locate the developers and testers so that day-to-day communication becomes much easier
Challenge whether too many requirements are classed as Must haves, and the assumptions behind them
Increase the time tolerance for the stage so that more of the features can still be delivered
Hold more frequent joint workshops with the supplier to raise the level of collaboration
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The book suggests that flexibility on what is delivered can be raised by checking whether too many requirements are Must haves and whether they, or their underlying assumptions, can be challenged (book 10.3.2.3).

n.0: Co-location helps ease of communication, a different slider; it does not address how much of the scope can be flexed (book 10.3.2.2).
n.2: Time has zero tolerance by default in PRINCE2 Agile; the book suggests flexing scope by challenging Must haves, not extending time (book Table 3.1, 10.3.2.3).
n.3: More joint workshops may lift the level of collaboration slider, but they do not explain how to improve flexibility on what is delivered (book 10.3.2.2, 10.3.2.3).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: During initiation of an agile project at an insurance broker, the project manager drafts the artifact that sets out how risk will be managed on the project, including the procedures, techniques and responsibilities to be used. Which artifact is this?
o: Risk register
Agilometer
Issue management approach
Risk management approach
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The risk management approach describes how risk will be managed on the project. It holds the procedure, techniques and responsibilities, not the individual risks (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 10.1; PRINCE2 7 manual chapter 9).

n.0: The risk register records the identified risks with their status and history; it does not describe how risk will be managed (book Table 10.1).
n.1: The Agilometer identifies and monitors the risks of agile working through its sliders; it does not set out the risk procedures and responsibilities (book 10.3.1).
n.2: The issue management approach describes how issues are captured and how baseline changes are controlled, not how risk is managed (book Table 11.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A product owner at a logistics company wants to check the current status of a supplier risk that was raised three iterations ago, and see how it has changed since then. Which artifact should she look at?
o: Risk register
Risk management approach
Cumulative risk burn-down chart
Daily log
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The risk register keeps a record of the identified risks, including their status and history, so it shows how an individual risk has developed (book Table 10.1).

n.1: The risk management approach describes how risk is managed; it does not list individual risks or their status (book Table 10.1).
n.2: The cumulative risk burn-down shows the total risk exposure across iterations, not the status and history of one particular risk (book 10.4.2, Table 10.1).
n.3: The daily log records informal issues, required actions and significant events; identified risks and their history are kept in the risk register (book Table 12.1, Table 10.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A delivery team at a ticketing company says it uses a 'risk-adjusted product backlog'. What does this mean in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Every story with a high risk rating has been removed from the product backlog until the risk has closed
A separate backlog of risks is kept by the project manager next to the release map for each stage
Risk responses are held in the product backlog alongside user stories, so both are prioritized together
Each epic in the project backlog has been re-estimated to add contingency time for the known risks
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: In a risk-adjusted product backlog, both stories and risk responses are documented in the product backlog, so the responses are prioritized and delivered like other work (book 10.4.1, Figure 10.3).

n.0: A risk-adjusted backlog adds risk responses to the backlog; it does not strip out risky stories (book 10.4.1, Figure 10.3).
n.1: The risk responses sit in the product backlog itself, not in a separate list kept by the project manager (book 10.4.1).
n.3: Time has zero tolerance by default and the technique does not add contingency to epics; it places risk responses among the stories (book Table 3.1, 10.4.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A team at a regional airport has started using a cumulative risk burn-down chart. What does this chart show?
o: The story points still to be completed in the iteration, compared with an ideal line falling to zero
The total risk exposure of the tracked risks across iterations, which should ideally fall over time
The number of tasks in each workflow state over time, showing where work is building up
The status and history of each individual risk recorded since the project was initiated
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: A cumulative risk burn-down chart (John Brothers) tracks the total risk level across iterations and shows trends in risk exposure, ideally decreasing over time (book 10.4.2, Figure 10.4).

n.0: Remaining work against an ideal line is a burn-down chart in the progress practice, not the cumulative risk burn-down (book 12.4.3).
n.2: Tasks per workflow state over time is a cumulative flow diagram, used to reveal bottlenecks (book 12.4.2).
n.3: The status and history of individual risks is held in the risk register; the chart shows the overall trend in exposure (book Table 10.1, 10.4.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: How is a cumulative risk burn-down chart kept up to date in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: The team sets the likelihood of each tracked risk at its first planning meeting and updates it in each later planning session
The project manager recalculates it at each stage boundary from the risk register and adds it to the end stage report
Project support updates it every day from the stand-up notes and publishes it on the project dashboard for the board
The project board updates it whenever an exception report is approved and the release map has been revised
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The team defines the risk likelihood for each tracked risk in its first planning meeting and updates the probability in every following planning session, so the chart shows how total exposure changes (book 10.4.2, Figure 10.4).

n.1: The chart is maintained by the team in its planning sessions, not recalculated by the project manager at stage boundaries (book 10.4.2).
n.2: The likelihood of each tracked risk is updated by the team in each planning session, not daily by project support (book 10.4.2).
n.3: The board does not maintain the chart; the team sets and updates risk likelihoods in its planning sessions (book 10.4.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q:
Which two statements about risk artifacts and techniques in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. The risk register shows the overall trend in risk exposure across iterations.
2. A risk-adjusted product backlog holds both user stories and risk responses.
3. The Agilometer is one of the artifacts of the risk practice.
4. The risk management approach is a list of the specific risks identified so far.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
1 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Statement 2 is true: the risk-adjusted product backlog documents stories and risk responses together (book 10.4.1). Statement 3 is true: the risk practice's artifacts are the risk management approach, the risk register and the Agilometer (book 10.3.2, Table 10.1).

n.0: Statement 1 is false: the risk register shows the status of individual risks; the overall trend in exposure is shown by the cumulative risk burn-down chart (book Table 10.1, 10.4.2).
n.2: Both statements are false: the register records individual risks rather than the overall trend, and the risk management approach describes how risk is managed rather than listing risks (book Table 10.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is false: the risk management approach sets out how risk will be managed; the specific risks are recorded in the risk register (book Table 10.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: At a progress review for a council housing project, the board asks whether the combined level of the project's tracked risks has been falling over the last six iterations. Which technique is designed to show this?
o: Risk register and its status history
Burn-up chart for the release
Trend of project Agilometer readings
Cumulative risk burn-down chart
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The cumulative risk burn-down chart tracks the total risk level across iterations and shows the trend in exposure, ideally falling (book 10.4.2, Figure 10.4).

n.0: The risk register gives the status and history of each risk, not a picture of total exposure across iterations (book Table 10.1).
n.1: A burn-up chart shows completed work against a deadline to forecast completion; it does not track risk exposure (book 12.4.3).
n.2: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working through its sliders, not the combined exposure of the project's tracked risks per iteration (book 10.3.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A team at a ferry operator is worried that the payment service it relies on may be unavailable at launch. It writes a story to build a manual fallback and ranks that story among its other user stories for the coming iterations. Which technique is the team using?
o: Trading with a similar-sized item
Swarming on the at-risk story
Risk-adjusted product backlog
Cumulative risk burn-down chart
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Putting a risk response into the product backlog and prioritizing it with the user stories is the risk-adjusted product backlog technique (book 10.4.1, Figure 10.3).

n.0: Trading swaps existing items for new ones of similar effort to absorb change; here a risk response is being added and prioritized as backlog work (book 11.4.1, 10.4.1).
n.1: Swarming is the whole team focusing on a stuck task or blocker; nothing is blocked here (book 11.4.2).
n.3: The cumulative risk burn-down tracks total exposure across iterations; it does not put risk responses into the backlog (book 10.4.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: Users of a public library's new catalogue app ask for an extra search filter by publication year. The filter is not part of the requirements agreed so far. Which type of issue is this?
o: Request for change
Off-specification
Problem
Business opportunity
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: A request for change is a proposal for a change to a baseline. Requests for change usually come from users and represent additional or changed requirements (book 11.3.1).

n.1: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification; here users want something new, not a fix to a failing product (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 11.3.1).
n.2: A problem has an immediate and negative impact on the project, such as a supplier going bankrupt; a request for a new filter is not that (book 11.3.1).
n.3: A business opportunity is an unanticipated positive consequence for the project or user organization, such as extra funding; this is a user asking for more scope (book 11.3.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: Testing at a leisure-centre chain shows that the new online booking screen will not meet the accessibility standard set out in its agreed quality criteria. Which type of issue has been found?
o: Request for change
Business opportunity
Off-specification
Problem
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications. A screen that will fail its agreed accessibility criteria fits this type (book 11.3.1).

n.0: A request for change proposes changing a baseline; here the product fails to meet what was already agreed (book 11.3.1).
n.1: A business opportunity is an unanticipated positive consequence; a product failing its quality criteria is negative (book 11.3.1).
n.3: Problem is the general type for an immediate negative impact; a product that will not meet its quality specification is defined separately as an off-specification (book 11.3.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: The company supplying sensors for a city's smart-parking project goes into administration, and deliveries stop with immediate effect. Which type of issue should the project manager record?
o: Request for change
Problem
Off-specification
Business opportunity
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: A problem is an issue with an immediate and negative impact on the project; a supplier going bankrupt is the book's own kind of example (book 11.3.1).

n.0: Nobody is proposing a change to a baseline; an event with an immediate negative impact has occurred (book 11.3.1).
n.2: No product has failed its quality specification; the supply of components has stopped (book 11.3.1).
n.3: A business opportunity brings unanticipated positive consequences; a supplier failure is negative (book 11.3.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: Halfway through an agile project to digitize a county archive, the regional government unexpectedly offers extra funding that could extend the benefits for the archive's users. Which type of issue is this?
o: A request for change
An off-specification
A problem
A business opportunity
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: A business opportunity is an issue representing unanticipated positive consequences for the project or the user organization, such as additional funding becoming available (book 11.3.1).

n.0: No one has proposed a change to a baseline yet; the funding offer is an unexpected positive event (book 11.3.1).
n.1: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification, which has nothing to do with new funding (book 11.3.1).
n.2: A problem has an immediate and negative impact; extra funding is a positive consequence (book 11.3.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: Which statement describes the purpose of the issues practice in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: To identify, assess and control uncertainties that would affect the project's objectives
To monitor and compare actual achievements against those planned and control any deviations
To document the users' requirements of the project products and how they will be met
To collect and assess issues and to control changes to the project's baseline
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The issues practice exists to collect and assess issues and to control changes to the project's baseline (book 11.1).

n.0: Identifying, assessing and controlling uncertainties is the purpose of the risk practice (book Table 10.1).
n.1: Monitoring achievement against plan and controlling deviations that cause an exception is the purpose of the progress practice (book 12.1).
n.2: Documenting user requirements and the means of meeting them is the purpose of the quality practice (book Table 9.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A board member at a pharmaceutical distributor is worried that the agile teams keep receiving changes to their requirements. How does PRINCE2 Agile view change in an agile project?
o: Iterative, incremental work creates many product versions, so change is inevitable and should be embraced and supported
Change shows that requirements were poorly defined, so scope should be fixed during initiation to keep it to a minimum
Change disrupts the iterations, so every new request should be deferred until the final stage of the project is reached
Change is a governance matter, so the project board should decide every change, however small it is or wherever it arises
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: In agile, the iterative and incremental way of working produces many product versions and makes change inevitable; the issue management approach should embrace and support it (book Table 11.1).

n.1: PRINCE2 Agile does not treat change as a failure to be minimized; it expects and supports it because of iterative delivery (book Table 11.1).
n.2: Deferring all change would lose the benefit of feedback; change is handled continuously, at the lowest sensible level (book Table 11.1, 11.3.2).
n.3: Only changes that affect the baseline need formal decisions; detail changes are handled informally at team level (book 11.3.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q:
Which two statements about the types of issue in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. A business opportunity is an issue with an immediate and negative impact on the project.
2. A request for change is a proposal for a change to a baseline.
3. An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications.
4. A problem is an issue that represents unanticipated positive consequences for the project.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Statement 2 is true: a request for change proposes a change to a baseline. Statement 3 is true: an off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications (book 11.3.1).

n.0: Statement 1 is false: an immediate and negative impact describes a problem; a business opportunity brings unanticipated positive consequences (book 11.3.1).
n.1: Both statements are false: they swap the definitions of a business opportunity and a problem (book 11.3.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is false: unanticipated positive consequences describe a business opportunity; a problem has an immediate negative impact (book 11.3.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: At a museum's digital project, the team's accessibility tester has resigned and leaves on Friday, which will affect the next iteration. The project manager records this as an issue rather than as a risk. Why is this correct?
o: Staffing matters belong to the issues practice, while the risk practice covers technical uncertainty
It has already happened and needs management attention, whereas a risk is an uncertain event
It was raised during an iteration rather than in a planning session or a retrospective
It affects time, which has zero tolerance, so it has to be escalated to the board as an issue
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: An issue is a relevant event that has happened and needs project management consideration; a risk is an uncertain event that may happen. The resignation has already occurred, so it is an issue (PRINCE2 7 manual 10.1, which PRINCE2 Agile builds on; book 11.3.1).

n.0: Both practices can cover any subject; the difference is whether the event is uncertain (risk) or has occurred (issue) (PRINCE2 7 manual chapter 9 and 10.1).
n.2: When or where something is raised does not decide whether it is an issue or a risk; risks can also be raised at any time (book 10.3.1).
n.3: Recording an issue does not mean escalating it; the reason it is an issue is that the event has already occurred (book 11.3.2; PRINCE2 7 manual 10.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A project manager at a rail operator is explaining the issues practice to new product owners. In PRINCE2 Agile, when is a change to a requirement treated as a change to the project baseline?
o: When the change is estimated to take the team more than one iteration to build
When a developer and a tester disagree about a story's acceptance criteria
When the new or changed requirement means the project backlog has to change
When the product owner reorders the user stories in the team's product backlog
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: If a new or changed requirement means the project backlog needs to change, it is a change to the project baseline and must be handled formally (book 11.3.2).

n.0: The size of the work does not decide the route; what matters is whether the project backlog, the project baseline, must change (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 11.3.2).
n.1: A disagreement over acceptance criteria inside a story is team-level detail and does not by itself alter the project backlog (book 11.3.2).
n.3: Reordering a team's product backlog is normal prioritization at team level; it does not change the project backlog (book 11.3.2, 8.3.2.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: Users of a payroll system ask for a new Must have feature that is not in the agreed project backlog, so the approved scope would change. In PRINCE2 Agile, who decides whether this change goes ahead?
o: The product owner, after trading it with the team at iteration planning
The team coach, after discussing it at the next team retrospective
The developers, by reaching a consensus at the next daily stand-up
The project board, or whoever holds delegated change authority
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: A new Must have that changes the agreed project backlog is a change to the project baseline, so it is handled formally and decided by the project board or by the person or people given delegated authority to decide on changes (book 11.3.2).

n.0: Trading at team level suits detail changes inside the backlog; a new Must have that changes the agreed project backlog needs a formal decision (book 11.3.2, 11.4.1).
n.1: The team coach supports self-management and facilitates workshops; the coach does not hold authority over baseline changes (book 11.3.2, Table 7.2).
n.2: Self-managing developers handle detail at team level, but a change to the project baseline is decided formally at management level (book 11.3.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: During an iteration, users of a garden-design app ask for a clearer wording of an error message. The change sits within an existing story and does not affect the project backlog. How does PRINCE2 Agile regard this change?
o: As a detail change that makes the final product more accurate, handled informally at team level
As an off-specification that must be logged in the issue register before the team acts on it
As a baseline change that needs an issue report so that the board can decide on it formally
As a new risk to agile working that should be assessed at the next agile enablement workshop
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change. It is seen positively, as making the final product more accurate, and is handled informally at team level (book 11.3.2).

n.1: No product is failing its quality specification; the users are refining a requirement within the backlog (book 11.3.1, 11.3.2).
n.2: The project backlog is unaffected, so the baseline is not changing and formal handling by the board is not needed (book 11.3.2).
n.3: The agile enablement workshop reviews risks to agile adoption; a refined requirement is an issues matter handled by the team (book Table 13.5, 11.3.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
A change that leaves the project backlog untouched is a detail change and is dealt with informally at [?] level, whereas a change to the project backlog is decided formally.
o: board
executive
stage
team
