Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Issues that do not affect the agreed baseline are handled informally at team level; issues that do affect it are handled and decided formally at the appropriate management level (book 11.3.2).

n.0: The board, or a delegated change authority, decides baseline changes; detail changes do not need to reach it (book 11.3.2).
n.1: The project executive is part of the board and is involved in formal decisions, not in informal detail changes (book 11.3.2, Table 7.2).
n.2: Stage-level planning is shown in the release map; detail changes are dealt with by the team and product owner within the iterations (book 11.3.2, 8.3.2.5).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: The user group for a hospital's patient portal asks for a new Must have epic, covering repeat prescriptions, that is not in the agreed project backlog. How should this change be handled?
o: Informally, by the team trading it against an existing story of similar effort
Formally, as a baseline change decided by the board or a delegated change authority
By adding it directly to the team's next iteration because it is classed as a Must have
Through an Agilometer reassessment of the flexibility on what is delivered slider
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: A new Must have epic would change the project backlog, which forms part of the project baseline, so formal handling is essential and the decision lies with the board or whoever holds delegated change authority (book 11.3.2).

n.0: Adding a new Must have epic changes the project backlog, so it is a baseline change; trading is for detail changes at team level (book 11.3.2, 11.4.1).
n.2: Being a Must have does not let the team bypass formal handling; the change alters the baseline and needs a formal decision (book 11.3.2).
n.3: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working; it is not used to deal with baseline changes (book 10.3.1, 11.3.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: Feedback from a demo leads users to refine a story about invoice reminders. The epic in the project backlog is unchanged, and the refined story is more valuable than another story of similar effort that is planned for the iteration. What should the team do?
o: Raise an issue report so that the project board can approve the refinement before work starts
Set the refinement aside until the stage boundary, because the baseline is fixed for each stage
Agree the priority with the product owner and trade out the lower-priority item of similar effort
Record it as an off-specification and ask the chief product owner to grant a concession
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: A detail change should not be ignored: it is prioritized and, if it is more valuable than existing work, traded with a lower-priority item of similar effort, agreeing priorities with the product owner (book 11.3.2, 11.4.1).

n.0: The project backlog is unchanged, so this is a detail change handled at team level, not a matter for the board (book 11.3.2).
n.1: Detail changes are welcomed as improving accuracy and should be prioritized and traded, not parked (book 11.3.2, 11.4.1).
n.3: Nothing has failed its quality specification; a refined requirement inside the backlog is a detail change (book 11.3.1, 11.3.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, what decides whether a change to a requirement must be handled formally or can be handled informally?
o: Whether the change was raised by a user or by a member of the delivery team
Whether the change affects the project backlog, which forms the project baseline
Whether the change arises during an iteration or at the boundary between stages
The number of story points the team estimates the change will need to complete
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Changes that affect the project backlog are baseline changes needing formal handling at the right management level; changes that do not affect it are detail changes handled informally at team level (book 11.3.2).

n.0: Anyone can raise a change; the route depends on its effect on the project backlog, not on who raised it (book 11.3.2).
n.2: Timing does not decide the route; a baseline change is formal whenever it arises (book 11.3.2).
n.3: The estimate does not decide the route; the test is whether the project backlog has to change (book 11.3.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A tester at a council tax project suggests rewording a story's acceptance criteria so they are easier to test. The change stays within the story's epic, and the project backlog is unaffected. Who is best placed to agree the change?
o: The product owner, working with the team
The project board, at its next review
The project executive, by formal approval
The change authority, after an issue report
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: A detail change does not affect the project backlog, so it is handled informally at team level; the product owner, who owns the product backlog, agrees it with the team (book 11.3.2, Table 7.2).

n.1: The board decides baseline changes; a change that leaves the project backlog untouched is handled at team level (book 11.3.2).
n.2: Formal approval by the executive is for matters that affect the baseline or exceed tolerances, not for detail changes (book 11.3.2).
n.3: Delegated change authority and issue reports belong to formal handling of baseline changes, not to detail changes (book 11.3.2, Table 11.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A product owner at a travel insurer hears the team talk about 'trading' when a new requirement arrives mid-iteration. What is trading (or swapping) in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Moving a developer between teams so that the velocity of each team stays roughly equal
Replacing one or more backlog items with new ones of similar effort to absorb emerging change
The whole team working together on one blocked story until it can move forward again
Swapping the order of iterations in the release map so that a release arrives sooner
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Trading, or swapping, handles emerging change by replacing one or more requirements, features or user stories with others of a similar size in terms of effort (book 11.4.1).

n.0: Trading swaps requirements, features or stories, not people between teams (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 11.4.1).
n.2: The whole team focusing on a blocked story is swarming, not trading (book 11.4.2).
n.3: Trading works on backlog items within the planned work, not on the sequence of iterations in the release map (book 11.4.1, 8.3.2.5).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A team at a recycling company wants to absorb a new user request by trading. Which statement describes how trading should be carried out?
o: Items of any size can be swapped, and the project manager approves each swap by recording it in the daily log
New items are added on top of existing ones, and the chief product owner extends the iteration so that both fit
Items of similar effort are swapped, and the priority of the new and existing items is agreed with the product owner
Swaps are agreed with the team coach, who owns the product backlog and sets the order of the user stories
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The key to trading is that only items needing a similar amount of effort are swapped, in line with the project's goals, and the team communicates closely with the product owner to agree the priority of new and existing items (book 11.4.1).

n.0: Successful trading swaps items of similar effort, and priorities are agreed with the product owner rather than approved by the project manager (book 11.4.1).
n.1: Trading replaces lower-priority items instead of adding work on top, and iterations are timeboxes that are not extended (book 11.4.1).
n.3: The product owner owns the product backlog; the team coach supports self-management but does not set backlog priorities (book 11.4.1, Table 7.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: At a housing association, a story has been stuck for two days because of a data-migration fault that one developer cannot fix alone. The rest of the team pauses other work and focuses together on the fault until it is resolved. Which technique is the team using?
o: Trading
Refactoring
Timeboxing
Swarming
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Swarming is particularly effective for resolving issues: when a task or story is stuck, or an obstacle arises that one person cannot resolve, the team focuses on it together (book 11.4.2).

n.0: Trading swaps backlog items of similar effort to absorb change; it is not used to clear a blocker (book 11.4.1).
n.1: Refactoring improves a product's internal structure without changing its behaviour; it is not a team response to a blocked story (book 9.4.1).
n.2: Timeboxing fixes the length of a piece of work; the team here is concentrating its effort on a blocker (book Glossary, 11.4.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: Which statement describes what trading allows a delivery team to do?
o: Adapt to new priorities without increasing the overall scope of work or disrupting the current iteration
Extend the current iteration so that both the new and the existing items can still be delivered
Accept small changes from users directly, so the product owner does not need to be involved
Increase scope within the cost tolerance by bringing extra developers into the team for a while
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Trading lets the team stay flexible and adapt to new priorities without increasing overall scope or disrupting the current iteration, because a lower-priority item is traded out for the new one (book 11.4.1).

n.1: Trading keeps the iteration intact by removing lower-priority work; it does not extend the timebox (book 11.4.1).
n.2: Trading relies on close communication with the product owner to agree priorities, not on bypassing the PO (book 11.4.1).
n.3: Trading keeps overall scope the same; cost has zero tolerance by default and adding people is not trading (book 11.4.1, Table 3.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: Which of the following is NOT an appropriate use of trading in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: Absorbing a new requirement by removing a lower-priority item of similar effort
Keeping the workload of an iteration balanced when the priorities change
Resolving a technical blocker that has stopped progress on a story
Responding to a detail change that is more valuable than an existing story
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Trading handles emerging change by swapping items of similar effort; it is not a way of resolving blockers. Blockers are tackled by swarming and escalated if the team cannot resolve them (book 11.4.1, 11.4.2).

n.0: This is an appropriate use: trading replaces a lower-priority item with the new requirement of similar effort (book 11.4.1).
n.1: This is an appropriate use: trading keeps the workload balanced instead of adding tasks on top (book 11.4.1).
n.3: This is an appropriate use: detail changes should be prioritized and traded if more valuable than existing work (book 11.3.2, 11.4.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A team at a broadband provider has swarmed on an integration blocker for a day but still cannot resolve it within the team. What should happen next?
o: The project manager raises an exception report to the project board
The team trades the blocked story for another of similar effort and closes it
The board reassesses the Agilometer at the next agile enablement workshop
The team escalates the blocker as an issue to the project manager
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Swarming is tried first at team level; if the team still cannot handle the blocker, it is escalated as an issue to the project manager. An exception follows only if tolerances are forecast to be exceeded (book 11.4.2, Table 12.1).

n.0: An exception arises only when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; nothing here says that, so the next step is escalation as an issue (book Table 12.1, 11.4.2).
n.1: Trading absorbs change; it is not a way to resolve or close a blocker (book 11.4.1).
n.2: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working; it does not resolve a team-level blocker (book 10.3.1, Table 13.5).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: Apart from resolving a blocker, in which other situation does PRINCE2 Agile say swarming can be useful?
o: To speed up the completion of time-sensitive work
To replace low-priority stories with new ones of equal effort
To assess how suitable the environment is for agile working
To track the total risk exposure from one iteration to the next
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Swarming can be applied in various contexts, such as accelerating task completion or responding to time-sensitive requirements, though it is especially effective for resolving blockers (book 11.4.2).

n.1: Replacing stories with others of similar effort is trading, not swarming (book 11.4.1).
n.2: Assessing suitability for agile working is the purpose of the Agilometer (book 10.3.1).
n.3: Tracking total risk exposure across iterations is done with the cumulative risk burn-down chart (book 10.4.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: At a theatre group, two things happen in one iteration: (a) users ask for a small new feature within an existing epic, more valuable than a planned story of similar effort; (b) a story is stuck on a problem that one developer cannot solve alone. Which techniques fit (a) and (b)?
o: (a) swarming, (b) trading
(a) trading, (b) swarming
(a) baseline change, (b) exception
(a) refactoring, (b) swarming
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: A valuable detail change is absorbed by trading it for a lower-priority item of similar effort, agreed with the product owner; a stuck story is tackled by the team swarming on it (book 11.4.1, 11.4.2).

n.0: The techniques are reversed: trading absorbs a valuable change by swapping similar-effort items, and swarming tackles a blocker (book 11.4.1, 11.4.2).
n.2: The new feature stays within an existing epic, so the project backlog is unchanged; and a blocker is not an exception unless tolerances are forecast to be exceeded (book 11.3.2, Table 12.1).
n.3: Refactoring improves internal structure without changing behaviour; it does not absorb a new user feature (book 9.4.1, 11.4.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: While initiating an agile project at a port authority, the project manager writes the artifact that describes how issues will be captured and reported, and how changes to the project baseline will be assessed and controlled. Which artifact is this?
o: Issue register
Issue report
Risk management approach
Issue management approach
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The issue management approach describes how issues will be captured and reported and how changes to the project baseline will be assessed and controlled (book Table 11.1).

n.0: The issue register records the formal issues themselves and their status; it does not describe the procedure (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 11.1).
n.1: An issue report describes one issue's impact on the baseline, the options and a recommendation; it does not set out the overall procedure (book Table 11.1).
n.2: The risk management approach describes how risk will be managed, not how issues and baseline changes will be handled (book Table 10.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A request for change on a school-admissions project needs formal handling. The project manager wants to record it so that its status can be tracked until it is closed. Where should it be recorded?
o: Issue register
Daily log
Lessons log
Risk register
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The issue register captures and maintains the formal issues on the project, including their status, so the request for change is tracked there (book 11.3.4, Table 11.1; PRINCE2 7 manual chapter 10).

n.1: The daily log holds informal issues, required actions and significant events; an issue needing formal handling goes in the issue register (book Table 12.1; PRINCE2 7 manual chapter 10).
n.2: The lessons log records lessons that can be applied to this or future projects, not formal issues awaiting a decision (book Table 12.1).
n.3: The risk register records uncertain events; a request for change is an issue and is tracked in the issue register (book Table 10.1, 11.3.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A request for change on a dental-practice booking project would alter the project backlog, but the work can be absorbed within stage tolerances. The project manager must describe its impact on the baseline, set out the options and recommend a decision. Which artifact should be used?
o: Exception report
Project dashboard
Issue report
Issue register
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: An issue report describes an issue's impacts on the project baseline, identifies ways to resolve it or address an off-specification, and recommends a decision. Within tolerance, an issue report rather than an exception report is used (book Table 11.1, Table 12.1).

n.0: An exception report is used when a stage or project plan is forecast to exceed tolerance; this change stays within tolerances (book Table 12.1).
n.1: The project dashboard shares regular status with the board; it is not the artifact for analysing one issue and recommending a decision (book Table 12.1).
n.3: The issue register records the issue and its status; the impact analysis, options and recommendation are set out in the issue report (book Table 11.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A team coach tells the project manager about a minor problem with access to a test environment, which the team expects to sort out informally within a day. Where should the project manager record it?
o: Issue register
Daily log
Issue report
Exception report
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The daily log records informal issues, required actions and significant events, so a minor problem being handled informally is recorded there (book Table 12.1).

n.0: The issue register is for formal issues; a minor matter handled informally belongs in the daily log (book Table 12.1; PRINCE2 7 manual chapter 10).
n.2: An issue report analyses one formal issue's impact and recommends a decision, which this minor matter does not need (book Table 11.1).
n.3: An exception report is for a forecast breach of tolerance; a minor problem expected to be fixed in a day is not that (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile tailor the issue management approach for an agile project?
o: It reflects that iterative, incremental delivery brings many product versions and inevitable change, which is embraced and supported
It replaces the approach with the Agilometer, which then becomes the means of controlling every change to the project baseline
It drops change control from the approach, because agile teams work without any baseline once the iterations have started
It gives every change decision to the product owner, including changes that would alter the agreed project backlog
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: In agile, iterative and incremental working produces multiple product versions and inevitable change, which the issue management approach should embrace and support while still describing how baseline changes are controlled (book Table 11.1).

n.1: The Agilometer is a risk tool for the risks of agile working; it does not replace the issue management approach or control change (book 10.3.1, Table 11.1).
n.2: The project backlog forms the baseline, and changes to it are still handled formally; change control remains (book 11.3.2, Table 11.1).
n.3: Baseline changes, such as a new Must have in the agreed project backlog, are decided by the board or delegated change authority, not by a team's product owner (book 11.3.2).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q:
Which two statements about the issue artifacts in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. The issue register holds a record of the formal issues and their status.
2. The issue report is used to forecast when a stage will exceed its tolerances.
3. The daily log can hold informal issues and required actions.
4. The issue management approach lists each issue raised so far.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: Statement 1 is true: the issue register captures and maintains formal issues and their status. Statement 3 is true: the daily log records informal issues, required actions and significant events (book Table 11.1, Table 12.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is false: a forecast breach of tolerance is reported in an exception report; an issue report analyses one issue and recommends a decision (book Table 11.1, Table 12.1).
n.2: Both statements are false: forecasting a tolerance breach is the exception report's job, and the issue management approach describes the procedure rather than listing issues (book Table 11.1, Table 12.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is false: the issue management approach describes how issues are captured, reported and controlled; the issues themselves are recorded in the issue register (book Table 11.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: On a council's waste-collection app project, an issue under investigation is now forecast to push the current stage beyond its agreed tolerances. Which artifact should the project manager now use to inform the project board?
o: Issue report
Team dashboard
Exception report
Project dashboard
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: When a stage or project plan is forecast to exceed tolerances, the project manager uses an exception report to inform the board and give options and a recommendation (book Table 12.1).

n.0: An issue report is used while an issue can be handled within tolerance; a forecast breach of tolerance needs an exception report (book Table 11.1, Table 12.1).
n.1: The team dashboard shows a team's progress in place of the checkpoint report; it is not used to escalate a forecast breach to the board (book Table 12.1).
n.3: The project dashboard gives the board regular status in place of the highlight report; a forecast tolerance breach is escalated in an exception report (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The issue [?] describes an issue's impacts on the project baseline, sets out ways of resolving it and recommends a decision.
o: register
management approach
log
report
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The issue report describes the issue's impacts on the project baseline, identifies ways to resolve it or address an off-specification, and recommends a decision (book Table 11.1).

n.0: The issue register records formal issues and their status; it does not analyse a single issue and recommend a decision (book Table 11.1).
n.1: The issue management approach describes the overall procedure for capturing, reporting and controlling issues and changes (book Table 11.1).
n.2: 'Issue log' is not a PRINCE2 Agile artifact; informal issues go in the daily log and formal ones in the issue register (book Table 12.1, Table 11.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A project manager at a regional bus operator is explaining to new team members how risk will be handled across the iterations. PRINCE2 Agile recommends adapting the PRINCE2 Project Management risk technique. Which sequence lists the steps of that technique?
o: Capture, assess, recommend, decide, implement
Identify, assess, plan, implement, review
Identify, assess, plan, implement, communicate
Identify, plan, assess, communicate, implement
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: PRINCE2 Agile adapts the five-step PRINCE2 Project Management risk technique: identify, assess, plan, implement and communicate, woven into the iteration cycle (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).

n.0: Capture, assess, recommend, decide and implement are the steps of the issues technique (PRINCE2 7 manual 10.3.1), not the risk technique adapted in PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 10.3.1.
n.1: The fifth step of the risk technique is communicate, not review; communication runs through the established feedback loops of the iterations (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).
n.3: Risks must be assessed (estimated and evaluated) before responses are planned, and implement comes before communicate in the technique (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: A delivery team at an online furniture retailer works in two-week iterations. According to PRINCE2 Agile, where is the 'identify' step of the risk technique suggested to be a fixed part of the team's routine?
o: In every planning session and in every team and project retrospective
In the project kickoff workshop, held once while the project is initiated
In the project closure workshop, when lessons for future projects are recorded
In the project board's review of each exception report from the manager
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The identify step is suggested to be a fixed part of every planning session and of team and project retrospectives, where risks are gathered and documented. Risks can still be raised at any other time (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).

n.1: The kickoff workshop builds teamwork, values and dashboards; a one-off workshop cannot be the fixed, recurring place for identifying risks (book Table 13.8, 10.3.1).
n.2: The closure workshop confirms the product, records lessons and prepares handover; identifying project risks there is far too late to act on them (book 13.8.4, 10.3.1).
n.3: Exception reports deal with forecast tolerance breaches; the book places risk identification in the team's planning sessions and retrospectives (book 10.3.1, Table 12.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: At a garden-centre chain, a delivery team has gathered and documented several new risks during its retrospective. The team now estimates the probability and impact of each risk and evaluates them against one another. Which step of the risk technique is the team carrying out?
o: Identify
Plan
Implement
Assess
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: In the assess step, risks are estimated and evaluated. Estimating probability and impact and comparing the risks is assessment (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).

n.0: Identify is where risks are gathered and documented, which the team has already done in its retrospective (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).
n.1: Plan is where the necessary risk responses are planned; the team is still estimating and evaluating the risks (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).
n.2: Implement is where planned responses are carried out within the iteration cycle; no responses have been chosen yet (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).

Agile: Risk & Issues.q: Which statement describes how the 'implement' and 'communicate' steps of the risk technique are handled in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: They are carried out by the project board at each stage boundary, once the planned responses have been approved
They are part of the continuous iteration cycles and the established communication procedures and feedback loops
They are deferred until the risk register has been baselined in the PID at the end of the initiation stage
They are performed in a separate risk review meeting held between iterations, apart from the team workshops
Agile: Risk & Issues.w: The fourth and fifth steps, implement and communicate, become part of the continuous iteration cycles and the existing communication procedures and feedback loops, so they happen in each iteration and stage (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).

n.0: The board does not carry out risk responses; implementing and communicating happen continuously within each iteration and stage (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).
n.2: Implementing and communicating are not postponed to a single point; they run through every iteration and feedback loop (book 10.3.1).
n.3: PRINCE2 Agile weaves these steps into existing iteration cycles and communication routines rather than adding a separate review meeting (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).

Agile: Progress.q: Halfway through an iteration, the team's burn-down chart shows the actual line well above the ideal line. What does this indicate, and what should the team do?
o: The team is behind and should focus on the highest-priority items in the product backlog
The team is ahead and can pull extra stories forward from the next iteration
Scope has grown and the iteration should be extended so that all stories are finished
The team is behind and should send an exception report straight to the project board
Agile: Progress.w: On a burn-down chart, an actual line above the ideal line means less work has been completed than planned; the team will not finish everything at this rate and should concentrate on the highest-priority items in the product backlog (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.4.3).

n.1: Being ahead would put the actual line below the ideal line; above it means more work remains than planned (book 12.4.3).
n.2: Iterations are timeboxes and time has zero tolerance, so the response is to flex what is delivered, not to extend the iteration (book Table 3.1).
n.3: The reading of 'behind' is right, but a slow iteration is handled by the team reprioritizing; exception reports are prepared by the project manager when a stage or project plan is forecast to exceed tolerance (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Progress.q: A team completed 24, 28 and 26 story points in its last three iterations, and 104 points remain in the release. Using the team's velocity, how many more iterations is the remaining work forecast to take?
o: About 3.7 iterations, using the best recent rate of 28 points
5 iterations, using the lowest recent rate of 24 points
6 iterations, adding a buffer iteration to the lowest-rate forecast
4 iterations, using the average rate of 26 points per iteration
Agile: Progress.w: Velocity is the average rate of story points delivered per timebox and is used to forecast empirically: (24 + 28 + 26) / 3 = 26 points, and 104 / 26 = 4 iterations (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.4.3, Glossary).

n.0: Velocity is an average, not the best single result; using 28 points gives an over-optimistic forecast (book 12.4.3).
n.1: Velocity is an average, not the lowest single result; 24 points understates the team's measured rate (book 12.4.3).
n.2: A velocity forecast divides the remaining points by the measured average rate (104 / 26 = 4); using the lowest rate and then adding a buffer iteration is not how velocity forecasts work (book 12.4.3).

Agile: Progress.q:
Which two statements about progress control in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. Baseline metrics can be set through assessments and then checked regularly using the same metrics.
2. Progress reporting is mainly formal and written, so workshops play little part in it.
3. Progress information is often shared visually, for example through burn charts and dashboards.
4. The team retrospective is the main way to track progress during an iteration.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Progress.w: The book describes setting baseline metrics through assessments and checking them regularly (statement 1), and reporting that is often informal and visual, using workshops, burn charts and dashboards (statement 3) (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: agile progress reporting is often informal and takes place in workshops such as planning, review and retrospectives (book 12.2).
n.2: Both are wrong: reporting is often informal and workshop-based, and retrospectives happen at the end of an iteration rather than to track progress during it (book 12.2, 4.2.4).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is wrong: retrospectives are held at the end of an iteration to learn and improve, not to track progress during it (book 4.2.4).

Agile: Progress.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.

A [?] tracks completed work against a deadline and is often used at project or product level, plotting story points across stages or iterations to forecast when the work is likely to finish.
o: cumulative flow diagram
burn-down chart
burn-up chart
release map
Agile: Progress.w: This describes a burn-up chart, which tracks completed work against a deadline at project or product level to forecast completion (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.4.3).

n.0: A cumulative flow diagram shows tasks in each workflow state over time to expose bottlenecks (book 12.4.2).
n.1: A burn-down chart plots outstanding work, usually at team level over the days of an iteration (book 12.4.3).
n.3: A release map is a visual plan clustering user stories into releases; it is a plan, not a run chart of completed work (book 8.3.2.5).

Agile: Progress.q: A product owner asks when a situation in a PRINCE2 Agile project becomes an exception. Which answer is correct?
o: When a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded
When a team's velocity drops in one iteration
When the product owner reorders the product backlog
When a user story fails the team's Definition of Done
Agile: Progress.w: An exception is a situation where tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; agile teams flex what is delivered within tolerance, so ordinary variation does not cause one (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1).

n.1: A dip in velocity is ordinary variation handled by the team; an exception needs a forecast breach of tolerance (book Table 12.1).
n.2: Reprioritizing the product backlog is normal product owner work within tolerance, not an exception (book 8.3.2.1).
n.3: A story that is not done is reworked or stays in the backlog; failing the Definition of Done is a quality matter, not an exception (book 9.3.2.2).

Agile: Progress.q: A project manager forecasts that the current stage plan will exceed its tolerances. Which product informs the project board of this, setting out options and a recommendation?
o: Issue report
Project dashboard
Lessons report
Exception report
Agile: Progress.w: The exception report tells the project board when a stage plan or project plan is forecast to exceed tolerance and offers options and recommendations for how to proceed (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1).

n.0: An issue report describes one issue's impact on the baseline with options for resolving it; a forecast tolerance breach on a plan calls for an exception report (book 11.3.4, Table 12.1).
n.1: The project dashboard gives the board regular status in place of the highlight report; it is not the product for escalating a forecast breach (book Table 12.1).
n.2: The lessons report shares lessons and triggers actions to embed them; it does not escalate a forecast breach (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Progress.q: PRINCE2 Agile prefers tolerance to be set mainly on one area so that teams can absorb variation without causing an exception. Where does it place most of that tolerance?
o: On the length of each iteration, which the team may extend if needed
On the project budget, through a contingency held by the PM
On what is delivered, such as Should-have and Could-have features
On the release dates, which the product owner may move back
Agile: Progress.w: PRINCE2 Agile allows tolerance on what is delivered and restricts tolerance on time and cost: scope is fixed for Must-haves and flexed for Should-haves and Could-haves (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1, Table 5.1).

n.0: Iterations are timeboxes and time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, so iteration length is not where variation is absorbed (book Table 3.1).
n.1: Cost has zero tolerance on all levels of plan in PRINCE2 Agile, so variation is absorbed in scope rather than budget (book Table 3.1).
n.3: Moving release dates would flex time, which has zero tolerance on all levels of plan (book Table 3.1).

Agile: Progress.q: Mid-iteration, a team hits a technical blocker. The whole team swarms on it, clears it within the iteration, and none of the team's tolerances are affected. How should this be treated?
o: As an exception, because the iteration plan was disrupted
As a team-level matter, because no tolerance is forecast to be exceeded
As an issue for the project board to decide on at the next progress review
As an Agilometer risk to be rated at the next agile enablement workshop
Agile: Progress.w: A blocker resolved at team level, for example by swarming, is not an exception because no tolerance is forecast to be exceeded; it would go to the project manager as an issue if the team could not resolve it (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 11.4.2, Table 12.1).

n.0: Disruption in itself does not create an exception; an exception needs a forecast breach of tolerance (book Table 12.1).
n.2: The team resolved the blocker itself; had it failed, the next step would be raising it with the project manager as an issue, not taking it straight to the board (book 11.4.2).
n.3: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working, such as the level of collaboration; it is not a record of resolved technical blockers (book 10.3.2).

Agile: Progress.q: An updated release-level burn chart shows that the Must-have stories cannot all be delivered by the fixed release date. According to the progress practice, what should happen first?
o: Extend the release by one iteration so that every Must-have story is delivered
Ask the board to raise cost tolerance so that more developers can join the team
Hold an immediate project meeting to discuss options before escalating to the board
Ask the team to swarm and record the shortfall in the lessons log for later review
Agile: Progress.w: An updated burn chart at iteration or release level can trigger an exception; the progress practice suggests an immediate project meeting to discuss the options before the matter is escalated to the project board (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1).

n.0: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, so extending the release is not the agile response (book Table 3.1).
n.1: Cost has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, and options are discussed in a project meeting before anything goes to the board (book Table 3.1, Table 12.1).
n.3: Swarming suits a stuck task or blocker, not a forecast shortfall in Must-haves, and the lessons log records lessons rather than escalating a breach (book 11.4.2, Table 12.1).

Agile: Progress.q: Significant technical debt means that a team can no longer deliver the remaining Must-have stories in the current stage. Which statement is correct?
o: It is a detail change, handled informally by the team with the product owner
It is an exception, so the project manager prepares an exception report for the board
It is best captured in a lessons report so that other teams can avoid the same debt
It is recorded in an issue report as it affects one product, and the team carries on
Agile: Progress.w: If the Must-haves cannot all be delivered, the scope tolerance is forecast to be breached, which is an exception; the project manager sets out options and a recommendation for the board in an exception report (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.4.2, Table 12.1).

n.0: Losing Must-haves breaches the fixed scope for Must-haves, so this cannot be absorbed informally at team level (book Table 3.1, 11.3.2).
n.2: A lessons report shares lessons to embed them in ways of working; it does not escalate a forecast tolerance breach (book Table 12.1).
n.3: An issue report covers one issue's impact and options; a forecast breach of stage tolerance needs an exception report to the board (book 9.4.2, Table 12.1).

Agile: Progress.q: After receiving an exception report, the project board carries out the 'authorize a stage or exception plan' activity. What does this involve in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: Re-planning the team's iterations and assigning new user stories to each developer
Running a team retrospective to agree the delivery team's improvement actions
Approving the team dashboard layout that every delivery team must then use
Reviewing the updated project dashboard and approving the updated release map
Agile: Progress.w: In this directing activity the board reviews the updated project dashboard and approves the updated release map (and updated PID), or instructs premature closure (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.4).

n.0: Detailed iteration planning happens in managing product delivery, in the team planning workshop, not in directing a project (book Table 13.13).
n.1: Team retrospectives belong to managing product delivery and are held by the team, not by the board (book Table 13.14).
n.2: Team dashboards are co-created within each team rather than dictated, and approving their layout is not part of this activity (book 13.4.4.2).

Agile: Progress.q:
Which two statements about tolerances and exceptions in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. Scope is fixed for Must-have features and flexed for Should-have and Could-have features.
2. An exception may be triggered by an updated burn chart at iteration or release level.
3. Benefits may fall below minimum viability so that the release date can be kept.
4. An exception arises each time a team's velocity falls below its average.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Progress.w: Scope is fixed for Must-haves and flexed for lower priorities (statement 1), and an updated burn chart at iteration or release level can reveal a forecast breach and trigger an exception (statement 2) (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1, Table 12.1).

n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: benefits are fixed at minimum viability and flexed above it (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: a dip in velocity is ordinary variation; an exception needs a forecast breach of tolerance (book Table 12.1).
n.3: Both are wrong: benefits are fixed at minimum viability, and a dip in velocity is not in itself an exception (book Table 3.1, Table 12.1).

Agile: Progress.q: A delivery team wants to report its progress to the project manager in a visual, continuously updated form. In PRINCE2 Agile, the team dashboard used for this replaces which management product?
o: Highlight report
Checkpoint report
End stage report
Daily log
Agile: Progress.w: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report; it is continuously updated and reviewed in team planning and retrospective workshops, and the project manager draws information from it as needed (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1).

n.0: The highlight report is replaced by the project dashboard, which reports from the project manager to the board (book Table 12.1).
n.2: The end stage report is also replaced by the project dashboard, not the team dashboard (book Table 12.1).
n.3: The daily log records informal issues, actions and events for the project manager; dashboards do not replace it (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Progress.q: A project board wants regular, visual information on stage progress instead of written reports. Which agile artifact replaces both the highlight report and the end stage report?
o: Team dashboard
Release map
Project dashboard
Cumulative flow diagram
Agile: Progress.w: The project dashboard replaces the highlight report and the end stage report; it is updated and reviewed in progress review workshops so the board can pull the information it needs (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1).

n.0: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report and reports from the team to the project manager (book Table 12.1).
n.1: The release map replaces the project and stage plans; it is a plan, not a progress report (book 8.3.2.5).
n.3: A cumulative flow diagram is a mostly team-level technique showing tasks in each workflow state; it does not replace either report (book 12.4.2).

Agile: Progress.q: A team coach is planning the agendas for the team's workshops. In which workshops is the team dashboard normally updated and reviewed?
o: Team planning and team retrospective workshops
Progress review and project closure workshops
Release planning and agile enablement workshops
Project canvas and starting up workshops
Agile: Progress.w: The team dashboard is kept up to date continuously and reviewed in the team planning and retrospective workshops, giving transparency to the team and the project manager (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1).

n.1: Progress review workshops are where the project dashboard is reviewed, and the project closure workshop updates the project dashboard at the end (book Table 12.1, Table 13.19).
n.2: Release planning defines OKRs and updates the release map, and the agile enablement workshop is for the board's Agilometer reviews (book Table 13.16, Table 13.5).
n.3: These starting up workshops shape the project canvas, roles and initiation planning, before delivery teams build their dashboards (book Table 13.2, Table 13.3).

Agile: Progress.q: A new project board member asks what she will find on the project dashboard. Which content would PRINCE2 Agile expect it to show?
o: Each developer's task estimates for the current iteration
The detailed acceptance criteria for every user story
The signed contract and payment terms with each supplier
Burn charts, release status and current risks and issues
Agile: Progress.w: The project dashboard shows items such as release status or plan, burn charts, current risks and issues, the communication plan and Agilometer or agile assessment trends (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.3.2.1).

n.0: Task-level estimates belong to the team's own planning in the team planning workshop, not the board's dashboard (book Table 13.13).
n.1: Acceptance criteria sit with the user stories in the product backlog, managed by the team and product owner (book 8.3.2.1, Table 13.13).
n.2: Contract terms belong to the commercial management approach in the organization practice, not the project dashboard (book chapter 7).

Agile: Progress.q: Which statement best describes how dashboard information reaches the project manager and the project board in PRINCE2 Agile?
o: The project manager pushes a weekly written report to the board in place of a dashboard
The board completes the project dashboard after each progress review for the teams
Project assurance compiles the team dashboards into a monthly highlight report
Dashboards are kept up to date so the project manager and board can pull what they need
Agile: Progress.w: Dashboards are pulled, not pushed: teams update the team dashboard so the project manager can pull information, and the project manager updates the project dashboard so the board can pull it (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.9, Table 13.12).

n.0: Written reports pushed to the board are what dashboards replace; the board pulls information from the project dashboard (book Table 12.1).
n.1: The project manager updates the project dashboard in 'report highlights'; the board reviews it rather than completing it (book Table 13.9).
n.2: Project assurance gives independent monitoring, and the highlight report is replaced by the project dashboard, so assurance does not compile one (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Progress.q: At the project kickoff workshop, a project manager presents one fixed team dashboard design that every delivery team must adopt. Why does this conflict with PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Team dashboards should be co-created within each team to support self-management
Team dashboards are designed by the board during the agile enablement workshop
Team dashboards are not created until the first release planning workshop
Team dashboards should be designed by project assurance to keep them independent
Agile: Progress.w: In the project kickoff workshop each team co-creates its own dashboard for transparency, accountability and quick insight into progress; dictating one design works against self-management (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 13.4.4.2, Table 13.8).

n.1: The agile enablement workshop is where the board and agile coaches review Agilometer assessments, not where team dashboards are designed (book Table 13.5).
n.2: Team dashboards are a topic of the project kickoff workshop in initiating a project, earlier than release planning (book Table 13.8).
n.3: Project assurance monitors adherence to principles and practices; designing team dashboards is the teams' own work (book Table 7.2, 13.4.4.2).

Agile: Progress.q: During the 'evaluate work package status' activity, how should the project manager normally find out how a delivery team is progressing?
o: By attending every daily stand-up as the person who directs the team's work
By asking the board for the latest figures shown on the project dashboard
By pulling progress from the team dashboard and talking with the product owner
By waiting for the checkpoint report the team sends at the end of each iteration
Agile: Progress.w: In 'evaluate work package status' the project manager has informal conversations with the product owner and pulls progress from the updated team dashboard (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.9).

n.0: The project manager may attend stand-ups with the delivery team's agreement, and does not direct the team's daily work, which is self-managed (book Table 12.1).
n.1: The board pulls information from the project dashboard that the project manager maintains; information does not flow from the board to the project manager this way (book Table 13.9).
n.3: The checkpoint report is replaced by the team dashboard, which is updated continuously rather than sent at intervals (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Progress.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.

In the 'report highlights' activity, the project manager brings together the team dashboards, project log and release map changes, and then updates the [?] so that the project board can pull the information it needs.
o: team dashboard
project dashboard
exception report
lessons report
Agile: Progress.w: In 'report highlights' (controlling a stage) the project manager assembles team dashboards, the project log and release map revisions and updates the project dashboard for the board to pull (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.9).

n.0: Team dashboards are the input here; they are updated by the delivery teams for the project manager (book Table 13.12).
n.2: An exception report is used when a stage or project plan is forecast to exceed tolerance, not for regular highlights (book Table 12.1).
n.3: A lessons report shares lessons to embed them in ways of working; it is not the board's regular status view (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Progress.q: A project manager wants somewhere to note informal issues, actions that need doing and significant events during a stage. Which PRINCE2 Agile product fits this purpose?
o: Lessons log
Issue register
Quality register
Daily log
Agile: Progress.w: The daily log records informal issues, required actions and significant events, and forms part of the project log in the progress practice (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1).

n.0: The lessons log is a repository for lessons that apply to this or future projects, not for day-to-day actions (book Table 12.1).
n.1: The issue register records the issues being handled formally, with their status and history; informal issues go in the daily log (book 11.3.4).
n.2: The quality register records planned quality activities and their results, not general actions or events (book chapter 9).

Agile: Progress.q: A team coach asks how the lessons report differs from other progress products. Which statement describes the purpose of the lessons report?
o: To provide a repository for lessons that apply to this or future projects
To share lessons and trigger actions that embed them in ways of working
To review how the project performed against the PID used to authorize it
To tell the board that a stage plan is forecast to exceed its tolerance
Agile: Progress.w: The lessons report shares lessons and triggers actions so that they become embedded in the relevant organization's ways of working (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1).

n.0: This describes the lessons log, where lessons are recorded as they arise (book Table 12.1).
n.2: This describes the end project report, prepared when evaluating the project during closure (book Table 12.1).
n.3: This describes the exception report, used when a plan is forecast to exceed tolerance (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Progress.q: At the end of the project, the board wants to see how the project performed against the version of the PID that was used to authorize it. Which product provides this?
o: End project report
Lessons report
Project dashboard
Issue report
Agile: Progress.w: The end project report reviews how the project performed against the version of the PID used to authorize it; the board approves it when authorizing project closure (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1, Table 13.4).

n.1: The lessons report shares lessons and triggers actions to embed them; it does not review performance against the PID (book Table 12.1).
n.2: The project dashboard gives regular and end-of-stage status during the project, in place of the highlight and end stage reports (book Table 12.1).
n.3: An issue report describes one issue's impact on the baseline, with options and a recommendation (book 11.3.4).

Agile: Progress.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, in which process and activity does the project manager first create the daily log?
o: Initiating a project, in the 'agree the management approaches' activity
Controlling a stage, in the 'capture issues and risks' activity
Starting up a project, in 'appoint the project executive and project manager'
Directing a project, in the board's 'authorize initiation' activity
Agile: Progress.w: The project manager creates the daily log in starting up a project, during 'appoint the project executive and project manager', so it is available from the very start (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.1).

n.0: By initiation the daily log already exists; this activity agrees the management approaches for the PID (book Table 13.6, Table 13.1).
n.1: Capturing issues and risks in controlling a stage uses the daily log, which was created earlier, in starting up (book Table 13.1, Table 13.9).
n.3: Authorizing initiation is a board activity in directing a project; the daily log is a project manager's product created in starting up (book Table 13.4, Table 13.1).

Agile: Progress.q: Which management approach, agreed in initiating a project, describes how data and information will be created, used and managed across the project and afterwards, including security and privacy?
o: Communication management approach
Digital and data management approach
Issue management approach
Quality management approach
Agile: Progress.w: The digital and data management approach covers how data and information are created, used and managed through the project lifecycle and afterwards, including security and privacy; it is one of the progress practice's artifacts (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1, Table 13.6).

n.0: The communication management approach covers two-way communication and tailored messaging with stakeholders, not how project data is managed and protected (book chapter 4).
n.2: The issue management approach covers how issues are captured and reported and how changes to the baseline are controlled (book Table 11.1).
n.3: The quality management approach covers quality methods, agile ways of working and testing, not data handling (book chapter 9).

Agile: Progress.q: A project manager is explaining the project log to a new product owner. Which statement correctly distinguishes the lessons log from the lessons report?
o: The log is created in closing a project; the report is created in starting up
The log is owned by the product owner; the report is written by the agile coach
The log records lessons as they arise; the report shares them and triggers action
The log holds lessons for later projects; the report holds lessons for this stage
Agile: Progress.w: The lessons log is a repository for lessons that apply to this or future projects, while the lessons report shares lessons and triggers actions to embed them in ways of working (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1).

n.0: This reverses the timing: the lessons log is set up early, in starting up, and a lessons report is produced later, for example when evaluating the project (book Table 13.1, Table 13.18).
n.1: The project manager sets up the lessons log in starting up and prepares the lessons report when evaluating the project; neither is a product owner or agile coach product (book Table 13.1, Table 13.18).
n.3: The lessons log holds lessons for this project and future ones, and the report's job is sharing and embedding lessons rather than storing one stage's lessons (book Table 12.1).

Agile: Progress.q:
Which two statements about logs and reports in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. The project log is made up of the daily log and the lessons log.
2. The lessons report can include trends from Agilometer and psychological safety assessments.
3. The end project report replaces the project dashboard at the end of each stage.
4. The daily log is first created in the project initiation workshop.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Progress.w: The project log combines the daily log and the lessons log (statement 1), and the lessons report topic of the project closure workshop draws on trends from Agilometer and psychological safety assessments (statement 2) (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1, Table 13.19).

n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: the project dashboard replaces the end stage report, and the end project report is prepared once, when closing the project (book Table 12.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: the daily log is created in starting up a project, in 'appoint the project executive and project manager' (book Table 13.1).
n.3: Both are wrong: the end project report is a closure product, and the daily log is created in starting up (book Table 12.1, Table 13.1).

Agile: Progress.q: In the 'evaluate the project' activity of closing a project, which products does the project manager prepare?
o: The exception report and the issue report
The end stage report and the checkpoint report
The project canvas and the project backlog
The end project report and the lessons report
Agile: Progress.w: Evaluating the project compares it with the original PID and approved changes, and produces the end project report and the lessons report (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.18).

n.0: These products handle forecast tolerance breaches and individual issues during the project, not the evaluation at closure (book Table 12.1, 11.3.4).
n.1: In PRINCE2 Agile these are replaced by the project dashboard and the team dashboard and serve stage and team reporting, not closure (book Table 12.1).
n.2: The project canvas and project backlog are created in starting up; at closure the board confirms the updated project canvas rather than the project manager creating these products (book Table 13.1, Table 13.4).

Agile: Progress.q: The progress practice in PRINCE2 Agile includes objectives and key results (OKRs) as an artifact. Who is credited with this goal-setting framework?
o: Mike Cohn
Rachel Davies
John Doerr
Robert Greenleaf
Agile: Progress.w: OKRs are attributed to John Doerr: a goal-setting framework that helps organizations define and track ambitious goals (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.3.2.3).

n.0: Mike Cohn is credited with the term epic user story (book 8.3.2.2).
n.1: Rachel Davies is credited with basing user stories on the 'who, what and why' of a requirement (book 8.3.2.3).
n.3: Robert Greenleaf is associated with servant leadership (book 2.7.3).

Agile: Progress.q: A delivery team is writing its first OKRs. In the OKR framework referred to by PRINCE2 Agile, what is an objective?
o: A specific, measurable outcome that shows progress towards a goal
A prioritized list of epic user stories for the coming release
A tolerance on scope agreed between the product owner and the PM
A clear, aspirational goal describing what the team wants to achieve
Agile: Progress.w: Objectives are clear, aspirational goals; key results are the specific, measurable outcomes that show progress towards them (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.3.2.3, Glossary).

n.0: This describes a key result, the measurable part of an OKR (Glossary).
n.1: A prioritized list of epics is the project backlog, owned by the chief product owner (book 8.3.2.1).
n.2: Tolerances agreed between the product owner and project manager govern work packages; they are not the objective in an OKR (book Table 7.2).

Agile: Progress.q: A product owner reviews the draft OKRs for her team. Which statement correctly describes a key result?
o: An aspirational statement of what the team hopes to achieve next
A specific, measurable outcome that indicates progress to the objective
A user story that has been accepted against the team's Definition of Done
A feature shown to users in the final product demonstration
Agile: Progress.w: Key results are specific, measurable outcomes that indicate progress towards the objective; the objective itself is the clear, aspirational goal (PRINCE2 Agile V2 Glossary, book 12.3.2.3).

n.0: An aspirational goal is the objective, not a key result (Glossary).
n.2: A story meeting the Definition of Done is a completed piece of work, not a measurable outcome set as part of an OKR (book 9.3.2.2).
n.3: Demonstrating features gathers user acceptance at a demo; it is not how a key result is defined (book Table 13.19).

Agile: Progress.q: A project manager is preparing workshop agendas. In which PRINCE2 Agile workshop is 'OKR definition', where team OKRs are defined or updated, an agenda topic?
o: Release planning workshop
Team planning workshop
Project kickoff workshop
Agile enablement workshop
Agile: Progress.w: OKR definition is a topic of the release planning workshop: OKRs are introduced as a link between high-level goals and measurable outcomes, and team OKRs are defined or updated (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.16).

n.1: The team planning workshop covers backlog and story refinement, effort estimation and iteration planning (book Table 13.13).
n.2: The project kickoff workshop covers introductions, psychological safety, team values, skill and delegation matrices and dashboards (book Table 13.8).
n.3: The agile enablement workshop is for the board and agile coaches to review Agilometer assessments and agile-adoption risks (book Table 13.5).

Agile: Progress.q: What is the main reason PRINCE2 Agile includes OKRs among the progress practice artifacts?
o: To help organizations focus on what matters most and align teams on goals
To assess psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability
To record each team's velocity so that release dates can be forecast
To replace the project canvas as the project's business justification
Agile: Progress.w: OKRs are designed to help organizations focus on what matters most and align their teams around common goals, guiding progress and measuring success (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.3.2.3).

n.1: These are the key metrics for agility used in agile maturity assessments; OKRs are not used to assess agile maturity (book 12.4.1, 12.3.2.3).
n.2: Velocity is the average of story points delivered per timebox and is used with burn charts; it is not what an OKR records (book 12.4.3).
n.3: The project canvas remains the agile form of the business case; OKRs set goals and do not replace it (book 6.3.2.1).

Agile: Progress.q: The release planning workshop, where teams define or update their OKRs, supports which PRINCE2 Agile process?
o: Controlling a stage
Managing a stage boundary
Managing product delivery
Directing a project
Agile: Progress.w: The release planning workshop supports managing a stage boundary, planning the next stage and updating the release map, with OKR definition as one of its topics (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 13.7.4.1, Table 13.16).

n.0: Controlling a stage is supported by the progress review workshop and the project retrospective, not release planning (book 13.5.4.1).
n.2: Managing product delivery is supported by the team planning and team retrospective workshops (book 13.6.4.1, 13.6.4.2).
n.3: Directing a project is supported by the agile enablement workshop for the board (book Table 13.5).

Agile: Progress.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, who normally defines a delivery team's OKRs, and in which workshop?
o: The project board, which hands them to teams in the agile enablement workshop
The agile coach, who sets them for each team at the project kickoff workshop
Project assurance, which uses them to audit each team at the progress review
The team itself, with other teams and the PM, in the release planning workshop
Agile: Progress.w: Teams define their own OKRs in a workshop with other teams and the project manager during managing a stage boundary, which is the release planning workshop (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.3.2.3, Table 13.16).

n.0: The agile enablement workshop is where the board reviews Agilometer assessments; it does not hand OKRs to teams (book Table 13.5).
n.1: The agile coach supports agile adoption across the organization; OKR definition is not a kickoff topic, and teams set their own OKRs (book Table 13.8, Table 13.16).
n.2: Project assurance monitors adherence to principles and practices; it does not define team OKRs, and the progress review looks at the project dashboard (book Table 7.2, 13.5.4.1).

Agile: Progress.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.

In an OKR, the [?] are specific, measurable outcomes that show how far a team has moved towards its clear, aspirational goal.
o: objectives
acceptance criteria
key results
story points
Agile: Progress.w: Key results are the specific, measurable outcomes that show progress towards the objective, which is the clear, aspirational goal (PRINCE2 Agile V2 Glossary, book 12.3.2.3).

n.0: Objectives are the clear, aspirational goals themselves, not the measures of progress towards them (Glossary).
n.1: Acceptance criteria state what a user story must satisfy to be accepted; they are not part of an OKR (book Table 13.13).
n.3: Story points are relative estimates for user stories, not outcomes set in an OKR (book 8.4.3).

Agile: Progress.q: A team coach introduces a cumulative flow diagram to the delivery team. What does this diagram show?
o: Total risk exposure across successive iterations
The number of tasks in each workflow state over time
Completed story points plotted against a deadline
Agilometer slider ratings from successive assessments
Agile: Progress.w: A cumulative flow diagram is a visual representation of tasks in the different states of the workflow over time, which helps identify bottlenecks and assess overall progress (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.4.2).

n.0: Total risk exposure across iterations is shown by a cumulative risk burn-down chart (book 10.4.2).
n.2: Completed work against a deadline is shown by a burn-up chart (book 12.4.3).
n.3: Agilometer readings and their trends appear on the project dashboard; they are not what a cumulative flow diagram plots (book 12.3.2.1).

Agile: Progress.q: Agile maturity assessments in PRINCE2 Agile are based on three key metrics for agility. Which are they?
o: Psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability
Velocity, lead time and cycle time
Level of collaboration, ease of communication and flexibility
Transparency, empowerment and respect
Agile: Progress.w: Agile maturity assessments are based on the key metrics for agility: psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.4.1, 2.7.6).

n.1: These are delivery flow measures, such as Kanban metrics, that track how fast work moves; they are not the key metrics for agility (book 12.2).
n.2: These are Agilometer sliders, used in the risk practice to assess the risks of agile working (book 10.3.2).
n.3: These are characteristics of the agile mindset, not the three key metrics used in agile maturity assessments (book 2.6.2).

Agile: Progress.q: A project manager is planning when to assess the project's agility. When are agile maturity assessments first carried out in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
o: In the project closure workshop, as input to the lessons report
At the first stage boundary, in the release planning workshop
When the board receives the first exception report of the project
During starting up a project or initiating a project
Agile: Progress.w: Agile maturity assessments are first carried out during starting up a project or initiating a project, giving a baseline that can be checked again later (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.4.1, 12.2).

n.0: Closure reviews trends from earlier assessments in the lessons report; the first assessment comes much earlier (book Table 13.19, 12.4.1).
n.1: Release planning defines OKRs and updates the release map; maturity is first assessed before this, in starting up or initiating (book Table 13.16, 12.4.1).
n.2: Assessments are planned from the start of the project, not triggered by an exception report (book 12.4.1).

Agile: Progress.q: A team notices that work keeps piling up in its 'testing' state while items move steadily through the other states. Which technique is designed to make this kind of bottleneck visible over time?
o: Burn-down chart
Agile maturity assessment
Cumulative flow diagram
Risk-adjusted product backlog
Agile: Progress.w: A cumulative flow diagram shows tasks in each workflow state over time and helps identify bottlenecks, such as work collecting in one state (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.4.2).

n.0: A burn-down chart shows total outstanding work over time, not where work collects between workflow states (book 12.4.3).
n.1: Agile maturity assessments measure psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability, not workflow bottlenecks (book 12.4.1).
n.3: A risk-adjusted product backlog holds risk responses alongside user stories; it does not show flow between states (book 10.4.1).

Agile: Progress.q: The progress practice describes setting baseline metrics and checking them regularly. Which metric, often taken from Kanban, tracks how fast delivery cycles are?
o: Risk exposure
Business value
Psychological safety
Lead time
Agile: Progress.w: The book gives Kanban metrics such as lead time as examples of tracking how fast and how well delivery cycles run, using baseline metrics that are checked regularly (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.2).

n.0: Risk exposure is tracked with a cumulative risk burn-down chart in the risk practice; it does not measure delivery speed (book 10.4.2).
n.1: Business value is set out in the project canvas as part of the business justification, not a measure of delivery speed (book 6.3.2.1).
n.2: Psychological safety is a key metric for agility in maturity assessments, not a measure of delivery speed (book 12.4.1).

Agile: Progress.q: At which level of a PRINCE2 Agile project is a cumulative flow diagram mostly used?
o: Project board level, to approve stage and exception plans
Project level, in place of the burn-up chart on the project dashboard
Team level, to follow how tasks move through the workflow
Organization level, to compare the agile maturity of projects
Agile: Progress.w: The cumulative flow diagram is mostly a team-level technique that follows tasks through workflow states; it is unlikely to be used at project level (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.4.2).

n.0: The board decides on stage and exception plans using the project dashboard and release map, not a cumulative flow diagram (book Table 13.4).
n.1: At project level a burn-up chart forecasts completion; a cumulative flow diagram is unlikely to be used at that level (book 12.4.2, 12.4.3).
n.3: Comparing agile maturity uses agile maturity assessments based on the key metrics for agility, not a cumulative flow diagram (book 12.4.1).

Agile: Progress.q: Where would the project board expect to see trends from Agilometer and other agile assessments while a stage is in progress?
o: On the project dashboard
On each delivery team's dashboard
In the daily log
On the release map
Agile: Progress.w: The project dashboard can show release status, burn charts, current risks and issues, the communication plan and Agilometer or agile assessment trends, and the board pulls information from it (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.3.2.1).

n.1: A team dashboard reports from its team to the project manager and replaces the checkpoint report; the board pulls from the project dashboard (book Table 12.1).
n.2: The daily log records informal issues, actions and events for the project manager; it is not the board's status view (book Table 12.1).
n.3: The release map is the visual project and stage plan clustering user stories into releases, not a record of assessment trends (book 8.3.2.5).

Agile: Progress.q:
Which two statements about progress techniques in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?

1. OKRs are the main technique for assessing a team's agile maturity.
2. A cumulative flow diagram can help a team spot bottlenecks in its workflow.
3. Trends from agile assessments can be tracked on the project dashboard.
4. A cumulative flow diagram is mainly used by the board to approve stage plans.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Progress.w: A cumulative flow diagram helps identify bottlenecks (statement 2), and the project dashboard can show Agilometer and agile assessment trends (statement 3) (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.4.2, 12.3.2.1).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: OKRs align teams around common goals, while agile maturity is assessed through agile maturity assessments (book 12.3.2.3, 12.4.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: a cumulative flow diagram is mostly a team-level technique and is unlikely to be used at project level (book 12.4.2).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is wrong: the board does not use a cumulative flow diagram to approve stage plans (book 12.4.2, Table 13.4).

Agile: Progress.q: A project manager new to PRINCE2 Agile asks what the progress practice is for. Which statement describes its purpose?
o: To identify, assess and control uncertainties that would affect the project's objectives
To collect and assess issues and control changes to the project's baseline
To compare actual achievements with plans and forecast the project's objectives and viability
To document the users' requirements and establish how they will be met
Agile: Progress.w: The progress practice monitors and compares actual achievements against those planned, forecasts the project's objectives and continued viability, and controls any deviation that would cause an exception (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.1).

n.0: This is the purpose of the risk practice, which deals with uncertainty rather than tracking achievement against plan (book chapter 10).
n.1: This is the purpose of the issues practice, which handles issues and controls changes to the baseline (book 11.1).
n.3: This is the purpose of the quality practice, which sets out what users need and how it will be achieved (book Table 9.1).

Agile: Progress.q: According to the progress practice, which aspect of performance is usually of most interest to the whole project management team, making burn charts a natural choice at any level of the project?
o: Flexibility in what is delivered
Spend measured against the budget
Time used against the time tolerance
Hours logged against each team task
Agile: Progress.w: The book treats flexibility in what is delivered as probably the primary performance aspect of interest to the whole project management team, so showing it on burn charts suits any project level (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.3.1).

n.1: Cost has zero tolerance on all levels of plan in PRINCE2 Agile, so there is little point tracking spend against budget as the main measure (book 12.3.1, Table 3.1).
n.2: Time also has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, so tracking use of a time tolerance tells the team little (book 12.3.1, Table 3.1).
n.3: Agile estimating is relative (for example story points), and progress is shown by what is delivered, not by hours logged on tasks (book 8.4.3, 12.3.1).

Agile: Progress.q: A team coach wants a chart for the daily stand-up that shows how many story points of work are still outstanding on each day of the current iteration. Which technique fits best?
o: A burn-up chart
A burn-down chart
A cumulative risk burn-down chart
A cumulative flow diagram
Agile: Progress.w: A burn-down chart is a run chart of outstanding work over time, typically used at team level to show story points over the days of an iteration (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.4.3).

n.0: A burn-up chart plots completed work against a deadline and is typically used at project or product level across stages or iterations (book 12.4.3).
n.2: A cumulative risk burn-down chart shows the total risk exposure across iterations, not outstanding story points (book 10.4.2).
n.3: A cumulative flow diagram shows how many tasks sit in each workflow state over time to reveal bottlenecks; it is not a run chart of work remaining (book 12.4.2).

Agile: Progress.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile see little value in tracking spend against budget, or use of time tolerance, as the main measure of progress?
o: Because cost and time are reported by the senior supplier rather than the project manager
Because budgets are reviewed at the end of each release rather than during it
Because the product owner holds the cost tolerance and reports it on the team dashboard
Because time and cost have zero tolerance on all levels of plan, so scope is what flexes
Agile: Progress.w: PRINCE2 Agile sets zero tolerance for extra time and extra cost on all levels of plan, so tracking them adds little; progress is shown by what is delivered, which is where the flexibility lies (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 12.3.1, Table 3.1).

n.0: The progress practice gives the senior supplier no such reporting duty; the reason is that time and cost are fixed with zero tolerance (book Table 3.1).
n.1: The timing of budget reviews is not the point: with zero cost tolerance on every level of plan, spend is not where variation is absorbed (book 12.3.1).
n.2: The product owner works within tolerances agreed with the project manager, but cost has zero tolerance, and the team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report rather than tracking budget (book Table 3.1, Table 12.1).

Agile: Processes & Wider Context.q: Which statement about the 'controlling a stage' process in PRINCE2 Agile is correct?
o: It begins with the first delivery stage, so the work of the initiation stage is controlled by directing a project
It is the process in which the board approves each release map update and confirms continued business justification
It is normally first used once the project is authorized, but it can be used during initiation for large or complex projects
It is the process in which the delivery team produces a team plan and agrees to deliver each work package
Agile: Processes & Wider Context.w: Controlling a stage assigns and monitors work, handles issues, reports progress and takes corrective action to keep the stage within tolerances. It is normally first used after authorization but may be used in initiation for large or complex projects (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 13.5.1).

n.0: The book allows controlling a stage to be used during initiation for large or complex projects; directing a project is the board's process, not day-to-day control (book 13.5.1, 13.3.1).
n.1: Approving the next stage plan and confirming business justification happen at stage boundaries, supported by managing a stage boundary and directing a project (book 13.7.1).
n.3: Producing a team plan and agreeing to deliver work belong to the 'accept a work package' activity in managing product delivery (book Table 13.12).

Agile: Processes & Wider Context.q:
Which two statements about the purposes of the PRINCE2 Agile processes are correct?

1. Managing a stage boundary gives the board the information to review the current stage, approve the next stage plan and confirm continued business justification.
2. Starting up a project establishes solid foundations so that the business understands the work before committing significant expenditure.
3. Managing product delivery controls the link between the project manager and the delivery team.
4. Directing a project transfers the board's accountability for success to the project manager.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
Agile: Processes & Wider Context.w: Statement 1 matches managing a stage boundary (book 13.7.1) and statement 3 matches managing product delivery (book 13.6.1).

n.1: Statement 2 is wrong: establishing solid foundations before significant expenditure is the purpose of initiating a project, not starting up (book 13.4.1).
n.2: Both are wrong: statement 2 describes initiating a project, and in statement 4 the board stays accountable while delegating day-to-day management (book 13.3.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: directing a project keeps the board accountable for success and delegates day-to-day management, not accountability (book 13.3.1).

Agile: Processes & Wider Context.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
